News.title: Donald Trump congratulates Robert Pattinson on being named James Bond - but wants to know if he's 'a conservative'
News.content:
Donald Trump congratulates Robert Pattinson on being named James Bond - but wants to know if he's 'a conservative'

US president Donald Trump has given his verdict on Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond – years after he urged the British actor to break up with Twilight co-star Kristen Stewart

View 2 Images Donald Trump has congratulated the new James Bond actor (Image: BONNIE CASH/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Donald Trump has congratulated Robert Pattinson on becoming James Bond - before immediately asking his aide to find out whether he's a conservative.

‌



‌



Pattinson was named the new 007 by Amazon-owned MGM studios last week - ending years of speculation over who would succeed Daniel Craig in the role as cinema's most famous spy.

‌



His casting attracted the attention of high-profile figures around the world, with the Royal Family commenting via social media on the day of the announcement: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

‌



And now the US president - known to closely follow Pattinson's personal life - has weighed in on the news.

View 2 Images Robert Pattinson will become the seventh actor to play 007 (Image: Amazon MGM Studios via AP)

New 007 Robert Pattinson’s early licence for talent showcased in youth theatre snaps READ MORE :

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



Trump told the New York Post: "He looks nice. You know, I wish him luck."

The 80-year-old then asked Natalie Harp - an assistant known for printing out physical copies of news articles for him to read - what James Bond's political leanings were.

‌



"Is James Bond conservative? Natalie..." he reportedly shouted down the corridors of the White House, through the Oval Office door.

The US president has previous when it comes to commenting on the career of the 40-year-old British actor.

‌



In 2012, he posted a string of tweets urging Pattinson, then aged 36, to dump his Twilight co-star Kristen Stewart, warning she "cheated on him like a dog and will do it again."

He later wrote: "Robert I'm getting a lot of heat for saying you should dump Kristen- but I'm right. If you saw the Miss Universe girls you would reconsider."

‌



Pattinson commented on the bizarre posts after Trump began his first term in 2017, telling an interviewer they "didn't really mean anything" at the time and joking: "Can I use this in my acting?"

Kristen Stewart also referenced the tweets during her Saturday Night Live opening monologue the same year, where she quipped that Trump was "in love with my boyfriend".

Article continues below

Donald Trump is a fan of the 007 series, having previously named Sean Connery as his "all-time favourite Bond".

Shortly after Amazon MGM Studios announced that auditions for Daniel Craig’s successor were underway last year, the White House X account posted an AI-generated poster showing Trump in a dinner jacket holding a gun, stamped with the words: 'MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN' and '007'.

News.title: Ade Adepitan faced judgement over 17-year age gap with celebrity wife
News.content:
Ade Adepitan faced judgement over 17-year age gap with celebrity wife

I'm A Celebrity star and Paralympic medallist Ade Adepitan and his wife Linda Harrison have been together for more than 16 years, but their 17-year age gap caused some initial reservations for the TV presenter

View 3 Images Ade Adepitan and Linda Harrison have been together for over 16 years (Image: Dave Benett, Dave Benett/Getty Images for National Geographic & Disney+)

I'm A Celebrity...Get Me Out of Here! contestant Ade Adepitan has lived a remarkable life, conquering challenges to become a Paralympic medallist and one of Britain's most familiar faces on television. Yet behind the scenes, the 53-year-old has also discovered love with his wife, Scottish singer-songwriter Linda Harrison, who is 17 years his junior.

‌



‌



The duo have been an item for over 16 years, having first encountered each other at the National Television Awards in January 2010. Linda was just 19 at the time, while Ade was already a well-known television figure and ex-Paralympic competitor.

‌



Their initial encounter was rather unconventional, with Ade noticing Linda seated alone after her mates had momentarily vanished. Speaking to The Guardian, he said he clocked her beaming grin and felt instantly attracted to her.

‌



Linda recalled Ade making his way over and remarking on her stripy tights, before they engaged in effortless chat. Ade snapped a photo of them both and requested her email so he could forward it.

What transpired was a series of exchanges that would ultimately result in matrimony. Of course, Linda quipped that she chose to do some digging of her own after he disclosed he'd discovered clips of her performing online.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



"If he's going to stalk me, I'm going to stalk him," she recalled. She looked him up online and uncovered the remarkable feats he'd already achieved, including securing bronze at the 2004 Paralympic Games and scaling a volcano on his hands and knees for five hours when his wheelchair couldn't go any further.

Linda subsequently confessed she was astounded by what she found. She said: "I just went: 'That's my person.'"

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

At that point, Linda was studying music while chasing her dream as a vocalist performing under the stage name Elle Exxe. Their first real date happened in Guildford, where she was at university, though Ade turned up an hour behind schedule.

‌



The couple rapidly realised they relished each other's presence, with Linda even perching on Ade's lap as they tumbled down a hillside heading back towards the car park.

The 17-year age gap

Despite the immediate spark, their romance wasn't without its challenges. Ade has openly acknowledged that their 17-year age difference initially left him uncertain, especially given Linda was still in her teens when they first crossed paths.

‌



He also found himself out of his comfort zone when he turned up at one of her performances, with Linda's musical preferences and edgy look being completely alien to his own world. He even dubbed her 'Indie Lindie' after experiencing her music scene.

Yet it was the gap in their ages that proved most troubling for him. He confessed: "It definitely threw me at first."

‌



He revealed that he was mindful of the different life stages they occupied and wished to allow Linda time to mature before contemplating marriage. He added: "I felt I had to wait until Linda was in her mid-20s," explaining that if they remained together and content, marriage would follow naturally.

Their romance also endured a temporary split when professional obligations and differing priorities risked driving them apart. Ade was regularly absent, travelling extensively on the wheelchair tennis circuit, while Linda was focused on finishing her degree.

‌



Nevertheless, an invitation to accompany him on a Portuguese holiday marked a pivotal moment. Linda was initially hesitant, but the couple enjoyed themselves to such an extent that she confessed she didn't want to resume normal life.

She ultimately relocated to London, though they maintained separate residences for approximately five years before cohabiting shortly ahead of their wedding.

‌



View 3 Images Ade Adepitan's wife is 17 years his junior (Image: Jeff Spicer, Getty Images for Great Show Productions Ltd.)

Confronting prejudice surrounding their partnership

The couple have also discussed openly the assumptions and discrimination they have faced, with Ade disclosing that their age gap, his disability and their contrasting backgrounds have all shaped how certain people view their relationship. He explained: "Disability, race, age, all of that. People judge all the time."

‌



Linda has been especially vocal about some of the responses she has encountered, remembering how people would essentially praise her for being in a relationship with a disabled man. She characterised the mindset as peculiar and said it was one of the reasons the couple chose to launch a YouTube channel, hoping to challenge the presumptions people made about them.

"They seem to need a motive for us to be together, other than love," she said. Ade, meanwhile, has described their relationship as a partnership founded on understanding each other's strengths and weaknesses, supporting one another and enabling both of their careers to thrive.

‌



View 3 Images Ade Adepitan is currently on I'm A Celeb (Image: Molly Darlington, Getty Images)

Fairytale wedding and family life

Ade's prediction that he would one day marry Linda ultimately came true in August 2018, when they wed at the iconic St Paul's Cathedral. The wedding followed a romantic proposal beside Lake Como in Italy, although the moment itself came with a humorous exchange between the pair.

‌



Recalling the proposal to HELLO!, Ade revealed that Linda insisted he needed to get down on one knee, despite his disability making the movement difficult. He eventually got down on both knees instead, before asking her to marry him.

Their wedding was covered exclusively by HELLO!, with Ade later describing it as an occasion that exceeded even his expectations.

Article continues below

"Everyone says it's the best day of your life but it was probably better than that," he said. The pair have since started a family, with their first child, son Bolla, arriving in January 2021.

Their family expanded further in March 2025 with the arrival of daughter Zayla. Ade has previously discussed the delights of being a father, remarking that their son tends to mimic everything his parents say, requiring them to be mindful of conversations held in his presence.

News.title: Claudia Lawrence case: Police urged to enhance CCTV to reveal mystery man's face
News.content:
Claudia Lawrence case: Police urged to enhance CCTV to reveal mystery man's face

EXCLUSIVE: Police are being urged to send their original CCTV to forensic experts with a leading criminologist saying; 'There are ways of unlocking this case by identifying the man with something to hide.'

COLD CASE: Fresh evidence in the search for Claudia Lawrence

The police searching for missing chef Claudia Lawrence are being urged to enhance this CCTV of a mystery man lurking near her home - as it could reveal a face.

‌



‌



A leading criminologist, who had experts enhance the compressed footage released by police, believes the original CCTV which North Yorkshire Police hold, could produce even more crucial detail.

‌



Claudia, 35, a chef at the University of York, vanished from her pretty terraced home in March 2009, sparking one of the largest police searches the country has ever seen. Six years after she vanished, police released footage of two men - one described as having a ‘strange gait’ and behaving suspiciously near Claudia’s house in Heworth, York.

‌



This week The Mirror revealed how experts using forensic imaging, commissioned by Professor David Wilson, concluded footage of a man seen during the night and again in the morning around the time Claudia vanished - was one and the same person. They concluded the stranger appears to have a receding hairline of grey-coloured hair and may even be bald.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 7 Images 'Critical' new information has been uncovered about 'the man with something to hide' in the shadows

‌



In the CCTV this man freezes when he sees another pedestrian crossing the road ahead of him, hiding away in the shadows and avoiding a bright street lamp which would have exposed him. Police six years after Claudia vanished parked a huge screen near her home showing this footage.

North Yorkshire Police are now being urged to have forensic experts look at the original footage with criminologist Prof Wilson saying: “There are ways of unlocking this case by identifying the man with something to hide.”

‌



Joan Lawrence said of the Professor's research “It is obviously crucial. So I think they should look into it immediately. Because surely we both want the same result - the police and me - we want answers. For me 17-and-a-half years is too long. I don’t want to see this pushed in a drawer.”

View 7 Images Missing chef Claudia Lawrence (Image: PA)

‌



Professor Wilson, who commissioned the analysis for his podcast ‘This Much is True Crime’ podcast, which he co-presents with Martin Frizell, said in an update to the Mirror: “The firm who carried out the analysis do this regularly for police forces. This was done for the podcast based on compressed footage but North Yorkshire Police would have the original footage, which would give a much better response and might even reveal a face.”

He said he didn’t understand why North Yorkshire Police had not sent the original footage for enhancement.

‌



Reacting to social media claims the enhancement was done using AI, he pointed out it was enhanced using Amped Five, forensic enhancement software used by law enforcement, military and forensic labs worldwide.

He said for a podcast update: “This has nothing to do with AI, this has not been done by AI tools, this is done through a state of the art system called Amped Five which is regularly used by forensic laboratories to analyse low quality CCTV.

‌



View 7 Images Claudia has been missing since 18th March 2009, the first photo released of the missing chef was with the wrong hair colour (Image: rossparry.co.uk/ Rossparry.co.uk SWNS)

“The experts we sent the CCTV to used Amped FIVE - an all-in-one software suite used by forensic labs to convert, enhance, and analyse digital evidence to present in court. " He explained how AI invents pixels based on other data which undermines results and so can’t be used in court. But he added: "Amped FIVE does not use AI and therefore has come to be regarded as the industry standard."

‌



View 7 Images 'This case can be solved' Britain's leading criminologist, Professor David Wilson, (l) and journalist and TV producer Martin Frizell (r)

He explained Amped FIVE was developed in 2008 in Italy and has had major updates in 2012, 2019, 2023, 2025 and most recently 2026. "In layman’s language, it uses 140 specified filters to clarify low quality footage so that it can be 'read' eg a car number plate, or identify a face.

‌



“This means it does not rely on a single magical sharpening tactic, although we only had access to the compressed CCTV footage of the man with something to hide - which was very low quality footage with few pixels - and not the original CCTV which would have a significantly higher number of pixels that could be enhanced. That original footage is presumably still in the possession of North Yorkshire Police. “ He said he would urge the force to contact him as they have his number.

Martin Frizell, in their podcast update, said it is "astonishing" technology and added: “I am a bit disappointed with the North Yorkshire Police’s response to it.” And he pointed out the firm who did this work with police forces and their results are acceptable in court.”

‌



View 7 Images Peter Lawrence MBE told The Mirror how he felt the CCTV would hold the key (Image: PA)

Martin said they are happy to hand over to the North Yorkshire Police everything they have uncovered within their investigation. During their research they said they'd time how far the mystery man would bet in the time he goes out of shot. They found he had time to get down to Claudia's back gate or to check if there was a light on in her house.

‌



“The point is police need to find that person, either to rule him out or rule him in. Why has it been left to us to do our own Sherlock Holmes and send it off for forensic analysis, why have the police not done that?" Martin has said.

“The company we used, who don’t wish to be named because they are busy with other forces, who are using them now. I’m just surprised that North Yorkshire didn’t. The forensic analysts are happy to receive the original from the police from which they can probably deduce even more.”

‌



View 7 Images Joan, pictured with Tom McDermott, says she hopes police act immediately and get the CCTV enhanced. (Image: Andy Commins / Daily Mirror)

A spokesperson for North Yorkshire Police said: “Over the course of the investigation, officers have pursued a wide range of investigative opportunities, reviewed extensive evidence and committed considerable policing resources to determine the circumstances of Claudia's disappearance. This work has also been the subject of detailed review by independent experts.

‌



“We continually assess information that may assist the investigation. While we can’t comment on specific investigative opportunities, we keep developments in forensic techniques under review and, where appropriate, consider whether they may support our enquiries.

“The CCTV footage referred to was released by North Yorkshire Police during the investigation in an effort to identify the individual shown, and we continue to urge anyone with information to come forward. We remain committed to establishing what happened to Claudia, and securing answers for her family.”

‌



View 7 Images Claudia Lawrence's terraced home in Heworth in York (Image: Andy Commins / Daily Mirror)

TIMELINE

March 18, 2009

‌



- 5.57am - Miss Lawrence is captured on CCTV arriving for work at the University of York's Goodricke College.

- 2.31pm - The chef leaves work to walk the three miles to her home on Heworth Road. A female colleague sees her as she drives past in her car and gives her a lift, dropping her off outside her house.

‌



- A short time later, Miss Lawrence leaves her house and walks past the Nags Head pub. She has a brief conversation with a woman with a pram.

- 3.05pm - The last sighting of Miss Lawrence as she walks back to her house.

‌



- 8.10pm - Miss Lawrence has a telephone conversation with her father, Peter, and then another with her mother, Joan. They make arrangements to celebrate Mother's Day.

- 8.23pm - She sends a text message to a friend.

‌



- 9.12pm - Miss Lawrence receives a text on her mobile phone from a friend in Cyprus but it is not known if she read the message.

The following day, March 19th.

‌



- 6am - Claudia fails to arrive for her morning shift as a chef.

- 10am. Her manager calls her mobile phone, which rings out to voicemail.

Article continues below

- 12:10 PM: Her mobile phone is deliberately switched off. Up until this point, the device was connected to a mobile mast in the Heworth area. Neither her phone nor her Karrimor rucksack containing her chef's whites were ever found.

“The Man With Something to Hide”, is produced by Podcast House, executive producer Jack Suddaby, producer, videographer & editor Aidan Collins.

News.title: CCTV footage shows moment father and daughter wheeled murder victim's body to canal
News.content:
CCTV footage shows moment father and daughter wheeled murder victim's body to canal

Security footage shows the moment ‘evil’ murderer John Anslow and his daughter Hayley-Marie Ferguson pushed his victim in a wheelchair before dumping her lifeless body in a canal

Father and daughter push corpse in wheelchair to dump body in canal

CCTV footage has captured the chilling moment an ‘evil monster’ pushed a mother-of-one he murdered in his wheelchair before dumping her body in a canal.

‌



‌



‌



The footage, from the early hours of September 29, shows John Anslow, 65, walking unaided alongside his daughter Hayley-Marie Ferguson pushing his victim’s body in the wheelchair along the darkened streets towards the well-to the Walsall Canal.

‌



They are both seen walking freely despite each purporting to be severely disabled. Police bodycam footage also shows officers going through Ferguson's wheelie bin where she had disposed of Ms Bailey's clothes.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 4 Images John Anslow duped his victim into helping wheel him home before he murdered her (Image: West Midlands Police /Press Association)

Anslow recruited his ‘daddy’s girl’ daughter, 42, to help him clean the murder scene. She arrived to meet him with paving slabs from her garden for their plot to weigh down the victim's body and dump it in a canal.

‌



Anslow described as "evil" and a "monster" in court by Bailey’s relatives was found guilty of murder in September after jurors heard how he met Ms Bailey by chance in Great Bridge, West Midlands, and asked the 36-year-old to push his wheelchair to his home, where he broke her jaw and inflicted injuries to her private parts before killing her.

‌



Today, he was sentenced to life with a minimum term of 26 years at Worcester Crown Court. The twice-convicted rapist was likely to die in jail, Judge Simon Drew Kc said.

View 4 Images The father and daughter pair wheeled Chereiss Bailey’s lifeless body to a canal (Image: West Midlands Police /Press Association)

‌



Mother-of-five Ferguson, 42, who attended a Peaky Blinders-themed event after helping her father dispose of evidence, was jailed for six years for assisting an offender and preventing a lawful burial.

‌



The judge told Ferguson, who helped dispose of bloodstained clothing and bedding: “You played an active and crucial part in a carefully planned and executed enterprise.”

Judge Drew also criticised Ferguson for taking a photograph of the victim’s body inside her father’s house “presumably as some form of trophy” and taking another picture of it in the wheelchair as “another ghoulish record of your actions”.

‌



View 4 Images CCTV footage showed the walk in the early hours to dispose of the body (Image: West Midlands Police)

In a statement issued after the sentencing, the family of the victim said: “We have waited a long time for this day, carrying a pain that no family should ever have to carry.

‌



“Throughout everything, we have stood together for Chereiss. On the days one of us has struggled, the rest of us have held them up and that is how we have made it this far.

“We would like to thank everyone who has supported our family and kept Chereiss in their thoughts. Every message, kind word and act of support has meant more than people probably realise.”

‌



View 4 Images Police found Ms Bailey's clothes in Ferguson's bin (Image: West Midlands Police)

‌



The family added of their loved one: “Chereiss was a much-loved daughter, sister, mother, auntie, granddaughter and friend, but those words alone could never explain what she meant to us.

“Most heartbreaking of all, her little boy has been robbed of growing up with his mum beside him. We will make sure he grows up knowing exactly who she was, how much she adored him and how fiercely she was loved.”

News.title: UK government set to publish new treaties agreed with EU
News.content:
Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.

Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

News.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
News.content:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisationâone that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.

The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.

Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.

Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

News.title: Stalking law simplified to become one offence
News.content:
A new standalone offence of stalking is to be created in England and Wales after a review found the law regarding the crime was "cluttered and confused" - but the maximum sentence will not be increased.

Specific stalking offences were introduced in 2012 but the underlying offence of harassment had to be established, and additional factors such as fear or distress proven, for it to be considered stalking.

A review was ordered by the government last year, led by Richard Wright KC, who prosecuted the man who stalked and murdered Alice Ruggles in Gateshead in 2016.

Victims of stalking have welcomed the change in law but said they were disappointed not all the recommendations have been adopted.

Katherine, from Newcastle, whose former partner was arrested 28 times for stalking her, welcomed the government's decision to introduce one stalking offence instead of two.

"I'm pleased about that one because my ex was charged with [the lesser offence] of stalking without fear to start with and I was terrified," she said.

"Anyone who's been stalked knows how terrifying it is, so that one [without fear] was just pointless."

But her ex had resumed his behaviour after being sentenced to three years and four months in prison, and she criticised the length of jail terms given to stalkers, which she described as "an absolute joke and an insult to the victims".

Ashley, from Washington, in Tyne and Wear, was also disappointed the maximum sentence would not be increased.

"Stalking can have a devastating and lifelong impact on victims and their families," she said.

"It affects your confidence, independence and ability to feel safe, even long after the relationship has ended and the perpetrator has been sentenced."

News.title: Expect fewer frosts and more hot days as UK seasons shift, says Met Office
News.content:
The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.

Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost â when the air temperature falls to 0C or below â was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.

In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.

The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.

"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.

"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.

"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."

The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.

News.title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
News.content:
The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.

The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.

Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".

But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.

The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.

The BBC said the partnership includes:

A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts

Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app

More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters

More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate

There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.

Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".

News.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
News.content:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the pop group Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.

Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits, including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film; and also worked with artists like Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.

In a statement, his bandmates said Taylor had fought "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer" and "passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23 November".

His wife, Tracey, said the musician "was the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day".

News.title: Moment Nasa spacecraft hit asteroid - and what happened next
News.content:
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

Video released by Nasa showed the moment of impact in 2022, while new images show the extent of the damage done to the asteroid.

Dimorphos, the asteroid, posed no threat to Earth, but the crash was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.

Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.

The BBC's science editor Rebecca Morelle explains.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
News.content:
Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.

"We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds.

"My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was "part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country".

He said the news of it going into administration just weeks before Christmas would be "deeply concerning for workers and their families".

He added: "While it is worrying, going into administration does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage and we will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome."

Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said they would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".

"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.

Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.

Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.

On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm Â£85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.

But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.

Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees.

Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament - two weeks after Gordon Brothers representatives last appeared at the committee to answer questions about Poundland, and where MPs said they were "deeply concerned" about the business.

Byrne said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration."

He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again".

News.title: Gordon Ramsay to host Top Gear as show revived after Flintoff crash
News.content:
TV chef Gordon Ramsay is to lead the new presenting line-up on BBC motoring show Top Gear, which is being revived four years after it was last on air.

Ramsay will take the driving seat alongside as yet unnamed co-presenters when the show starts filming next year. It will return to screens in 2028.

The long-running programme has been off air since 2022, when co-host Andrew Flintoff suffered serious facial and rib injuries after his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test-track.

In a statement announcing his new role, Ramsay said he wants to bring "a fresh energy and ambition" to the show's formula of being "surprising, entertaining and [with] just the right amount of chaos".

News.title: Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving
News.content:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has been given a suspended sentence after admitting dangerously driving his Lamborghini while inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon on a motorway.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, who later crashed into a metal gate during rush hour, gave no reaction as he was handed a 12-month jail term, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court.

Sterling had pleaded guilty to dangerous driving of a Lamborghini Urus and possessing nitrous oxide on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road on 28 May.

The judge said Sterling's use of the Class C drug had became a "maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period" in his career.

Sterling, who left the court without making any comment, was ordered to complete 100 hours unpaid work and was banned from driving for 24 months.

He was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire.

News.title: Wife drugged and raped by husband asked police if she was to blame, court hears
News.content:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A woman who had been drugged and raped by her husband for 20 years asked police: "Is it my fault he's done this?", a court heard.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's right to anonymity, has admitted a litany of offences against her - including rape, administering a substance with intent and inviting 13 other men to join the abuse.

Nine of those men have pleaded not guilty to sexual offences against her and are standing trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

Giving evidence in court for the first time, the woman also said claims she had been "pretending to be asleep" during the abuse were a "load of rubbish".

The victim, in her 60s, was formally interviewed by Greater Manchester Police on 7 November last year, around two weeks after officers had arrived at her family home to arrest her husband.

In the interview, played to the jury, she told Det Con Anouska Barker: "I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can't believe it's true, and I think you have made a mistake."

News.title: Hotels need 'minimum standards' to keep women safe
News.content:
Hotels should face national minimum standards to protect female guests, witnesses have told a parliamentary committee examining safety in the industry.

The hearing followed an independent review into security failings at Travelodge after a woman was sexually assaulted at one of its hotels in Maidenhead, Berkshire.

The review's author, Paul Greaney KC, said room intrusions had become so common they were treated as something to be tolerated, while Travelodge's interim chief executive admitted the company had not taken guest safety seriously enough.

Committee chair and Labour MP Olivia Bailey said the evidence showed not enough was being done to protect women and called for "concrete action".

The one-off parliamentary session heard evidence from hotel chains including Travelodge, Premier Inn UK and Z Hotels, alongside women's safety organisations.

Three women giving evidence revealed they had previously barricaded their hotel room doors to feel safer during their stays.

UK Hospitality chief executive Allen Simpson also recalled inadvertently revealing the location of a domestic violence victim to their abuser while working as a hotel receptionist earlier in his career.

News.title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
News.content:
Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

A typical bill will increase by about Â£37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to Â£60 extra a month in winter.

A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from Â£1,723 to Â£2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem.

The government will pay millions of households Â£100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.

News.title: MP calls for action after her likeness used for AI porn deepfakes
News.content:
A member of parliament whose name and image were used in AI content on porn sites said the issue could make women less likely to want to enter public life.

Mims Davies, the shadow Welsh Secretary, said she received an email in her parliamentary inbox which said "her likeness was found on forums in abusive and pornographic content".

The Conservative frontbencher said people making money from deepfakes was "grotesque", urging people to report it if it happens to them so that "culprits can be held to account".

"It's completely unacceptable, it's a violation and an outrage," she told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.

Deepfakes are videos, pictures or audio clips made with artificial intelligence to look real.

It is illegal, external to share or threaten to share intimate photos or videos of someone without their consent, including through deepfake images.

Davies said she had waived her right to anonymity to call for more resources to find and prosecute culprits.

Ofcom, the communications regulator, said "significant action is being taken to tackle intimate image abuse" but added there was "more to do".

Davies, MP for East Grinstead and Uckfield in East Sussex, said: "There are things you expect to be dealing with these days in public life and frankly this is not it.

"This could be any woman. This could be anyone in politics, in business, or down in your high street.

"We need to be able to protect ourselves from deepfakes."

She added: "This is going to have an effect on our daily lives, on our lifestyles. We need an answer to this.

"There's a problem, a new frontier which we need to battle."

She previously told the BBC she was spiked on a night out in 2019.

News.title: Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has challenged Andy Burnham over whether EU students in the UK could pay lower university tuition fees as part of his deal with the bloc.

The prime minister insisted the issue of tuition fees was "a separate deal", with discussions on this continuing.

Asked whether he could rule out EU students paying the same fees as British students, Burnham said this was "the European negotiating position" and "won't be put on the table".

At a UK-EU summit last Friday, the two sides agreed a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth travel scheme.

A joint statement said they would also work towards a "supplementing" agreement on tuition fees for EU students in the UK and British students in the EU, with negotiations concluding within six months.

EU sources had earlier suggested the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

But the UK has insisted the wider deal will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can reach an agreement on tuition fees.

News.title: EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
News.content:
The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans.

The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by EU governments.

It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme.

Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move.

The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry.

The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others.

Germany and France had previously agreed a joint position under which UK involvement would have been conditional on matching EU import restrictions and tariffs on imports of Chinese electric cars and hybrids.

Alignment in this area with the EU would increase the price of increasingly popular Chinese cars in the UK, as well as raising the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on British-made cars.

News.title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Kyiv says five military aircraft damaged in strike on airbase east of Moscow
News.content:
From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story.

And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls.
