World.title: Makinde’s campaign group questions Tinubu’s N3.15trn budget cut
World.content:
The Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) has questioned President Bola Tinubu’s decision to reduce the proposed expenditure of the 2026 federal budget by N3.15 trillion while retaining the original N31.46 trillion fiscal deficit and N9.22 trillion borrowing plan.

The organisation, which is campaigning for Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde’s presidential ambition on the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), said the decision raised questions about the federal government’s fiscal management and its commitment to transparency.

In a statement issued on Wednesday and signed by its Director of Strategic Communications, Richard Ihediwa, the organisation demanded that Mr Tinubu explain why the deficit and borrowing projections remained unchanged despite the reduction in overall expenditure.

“The N3.1 trillion expenditure profile reduction is infinitesimal when juxtaposed with the massive budget padding including the appropriation of billions of naira for reportedly duplicated and non-existence projects,” the statement read.

The revised proposal reduces the federal government’s expenditure from N68.32 trillion to approximately N65.18 trillion, representing a cut of about 4.6 per cent.

However, the fiscal deficit remains at N31.46 trillion, equivalent to about 5.64 per cent of Nigeria’s gross domestic product, while planned new borrowing remains at N29.22 trillion.

The borrowing plan comprises N18.43 trillion in domestic borrowing and N10.79 trillion in external borrowing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The campaign organisation described the adjustment as inadequate, alleging that it failed to address deeper problems in the country’s budget planning and implementation.

“The reduction in expenditure without a corresponding reduction in the fiscal deficit and borrowing plans further exposes the seething corruption in Nigeria’s fiscal coordination under the Tinubu administration while raising apprehension of a decoy by officials to siphon public funds,” the statement said.

The organisation also alleged that the original budget contained billions of naira in duplicated and non-existent projects, describing the expenditure reduction as insignificant when compared with what it called extensive budget padding.

It further criticised the timing of the proposed revision, arguing that the recognition of existing government obligations shortly before the end of the fiscal year reflected weaknesses in budget planning and implementation.

Tinubu’s explanation for budget revision

Mr Tinubu had asked the National Assembly to consider a revised 2026 Appropriation Act, reducing total expenditure from N68.32 trillion to N65.18 trillion while retaining the deficit and borrowing provisions.

In his communication to lawmakers dated 20 November, the president said the adjustments were intended to regularise certain expenditures incurred by the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited on behalf of the federal government, address under-provided debt-service obligations and recognise issued capital warrants and supplementary commitments.

READ ALSO: Tinubu pledges rescue of schoolchildren at Maiduguri rally

He also said the revised framework would provide for refunds to ministries, departments and agencies and accommodate priority national interventions.

The president maintained that the revised budget would prioritise existing commitments and improve the credibility and implementation of the capital budget.

The Makinde-Daura campaign organisation, however, questioned the decision to retain the borrowing plan despite the reduction in planned expenditure.

It also demanded an explanation for the government’s handling of capital budget implementation, alleging that funds had not been released for the 2026 capital budget despite substantial borrowing.

World.title: Wole Olanipekun on law, democracy and the limits of power
World.content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri

Chief Wole Olanipekun (SAN), former Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of old Ondo State, former President of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) and former Chairman of the Body of Benchers, has been involved in landmark cases spanning constitutional interpretation, commercial law, electoral disputes and the protection of democratic institutions.



The learned Silk, who recently launched a six-volume compendium: Wole Olanipekun Through the Cases, spoke on the defining moments of his career, the state of the legal profession, judicial independence, mentorship and the responsibility of lawyers to society.



He also reflected on the cases that tested his convictions, the lessons of nearly five decades in practice and the legacy he hopes to leave behind.

Having spent nearly five decades in legal practice, what experiences have tested you most and what lessons have remained with you?



The experience that tested me most came on my very first day in court. After my National Youth Service year in Kwara State, I joined the Chambers of Alhaji Akanbi Oniyangi & Co. at No. 107, Emir Road, Ilorin, as its first junior counsel. My Principal, the late Alhaji Oniyangi, treated me like a nephew, and I regarded him as an uncle.



That first day, we appeared before the Honourable Justice Gilbert Obayan in a divorce matter, Okin v. Okin. The Court sat at 9:00am and stood the case down to 12:00 noon for definite hearing.



Alhaji Oniyangi drove back to the office, promising to return by noon, but exigencies took him out of Ilorin, and he sent word that I should plead for an adjournment. I did, but the Judge insisted that I proceed, and counsel to the respondent was ready. I had never appeared in any court, not even a Magistrate Court. I was nervous and had the shakes.



I told His Lordship I was a greenhorn, just called to the Bar, but he held that the case had been on the cause list for too long. He graciously granted me a 45-minute stand-down, which I used to study the file and hold a pre-trial session with our client. When the Court resumed at 12:45pm, I led our client in evidence-in-chief; he was cross-examined, and I closed our case.



Respondent’s counsel called his sole witness and closed his. The Judge then directed us to address the Court, with another 45 minutes to prepare. In those days, oral advocacy was in primacy, unlike now, when written addresses are simply adopted. I fell back on my notes from the Nigerian Law School and extracted some relevant decisions.



By the time the Court resumed, I had built enough confidence to present our address, and respondent’s counsel did the same. Before adjourning for judgment, the Judge commended my performance and encouraged me to keep it up. That was the tonic I needed to dive into active practice without further trepidation.



Some of the cases you have handled have had far-reaching implications for Nigeria’s constitutional and democratic development. Looking back, which of your interventions do you consider particularly consequential?



To isolate a single case from over five decades of active and uninterrupted legal practice and identify it as the most consequential would be both difficult and, perhaps, a disservice to the richness of a journey shaped by many defining encounters. Constitutional development, much like nation-building itself, is rarely the product of one event.



It is the cumulative consequence of many interventions, each contributing in its own way to the strengthening of institutions, the preservation of democratic ideals, and the advancement of the rule of law.



If, however, one were to speak of interventions whose impact on Nigeria’s constitutional and democratic landscape has been particularly enduring, Inakoju v. Adeleke (2007) 4 NWLR (Pt. 1025) 423 must occupy a prominent place. The case arose from the purported impeachment of Governor Rashidi Ladoja of Oyo State by a faction of legislators who convened outside the constitutional precincts of the House of Assembly.



At the time, many considered the matter foreclosed by Section 188(10) of the Constitution, which purported to oust the jurisdiction of the courts in impeachment proceedings. Yet the fundamental issue before us was whether constitutional safeguards could simply be ignored and then shielded by the very Constitution that had been violated.



Following a request by the then Governor of Lagos State, Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu, I assembled and led a distinguished team of advocates, including the late Rotimi Akeredolu, SAN, Kola Awodein, SAN, Chief Adeniyi Akintola, SAN, Professor Taiwo Osipitan, SAN, Femi Falana, SAN, and Dele Adesina, SAN.



We painstakingly examined the constitutional architecture of impeachment and advanced the argument that Section 188(10) could not be interpreted in isolation from the procedural safeguards embedded in Section 188(1)-(9).



The Court of Appeal accepted our arguments and the Supreme Court subsequently affirmed them. The decision became a constitutional watershed. It effectively halted the era in which elected governors and deputy governors could be removed through political contrivance masquerading as constitutional process.



More fundamentally, it reaffirmed that constitutional power must always be exercised constitutionally.



I would place alongside it a number of landmark electoral cases which strengthened public confidence in democratic governance. In Agagu v. Mimiko (2009) 7 NWLR (Pt. 1140) 342, after protracted proceedings at both the Election Tribunal and the Court of Appeal, the lawful mandate of Dr. Olusegun Mimiko was restored, thereby reinforcing the principle that electoral victory belongs not to the declared winner but to the candidate whom the electorate truly chose.



Similarly, in Osunbor v. Oshiomhole (2007) 18 NWLR (Pt. 1065) 32, where I led the legal team at the Court of Appeal, the mandate of Comrade Adams Oshiomhole was judicially vindicated.



Both cases powerfully demonstrated that the judiciary remains the ultimate guardian of electoral legitimacy and that democratic mandates cannot be permanently suppressed by administrative declarations.



Equally noteworthy was Fayemi v. Oni (2009) 7 NWLR (Pt. 1140) 223. Although I deliberately chose not to make a physical appearance in court, I was deeply involved in preparing the processes filed for Dr. Kayode Fayemi at both the Tribunal and Court of Appeal levels, and in assembling the legal team that prosecuted the matter.



An enormous amount of research, strategic planning and constitutional analysis went into that case. Together, the Mimiko, Oshiomhole and Fayemi litigations helped shape modern Nigerian election jurisprudence by reinforcing the proposition that electoral disputes must ultimately be resolved on the basis of lawful votes rather than political convenience.



Another intervention that readily comes to mind is the successful challenge to the purported removal of Vice-President Atiku Abubakar in 2007. At the height of the disagreement between the President and his Vice-President, the nation was confronted with an unprecedented constitutional situation.



There was no impeachment, no resignation, no allegation of permanent incapacity, and none of the constitutional procedures stipulated under Sections 143, 144 or 146 of the Constitution had been followed. Nevertheless, an attempt was made to remove the Vice-President from office through executive action.



The legal team I led successfully challenged that constitutional aberration. From the Court of Appeal to the Supreme Court, we maintained that no public officer, including the President, possesses powers beyond those expressly conferred by the Constitution.

The Supreme Court agreed, affirming that the Vice-President could only vacate office through the means prescribed by the Constitution and not by executive whim or political disagreement. The Court further accepted the distinction we drew between constitutional executive offices and legislative seats with respect to party affiliation.



That decision remains one of the clearest judicial affirmations of the supremacy of the Constitution over executive power. Around the same period, we also successfully challenged attempts to subject the sitting Vice-President to criminal proceedings notwithstanding the immunity guaranteed by Section 308 of the Constitution, resulting in another significant constitutional pronouncement in A.-G. Federation v. Abubakar (2007) 8 NWLR (Pt. 1035) 117.



These cases have strengthened constitutionalism, preserved democratic order, protected the sanctity of the ballot, restrained arbitrariness in the exercise of power, and reinforced public confidence in the rule of law; and if there is a common thread running through them, it is the enduring principle that in a constitutional democracy, power is never above the Constitution, and legitimacy can only be derived from fidelity to its provisions.

World.title: 2027: FCT, Rivers in the bag, give me Imo and Kwara, Wike begs Tinubu
World.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: Minister of the Federal Capital Territory FCT, Nyesom Wike, has asked President Bola Tinubu to hand him two more states, Imo and Kwara, to mobilise for the President’s re-election in 2027, declaring that his work in Rivers State and the FCT is done.

He made the request on Wednesday at a Rainbow Coalition Town Hall meeting in Gokana Local Government Area of Rivers State.

Wike has been at loggerheads with the Imo state governor, Senator Hope Uzodinma who chairs the Progressive Governors’ Forum PGF, and his Kwara counterpart, Abdulrazaq Abdulrahman who chairs the Nigeria Governors’ Forum NGF over the minister’s floating of a multi-parry campaign machinery known as the Rainbow Coalition.

“I was assigned to coordinate Rivers and the FCT. Frankly speaking, I am done with these states. All adequate political machineries have been set in motion to deliver Rivers State and the FCT for the President. So, I have no much work to do again,” Wike said.

He addressed his plea to Tinubu and to the Director General of the All Progressives Congress APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdul’aziz Abubakar Yari.

“As I am going now, I will plead with the DG and Mr President to give two more states for me to deliver,” he said.

The former Rivers State governor used the gathering to canvass a second term for the President, whom he described as a courageous leader willing to take difficult decisions in the interest of the country.

He listed the removal of fuel subsidy, increased financial allocations to state and local governments, and the establishment of the Federal University of Environment in Ogoniland among the interventions he said justified continued support for the administration.

Wike urged the people of Gokana to sustain their relationship with Tinubu, insisting that abandoning an existing political relationship for an uncertain alternative would be unwise.

He also commended stakeholders in the area for setting aside their differences to work together under the Rainbow Coalition, saying political unity was necessary to achieve common objectives.

The Coordinator of the Rainbow Coalition in Gokana and former Secretary to the Rivers State Government, Chief Kenneth Kobani, described the meeting as unprecedented, saying it brought together different segments of the community.

The APC National Vice Chairman for the South-South, Chief Victor Tombari Giadom, expressed confidence that the coalition would mobilise up to 90 per cent of the votes in Gokana in the 2027 elections.

Senator Magnus Abe also praised Wike for reconciling previously divided political leaders, saying the people of Gokana were united in their expectations from the coalition.

The town hall was attended by political leaders, traditional rulers, religious leaders, women, youths and other stakeholders from Gokana and neighbouring communities.

Wike said his interest in Imo State stemmed from what he had heard about the state’s political situation.

“From what I am told, they are having some problems in Imo State. So, I will love to go there and deliver the State for Mr President,” he stated.

On Kwara State, he conceded that he had not verified the reports of division he was relying on.

“Secondly, I have not confirmed, but what I read on social media is that there are some divisions in Kwara. So I plead with the DG of the APC Presidential Council, Senator Yari, and Mr President to allow me take over Imo and Kwara States, because I am done with Rivers and FCT,” Wike added.

World.title: Awka City chosen for AfDB -funded Action Plan for Africa’s coordinated urban development
World.content:
By Vincent Ujumadu

Awka, the capital city of Anambra State, has been selected for the African Development Bank, AfDB, – funded action plan for coordinated urban development in Africa.

Under the programme, government would provide the policy direction, regulatory clarity, and institutional leadership, while development partners would support the mobilisation of technical expertise and catalytic resources.

Also, the private sector is expected to play a decisive role in financing and delivering viable infrastructure and urban projects, traditional institutions, community leaders, professional bodies and residents will remain vital in safeguarding public ownership and ensuring that development stays centred on the people in the new city.

At the launch of the plan on Wednesday in Awka, the state governor, Professor Chukwuma Soludo said it is part of the strategic plan to create the envisioned Anambra mega city.

Represented by his special Adviser on trade and commerce, Mr. Christian Udechukwu, the governor recalled that Awka is the only city chosen in Africa for the project, noting that it is because of the long term vision and the strategic implementation and the intentionality and purposeful focus of the administration.

According to Udechukwu, it is the governor’s determination to transform Anambra State that drew the attention of the African Development Bank to the state.

“The reforms they see here are of significance that it would serve to use Awka City as a model to prove the sustainability of the project and we are happy that this is happening under this administration”, he said.

He said that a substantial amount of next year’s budget would be devoted to the development of the new Awka City, while other cities of Onitsha, Nnewi, and Ekwulobia would also undergo transformation, in addition to the new cities planned for the state.

“When Awka 2.0 joins the planned industrial city, the proposed axis of prosperity would have been created. So Anambra is being positioned to become the economic hub of Nigeria and that is why the selection of Awka as a primary model sustainable city in Africa is important to us as a government. We should therefore not waste more time to move into the project preparatory stage”, Udechukwu said.

Speaking at the launch, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Awka Capital Territory Development Authority, ACTDA, Dr Osita Onuko said the coordinated development framework is aimed at addressing the growing infrastructure and environmental challenges confronting Awka and guiding the capital city’s expansion towards a more liveable and inclusive future.

The ACTDA boss said the action plan should be viewed not merely as a technical document, but as a shared commitment to building a productive, resilient and inclusive capital city for future generations

He said: “This ambition aligns directly with the vision of His Excellency, Governor Chukwuma Soludo, to transform Anambra into a liveable and prosperous smart megacity by 2050. Achieving that vision requires clear urban direction, sustained investment, and strong institutions capable of translating bold aspirations into tangible outcomes.

“Like many rapidly growing African cities, Awka is experiencing mounting pressure on its urban infrastructure, public services, and environment. The steady expansion of our built environment, rising demand for housing and utilities, traffic congestion, flooding, and gully erosion all highlight the urgent need for a more integrated approach to urban management.

“These challenges are deeply interconnected. Addressing them effectively means that decisions around land use, mobility, housing, utilities, environmental protection, and economic development must be considered together within one coherent framework. Without this alignment, interventions risk becoming fragmented, resources are inefficiently deployed, and opportunities for lasting impact are lost.

“The Awka City Action Plan provides that common framework. It establishes a shared direction for our capital’s growth, identifies clear priority areas for intervention, and creates a practical structure to align government spending, private sector investment, and development partner support.

“With the document now complete, our immediate focus turns to translating these priorities into bankable, well-prepared projects that can attract financing and deliver lasting value. For ACTDA, this means providing strong institutional leadership and coordination—working hand-in-hand with relevant ministries, departments, and agencies to ensure this plan actively guides our regulatory decisions and investment discussions. We are committed to accountability, continuity, and measurable results so that this becomes a living framework rather than a document left on a shelf.”

World.title: Malen penalty ends PSG’s perfect UCL run as Roma snatch 2-2 draw
World.content:
AS Roma’s Dutch forward #14 Donyell Malen (C) and PSG’s French midfielder #33 Warren Zaire-Emery (L) fight for the ball during the UEFA Champions League first round day 5 football match between Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) and AS Roma at the Parc de Princes stadium in Paris on November 25, 2026. (Photo by FRANCK FIFE / AFP)

Donyell Malen’s penalty gave Roma a 2-2 draw away to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday, as the injury-hit reigning champions saw their perfect record in this season’s competition come to an end.

Malen stroked in from the spot in the 78th minute on a bitterly cold and wet night at the Parc des Princes, giving Roma a welcome point after their collapse from two goals up to lose 3-2 at Manchester United last time out.

Roma had earlier taken the lead through Mario Hermoso, only for Illia Zabarnyi to equalise before substitute Ousmane Dembele put PSG briefly in front with a penalty of his own.

The result ends PSG’s perfect record in this season’s league phase, and halts a run of 12 consecutive wins in all competitions for Luis Enrique’s team.

They fall two points behind Real Madrid, who are now clear at the top of the standings as the only side still with a 100 percent record after five matches.

It is only a minor setback for PSG in their quest to finish in the top eight of the 36-team table, and therefore qualify directly for the last 16 without having to go through the play-off round like in the last two campaigns.

But the Parisians could have done with the boost of a victory as they come to terms with the loss of the outstanding Desire Doue, who may not play again this season after rupturing the ACL in his right knee last weekend.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, another of their outstanding attacking players, recently succumbed to the same injury, while Dembele has been struggling for fitness too and PSG’s prospects of winning a third straight Champions League title are undoubtedly diminished as a result.

Dembele’s presence on the bench at kick-off meant that none of PSG’s five top scorers from last season were in their line-up here, with the others either injured or having departed in the case of Bradley Barcola and Goncalo Ramos.

Meanwhile, Roma coach Gian Piero Gasperini raised eyebrows by leaving Malen out of his starting XI. The Dutchman is running at an average of more than a goal a game this season and netted four against Parma last weekend.

– Dembele spot-kick –

However, Roma have been in prolific form in general, netting 26 goals in their last seven matches before arriving in the French capital.

They went ahead inside five minutes here as Matias Soule cut the ball back from the byline and Spanish defender Hermoso was on hand to convert.

Roma had blown even more promising leads already this season, though, losing 4-3 at home to Real Madrid after leading 3-1 with eight minutes left, and then going down 3-2 at Old Trafford despite being 2-0 ahead at half-time.

Ukrainian defender Zabarnyi levelled just after the half-hour mark as he found space at the near post to head in Senny Mayulu’s corner.

Evan Ndicka headed just off-target for Roma late in the first half and Niccolo Pisilli forced a good stop from Matvei Safonov early in the second half.

Joao Neves then headed agonisingly wide for PSG as he arrived unmarked in the area to meet a Nuno Mendes cross, before Dembele was introduced for the hosts in place of the ineffective Ferran Torres.

Moments after that PSG won a penalty when Achraf Hakimi stormed into the Roma box only to be pulled down by Wesley.

The French side had missed four penalties in the Champions League since the start of last season, but Dembele did score in the final against Arsenal in May.

He kept a cool head to convert his fifth goal of the campaign, but PSG could not make it five straight Champions League wins this season.

Malen entered the fray for Roma midway through the second half and looked on as Dembele was denied a brilliant solo goal by a Mile Svilar save.

Roma then won a penalty following a VAR check after Vitinha blocked a Soule shot with a raised hand in the box.

Up stepped Malen to score his 17th goal of a prolific campaign, boosting Roma’s hopes of reaching the knockout phase.

World.title: UCL: Pochettino still winless as Man United draw 2-2 with Sporting
World.content:
Sporting Lisbon’s Colombian forward #97 Luis Suarez (R) celebrates scoring his team’s second goal during the UEFA Champions League 1st round day 5 football match between Sporting CP and Manchester United at Jose Alvalade Stadium in Lisbon on November 25, 2026. (Photo by PATRICIA DE MELO MOREIRA / AFP)

Mauricio Pochettino must wait for his first win as Manchester United coach after a wild 2-2 Champions League draw at Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday, with the hosts equalising thanks to a goalkeeping error from Senne Lammens.

The Belgian stopper’s poor handling allowed Luis Suarez to complete a brace for the hosts, cancelling out United playmaker Bruno Fernandes’s double against his former side.

United gave away two penalties in the first half, the second converted by Suarez, before Fernandes equalised from the spot early in the second half.

Fernandes sent United ahead with a lucky bounce taking his effort over the Sporting goalkeeper, before Suarez’s acrobatic effort levelled the game.

United midfielder Youri Tielemans was sent off in stoppage time for a second yellow card to end a compelling and often erratic match.

A crushing 4-0 defeat by rivals Liverpool in the Premier League at the weekend, leaving United 19th, was a disastrous first game at the helm for Pochettino after replacing Michael Carrick.

Pochettino brought Harry Maguire into the three-man defence as he shuffled his pack, as well as starting Joshua Zirkzee in place of the suspended Matheus Cunha.

Neither side took many risks in the opening stages, with few chances of note until the game burst into life midway through the first half as United lost control.

Lisandro Martinez brought down Geny Catamo in the area and Sporting were awarded a penalty.

The hosts blew their chance from the spot, with Suarez’s scuffed effort easily saved by Lammens, but the Red Devils gave away another spot kick just a couple of minutes later.

Goalkeeper Lammens came flying off his line and clattered Maxi Araujo, and this time Colombian striker Suarez made no mistake from the spot.

– United unhappy with disallowed goals –

United thought they had equalised when Amad Diallo hit the crossbar and then nodded home the rebound, but the goal was disallowed to their dismay.

Youri Tielemans was ruled to have fouled Goncalo Inacio, although he seemed to win the ball, upsetting United further after Leny Yoro’s controversial red card against Liverpool on Sunday that was later rescinded.

Fernandes pulled United level early in the second half from the spot after Eduardo Quaresma brought down Martinez.

The former Sporting playmaker calmly stroked his penalty beyond the dive of Kaique Pereira into the bottom left corner.

Fernandes said on the eve of the game he had stopped contract talks because he wanted to focus on helping United improve their form after a dire start to the season.

The midfielder soon had his second goal, with the help of a bizarre bounce off a divot on the pitch.

Fernandes’s low effort from distance seemed bound for Pereira’s hands, but suddenly bounced up off a patch of uneven turf and fortuitously over the goalkeeper’s head.

The Portugal international bent a free-kick narrowly off target as he looked to complete his hat-trick.

Lammens saved well from Sergi Altimira to protect United’s lead as Sporting battled to find an equaliser.

It eventually came from a howler from Lammens, who failed to claim a cross dropping out of the sky, spilling the ball in front of Suarez, who produced a hooked acrobatic effort to score.

Moments later United had the ball in the net at the other end after another goalkeeping error by Pereira, who mishandled Fernandes’s corner, pushing the ball into his own net.

However what would have been the winner was disallowed for an elbow by Patrick Dorgu on the goalkeeper, a decision the visitors were also unhappy about.

World.title: Dangote Refinery to list on Nigerian Exchange December 1
World.content:
The Dangote Petroleum Refinery says it will begin trading on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) Group on December 1, marking its entry into the Nigerian stock market following its initial public offering (IPO).

Devakumar Edwin, vice-president of oil and gas at Dangote Group, announced the development on Wednesday, according to a Reuters report.

The listing comes after the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved the refinery’s share allocation plan following its heavily oversubscribed IPO, which closed last month.

The regulatory approval cleared the way for the company to distribute shares to investors and proceed with preparations for its stock market debut.

The refinery had earlier sought to increase the size of its IPO by up to 30 per cent to approximately $2.1 billion following strong investor demand.

On September 11, Aliko Dangote, president of Dangote Industries Limited (DIL), said the refinery planned to pursue a listing on a United States stock exchange after expanding its production capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day within the next two and a half years.

However, on November 8, Dangote disclosed that the refinery’s IPO fell short of its target of attracting 10 million investors.

Despite missing the target, Africa’s richest person said the offer attracted “millions of investors”.

He described the level of participation as significant when compared with some of the largest public offerings in Africa and globally.

World.title: Troops rescue 5 kidnapped victims, arrest 2 suspected terrorists in Kaduna
World.content:
FILE IMAGE

By Kingsley Omonobi

Troops of Operation Fansan Yamma in furtherance of ongoing counter-terrorism operations, on Wednesday successfully rescued 5 kidnapped victims and arrested of 2 suspected terrorists in separate operations conducted in Kaduna State.

Confirming the rescue operation, Captain Sinivie Tamuno, Spokesman said, “On Wednesday, 25 November 2026, troops of Sector 1 responded to distress calls following attacks by suspected terrorists on Dan Bushiya community in Chikun Local Government Area, during which some residents were abducted.

“Despite encountering an ambush, troops continued their rescue efforts without sustaining any casualties.

“The operation led to the rescue of a woman and her baby, who were abandoned by the fleeing terrorists following sustained pressure from the troops.

“Similarly, on the same day, troops responded to another distress call following the abduction of 5 residents of Kakura village in the same Local Government Area.

“The swift intervention of the troops forced the terrorists to abandon 3 of the kidnapped victims, who were subsequently rescued.

“Efforts are ongoing in conjunction with other security agencies to track and eliminate the terrorists.

“In a related development, on the same day, a joint patrol team conducting search and rescue operations following a kidnapped incident in Danbushiya community, found a national ID card along the terrorists’ withdraw route.

“The discovery subsequently led to the arrest of the bearer identified as Mr Shauibu Musa and another suspect named Aliyu Ahmed.

“The suspected terrorists are in troops custody for further investigation.

The Joint Task Force Operation Fansan Yamma remains resolute in its commitment to combating terrorism and other forms of criminality, securing lives and property, and restoring lasting peace across the North West.

“Members of the public are urged to continue supporting ongoing operations by providing timely and credible information on suspicious activities to the troops and other security agencies.”

World.title: ‘Five bullets’ — NDC supporter recounts attack on Omo-Agege’s campaign team in Delta
World.content:
A supporter of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has recounted how gunmen allegedly shot him five times during an attack on the campaign team of Ovie Omo-Agege, the party’s candidate for Delta Central, in Uduere, Ughelli North Local Government Area of Delta State.

The survivor, who sustained gunshot injuries to his chest and mouth, narrated his ordeal in a video shared on the NDC’s X page on Wednesday.

The video showed him speaking from his hospital bed during a visit by Peter Obi, the party’s presidential candidate, and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, its vice-presidential candidate, to survivors of the attack.

Recounting events leading up to the shooting, the man said he had received threats after participating in a 10,000-man march organised by the NDC in Delta State.

According to him, his wife received a telephone call from individuals who threatened to shut down his business.

“To be very precise, on Sunday, when we were in church, in the early hours of the day, they went and sealed the whole business premises. I could not get access to the premises; I could not offload my goods,” he recalled.

“A week later, my truck that brought goods from Lagos, they seized the truck and drove it to the local government secretariat.”

He said the truck was detained for more than four days, adding that no explanation had been provided for its seizure.

The supporter said the attack occurred on Monday while Omo-Agege was addressing supporters at the campaign venue, when gunmen stormed the gathering and opened fire.

He said one of the attackers called out his name before shooting him as he attempted to escape towards his car.

“One of them started shouting, ‘That is Agba, shoot Agba, that is Agba, look at Agba going.’ Before I could say Jack, the gunshot came straight to my chest,” he said.

“There is a bullet here, through the throat. There is a bullet here…five bullets on the chest and the mouth.

“So, the target was just to kill me, but to God be the glory, I’m alive.”

He attributed the attack to his political affiliation and support for the NDC’s presidential and vice-presidential candidates.

“The whole thing is because I’m supporting NDC; I’m supporting Obi and Kwankwaso,” he said.

Another survivor receiving treatment at the hospital also expressed determination to continue supporting the party despite the violence.

“No matter the number of persons they shoot or attempt to kill in their time, Peter Obi will become president, Rabiu Kwankwaso will become vice-president, and Nigeria will be okay,” he said.

Recall in a statement issued on Tuesday, the Nigeria Police Force spokesperson, Ani Iniedu, said preliminary reports indicated that six people were killed and several others injured during the attack.

Iniedu said the police would sanction any officers found to have acted improperly, unlawfully or breached professional standards during the incident.

He added that an investigation was ongoing to establish the confirmed casualty figure and determine the circumstances surrounding the violence.

According to him, the Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, had ordered increased security deployment, intelligence-led operations and sustained patrols to prevent further violence and restore normalcy in the affected communities.

Meanwhile, the Delta State Government imposed a curfew across Ughelli North Local Government Area from 6pm to 6am daily until further notice following the attack.

World.title: Uzodimma: More Garlands, More Fury
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

By Declan Emelumba





A maxim has it that the more successful you become, the more enemies you attract. Put another way, nobody envies a failure, but many grow jealous at the meteoric rise of a successful man. Governor Hope Uzodimma has lived out that maxim in a peculiar way in recent weeks: every fresh garland placed on his neck has been met with a fresh wave of fury from his enemies, and the louder the applause for him grows, the louder their howling becomes.

The latest garland came from an unlikely quarter. The Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR), a body known to be conservative and sparing with its honours, named its auditorium after the Imo State Governor. In its 63-year history since 1963, the Institute had never named that auditorium after any individual or institution. The announcement was made by the NIPR President, Dr Ike Neliaku, shortly after Uzodimma delivered the keynote address at the World Public Relations Forum (WPRF), which was being held in West Africa for the first time. The more than 3,000 delegates from over 126 countries in the hall rose to their feet.

The Global Alliance for Public Relations and Communication Management, organisers of the WPRF, had invited Uzodimma on the strong recommendation of the NIPR to share his governance experience, which it said had produced massive improvement in infrastructure, social services, human capital development, and engagement with the people of Imo State. He spoke on “Responsible Governance and Communication: Building Trust Through Community Engagement, Stakeholder Relations and Inclusive Impact – Spotlight on Imo State”. He spoke confidently and eloquently, with facts, figures, and candour, and his conversational style connected with the audience. He linked the results of his administration to inclusive governance, transparency, accountability, and steady feedback from the people under his Shared Prosperity agenda. He cited about 150 roads constructed, more than 65,000 youths trained in digital skills and technology, linked to roughly 80,000 jobs, the digitalisation of land administration, the Orashi Electricity Power Plant, the OKOBI Initiative supporting hundreds of businesses, and a health insurance scheme covering more than 2.5 million residents. When he was done, it was a standing ovation, and the naming of the auditorium drew another.

That garland did not hang alone. A few days earlier, the Lagos Country Club had nominated him to deliver its maiden lecture on dialogue with policymakers. The Sun named him its Man of the Year for 2026. Abroad, the African Leadership Organisation conferred on him its African Inspirational Leadership and Good Governance Award at a ceremony held at the House of Lords in London, and the South Carolina House of Representatives in the United States passed a formal motion recognising his work in infrastructure, urban renewal, and digital innovation. At home, Vanguard, Leadership, Silverbird Television, and other reputable media organisations have also honoured him for a transformation and transparency that have rewritten the story of development and democracy in Imo State.

Yet with every garland, the fury of his enemies has grown. The speed with which some political turncoats and charlatans celebrated the procured judgement that temporarily halted his senatorial ambition for Imo West showed clearly that not everyone who has been laughing with him is his true friend. Some have been plotting his downfall all along, for the simple reason that Uzodimma has not allowed his humble beginnings to limit his political growth, nor obstacles to stop him from posting a superlative performance as Governor of Imo State.

Place the two camps side by side. While Uzodimma was collecting garlands in Abuja, Lagos, and London, his chief accuser was collecting a bench warrant from a magistrate’s court on charges of forgery and perjury, and spending his evenings in television studios explaining why he was never arrested. One man is being invited by professional bodies to teach governance; the other is being invited by the police to explain documents. Ask those dancing over the Abuja judgement to name one institution that has honoured their principal in the last seven years, and the silence will be deafening. A man with no garlands of his own can only hope to tear down another man’s, and that is the whole story of this fury.

Having failed to stop him at the polls, they have taken to twisting his statements, inciting people against him, and hyping an imaginary wedge between him and the APC on one hand and the Presidency on the other. Social media was recently awash with a phantom claim that the Imo State Governor had directed his people not to vote for President Tinubu because the President failed to intervene in his court case. Can anyone imagine such insanity? Discerning Nigerians know that Uzodimma would never say such a thing against a party in which he is a critical stakeholder, but what about the gullible? He is the Chairman of the Progressive Governors’ Forum, the Director-General of the Renewed Hope Ambassadors, the Secretary of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, and the leader of the party in the South-East. Everyone who knows him knows he would never utter such words, even in his dreams.

Still hunting for a way to set the Imo helmsman against the Presidency, someone had the audacity to publish a headline claiming that Uzodimma had criticised President Tinubu over the removal of fuel subsidy. The irony is that they took that headline from the very WPRF speech that earned him the NIPR auditorium. In every major speech he has delivered since 2023, Uzodimma has defended the subsidy removal as the saving grace of Nigeria’s economic stability, and he has praised the President for a policy that has released more money to every tier of government for development across the country. At the WPRF, he noted that the temporary hardship was necessary for Nigeria’s future growth and overall development. The mischief-makers thought they could embarrass him by twisting his words. Unknown to them, the 3,000 delegates in that hall had understood him perfectly, and had already given him a thunderous applause for a presentation that left no room for ambiguity.

Anyone who has followed this saga will notice a pattern. The same camp that produced a forged primary result sheet, which INEC itself disowned and handed to the security agencies, is now producing forged statements and doctored headlines. When you cannot win at the ballot, you manufacture a result. When you cannot fault a man’s speech, you manufacture a quote. It is the same workshop and the same craftsmen, only the product has changed. Imo people have seen this trade before, and they are no longer buying.

So why the fury? Those who are weeping today that they suffered humiliation at the hands of the governor are doing so because Uzodimma had the courage to stand with Imo people in recovering their looted land, assets, and money. Those who wrote him off when he assumed office are angry because he refused to let the politically contrived insecurity of that period slow him down, and that steadiness is now recorded as one of his greatest strengths. He subdued those who wanted to overwhelm him, he shamed those who had written him off, and he won the hearts of Imo people through the faithful and transparent implementation of his Reconstruction, Rehabilitation, and Recovery agenda. The same courage that rattles his enemies is what Imo people celebrate in him. It changed the narrative of the state, and it is what has drawn the garlands.

There is also a deeper fear at work. A governor who is honoured in London, invited in Lagos, and celebrated by a global gathering of communication professionals in Abuja is a governor whose voice will reverberate far beyond Imo. His opponents understand that a Senator Uzodimma would take that voice, and the South-East’s place at the national table, into the red chamber. That is what they are truly fighting. Their quarrel is less with one senatorial ticket than with the prospect of an Igbo voice they cannot shout down.

Like the proverbial animal that keeps galloping to safety even as it is being shot at, Uzodimma has kept rising in national politics, attracting weightier appointments, delivering democracy dividends in Imo State, and being honoured locally and internationally for his honest hard work. Those after him will need far more energy to catch him, because the more stones they throw, the faster he gallops, and the more garlands he gathers along the way. Happily, the governor is far more interested in his place in history than in the shenanigans of his enemies and political opponents.

There is no longer any doubt about his performance over the last seven years. Those who never expected him to go this far are simply angry that he has disappointed them. But to the great majority of Imo people, who are enamoured of his style of governance and the development it has brought, the chorus remains the same: CARRY GO, WE DEY YOUR BACK.

•Emelumba is the Commissioner for Information, Public Orientation and Strategy, Imo State.

The five finalists were selected from an initial list of 10 nominees following their exceptional contributions for club and country during the period under consideration.

The winner will be revealed during the CAF Awards 2026 ceremony in Lagos, which returns to Nigeria’s commercial capital for the first time since the 2014 edition.

World.title: The DSS’s New Push For Accountability And Rule Of Law
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

By Suleiman Tajudeen

Something has changed at the Department of State Service (DSS) and I hope it is sustained. On November 3, 2026, the Presidential Candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) accused the DSS at a press conference of planning to hire protesters to disrupt the party’s campaign in Sokoto.

It was a grave allegation which could damage the image of the DSS beyond repair if proven to be true. So, I waited eagerly for the response of the DSS. The agency replied the same day.

In its initial statement—issued by Deputy Director of Public Relations and Strategic Communications Favour Dozie—the DSS stated that its Director-General had ordered an internal investigation into the claim. The agency also rejected the allegation as inconsistent with its operations, pointing to its operatives’ rescue of Sokoto ADC governorship candidate Mannir Daniya during an October 31, 2026 attack.

It said two of its operatives were assaulted during the incident and were still being treated in the hospital. The statement said Daniya personally called to thank the DSS for saving his life, and warned against demoralising its operatives. It added that the DG had ordered an investigation into the claim.

Then on November 17, the agency issued a final response. It said after activating its internal investigation protocol, which was expanded to include interviews with the ADC leadership in Sokoto State, members and relevant stakeholders, it found the allegation to be untrue.

The agency then issued a subtle challenge to Atiku Abubakar: “While the Service acknowledges the Letters of Appreciation from the ADC chairman and governorship candidate in Sokoto State, the DSS still requests that, in view of the fact that the allegation was made in public, His Excellency should set the records straight publicly or provide concrete evidence (if any) to enable further investigation.”

But since then, neither Atiku Abubakar nor the ADC has responded to the challenge.

It’s refreshing to see the DSS embrace accountability and professionalism under its current Director General, Oluwatosin Adeola Ajayi. In the statement issued by Favour Dozie, it stated that the “DSS, under its present DG, remains deeply committed to its constitutional mandate, set standards of professionalism and neutrality.”

Speak with any staff of the DSS or the National Assembly committees performing oversight on the agency, and you would understand that the place has turned around since August 26, 2024 when Ajayi was appointed the DG.

Ajayi joined the DSS as a cadet officer in 1990 and rose through the ranks to attain the position of Assistant Director-General before being named DG. He has participated in several domestic and international training programs covering management, security leadership, critical thinking, and human resources, and is said to be one of the most professional operatives in the service.

As DSS Director-General, Ajayi oversees internal security operations, domestic intelligence gathering, counterterrorism, protection of critical national infrastructure, election security support, and security advisory to the federal government.

One of the first things he reportedly did was to restore professionalism to the agency by ensuring only those qualified and competent are in the system. The man reportedly weeded out some bad eggs and those the merit system he instituted could not accommodate.

In November 2025, the service announced the dismissal of 115 personnel as part of ongoing reforms. The agency also published the names and pictures of the 115 disengaged officers on its website. Some of them are reportedly being prosecuted for some crimes allegedly committed.

The man is said to be tough on the job without bending decisions on account of ethnicity, religion or connection. Staff of the agency I’ve spoken with described the DG as an ethical, non-corrupt leader who’s leading by example with honesty, fairness, and transparency, treating organizational resources as a trust rather than a tool for personal gain.

By rewarding merit and actively discouraging nepotism and other corrupt acts by enforcing clear rules and holding everyone accountable—including himself, Ajayi has been able to restore professionalism to the DSS.

This is why the DSS has become one of the most critical security agencies in Nigeria today. It is bursting crimes, gathering valuable intelligence especially terrorism-related intelligence. Unlike in the past when terrorists’ suspects are detained for prolonged periods due to lack of credible evidence for prosecution, cases are now charged to court without delay.

His tenure has included initiatives such as reviewing prolonged detentions without trial, complying with court-ordered compensation and medical support for affected individuals, and advocating for community-level security participation and local government empowerment.

He is certainly getting good results. A good example was the arraignment of seven persons before a federal high court in Birnin Kebbi on Monday barely four months after their arrest. They allegedly committed the crime on May 20, 2026. They were arraigned over alleged involvement in terrorism, kidnapping and illegal possession of firearms. The DSS filed three separate cases against the accused.

But I was fascinated by the first charge which bothers on conspiracy, providing support to a terrorist group and withholding information about terrorist activities. The prosecution alleged that the defendants bought and sold cattle rustled by members of the Islamic State in Sahel Province (ISSP), also known as Lakurawa, operating in parts of Argungu and Augie LGAs of Kebbi.

The DSS said the offences amounted to providing material support to the group and concealing information about its operations.

What was obvious from the court proceedings was that the DSS successfully infiltrated the communication channels of the criminal gang before their arrest. One of the defendants, an informant, was accused of communicating with a suspected terrorists’ leader by telephone and providing information to him. The prosecutor stated details of conversations, including how an attack was conducted.

The DSS diligence had shown before last Monday’s arraignment. In June 2025, it secured life imprisonment for four suspects in the Owo Church attack. Following evidence presented by the DSS, a Federal High Court in Abuja convicted—Idris Ojo, Al-Kasim, Abdulmalik, and Momoh Abubakar— for belonging to a terrorist group.

Mahmud Usman (Mahmud Al-Nijiri) and Abubakar Abba (Abu Bar), two Ansaru commanders, were prosecuted on a 32-count charge covering terrorism financing, kidnapping for ransom, illegal mining, and fabricating improvised explosive devices. They were sentenced in September 2025,with Usman getting 50 years in jail.

The DSS also closed its case against Tukur Mamu, the alleged terrorist negotiator, at the Federal High Court in Abuja.

Earlier this month, the DSS DG ordered the release of four suspects cleared of alleged Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) membership after finding they were misled about a monthly amnesty payout, and approved ₦5 million in initial compensation for each.

All these are indications of an agency that respects the law and cherishes professionalism. The days when DSS officers behaved like lawless goons appear to be over, thanks to the house-cleaning embarked upon by the DG. The DSS has repeatedly issued statements to the effect that it has zero tolerance for misconduct, and everyone seemed to have keyed into the new culture civility and ethical discipline.

We do not want to see the DSS go back to its old ways. It must continue on this trajectory and institutionalise the current reforms in order to serve Nigeria and the government better. Our secret police must be strong on intelligence gathering and have the skill to burst crimes before they happen. But when crimes are committed, it must be well equipped to apprehend criminals.

This is the secret police Nigeria deserves.

*Tajudeen Suleiman is an Abuja-based journalist. He can be reached via email: tajudeensuleiman64@gmail.com

World.title: From the Bench to Blueprint: The Adumein Legacy of Excellence
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

POLITY

By Louis Achi





Undeniably, there is something profoundly symbolic about the convergence of two disciplines in one family. In this case – social engineering, which seeks to shape institutions, strengthen societies and improve the human condition, and civil engineering, which gives physical expression to civilisation through roads, bridges, buildings and other infrastructure.

One operates largely in the realm of institutions and human relationships; the other transforms landscapes through science, technology and innovation. Both, however, are ultimately concerned with building a better society.

It is against this compelling backdrop that the academic distinction of Adumein Ayibaingo Adumein, a Civil Engineering graduate of Nile University of Nigeria, who bagged First-Class Honours Degree, deserves particular attention. Mint new Engr. Adumein Ayibaingo Adumein is the son of His Lordship, Justice Moore Aseimo Abraham Adumein of the Supreme Court.

Significantly, at the Nile varsity’s 14th Convocation in Abuja, Ayibaingo emerged among the outstanding graduates recognised for exceptional academic performance as the university inducted 261 engineering graduates into the Nigerian Society of Engineers (NSE) and administered the professional oath of the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN).

His recognition for academic excellence in the Civil Engineering Department was not merely another entry in a graduation honours list. It was an affirmation of intellectual discipline, academic commitment and the promise of a young professional preparing to enter a field whose importance to Nigeria’s development can hardly be overstated.

Meanwhile, in a letter to the Vice Chancellor Nile University of Nigeria, through the Dean, Faculty of Engineering, the Nigerian Institution of Civil Engineers (NICE), pledged: “To sponsor the best graduating Civil Engineering student, Mr. Adumein Ayibaingo in all NICE conferences and Major events with effect from January 01, 2027 till December31, 2028. Following his excellent performance culminating in a graduating GPA of 4.97, this offer would serve as an excellent exposure to him (Mr. Ayibaingo) into the world of Civil Engineering.”

The letter was signed by Engr. Prof. Sony Emeka Ali fnse, fnice, fnistructe, the incoming national chairman of NICE.

But Ayibaingo’s story carries an additional dimension of further human interest. And this bears repeating. He is the son of Justice Moore Adumein of the Supreme Court of Nigeria, a jurist whose professional calling places him at the heart of the country’s judicial and constitutional architecture.

The coincidence is striking, even if the significance is ultimately his own. While his father occupies an important place in the architecture of Nigeria’s justice system and the complex enterprise of social engineering, his son appears poised to make his contribution to the country’s physical infrastructure through civil engineering.

One builds through the law and the institutions that sustain society; the other is preparing to build through mathematics, materials, design and the science of infrastructure. Different professional pathways, but a shared encounter with the larger question of nation-building.

Academic excellence is often celebrated as a personal achievement, but its deeper significance lies in what it suggests about capacity and potential. In a demanding discipline such as civil engineering, outstanding performance requires more than the ability to memorise formulae or reproduce theoretical principles. It demands analytical rigour, precision, patience, creativity and the capacity to translate abstract knowledge into practical solutions.

These are qualities that matter enormously in a country confronted by an expanding infrastructure deficit. Nigeria needs a new generation of engineers capable of designing resilient roads, constructing durable bridges, developing sustainable housing, improving water systems and delivering infrastructure that can withstand environmental pressures and the demands of a growing population.

The country also needs professionals who understand that engineering is not simply about putting structures on the ground. It is about public safety, economic productivity, environmental responsibility and the quality of human life.

This is why the recognition accorded to Ayibaingo deserves to be viewed beyond the immediate excitement of an academic award. It represents the emergence of another young Nigerian professional whose intellectual preparation could become an asset to national development.

His father’s distinguished career may provide an interesting family backdrop, but the young graduate’s achievement must stand on its own merit. Indeed, the most meaningful legacy a parent can bequeath to a child is not a title or privileged access, but an appreciation of discipline, responsibility, intellectual honesty and service. Ayibaingo’s academic recognition offers an encouraging glimpse of those possibilities.

The induction ceremony – an oath beyond graduation – itself carries significance beyond the usual rituals associated with university valediction. For the 261 graduates, admission into the Nigerian Society of Engineers and the administration of the COREN oath represented an important transition from academic preparation towards the ethical and professional obligations of engineering practice.

As the Dean of the Faculty of Engineering, Engr. Prof. Abdulhameed Danjuma Mambo, aptly observed: “Graduation shows that you have learned, but induction shows that you have become a professional.”

A poorly designed bridge, an inadequately constructed building or a compromised drainage system can become a public hazard long after the engineers responsible have moved on. The public may never see the calculations, technical drawings, material assessments or structural evaluations behind a completed project. Yet it entrusts its safety to the competence and integrity of the professionals responsible.

This places a special obligation on the newly inducted engineers, including Ayibaingo, to appreciate that their professional calling must be governed by ethical conduct as much as technical competence.

The keynote speaker, Engr. Dr. Adamu Muhammed, Terminal Manager of NNPC Limited, reinforced this point by challenging the graduates to uphold honesty, embrace continuous learning and deploy their knowledge towards solving Nigeria’s developmental problems.

It was a timely message for a generation entering a profession increasingly transformed by artificial intelligence, digital modelling, advanced construction materials, automation and climate-conscious infrastructure design.

The engineer of tomorrow must be more than technically qualified. He must be adaptable, innovative and conscious of the wider social consequences of his professional decisions.

Ayibaingo’s distinction also reflects the broader academic ambitions of Nile University of Nigeria. Established in 2009, the university’s Faculty of Engineering has developed into one of its major academic units, offering programmes in Civil Engineering, Computer Engineering, Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Mechatronics Engineering, and Petroleum and Gas Engineering.

The institution’s maiden induction and oath-taking ceremony, involving 261 graduates, represents an important step in consolidating its relationship with professional engineering institutions and strengthening the transition from classroom learning to professional practice.

Particularly noteworthy was the commendation by the Registrar of COREN, Engr. Prof. Okorie Austine Uchegbusi Uche, who praised the university’s implementation of Outcome-Based Education (OBE). The approach places emphasis on measurable competencies and demonstrable graduate capabilities rather than simply the completion of prescribed academic programmes.

Such a framework is increasingly important in a world where employers and professional regulators are concerned not only with what graduates know but also with what they can competently deliver.

The university’s engagement with officials of COREN and international experts from the International Engineering Alliance (IEA) further underscores its internationalisation ambitions. The exercise is connected to Nigeria’s broader efforts to align engineering education with the Washington Accord framework, which promotes internationally benchmarked standards for engineering qualifications.

There is, perhaps, a philosophical lesson in Ayibaingo’s emergence. It significantly mirrors an interesting family portrait of nation-building. The business of building a nation is never the responsibility of one profession or generation. It is an interconnected enterprise involving institutions, ideas, infrastructure, leadership, knowledge and the values that bind society together.

Justice Moore Adumein’s professional vocation belongs to the administration of justice and the preservation of constitutional order. His son’s chosen discipline belongs to the engineering of the physical environment within which citizens live, work, travel and conduct their economic activities.

The metaphor of social engineering should not be mistaken for a claim about the judge’s specific professional specialisation. Rather, it captures the broader societal significance of his judicial calling – the strengthening of institutions, the interpretation of law and the maintenance of the constitutional framework upon which orderly society depends.

Civil engineering gives tangible form to development. It creates the infrastructure that connects communities, facilitates commerce, supports industrialisation and improves living conditions. The convergence of these two professional trajectories in one family offers an attractive illustration of the many dimensions of nation-building.

For Nigeria, where infrastructure development remains central to economic transformation, young engineers of promise represent an important national resource. And for a father whose professional life has been devoted to the institutions of justice, there must be a special satisfaction in seeing his son earn recognition in an entirely different but equally consequential field of public relevance.

Hear Justice Adumein: “I give all glory and gratitude to Almighty God for this remarkable milestone in the life of my son, Adumein Ayibaingo Adumein, who has graduated with distinction in Civil Engineering from the Nile University of Nigeria, Abuja.

“Few moments can compare with the profound satisfaction of witnessing one’s child translate years of discipline, sacrifice, perseverance and intellectual exertion into an accomplishment of this nature.

“My profound appreciation goes to the management, faculty and entire academic community of Nile University for their contribution to his intellectual development and for recognising his efforts. However, I must remind my dear son that distinction is not an arrival point; it is an obligation. Academic excellence confers not just privilege but responsibility.”

Ultimately, the most enduring family legacies are not necessarily those in which children reproduce their parents’ professions. They are those in which succeeding generations inherit the values of excellence and service, then deploy them in new fields of endeavour.

Justice Moore Adumein has made his mark in the judicial architecture of Nigeria. Adumein Ayibaingo Adumein has taken an impressive first step towards making his own mark in the engineering architecture of the nation.

One is associated with the interpretation and defence of the law; the other is preparing to master the science of building structures upon which society depends. The father helps sustain the architecture of justice. The son will now help construct the architecture of development.

And therein lies the promise of a new generation. Not merely inheriting a name, but earning a place in the demanding business of building a nation.

Kayode Tokede

The Nigerian stock market yesterday extended its downward trends, as persistent selling pressure in 34 stocks dragged the market capitalisation lower by N1.10 trillion.

The Nigerian Exchange Limited All-Share Index (NGX ASI) fell by 1,696.56 basis points or 0.69 per cent to close 243,989.31 basis points, its lowest level in 10 weeks, dating back to mid-September 2026, moderating its year-to-date return to 56.80 per cent

Consequently, market capitalisation decreased by N1.10 trillion to close at N158.42 trillion.

The downturn was impacted by losses recorded in medium and large capitalised stocks, amongst which are; MTN Nigeria Communications (MTNN), Nigerian Aviation Handling Company (NAHCO), NASCON Allied Industries, among ofhers.

Market sentiment remained negative, with 34 decliners, outweighing 24 advancers. Fortis Global Insurance topped the gainers’ list by 10.00 per cent to close at N1.65, per share. Cornerstone Insurance followed with a gain of 9.92 per cent to close at N6.65, while Transnational Express rose by 9.91 per cent to close at N2.33, per share.

Omatek Venture also advanced by 6.87 per cent to close at N1.40, and Sunu Assurance gained 6.29 per cent to close at N3.04, per share.

On the flip side, Nigerian Aviation Handling Company (NAHCO) led the losers, shedding 10.00 per cent to close at N130.50, while McNichols followed with a decline of 9.57 per cent to close at N4.25, per share.

AIICO Insurance fell by 9.43 per cent to close at N4.32, while Learn Africa and NEM Insurance dropped by 9.09 per cent each to close at N7.00 and N28.00 respectively, per share.

Meanwhile, the total volume traded increased by 236.48 per cent to 1.647 billion units, valued at N40.919 billion, and exchanged in 29,893 deals. Transactions in the shares of FCMB Group topped the activity chart with 704.657 million shares valued at NN9.532 billion. Fidelity Bank followed with 614.770 million shares worth N13.523 billion, while NEM Insurance traded 57.720 million shares valued at N267.548 million.

Linkage Assurance traded 33.217 million shares valued at N60.492 million, while Access Holdings sold 28.570 million shares worth N730.533 million.
