The head of the National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority has emphasized that the spread of this game poses a risk to the younger generation and must be addressed.”

Badawy noted that the game is not yet widespread in Egypt with far less than one million players so far.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Egypt and Sudan call on Ethiopia to change its unilateral policy
World.content:
The Egyptian Cabinet issued a joint statement on Tuesday on the conclusion of the state visit of the Sudanese Prime Minister Professor Kamel al-Tayeb Idris.

Both sides stressed the inseparable nature of the Sudanese and Egyptian water security and agreed on the necessity of defending both countries’ full water rights and uses under the 1959 Agreement and not permitting any encroachment upon those rights.

They confirmed that their position is based on a call for cooperation and dialogue to protect the right to life and support the right to development, and on joint action to achieve mutual benefit in accordance with international law.

Egypt and Sudan both welcomed African positions that recognize the entitlement of the both Nile Basin downstream states to defend their water rights alongside the interests of their peoples, and to pursue development on an equal footing with the rest of the continent.

The two parties agreed to follow up on the implementation of the outcomes of the coordination meetings within the framework of the Permanent Joint Technical Body for Nile Waters under the 1959 Agreement, to study and formulate the unified position to be adopted by the two countries on all matters related to Nile waters, in addition to meetings of the 2+2 mechanism between the foreign and irrigation ministers of the two countries.

Both sides reiterated their complete rejection of any unilateral measures in the Eastern Nile Basin and agreed that the unlateral actions of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), which violates international law, has grave consequences and constitutes a continuing threat to the downstream Nile states.

They called on Ethiopia to change its unilateral policy and restore cooperation in accordance with rules applicable under international law, particularly the principles of no significant harm, prior notification, consultation and consensus.

Restoring stability

The two sides affirmed their determination to enhance joint coordination to restore stability in Sudan.

Egypt reiterated its rejection of any threat to Sudan’s unity and territorial integrity, and stressed its continued support for the Sudanese people and their national institutions.

Both sides reaffirmed the principles set out in a statement from the Egyptian Presidency, dated December 18, 2025, regarding the direct link between Egyptian and Sudanese national security: foremost among them preserving Sudan’s sovereignty, territorial unity and integrity, safeguarding its resources and the rights of the Sudanese people, categorical rejection of the establishment of or recognition of parallel entities, and the protection of Sudanese state institutions from interference.

Egypt reiterated its full readiness to take all measures and actions permitted under international law and the mutual defense agreement between both countries to support Sudan and ensure these red lines are never crossed.

Both sides condemned the targeting of civilians and infrastructure in Sudan by rebel militias, in particular power stations and water installations, including through the launch of drones from a neighboring country.

They renewed their call for respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity, and for supporting its national institutions, foremost the Sudanese Armed Forces, in fulfilling their constitutional duty to preserve Sudanese national security, protect its borders, defend its resources, prevent the dissipation of its assets and safeguard its water rights.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: The Trump team is getting more and more evasive about Jensen Huang
World.content:
When Jensen Huang was shockingly reinstalled as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, both Nvidia’s board of directors and President Donald Trump cast it as the result of the administration’s assurances that he wasn’t a national security risk and faced no legal jeopardy.

But pretty much ever since then, those assurances have appeared less than ironclad.

All of which reinforces what a massive risk both Trump and Nvidia just took, which should be ratcheting up concerns among some very skeptical GOP lawmakers.

What Nvidia and Trump initially said

The board said in its initial statement Monday morning that its talks with senior government officials left it “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk” — despite the fact that he had an affair with a woman who US officials feared could be working with Chinese intelligence.

Trump said shortly thereafter on social media that the US government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

Trump also said that, despite questions about prohibited Nvidia chips making their way to China, Attorney General Todd Blanche “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

But other officials have yet to publicly double down on those assurances. And Blanche was rather evasive in an interview Monday night. Even Trump has repeatedly emphasized very real caveats.

In addition to the assurances he offered on Truth Social on Monday morning, Trump in a later CNBC interview claimed the Justice Department had “exonerated” Huang.

“They did a study. They did a pretty good investigation,” Trump said. “And they felt that he himself was exonerated. I don’t know what word you want to use.”

The US Commerce and Justice Departments previously said investigators had conducted an in-person interview with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as part of an investigation into whether the Singaporean-based company had been diverting US semiconductors.

But now Blanche is talking around all that, with increasingly evasive comments about what sort of investigations have occurred or been opened — even accusing reporters of “mocking” him by asking the questions.

“What I said last week is that we were looking into it,” Blanche said at the Justice Department on Tuesday. “The FBI, law enforcement, looks into things all the time. That doesn’t necessarily become a criminal investigation. Doesn’t necessarily become an indictment. It just literally is that it’s looking into things.”

Pressed on whether Jensen Huang had been investigated, Blanche threw the question back at reporters. “What does that mean, had Huang been investigated? For what?”

He went on to say, “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.”

And the night before, when Fox News host Laura Ingraham asked whether Huang had been cleared of being a national security risk and of illegal activity, Blanche never offered a direct answer.

He instead referred to a Wall Street Journal story Ingraham had mentioned in her lead-up, and declined to comment on it. Then he mentioned extensive discussions within the administration — but without ever saying that those discussions had confirmed Huang was in the clear.

Blanche eventually landed on saying: “A lot of thoughtful process by administration officials went into this decision, and the right decision was reached, I believe.”

And perhaps most strikingly, despite Trump’s claim that the DOJ had “exonerated” Huang, Blanche wouldn’t even confirm the DOJ had opened an investigation.

Ingraham asked twice whether the investigation was now closed, and Blanche balked.

“That assumes there’s an investigation that’s open. And I — that’s never been discussed publicly,” Blanche said.

That’s a long way from Trump’s claim about Huang having been “exonerated.”

While Blanche was evasive, others in the administration were non-existent when it came to vouching for Trump’s assurances.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio was a case in point.

It was Rubio who disseminated a memo to senior US officials warning about potential counterintelligence risks posed by Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation).

But on Monday, Rubio said nothing publicly about Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.

He ignored a CNN reporter’s shouted question about it during a public event with a foreign dignitary.

Maybe that wasn’t the forum for an in-depth answer on the subject. But Rubio would seem to be a hugely significantly witness for Trump’s assurances. And the fact that the administration didn’t put him forward was conspicuous.

Trump watered down his assurances, too

And even Trump, later Monday morning in his CNBC interview, qualified his assurances.

When talking about whether Huang might have known about prohibited chips making their way to China, Trump said that “he certainly did not know about it.”

But then he quickly added a less-than-certain caveat, appending “or at least that’s been our very powerful impression.”

Later in the interview, Trump twice qualified his assurances about Huang’s lack of legal liability by saying that “we believe” Huang is in the clear.

“I gave them enough assurance,” Trump added.

He later said: “You can only give the assurance as to what you know. But we feel very strongly that he’s in good shape — very good shape.”

What it means

None of these comments preclude something else coming out about Huang.

Perhaps Trump and those around him are indeed very confident that nothing is going to come out to undercut their assurances. But they just won’t completely own those assurances yet.

And Blanche’s evasive interview and Rubio’s lack of comment both suggest this could be a familiar dynamic: Trump coming to a conclusion based upon what he wants to believe, and those around him scrambling to justify and bolster his preferred narrative.

But there seem to be plenty of people bent on learning more. And time will tell how well the administration’s qualified assurances hold up.

World.title: Like ‘family businesses’: Inside the Nvidia board that ousted and rehired Jensen Huang
World.content:
New York — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang gushed last year that support from longtime board members Tench Coxe, Mark Stevens and Harvey Jones was crucial to helping him navigate three decades of running the company.

“They not one time gave up on the company and us,” Huang told the Acquired podcast of the board members and other early employees.

Those same supporters have now helped see Huang through his biggest challenge yet — restoring his role as CEO following an unprecedented corporate scandal. But their close relationships have also raised questions about the board’s independence and whether it was equipped to hold Huang accountable and protect shareholders’ interests.

Including Huang, nearly half of Nvidia’s 11-person board has been with the company since its early days. Its three longest-serving members — Coxe, Stevens and Jones — saw the value of their combined holdings in the company jump by nearly $2.5 billion from Friday to Monday, after Huang was brought back.

His reinstatement marks a sharp turnaround from a week ago, when Jones said the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation, and had no intention of bringing him back. And it comes despite Huang’s relationship with a woman that US officials feared could be a Chinese intelligence asset, as well as multiple reports about an extramarital affair with a subordinate. President Donald Trump has also been open about his role in pushing the board to give Huang his job back.

“The appearance of the relationship between the board and Jensen is most akin to family businesses that go public — that’s a domain in which it’s not uncommon for directors to be there for a long time,” said Jo-Ellen Pozner, management professor at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business. “But those kinds of companies are not major players in the global economy.”

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the Yale professor known as the “CEO Whisperer,” on Monday called the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Huang a “complete failure of corporate governance” and urged them to resign.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.

The Board

Aside from Huang, whose board seat was restored along with his CEO title, four members of Nvidia’s board have been with the company for around three decades.

That includes Jones, who was named last week as Nvidia’s first-ever board chair after joining the company at its inception in 1993. At the time, he’d been serving as CEO of software firm Synopsys, where Nvidia’s original founders had been customers before they approached Jones to bring his operational expertise to the board of their new company.

Coxe and Stevens, early Nvidia investors, have also served on the board since 1993, although Stevens took a two-year hiatus from 2006 to 2008. Brooke Seawell, who previously worked alongside Jones at Synopsys, joined Nvidia’s board in 1997.

Having long tenured board members means having a “longstanding mission and espirit de corps that a lot of people pointed to as a source of strength for the company,” said Eric Talley, professor at Columbia Law School and co-host of the Beyond Unprecedented podcast. But “it does set up situations where a board might be very, very reluctant to exercise real oversight over someone who’s now become their old friend and someone who has given them loyalty over the years.”

That may be why, for example, the board had been reluctant to challenge Huang’s opposition to succession planning that left them flat-footed, causing investors to panic when news of his affairs and concerns about national security risk came to light.

Even many of the board members who have joined, by Nvidia’s standards, more recently, have, by current, typical corporate governance standards, been there a relatively long time.

Research on corporate boards suggests that the “maximum efficacy” of a board member peaks around eight to 10 years and then “trails off dramatically,” Pozner said.

“Boards that have longer tenures are referred to as zombie boards,” she said, “because the implication is that people then are asleep at the wheel in terms of their ability to engage in active oversight because they become like insiders.”

Reinstating Huang

Still, Talley noted that when it came to reinstating Huang, the board was in a difficult position: stick with their original decision to move on without Huang and risk angering some of their biggest customers and the president “who can wield a fairly heavy governmental and regulatory hammer.” Or it could reverse course, which “makes the board look weaker,” and puts them at risk if additional issues arise from the ongoing internal, state and federal investigations.

Going forward, the board may be mindful of keeping a tight leash on Huang to ensure it doesn’t look ineffective, Talley said. It appointed its newest member, Suzanne Nora Johnson, the retired vice chair of Goldman Sachs who joined Nvidia in May, to lead the National Security and Export Controls Oversight Committee it created last week amid the scandal.

Jensen Huang reacts as employees applaud his return to office after Nvidia reinstated him as the company’s CEO, in Santa Clara, California, on November 23, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video. Zhengzhong Tu/UGC/Reuters

Nvidia’s longtime board members also stood to gain financially from Huang’s return. Jones, Coxe and Stevens together own more than 62 million shares in the company, according to data compiled by FactSet based on the most recent filings to the Securities and Exchange Commission. The combined value of their holdings declined by nearly $5 billion from the end of October, before the Huang debacle began, through Friday, before making up around half of those losses Monday when Haung’s return boosted the stock by more than 30%.

It is typical for corporate board members to own stock in the company; it aligns their interests with those of the shareholders they represent. Nvidia’s board may have decided that, like for them, Huang’s return was in the best interest of all shareholders given the dramatic decline in the stock price following his exit.

However, experts say significant holdings could lead to short-term decision making. Nvidia’s longtime board members have all seen their personal wealth rise dramatically in recent years as the company’s valuation skyrocketed.

“Now you’re an insider to that company, your portfolio starts to take on the look of an employee’s portfolio,” Pozner said. “It’s impossible then to separate yourself from the company in a way that allows you to maintain the kind of distance that board independence is supposed to ensure.”

World.title: Iran’s leaders want a baby boom. A struggling economy stands in the way
World.content:
Iran must address its declining population by encouraging young people to marry and have children, according to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.

The country of 93 million faces a demographic crisis, with an aging population and falling birthrate as young couples struggle to afford homes and start families amid a deepening economic slump.

In a statement attributed to him on Tuesday, Khamenei said Iran must address shortcomings in past population policies, describing population growth as a “strategic priority.”

His message was read at a ceremony for the National Population Rejuvenation Award, which honors efforts to help families and increase Iran’s birth rate.

Khamenei, who has not made a public appearance since becoming Supreme Leader in March, urged officials to make it easier for young people to marry, support childbearing, improve individual health and promote “a family-centered culture” to help Iran overcome what he called “a critical period.”

His message follows several warnings from Iranian officials about the consequences of a spiraling rate of marriages and births.

“The country’s demographic situation is extremely critical,” Marzieh Vahid Dastjerdi, secretary of the National Population Headquarters, said last month.

The fertility rate has fallen from 6.7 children per woman in the 1980s to 1.34, Dastjerdi said, with several provinces now seeing their populations decline as a result.

“If we do not act today to reverse the decline in marriage and childbearing, our demographic opportunities will be lost one after another,” she said, predicting that the country’s population could shrink by two-thirds to just 31 million over the next 75 years.

An Iranian family sits at the water edge of Chitgar Lake, an artificial recreational lake and park officially known as the Lake of the Martyrs of the Persian Gulf, in northwestern Tehran on April 26. Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images

The speed at which Iran’s population is aging makes it a demographic outlier in the Middle East, where many countries are grappling with challenges of growing youth populations. In less than two decades, Iran has transitioned from a youthful and fast-growing society into below-replacement fertility.

Unlike advanced economies facing similar demographic challenges, Iran risks growing old before it becomes prosperous, with decades of crippling US sanctions and economic mismanagement leaving it ill-equipped to absorb the financial burden of an aging population.

One Iranian official called the country’s demographic trend a “mega-crisis.”

The number of births registered in 2012 was 1.3 million. In 2025, it was 892,000. Over the same period, the percentage of the population aged 14 and younger declined from 25.3 percent to 15.8 percent. At the other end of the scale, the population aged 60 and over rose from 8.2 percent to 12.6 percent.

Decline in marriage

Unless the trend is reversed, the over-sixties will account for nearly a third of the population by 2050. And caring for that aging segment of society will become more arduous.

“The growing trend of one-child families in recent years has created numerous educational, psychological and social problems,” according to Fatemeh Mohammadbeigi, who serves on the parliament’s health commission.

Within about 15 years, each young couple may have to care for two sets of elderly parents without any siblings to share the responsibility, she said.

At the heart of the crisis is a sharp decline in marriage.

The number of marriages fell by more than 50 percent between 2011 and this year, according to figures from Iran’s Civil Registration Organization.

It attributed the fall to economic pressures such as inflation, rising housing costs, unemployment, and the growing difficulty of affording the expenses of starting a family.

Eighteen million Iranians of marriageable age are still single, including 10 million men and 8 million women, according to state media. Roughly 2.4 million women over 35 are single.

“All of our population-related issues are tied to marriage,” Dastjerdi said last month.

Residents continue their daily routines across business centers, shopping districts, and city streets despite escalating tensions between Iran and the United States, on October 12, in Tehran, Iran. Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu/Getty Images

But the country’s demographic problems are also partly the result of its own policies. The Islamic Republic introduced a major family planning program in the late 1980s – offering free contraceptives and vasectomies and later scrapping some benefits for larger families – only to reverse course decades later.

Iran’s rapidly changing demography has played out starkly in the capital, Tehran, this year, amid the perpetual economic crunch. Births have fallen nearly 10 percent, and deaths have risen more than 6 percent since March, compared to last year.

Women are selling their hair

Iran is one of the world’s biggest producers of oil and gas, but its economy is likely to shrink by 7.6 percent this year, according to the International Monetary Fund, thanks to the US naval blockade that has brought seaborne foreign trade to a near halt, damage to infrastructure since the conflict began in February, and ongoing sanctions.

A lack of employment opportunities and growing poverty discourage young people from getting married. Iranians increasingly use credit apps to get by, incurring more debt.

Online s have begun appearing, offering basic food products for sale in installments. One can of tuna, priced at the equivalent of just over $1, was being offered in four installments.

Some young women have taken desperate steps to make ends meet – including selling their hair to be made into extensions.

Among those seeking to sell their hair are female heads of household, mothers trying to cover the cost of their children’s medical treatment and students struggling to pay for their education, according to a recent study.

“At first, I wanted to sell my laptop, but I needed it to write my thesis. So I decided to sell my hair instead. Hair grows back, but I can’t get back the time I would lose on my thesis,” Maryam, a 27-year-old master’s student, told the Iranian outlet Fararu.

Customers shopping for vegetables in Tajrish Bazaar, a traditional market in Tehran on October 7. Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images

Millions of young Iranians are focused on getting by rather than planning for the future.

Earlier this month, the official media outlet ILNA, which has been outspoken in reporting hardships among Iranians, said that poverty was at “unprecedented levels, leaving unemployed people, seasonal workers, single mothers, low-wage earners, and even skilled workers, nurses and teachers struggling to afford basic necessities.”

It also pointed to rising school dropout rates, giving some of tomorrow’s prospective parents even less chance of affording a family.

World.title: Two charged after break-in at country home of Prince William and wife Kate, UK police say
World.content:
Reuters/CNN — Two men were charged on Wednesday in connection with burglary and trespass after a break-in at the country residence of Britain’s Two men were charged on Wednesday in connection with burglary and trespass after a break-in at the country residence of Britain’s Prince William and his wife Kate, British police said.

Norfolk Constabulary said police were called on Monday night following a report of suspicious activity at a property on the royal family’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England. The property was unoccupied at the time, police added.

“Mirgen Doku aged 34, of Courtfield Gardens, London and Arilen Ndoci, of no fixed address, aged 32 have since both been charged,” Norfolk Constabulary said in a statement Wednesday, adding the charges included “entering a dwelling with intent to steal,” and “trespassing on a protected site.”

The pair were expected to appear at Norwich Magistrates’ Court later Wednesday.

The Sun newspaper first reported that police were investigating a break-in at Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house which the late Queen Elizabeth II gave William and Kate as a wedding present in 2011.

Although they use the country retreat for holidays and short breaks, their main home is on the Windsor Castle estate to the west of London.

A spokesperson for William said they did not comment on security matters.

Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales arrive at the BAFTA Film Awards 2026 at the Royal Festival Hall in London on February 22. Jaimi Joy/WPA/Getty Images

The news of the attempted break-in came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader’s office, 10 Downing Street, on Tuesday.

While the British royals often mingle with political leaders and government ministers at formal occasions, visits to Downing Street, the official residence of British leaders since 1735, are more infrequent.

The late Queen dined with Winston Churchill at “Number 10” in 1955 on the eve of his resignation and became the first monarch for possibly 200 years to attend a Cabinet meeting there in 2012 during her Diamond Jubilee year.

As heir, King Charles also made a number of trips to Downing Street to attend meetings and see how the government functioned, while William’s late mother Diana, Princess of Wales also visited almost exactly 37 years ago in 1989.

World.title: Liberia: City Builders and Royal Grand Hotel Founder, Philanthropist and Former WLCU President Ezzat Eid Dies
World.content:
Monrovia – Ezzat N. Eid, one of Liberia’s best-known Lebanese businessmen, has died. He arrived in Liberia in 1968 and built a group of companies spanning construction materials, real estate, manufacturing and hospitality. Over more than five decades he became a fixture of Liberia’s business community and a major donor to health, education and community causes. His family announced that he died on November 25, 2026. He will be buried in Lebanon.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Monrovia – Ezzat N. Eid, a businessman and philanthropist whose companies became household names in Monrovia, died on Tuesday, November 25, 2026, his family announced.



In a message to “our dear friends in Liberia,” the family said: “When Ezzat arrived in Liberia in 1968, he began building a life that would shape our whole family. Liberia became his home.”

Five Decades in Liberia

Eid first came to Liberia on January 26, 1968 and has remained in Liberia since then, through the country’s years of upheaval, according to a 2020 statement on his behalf. He began private entrepreneurship in Liberia in 1976 when he established Capital Electrical Company at Buzzi Quarters.

From there he built a diversified group. The same statement listed his interests as including importation and sale of construction materials, equipment and furniture (City Builders Inc.); real property development and management (“Realty Management Corporation”); hospitality, as well as the import and sale of Chinese-made vehicles through Tayo Motors Liberia.



His companies also included City Builders, International Aluminium Factory, Royal Grand Hotel, and Medina Rock. City Builders, based on Bushrod Island, became one of the country’s best-known building materials dealers.

The Royal Grand

His most visible investment was the Royal Grand Hotel on Tubman Boulevard in Sinkor. Eid originally built the structure as an apartment building in 1987; but decided to lease it to a Spanish businesswoman who remodeled it into hotel rooms. In 2002, Mr. Eid repossessed the building and continued running it as a hotel before building the new Royal Grand.

At the dedication of the new hotel, he explained why he kept investing. “I keep investing in this country because I consider Liberia my home,” he said, noting that he has a third generation of children here.

At that ceremony, President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf expressed appreciation to the Chairman of Royal Grand Hotel, Mr. Ezzat Eid, for the multi-million investment made in Liberia. Eid used the occasion to push for policy change. He appealed to the Government to consider the enactment of laws to grant permanent residence to all aliens who have resided in Liberia for long periods, and urged Liberians to consider using the value of their real property to acquire equity interest and participate in business ventures with foreign investors who cannot, under existing laws, own land in Liberia.

Voice of the Lebanese Community

Eid served as President of the World Lebanese Cultural Union (WLCU) in Liberia, the umbrella body of the Lebanese community. In May 2016, he led a WLCU delegation to President Sirleaf and presented a check in the amount of US$100,000 to Tubman University as WLCU contribution in support of on-going projects of the University. He told the government that the Community stands ready to support projects earmarked by the Government of Liberia once called upon.

Philanthropy

Through the Ezzat Eid Charity Foundation, led by his son Marwan, Eid supported health and education projects. During the Ebola outbreak in Liberia, the Ezzat Eid Charity Foundation made several donations and contributions to the fight against the deadly virus. More than 200 employees of his companies once volunteered to clean the grounds of the John F. Kennedy Medical Center at the request of its leadership, and the foundation donated chairs to a public school in Marshall, Margibi County.

He also backed Liberian entrepreneurs. The Liberia Chamber of Commerce and the Ezzat N. Eid Foundation in an effort to support local Liberian business held a fundraising event and pitch contest for 23 Liberian owned businesses in Monrovia, aimed at helping them reach the U.S. market.

Two Homes

His family said Liberia was where “he built his career in business, made dear friends, and gave back through his humanitarian work.” In Lebanon, he also served as mayor of his hometown, Bchamoun. “Both places were dear to him,” the family wrote, “and so were the people who made them home.”

Survivors

He is survived by his wife, Houda Eid; his children Marwan, Omar, Faris and Helen; his son-in-law, Wael S. Hariz; and his grandchildren Shams, Rayan, Nour, Jude, Sara, Adam, Kyce, Reef and Mars.

The funeral will take place in Lebanon. The family said details of a memorial gathering in Liberia will be announced later.

World.title: Liberia: McCARTHY HITS BACK: Ex-Deputy Mines Minister Disputes Sirleaf’s ‘Fired’ Claim as US$5.7B Bea Mountain Deal Heads for Signing
World.content:
Former President Calls for Independent AfDB Review; McCarthy Says He “Honorably Resigned”

By Rodney D Sieh

Monrovia – Walter McCarthy, a former Deputy Minister for Administration at the Ministry of Lands, Mines and Energy, has disputed former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf’s claim that he was fired from government. He says he resigned honorably at the end of her first term.



McCarthy’s response comes hours before the government is due to sign the US$5.7 billion Master Infrastructure Development Agreement (MIDA) with Bea Mountain Mining Corporation (BMMC) today, Wednesday, November 25, 2026. McCarthy is credited with a role in putting the deal together.

On ELBC Radio on Tuesday, Sirleaf said she had personally advised President Joseph Boakai to bring in an independent technical team from the African Development Bank to review the agreement before Liberia commits to it. She warned: “People should be careful with that Walter McCarthy; he was working for the Ministry of Mines and was fired.”

‘Differences in Recollection’

In a statement issued Wednesday, McCarthy said his memory of how he left government “differs from the account recently shared.” He said that after he resigned he set up a private consultancy and stayed active in Liberia’s mining and infrastructure sectors.



He was careful in tone. He said he holds the former President “in high esteem” and was privileged to serve under her. He added that “there may be differences in recollection given the passage of time,” and said his clarification was not meant to “challenge or diminish the stature” of Sirleaf.

McCarthy urged the public to focus on what the agreement offers. According to his statement, the MIDA covers:

• 10 billion cubic meters of reservoir capacity • 270 megawatts of power generation from four plants • More than 300 kilometers of transmission lines • Roads, bridges and highways • Upgrades to electrical substations

He said he hopes “any differences in recollection will not overshadow the collective aspiration of advancing Liberia’s economic and infrastructural development.”

Sirleaf: ‘It Has to Be Paid Back’

Sirleaf’s main concern is debt. She said Bea Mountain is already mining gold and, as she understands it, pays about US$175 million a year into the government’s central account. Liberia could lose that revenue, she said, because the US$5.7 billion has to be repaid through mineral extraction.

“US$5.7 billion is a lot of money,” she said. “We had to pay US$5 billion debt. … If something goes wrong because someone is not giving the president the right information, it keeps the country down.”

She said people “who are supporting Liberia and who love Liberia” have contacted her with worries about the deal. She said she has called the President and asked for one thing: an independent assessment.

“We want more roads; we want more lights, but we have to be careful,” Sirleaf said. “This one is from the company, and they are taking charge of the whole thing. … When you are dealing with these companies, there should be no missing pieces.”

“That’s all people are asking for,” she added. “I don’t think that’s too big to say, let’s check it; let’s get independent technical people to look at it to make sure that it’s the right thing.”

Sirleaf’s reference to “US$5 billion debt” points to the roughly US$4.9 billion in external debt that Liberia had cleared under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative in 2010, while she was President.

As of press time, the Executive Mansion had not said whether President Boakai will order an independent review or delay the signing.

World.title: LPRA to Launch Five-Year Strategic Plan to Strengthen Liberia’s Petroleum Sector
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia – The Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority (LPRA) is set to launch its Five-Year Strategic Plan on Thursday, November 26, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. at the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf (EJS) Ministerial Complex in Congo Town, Monrovia.

The launch, being held under the theme “Regulating the Frontier for Lasting National Value,” marks a significant milestone in the Authority’s institutional development and Liberia’s efforts to position its upstream petroleum sector as a competitive, transparent, and attractive destination for responsible investment.

Established by an Act of the National Legislature to separate the regulatory and commercial functions of Liberia’s petroleum sector, the LPRA operates as an independent regulatory institution mandated to regulate, license, and oversee upstream petroleum activities in the country.



The five-year plan outlines a strategic framework for strengthening regulatory effectiveness, building institutional capacity, attracting credible investors, advancing petroleum exploration, and promoting strategic partnerships and stakeholder engagement.

Through its Board of Directors, experienced professional workforce, and collaboration with national and international partners, the Authority aims to establish a modern, responsive, and internationally credible regulatory institution capable of meeting the evolving demands of the global petroleum industry.

The launch is expected to bring together government officials, industry representatives, development partners, and other key stakeholders, underscoring the importance of collective commitment to the responsible management and development of Liberia’s petroleum resources.

The LPRA says the strategic plan reinforces its commitment to ensuring that the exploration and development of the country’s petroleum resources generate sustainable economic and social benefits for the Liberian people, both present and future generations.



The Authority views the plan as a roadmap for strengthening petroleum governance, promoting responsible investment, and ensuring that Liberia’s upstream petroleum sector contributes meaningfully to long-term national development.

World.title: Liberia Issues Revised AML/CFT Regulations to Strengthen Fight Against Financial Crimes
World.content:
The Government of the Republic of Liberia has announced the issuance of revised regulations to strengthen the country’s fight against money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing.

The Gazette, Vol. XXVI, No. 39, dated Tuesday, August 11, 2026, the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) and the Financial Intelligence Agency (FIA) jointly formulated and issued Regulation No. CBL/FIA/AML/CFT/001/2026.

The regulation is titled: Anti-Money Laundering, Counter-Terrorist Financing, Counter-Proliferation Financing, Preventive Measures, and Proceeds of Crime Regulations, 2026.



The regulations were issued pursuant to the statutory powers and functions of the FIA under the Anti-Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing, Preventive Measures, and Proceeds of Crime Act, 2021, the Financial Intelligence Agency Act, 2021. Also, the joint regulation considers the Amendment and Restatement of the Act Establishing the Central Bank of Liberia, and other applicable laws.

This Regulation implements preventive measures requirements which are mandatory for financial institutions as defined by Section 15.3 of the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Act of 2021. It designates the National AML/CFT Ministerial Committee (IMC) as the central coordinating body for the formulation of national AML/CFT policies and strategies necessary to achieve the objectives of Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism and combating the Financing of the Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction.

Moreover, the joint regulation provides for the creation and implementation of internal controls and other procedures to deter criminals from using its facilities for money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing (ML/TF/PF).

Also, it adopts a risk-based approach in the identification, assessment, and management of their ML/TF/PF risks in line with the requirements of these regulations.



Accordingly, it provides for compliance without delay with requests made pursuant to current AML/CFT/CPF legislation and provides information to the Central Bank of Liberia, Financial Intelligence Agency of Liberia, and other competent authorities.

Additionally, it ensures their employees, agents, and others doing business with them clearly understand the AML/CFT/CPF program, and conduct ongoing Due Diligence and, where appropriate, Enhanced Due Diligence on all business relationships, and shall obtain information on the purpose and intended nature of the business relationships of their potential customers.

Meanwhile, the revised Regulation repeals and replaces the previous CBL AML/CFT Regulations No. CBL/RSD/002/2017.

Under the revised framework, financial institutions are required to adopt and fully implement effective internal AML/CFT/CPF control policies and procedures applicable to all customers, products, services, business lines, branches, and subsidiaries.

The revised regulations are expected to enhance Liberia’s compliance with international standards and strengthen preventive measures against financial crimes, coupled with filling regulatory parameters and international compliance requirements.

In another development, the Government of the Republic of Liberia has announced new regulations to strengthen anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing measures in the country’s real estate sector.

The Gazette, Vol. XXVI, No. 38, dated Tuesday, August 11, 2026, the Financial Intelligence Agency of Liberia (FIA) and the Liberia Land Authority jointly issued and published Regulation No. FIA/LLA/RES/001/2026 concerning AML/CFT Regulations for Real Estate Institutions in Liberia.

The regulations were issued by the FIA pursuant to its mandate and authority under the Financial Intelligence Agency of Liberia Act of 2021, specifically Section 67.3 (12), which empowers it to issue regulations, and Sections 15.2 and 15.3 of the Anti-Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing, Preventive Measures, and Proceeds of Crime Act of 2021.

The objective of this regulation is to implement Liberia’s laws and its international obligations pertaining to Anti-Money Laundering and combating the financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT), and specifically as it relates to the implementation of internal control requirements by the Real Estate Sector (RES), to enhance systems to prevent and detect money laundering and terrorist financing, as well as enhance financial integrity of the real estate sector against money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing.

This regulation shall apply to all classes of real estate institutions and professionals (real estate agents, brokers, appraisals, property managers, real estate investors, title agents/closers, mortgage, mortgage brokers/lenders, etc.) to adopt and fully implement effective internal AML/CFT control policies and procedures applicable to all customers, products, services, business lines, branches, and subsidiaries as defined by the FIA Act of 2021 and AML/CFT Act of 2021.

The publication was made by order of the President, through the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mme. Sara Beysolow Nyanti.

The new regulations are expected to enhance transparency and accountability in real estate transactions and strengthen Liberia’s efforts to prevent the sector from being used for money laundering and terrorist financing.

World.title: Liberia: Promise of Power and Roads Collides With Warnings of Hidden Debt as Bea Mountain Deal Heads for Signing, Legislative Debate
World.content:
Monrovia- Every dry season, Monrovia goes through the same routine. River levels on the St. Paul fall, the turbines at Mount Coffee slow down, and the lights flicker and go out across the capital. Generators start up in businesses, hospitals and homes. Liberians have lived with this for so long that many now treat it as normal.

By Rodney D Sieh

On Wednesday, President Joseph Nyuma Boakai is due to sign a deal his government says will change that. The Master Infrastructure Development Agreement (MIDA) with Bea Mountain Mining Corporation (BMMC) is valued at about US$5.7 billion. The President received the agreement from the Inter-Ministerial Concession Committee. After he signs it, the Legislature must ratify it.



Within days of the announcement, the deal had become one of the most hotly debated documents in the country. Churchmen, analysts, opposition figures and columnists have warned that Liberia may be signing away its future gold income on terms that heavily favor the company. The government calls it a once-in-a-generation opportunity.

Both sides could be right. This is what the deal promises, what its critics fear, and what lawmakers need to settle before they vote.

THE PROMISE

The power shortage the deal targets is real. Liberia’s installed capacity was about 126 MW in 2024, while officials put national demand at roughly 400 MW. MIDA’s 270 MW would more than double current capacity. Only about a third of Liberians had electricity in 2023, according to World Bank data, and rural access was below 10 percent.



Under the plan, the 270 MW would come from four plants: a 100 MW hydropower plant on the Via River, a 100 MW plant at SP3 on the St. Paul River, a 10 MW plant at SP4 further along the St. Paul, and a 60 MW biomass plant near the Via dam. The reservoirs are central to the design. Three of them, with combined storage of 10 billion cubic meters, would hold high-flow water and release it through the turbines when river flows fall. That is the government’s answer to the dry-season blackouts.

The package also includes US$230 million to upgrade substations, transformers and transmission lines on the national grid, along with the 146 km Liberia Development Road linking the power plants to key facilities.

The government’s pitch rests on how the deal will be paid for. Instead of new loans, it plans to ring-fence additional revenue payable by BMMC, made possible by high gold prices. BMMC is also pledging US$500 million in bridge financing and will keep making its regular payments to the Consolidated Account. Officials call this “innovative financing” that would reduce Liberia’s debt burden. The government statement goes further, describing the deal as “the single most transformative catalyst for the nation’s development in decades.”

The schedule is ambitious. The full program is meant to take five years, with the biomass plant and transmission lines targeted within two years.

THE PRICE

Critics are not arguing about whether Liberia needs power. They are asking what the country will pay for it, and who will decide.

The most detailed objection has come from Rev. Dr. Samuel B. Reeves, Jr., President of the Liberia Council of Churches. He is urging the Legislature not to ratify the current version of the agreement. He says the copy he reviewed is missing key documents: the Annex C payment milestones, the Annex E technical specifications and the EPC contracts. Without them, he argues, no one can independently assess pricing and delivery.

His figures suggest the bill may be larger than the headline number. The eight primary projects have a base cost of US$4.4513 billion, rising to about US$5.6813 billion with additional roads and grid work. A further project ceiling of about US$2.23 billion could apply, and he says the draft sets no all-in ceiling.

The repayment mechanism worries him most. BMMC could offset its corporate income tax, royalties, withholding taxes, the dividends on Liberia’s 5% stake and its employees’ PAY against project costs. He warns that the Treasury might receive no guaranteed cash.

Independent analyst George K. Fahnbulleh reaches a similar conclusion in a briefing note to officials. He calls the arrangement “undisclosed public debt” repaid outside the Public Financial Management Act and the national debt sustainability analysis. By his estimate, the three dams would cost US$3.88 billion for 210 MW, about US$18.5 million per megawatt. He compares that with roughly US$3.1 million per megawatt for Guinea’s Souapiti dam. He projects interest of about US$282 million a year once the works are built, against total BMMC payments to government of about US$33.5 million in 2023. If the offsets cannot keep up with the interest, he warns, the balance could grow indefinitely and pass to future governments.

Reeves singles out the smallest dam. SP-4 is priced at US$634.44 million for 10 MW, or about US$63.4 million per megawatt. He concedes that reservoir and water-transfer works mean this alone does not prove overpricing, but says it warrants independent review.

Both men raise concerns about how the contract was awarded. The draft exempts the contractor and EPC contracts from public procurement law, and MAPA is the exclusive initial contractor. The Auditor General can inspect payment certificates but not actual costs. Liability is capped at 10% of the contract price, and there is no performance bond.

Writing in The New Dawn, columnist Seltue Robert Karweaye Sr. puts the central question bluntly. He argues that if the deal is financed from Liberia’s own future gold revenues rather than new foreign capital, it is a commitment of public money, not a generous investment. He also notes that Bea Mountain is a mining company, not an infrastructure developer, and asks whether there was any competitive bidding.

The political reaction has been harsher. Commentator Martin Kollie has urged President Boakai to abandon the deal. Emmanuel C.D. Gonquoi of the Economic Freedom Fighters of Liberia called it “daylight corporate robbery” under the guise of development.

THE TRACK RECORD

Much of the skepticism comes from Bea Mountain’s history in Grand Cape Mount.

Critics point to the gap between what the mine produces and what the state collects. According to the 16th EITI report, BMMC exported about 12,146 kilograms of gold worth over US$653 million in fiscal year 2023. Both Grand Cape Mount senators have demanded renegotiation of the existing mineral agreement. Sen. Dabah Varpilah describes the flat 3% royalty as inadequate and inequitable as gold values climb.

Questions over taxes are also still open. In October, a preliminary review by Sen. Amara Konneh found that Bea Mountain lifted 16.4 million gallons of diesel over nine months without paying levies. The company claims a duty-free exemption, and final liability is unconfirmed. A House joint committee is reviewing three years of its corporate income tax payments.

Environmental and community grievances add to the pressure. A May 2022 cyanide spill from the tailings facility was linked to fish deaths near Jikandor, Marvoe Creek and the Mafa River. The EPA says corrective measures, including tailings dam reinforcement, have since been implemented. In July 2025, residents of Ngojah Town petitioned the Supreme Court over alleged illegal land seizure and contamination. These remain allegations, not court findings.

That record bears directly on MIDA, because the new deal would flood large areas for reservoirs. Reeves notes that Annex A covers at least 446.42 square kilometers, while only US$50 million is set aside for compensation.

The company also has supporters on the ground. Residents of the Matamo Corridor in Grand Cape Mount recently commended BMMC for its development initiatives. Their statement cited education, youth empowerment, healthcare and jobs.

WHAT NOBODY HAS ANSWERED

Several basic questions remain unanswered. The government statement does not say how much extra revenue is involved or how it differs from the company’s existing obligations. Nor does it say how the new plants would fit with the planned 150 MW SP2 dam, which the World Bank Group pledged US$300 million toward in 2023. The price Liberians will pay for the electricity has not been disclosed, and lawmakers will want to know what happens to the financing if gold prices fall.

BMMC has not publicly answered the specific charges raised by Reeves, Fahnbulleh or others.

A MIDDLE ROAD

Almost none of the deal’s critics are saying Liberia should walk away from building power plants and roads. What they reject is the agreement in its current form.

Their proposals have a lot in common. Reeves wants five conditions met before ratification: publish the full deal and independently verify its prices; cap total exposure and guarantee minimum cash payments to the Treasury; tie payments to certified, usable infrastructure; give the Auditor General full access to cost records; and make community and jobs commitments binding.

Fahnbulleh suggests splitting the program. A small, fully specified first phase covering biomass, transmission and a road would go ahead on corrected terms. Each dam would need its own feasibility study, an open tender with development-bank financing, and a separate ratification vote. In his framing, the MIDA would become “the benchmark to beat” rather than the only option.

Splitting the program could keep the projects that would deliver early benefits, such as the biomass plant and the transmission lines the government already wants within two years, while giving the far more expensive dams the scrutiny they need.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Timing matters. Fahnbulleh warns that once the agreement is ratified, its terms would be protected by Article 25 of the Constitution and the deal’s stabilization clause, so any problems have to be fixed before then.

Liberia needs the power and the roads. Higher gold prices have given it real bargaining power. The question for lawmakers is whether this agreement makes the most of that moment for Liberians, or ties up decades of the country’s gold income on terms few people have been able to read in full.

World.title: Liberia Ratifies Four Intellectual Property Treaties as Senate Concurs with House
World.content:
–As legislative actions advance Liberia’s efforts to build a robust intellectual property ecosystem and support economic transformation

The Liberian Senate has concurred with the House of Representatives to ratify four regional and international intellectual property (IP) treaties, marking a significant step toward strengthening the country’s legal framework for protecting innovation, creativity, agricultural development and traditional knowledge.

The four instruments are the African Regional Intellectual Property Organization (ARIPO) Kampala Protocol on Voluntary Registration of Copyright and Related Rights; the ARIPO Arusha Protocol for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants; the International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV Convention); and the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge.



The Senate’s decision follows the House’s earlier approval of the instruments, which formed part of eight IP treaties and protocols submitted by His Excellency Joseph Nyumah Boakai, Sr., to the 55th Legislature for ratification.

The remaining four instruments, including the UNESCO 2003 Convention on Intangible Cultural Heritage, the 2005 Convention on the Diversity of Cultural Expressions, the WIPO Copyright Treaty and the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty, are expected to receive legislative consideration in the coming months.

The development aligns with President Boakai’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development, particularly Pillar One, Economic Transformation, which prioritizes building a robust national intellectual property ecosystem.

Welcoming the legislative actions, the Director General of the Liberia Intellectual Property Office (LIPO), Hon. Garmai Koboi, described the concurrence as an important advancement in Liberia’s efforts to position intellectual property as an instrument of economic development. According to Hon. Koboi, these instruments will provide additional legal frameworks to help unlock the economic value of Liberia’s agricultural resources, creative industries, indigenous knowledge and innovations.



“These agreements represent an important investment in Liberia’s economic future. They provide opportunities to strengthen the protection of creative works, encourage the development of improved plant varieties, safeguard knowledge associated with our genetic resources and create a more predictable environment for innovation and investment,” Hon. Koboi noted.

Hon. Koboi further noted that, for Liberia, this means building a system in which its creators, researchers, farmers, entrepreneurs and businesses can better protect, develop and derive economic value from their intellectual contributions and resources.

The legislative action, according to LIPO, brings Liberia closer to an internationally aligned intellectual property system capable of supporting innovation, strengthening economic competitiveness and expanding opportunities for sustainable development.

Meanwhile, LIPO also expressed its appreciation to President Boakai, Sr., for his leadership and to the Honorable Members of the House of Representatives and the Liberian Senate for their support in advancing the ratification of the four intellectual property instruments.

World.title: Liberia: Sheriff Fights Personal Prosecution as LACC Defends Gbarpolu Yellow Machines Indictment
World.content:
GBARPOLU COUNTY – The legal battle surrounding the controversial procurement of earth-moving equipment for Gbarpolu County has intensified, with Omaru Sheriff, General Manager of City Lion Incorporated, seeking to have his name removed from an amended corruption indictment in his individual capacity.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Sheriff’s attempt to separate himself from the criminal proceedings, however, is facing opposition from the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission (LACC), which argues that his position as head of the company does not shield him from personal criminal liability for transactions prosecutors allege facilitated tax evasion and the misuse of public resources.



The dispute unfolded Monday, November 23, at the 16th Judicial Circuit Court in Gbarpolu County, where Sheriffs’s legal team argued that City Lion Incorporated, rather than its general manager personally, should answer for alleged contractual violations arising from the procurement of the county’s yellow machines.

The defense, in a motion filed November 20, maintained that City Lion is a legally incorporated entity with a separate legal personality and should therefore bear responsibility for transactions conducted in its corporate capacity.

But the LACC, represented by Cllr. Jimmy Saah Bombo of the Central Law Offices, rejected the argument, insisting that the allegations against Sheriff go beyond his position as a corporate officer and include conduct allegedly undertaken in his personal capacity.

The court has reserved ruling on the motion until Wednesday, November 26, leaving Sheriff facing the possibility of remaining an individual defendant alongside City Lion and several current and former county officials.



Sheriff Invokes Corporate Legal Protection

In his motion, Sheriff argued that City Lion Incorporated was the contracting party in the transactions under investigation and should therefore be held responsible for any alleged contractual breaches.

The defense cited paragraph nine of the amended indictment, which states that on October 30, 2023, Gbarpolu County entered into three separate sales contracts with City Lion, represented by Sheriff, for the procurement of one bulldozer, one excavator and one motor grader equipped with a ripper.

Paragraph 11 of the indictment further identifies three payments totaling LRD80,750,000 made to City Lion for the equipment.

According to the defense, the payments were made to the corporation, not Sheriff personally. It also argued that the indictment acknowledges the existence of the machinery at the Freeport of Monrovia following information supplied by the vendor.

Sheriff’s lawyer, Cllr. T. Sensee Sewah, contended that the prosecution had failed to sufficiently distinguish between alleged corporate contractual defaults and criminal conduct personally attributable to his client.

To support the argument, the defense relied on Section 2.5 of Liberia’s Associations Law, which recognizes the separate legal personality of incorporated entities and their capacity to sue and be sued in their own names.

The defense also cited Section 14.3 of the Criminal Procedure Law, arguing that an indictment must contain a clear and definite statement of the essential facts constituting the alleged offenses.

Citing John K. Perkins v. Republic of Liberia, 23 LLR 352 (1974), the defense maintained that identifying Sheriff as a corporate officer and associating him with the transactions does not, by itself, establish individual criminal responsibility.

The motion therefore requested that Sheriff be removed from the amended indictment as an individual defendant while allowing the prosecution against City Lion Incorporated to continue.

LACC Rejects Sheriff’s Argument

Opposing the motion, Cllr. Bombo argued that the defense was attempting to revisit an issue the court had already considered and decided.

He invoked the doctrines of res judicata and collateral estoppel, arguing that Sheriff had previously filed a similar application seeking to be removed from the proceedings and that the court rejected it.

According to Bombo, entertaining another motion seeking substantially the same relief could undermine the court’s earlier decision.

The prosecution also challenged the defense’s reliance on misjoinder, arguing that the doctrine, as presented by the defense, applies to civil proceedings and cannot be used in the manner proposed to remove an accused person from a criminal indictment.

More importantly, Bombo argued that City Lion’s separate incorporation does not automatically absolve its general manager of criminal responsibility for actions he allegedly undertook personally.

He specifically cited an alleged US$6,400 payment involving Sheriff and Gbarpolu County Superintendent Sam K. Zinnah.

According to the prosecution, the alleged transaction was not simply a payment made by City Lion as a corporate entity. Bombo argued that Sheriff personally made the payment in connection with the inclusion of two additional earth-moving machines beyond the three covered by the county’s duty-free arrangement.

The LACC contends that the alleged payment could expose Sheriff to individual criminal liability if the prosecution establishes that it was intended to facilitate the avoidance of legitimate government revenue.

The allegations have not been established in court and remain subject to proof at trial.

Five Machines, Three Contracts and the US$6,400 Question

Beyond the legal arguments, the proceedings have brought renewed attention to questions surrounding the number of machines involved in the procurement arrangement and the handling of their customs clearance.

The amended indictment identifies three machines covered by the October 30, 2023 contracts: a bulldozer, an excavator and a motor grader with a ripper.

However, the controversy also involves references to five earth-moving machines, raising questions about the additional two machines and whether they were properly covered by the duty-free privileges granted for the county’s equipment.

In a submission to the LACC, Superintendent Zinnah provided an account of how the machinery reportedly became entangled in port charges, customs clearance and an auction process at the Freeport of Monrovia.

According to his submission, the three machines procured for the county arrived at the port on May 6 and May 23, 2024.

Zinnah alleged that City Lion failed to clear the equipment within the required period, resulting in the machines remaining at the port for more than 90 days and eventually being declared abandoned.

The National Port Authority reportedly issued a public auction notice on October 22, 2024, as part of the process involving the equipment.

In a letter dated October 5, 2024, City Lion reportedly informed the county that the NPA had agreed to release the three machines in the county’s favor.

Zinnah’s account further stated that the county eventually took possession of the three machines after they were offloaded and assembled at the port.

However, the clearance process remains central to the LACC’s allegations.

The prosecution contends that the additional two machines were not covered by the duty-free privileges granted for the three machines intended for Gbarpolu County.

Bombo argued that the alleged US$6,400 payment involving Sheriff and the Superintendent was connected to the handling of those additional machines and could have facilitated the avoidance of customs duties.

In his submission, Zinnah said Brown’s Trucking Handling Services Enterprise was engaged to offload, assemble and load the machines onto transport vehicles at a cost of US$7,500.

He alleged that City Lion paid US$6,400 in two installments: US$2,500 to Randall Clarence and US$3,900 to Lucia Massaquoi.

The submission further stated that the company failed to pay the remaining US$1,100, which Zinnah claimed he personally paid to the service provider.

However, Bombo presented a separate allegation to the court, arguing that the LACC considers the alleged US$6,400 payment involving Sheriff and the Superintendent a critical component of its case.

The prosecution maintains that the money was allegedly paid directly to the Superintendent rather than to the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA), potentially depriving the government of legitimate tax revenue.

The circumstances surrounding the payment, including its purpose, recipients and connection to the additional machinery, will require proof during the proceedings.

Duty-Free Documents Under Scrutiny

Questions have also emerged about the documentation used to secure duty-free privileges for the equipment.

In his submission to the LACC, Zinnah alleged that an approved duty-free letter from the Ministry of Internal Affairs contained inaccurate information, including the inclusion of two additional machines on the bill of lading.

He questioned whether the additional machinery was improperly included in the documentation to avoid payment of government taxes.

The submission also raised questions about City Lion’s subsequent position concerning customs duties and whether the relevant documents were consistent with claims that duties had been paid.

Communications involving City Lion’s clearing broker, Amadu S. Mulbah, were also referenced.

In a communication dated November 22, 2024, Mulbah reportedly raised concerns about the handling of the machinery and the county’s involvement in the clearance process.

These issues have placed the transactions involving City Lion, the county administration, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the National Port Authority and the Liberia Revenue Authority under scrutiny.

At the center of the investigation is whether the duty-free privileges were properly obtained and applied, whether additional machinery was improperly included in the documentation and whether individuals involved in the transactions facilitated the alleged loss of government revenue.

Six Defendants Face Multiple Charges

Sheriff is among six defendants named in the amended indictment.

They include current Gbarpolu County Superintendent Sam K. Zinnah; former Superintendent J. Keyah Saah; former Fiscal Superintendent Anthony Yorkor; former Chairperson of the Gbarpolu Project Management Committee Robert Benda; Sheriff; and City Lion Incorporated as a corporate defendant.

The charges include economic sabotage, fraud against the Internal Revenue of Liberia, misuse of public money, property or records, theft or illegal disbursement and expenditure of public money, illegal compensation for assistance in government matters, theft of property, criminal facilitation, criminal conspiracy, violations of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission and Public Financial Management laws, criminal solicitation and tax evasion.

The charges place both public officials and a private contractor under scrutiny over the procurement, financing, clearance and delivery of the county’s earth-moving equipment.

For the prosecution, the case is not limited to whether City Lion fulfilled its contractual obligations. It also concerns whether individuals involved in the transactions allegedly facilitated the misuse of public resources or deprived the government of legitimate revenue.

The LACC will ultimately have to establish the specific conduct and responsibilities of each defendant through evidence rather than rely solely on their official positions or association with the procurement arrangement.

Court Decision Pending

Following arguments from both sides, Judge Zuballah A. Kizeku reserved ruling on Sheriff’s motion until Wednesday, November 26, according to the proceedings.

The decision will determine whether Sheriff remains personally listed as a defendant alongside City Lion Incorporated or whether the court grants his request to remove him in his individual capacity.

Even if the court grants the motion, questions surrounding the alleged US$6,400 transaction, the duty-free documentation and the handling of the machinery would remain relevant to the broader proceedings against the other defendants and the corporate entity.

For Gbarpolu residents, the controversy extends beyond Sheriff’s attempt to separate himself from the indictment. It raises broader questions about the management of public funds, the protection of government revenue and the accountability of public officials and private contractors involved in public procurement.

Ultimately, the case will test the distinction between corporate responsibility and individual criminal liability, while placing the procurement and handling of the county’s yellow machines under judicial scrutiny.

World.title: Liberia: Green Guard Eco Solutions Earns Waste Collectors’ Praise for Improving Efficiency and Transforming Waste Management Operations
World.content:
Montserrado County– A Liberian waste management company, Green Guard Eco Solutions, is receiving commendation from independent waste collectors for improving waste disposal operations at its facility outside Dixville, with operators reporting reduced waiting times, faster offloading of garbage and increased opportunities to expand their businesses.

By Jaheim T. [email protected]

The improvements are providing relief to waste collection companies that previously struggled with long queues and accumulated garbage at the Stockton Creek disposal facility, sometimes spending several hours and, on some occasions, an entire day waiting to dispose of waste collected from households and businesses.



For operators whose businesses depend on regular waste collection and disposal, the improved efficiency is translating into more working hours, additional collection trips and the potential to serve more customers.

In interviews on Monday, November 23, 2026, Prince Freeman, Chief Driver of Zero Waste, and Dennis Cheyou, Supervisor of CleanPath Waste Solutions, praised the changes at the facility, describing the current operations as an improvement over the delays they previously experienced.

Freeman said he has witnessed a noticeable difference in the pace of waste disposal, explaining that the situation was previously challenging for independent collectors who had to wait for extended periods before they could offload their garbage.

“Everywhere was a lot of dirt. It used to take us some time. We would sit out there for about two to three hours waiting. Sometimes, it takes us the whole day because we cannot leave without dumping the dirt,” Freeman said.



According to him, the delays affected the ability of waste collectors to return to their assigned communities and continue collecting garbage from customers.

However, he said operations have improved, allowing drivers to dispose of waste more quickly and make additional trips.

“But now we are dumping the dirt with speed. We are speeding with our work, and this is helping us come back fast and do more trips,” he said.

For Freeman, the improvement is not simply about spending less time at the disposal site. It also creates opportunities for waste collection businesses to increase their earnings by serving more customers.

“Now that it is clear, it means we can grow our business and bring more waste. I think my business will be growing,” he added.

He expressed hope that the management would sustain the improvements, noting that consistent performance was important to the businesses that rely on the facility.

Freeman said he was encouraged by the changes but hoped the company would maintain its current pace of operations instead of allowing the facility to return to the conditions that previously caused delays.

He also emphasized the importance of time in the waste collection business, explaining that customers depend on collectors to remove household waste regularly.

A similar endorsement came from Dennis Cheyou, Supervisor of CleanPath Waste Solutions, who also commended the improvements at the disposal facility.

Cheyou said he was pleased with the efforts being made by the municipal authorities and the company managing the facility. “I would highly applaud them because they are trying their best,” he said.

CleanPath Waste Solutions operates directly within communities, collecting household waste from residents and transporting it to the disposal facility.

Cheyou’s comments reflect the importance of efficient disposal services to independent waste collection operators, whose daily operations depend on the ability to transport and offload garbage without unnecessary delays.

The commendations from the two operators provide an indication of how improvements at the disposal facility can benefit businesses beyond the company responsible for managing it.

When waste collectors spend less time waiting to dispose of garbage, they can return to communities sooner, complete additional trips and attend to more customers.

A Liberian Company’s Broader Environmental Ambition

The improvements in waste disposal operations form part of the broader ambitions of Green Guard Eco Solutions, a Liberian company seeking to transform the country’s waste management sector through investments in environmental protection, renewable energy and resource recovery.

In an earlier report published in January 2026, Green Guard outlined its ambition to position Liberia as a regional hub for waste-to-energy innovation, climate mitigation and sustainable livelihoods through a partnership with Philippines-based Alterna Verde Cooperation.

The partnership is designed to combine Green Guard’s local waste management operations with Alterna Verde’s technical expertise in waste processing and anaerobic digestion technology.

Green Guard broke ground on its facility outside Dixville on May 5, 2024, as part of its plan to establish an integrated waste management and resource recovery system.

The company also secured a 10-year renewable agreement with the Paynesville City Corporation (PCC), designating Green Guard as the primary entity responsible for solid waste collection. The arrangement extends beyond conventional garbage disposal to include waste-to-energy initiatives and revenue-sharing arrangements.

One of the project’s major objectives is to convert waste into cleaner energy, particularly cooking gas, as an alternative to charcoal, which remains widely used by Liberian households.

For decades, charcoal production has contributed to deforestation, while smoke from charcoal use has exposed households to harmful air pollutants associated with respiratory illnesses.

Green Guard has said its proposed clean cooking gas will be packaged in high-density polyethylene (HDPE) containers designed to make handling safer and the product more accessible and affordable.

The company has also outlined a reforestation commitment as part of its environmental compliance measures.

According to the company, it plans to plant more than 1,000 trees in an area where the applicable requirement would call for approximately 250 trees.

“Every acre you clear, you need to replant 50 trees. The place we are clearing is not more than five acres. Instead of 250, we are doing over 1,000, meaning we are doing more. We are sending more oxygen into the environment,” the company stated.

Philippines Partnership Targets Renewable Energy Production

Through its partnership with Alterna Verde Cooperation, Green Guard is pursuing a waste-to-energy model intended to transform organic waste into methane and subsequently electricity.

Alterna Verde Chief Executive Officer Dr. Nervy Santiago has described the initiative as an opportunity to apply decades of experience in anaerobic digestion technology to Liberia’s waste management challenges.

The proposed development covers approximately 30 acres and is designed around four major components.

These include a lined landfill intended to protect groundwater from contamination, an anaerobic baffled reactor (ABR) to break down organic waste and produce methane, a phytoremediation system to absorb heavy metals from contaminated liquid waste, and a power station designed to convert methane into electricity.

The project also incorporates the use of citronella and vetiver grasses as part of its environmental management strategy.

Citronella grass is expected to help absorb heavy metals from leachate, the contaminated liquid generated when water passes through waste materials.

The process could also support the production of citronella oil, a commercially valuable product with international demand.

The approach is expected to provide environmental and economic benefits by addressing waste contamination while creating opportunities for additional revenue generation.

Plans to Expand Waste Collection Beyond Montserrado

To support the proposed facility’s capacity, Green Guard has outlined plans to collect waste from several communities and cities beyond its immediate operational area.

The company’s targeted collection areas include Montserrado County, Kakata, Buchanan and Harbel, particularly Unification Town.

The expansion is expected to provide the facility with sufficient waste to support its broader waste processing and energy production ambitions.

If successfully implemented, the initiative could create opportunities in renewable energy production, environmental protection, clean cooking fuel distribution and employment across the waste management value chain.

The company’s ambition also extends to establishing Liberia as a regional player in waste-to-energy innovation, with the potential to demonstrate how waste can be converted from an environmental burden into an economic resource.

For the independent waste collectors already using the facility, however, the immediate benefits are reflected in their daily operations.

Freeman’s account of reduced waiting times and the opportunity to complete more collection trips, alongside Cheyou’s commendation of the company’s efforts, suggests that improvements in waste disposal services can have a direct impact on businesses operating within Liberia’s sanitation sector.

Their experiences also underscore the importance of maintaining efficient waste management operations as Green Guard advances its broader plans for renewable energy production, environmental sustainability and regional leadership.

World.title: ZESCO assures sufficient power supply
World.content:
ZESCO Limited has assured the nation that the country has sufficient electricity resources to sustain power supply.

The utility said the projected reduction in water allocation at Kariba Dam by the Zambezi River Authority for 2027 has been factored into its supply plans and is not expected to result in a national electricity deficit.

In a media statement issued to ZANIS by ZESCO Corporate Affairs Department, ZESCO said stability of the national power system has been sustained through increased electricity generation from thermal and solar power plants, partnerships with Independent Power Producers and participation in regional electricity markets.

The utility noted that it expects to add 135 megawatts of thermal power by December 2026, followed by an additional 300 megawatts in March 2027 and another 300 megawatts by June 2027.
