Aimée-Noël Mbiyozo, Senior Research Consultant, Migration, ISS

World.title: South Africa: SA Company Prepares to Make the Monthly Anti-HIV Pill. But Will the Govt Buy It?
World.content:
South African drug maker Aspen is preparing to manufacture alimatravir, a new monthly HIV prevention pill, before scientists have proved it works. But the government could still buy it from a cheaper supplier outside South Africa.

South African drug maker Aspen is preparing to manufacture a new monthly HIV prevention pill before scientists have proved it works. But the government could still buy it from a cheaper supplier outside South Africa.

The South African drug maker, Aspen, is preparing to manufacture a new monthly HIV prevention pill before scientists have even proved it works.

But there's a catch: the South African government may not buy the locally made pill if it can get cheaper versions from outside South Africa, for instance, from Indian manufacturers instead.

Aspen is one of seven companies licensed to make the pill, alimatravir. Four have manufacturing operations in India, where production could be less expensive.

Final study results will become available in mid-2027.

The dilemma: South Africa wants to grow its local pharmaceutical industry, but government medicine tenders often favour cheaper suppliers. Will Aspen's investment pay off?

Six months into South Africa's roll-out of lenacapavir, the injection that protects against HIV for six months , the local drug maker Aspen Pharmacare is preparing to manufacture alimatravir , a pill you'd swallow just once a month .

It's the first time the company has started preparing to make a medicine before the final trial results are in, says Aspen executive Stavros Nicolaou.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Aspen is one of seven generic manufacturers that MSD , the company developing the pill, licensed in July , to make cheaper versions for 129 low- and middle-income countries if the drug is approved.

MSD granted the generic licences before recruitment for the final-stage trials was complete, a move the company says is a first in HIV prevention .

The aim? To get the pill to people faster if it works.

But making the pill here doesn't mean the health department will buy it from Aspen. We don't yet know what any of the manufacturers would charge for this pill. But the government has a history of awarding its medicine contracts to cheaper suppliers, often from India.

That's a concern for Nicolaou, who says the government encourages local medicine manufacturing but doesn't always support it when awarding contracts, as has happened with recent HIV treatment tenders .

Meanwhile, the science is moving fast.

On 2 November, MSD, known as Merck in the US and Canada, announced that adult recruitment had been completed for two large, final-stage trials . Results could be available in the second half of 2027.

Early studies and modelling suggest that alimatravir reaches potentially protective levels in the body within about an hour of taking it. That's much faster than lenacapavir (LEN), which, according to South Africa's health department , starts protecting against HIV on day three, provided the injections and oral loading doses have been taken as prescribed.

But whether this translates into protection against infection in the case of alimatravir still needs to be confirmed in large clinical trials.

Why start making a pill that may not work?

Usually, manufacturers wait for final trial results before investing in production. But that can delay access to new medicines by months, even years, because it takes a long time to get the technology, equipment and facilities in place to make a particular medicine.

MSD wants to change that.

It's giving manufacturers technical information on how to make alimatravir — what Paul Schaper, MSD's associate vice president for global public policy, calls a "recipe book" — and helping them prepare applications for regulatory approval.

MSD learnt this approach during COVID-19, when it licensed manufacturers to prepare production of its treatment, molnupiravir , before the treatment was approved for emergency use.

If alimatravir passes its trials and receives regulatory approval, MSD plans to supply it until generic manufacturers are ready .

Schaper told Bhekisisa MSD would supply it at a no-profit price in the 129 countries, including South Africa, covered by the licences. The company hasn't announced what price that would be.

Aspen wasn't among the companies initially licensed by Gilead Sciences, the company that makes lenacapavir, to make generic LEN and has since stopped pursuing a licence .

Its caution comes partly from COVID-19. Aspen manufactured Johnson & Johnson's vaccines and secured the right to supply its own branded version , Aspenovax, across Africa. But production for Johnson & Johnson ended and no orders for Aspenovax materialised .

Nicolaou says the monthly pill is a smaller gamble and makes more sense for Aspen because tablets are easier and cheaper to make than injections. Injections need specialised equipment and extra care to keep them sterile.

"Once bitten, twice shy," Nicolaou says.

Will SA buy the locally made pill?

A published estimate puts the cost of making a generic version of alimatravir at as little as $4.49 (roughly R77) per person per year to make, including a profit margin.

But that's not the price governments would necessarily pay. And Aspen hasn't said what it would charge.

But when the national health department chooses which supplier to buy from, price is only one factor, spokesperson Foster Mohale told Bhekisisa . If South Africa's medicines regulator approves and registers alimatravir, the department would consider buying it under its usual rules. Mohale said the department gives priority to local manufacturing but also weighs affordability, how well a medicine works and whether it can be provided over the long term. That still leaves Aspen without an answer on whether making the pill here would give it an edge in a tender.

A recent court case illustrates the difficulty local manufacturers face.

In October, the Pretoria High Court ordered the health department to reconsider suppliers for two HIV treatment medicines after Cipla Medpro Manufacturing , the Durban-based subsidiary of an Indian drug maker, challenged the tender process.

The ruling put Cipla back in contention, but didn't guarantee it a contract.

The case raises a wider question: how much should making a medicine here count when the government decides who to buy from? The government and drug makers are looking at that question through a joint task force set up at President Cyril Ramaphosa's request.

One of its priorities is giving preference to locally made medicines .

Nicolaou, who leads the industry's delegation, hopes the task force will help the government support local manufacturing while keeping medicines affordable.

Until then, Aspen can't be certain that government orders will justify its investment.

How can one pill protect someone for a month?

When HIV prevention activist Yvette Raphael heard about the monthly pill, she had a question: "Where is the medicine sitting?" After someone swallows the pill, the medicine travels through their bloodstream into your cells, where it becomes active. When HIV gets into a cell, it starts making copies of itself. Alimatravir stops the virus mid-copy .

In experiments involving primates , none of the animals given alimatravir weekly became infected, even when scientists repeatedly tried to infect them with a virus similar to HIV.

Studies in people have also found that the medicine remains inside cells for a long time. In one study, it took about nine to 12 days for the amount to fall by half after repeated doses.

That doesn't mean it stops working after 12 days. Researchers believe enough medicine could remain to protect someone until their next monthly dose.

A Phase 2 trial also investigated the medicine's safety and how long it remains in the body.

But none of this proves that one pill a month will prevent HIV infection in people.

That's what the final-stage trials, EXPrESSIVE-10 and EXPrESSIVE-11 , are testing: whether alimatravir prevents HIV infection and how it compares to existing daily HIV prevention tablets.

Will people remember to take a pill once a month?

Raphael, co-chair of the African Women Prevention Community Accountability Board , thinks a monthly tablet could appeal to people who struggle to take daily medication. "I may struggle by a daily, but I will not struggle by a monthly," she told Bhekisisa .

But taking a tablet less often creates another challenge: remembering when the next dose is due.

MSD's calculations suggest that after several monthly pills taken on time, people might have up to seven extra days to take their next pill. Researchers still need to verify that they would remain protected during that time.

In Tshwane, researchers at Wits RHI are already investigating whether people would choose the monthly pill.

They've received approval to add questions about alimatravir to their LEN4PrEP study . The study looks at what people choose when they're offered either LEN or the daily pill at government clinics in Tshwane. From the second half of November, they'll ask HIV-negative participants finishing the study whether they'd consider monthly oral HIV prevention.

They expect responses from about 1 500 people.

Study leader Saiqa Mullick calls this "planning for success": preparing for a new medicine while researchers are still establishing whether it works.

There's good reason to investigate people's preferences.

In LEN4PrEP , more than half of those who chose the six-monthly injection had never used HIV prevention medicine before. And Bhekisisa's analysis of early LEN roll-out data found that about one in three recipients were new to HIV prevention medication.

Close 

But preferences can change. In the INSIGHT study , young women initially preferred a monthly pill, then chose the six-monthly injection a month later — without having tried either.

Community representatives have also helped shape the alimatravir trials . HIV prevention advocacy organisation Avac supports groups of about 15 people for each trial.

Now they're considering practical questions, including where people could collect the pill and what would help them remember their doses.

Would the monthly pill be worth the money?

An early modelling study that hasn't yet been checked by other scientists , compared what might happen if health services in South Africa and Western Kenya offered alimatravir, LEN or both.

It suggested LEN could prevent more HIV infections, while the monthly pill could cost less to provide. Offering both might prevent the most infections, but would also cost the most.

The researchers assumed people would take only two of every three monthly pills and that the pill would cut their risk of getting HIV by 95% during the months they took it.

Health economist Lise Jamieson of South Africa's Health Economics and Epidemiology Research Office (HE²RO) calls that assumption (the 95% figure) "brave".

HE²RO is conducting its own calculations, but the results aren't available yet. For now, neither the pill's effectiveness nor its eventual price is known.

What is clear is that getting manufacturers ready, understanding what people want and planning how to deliver the medicine needn't wait for the final trial results. By granting licences early , MSD gave generic manufacturers a head start.

"We shouldn't be doing those things sequentially," Mullick says.

The stakes are high. In 2025, an estimated 360 people acquired HIV each day in South Africa, according to UNAids .

If alimatravir works, preparing early could shorten the wait for another choice of HIV prevention medication.

But for Aspen, success in the laboratory won't necessarily mean success at the factory. Even if the pill works, the South African government may buy it elsewhere.

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 25, 2026
World.content:
press review

Zambia Opposition Leader Indicted on Treason Charges

Zambia's main opposition leader Brian Mundubile and 12 others have been formally indicted on treason charges over an alleged plot to overthrow President Hakainde Hichilema's government. Prosecutors allege the group planned the operation between April and August 2026, with Mundubile and a businessman accused of funding military training in Russia. Mundubile, who challenged Hichilema in the August election, has denied wrongdoing. The case comes amid growing concerns over political repression. Rights groups have accused Zambian authorities of political repression in the wake of the August election, which international observer missions said was marred by irregularities. If convicted, Mundubile faces up to life imprisonment. Hichilema's first term also drew concerns over political freedoms, with opposition parties and civil society groups accusing his government of curbing dissent, allegations the government has rejected.

Veteran Nollywood Actor Pete Edochie Dies



Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Nollywood's most celebrated stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced. He died in the south-eastern city of Enugu. The cause of death has not been disclosed. Edochie rose to international prominence in 1987 for his portrayal of Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart. His career spanned several decades, with film appearances including Igodo, Rituals, and Lionheart. He received Nigeria's Member of the Order of the Niger honour in 2003. He is survived by his wife and six children, including actors Yul and Linc Edochie. In recent years, his memorable film scenes and distinctive expressions also gained popularity among younger audiences through social media memes.

UNAIDS Warns Funding Cuts Threaten HIV Progress

UNAIDS has warned that decades of progress in the fight against HIV and AIDS could be reversed by international funding cuts and growing attacks on human rights and gender equality. Its latest report highlights a $4.3 billion funding gap in low- and middle-income countries, despite 32.1 million of the estimated 40 million people living with HIV receiving treatment. Prevention services have been particularly affected, with 446,000 fewer people accessing pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in 2025 compared with the previous year. The agency warned that reduced funding for testing, treatment and community organisations could drive up infections and deaths, threatening the global target of ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. UNAIDS said that achieving the target could prevent 3.2 million new infections and avert 1.3 million AIDS-related deaths by the end of the decade.

Amnesty Urges Egypt to Reverse Mada Masr Closure

Amnesty International has urged Egyptian authorities to reverse the closure of independent news outlet Mada Masr and drop charges against its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, ahead of an appeal hearing scheduled for 25 November. Attalah was convicted in October of operating a website without a licence, fined three million Egyptian pounds and ordered to close the publication. Amnesty says the case forms part of a wider crackdown on independent journalism and freedom of expression in Egypt, where journalists and human rights defenders face arrests and prosecution over their work. The organisation has called on international partners, including the European Union, to pressure Cairo to protect press freedom. Attalah also faces a separate case involving allegations of publishing false news, which could carry a prison sentence of up to one year.

Women's Rights Network Sounds Alarm Over Abductions and Sexual Violence in Sudan

The Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa (SIHA Network) has reported the abduction of 28 women and girls fleeing fighting in Sudan's Blue Nile state, alongside 15 cases of conflict-related sexual violence against girls under 18. The organisation alleged that Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters and allied militias were responsible for the abductions as civilians fled renewed clashes. More than 7,000 families are reportedly heading towards Damazin, with many facing shortages of food, safe drinking water, transport and healthcare. SIHA has warned that the withdrawal of international aid organisations is placing additional pressure on local responders and called for urgent protection and humanitarian assistance for displaced communities. The International Organization for Migration estimates that Blue Nile state was hosting about 443,494 internally displaced people by the end of October.

Malawi Denies Receiving Request From Pakistan to Deport Fake Honorary Consul Suspect

Pakistan is facing accusations of misleading the public after Malawi denied receiving any formal request from Islamabad to arrest and deport businessman Mahmood Azhar Chaudhry. An investigation by Nyasa Times found that Pakistan claimed to have engaged Malawian authorities over Chaudhry, who allegedly posed as its honorary consul in Malawi between 2018 and 2022, despite Pakistan denying he ever held the position. Malawi's Foreign Affairs Ministry said that it received no diplomatic note or official communication seeking his deportation. The controversy is linked to land disputes in Lilongwe, where more than 15,000 households claim to have lost land through transactions involving companies associated with Chaudhry. Critics said that Pakistan must produce documentary evidence of its alleged diplomatic engagement with Malawi to demonstrate that it took action.

Close 

Morocco Threatens Legal Action After Senegal Reinstated as 2025 AFCON Champions

Morocco's football federation has rejected the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling restoring Senegal's 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title, alleging irregularities in the arbitration process and threatening further legal action. The Moroccan federation questioned alleged communication between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and the Senegalese Football Federation president shortly before the verdict. CAS overturned the CAF Appeal Board's decision to award Morocco a 3-0 victory, reinstating Senegal's original 1-0 win in the January final. It ruled that the match had resumed under the referee's authority and was completed, meaning Senegal had not forfeited. CAF has said it respects the ruling and will take the necessary steps to implement it. The unanimous CAS decision brings Senegal's title dispute to a close at the arbitration level. Morocco's threat of further legal action leaves the possibility of another challenge open.

World.title: Nigeria: Fabricated Newspaper Front Page Falsely Claims Nigerian President Bola Tinubu Promised Petrol At N200 Per Litre If Re-Elected
World.content:
Fabricated newspaper front page falsely claims Nigerian president Bola Tinubu promised petrol at N200 per litre if re-elected

IN SHORT: According to this newspaper-style graphic, Nigerian president Bola Tinibu promised to reduce the price of petrol to N200 per litre if he won a second term. But we found no evidence that such a newspaper exists or that Tinubu made the promise.

Fuel prices remain a major political issue in Nigeria ahead of the general election scheduled for 16 January 2027.



On 29 May 2023, his first day in office, president Bola Tinubu announced the removal of the petrol subsidy. Prices subsequently rose from around N200 to above N1,000 per litre, driving up the cost of living for many Nigerians.

Against this backdrop, a graphic resembling the front page of a newspaper called "The Daily Tribune" began circulating on Facebook.

Dated 1 September 2026, it carries the headline: "Tinubu: I will reduce Petrol Pump Price to N200/ltr after 2027 Election."

The graphic also claims Tinubu promised to make N1 equal to $1 before March 2027, and that Nigerians would no longer pay for electricity.

Tinubu is seeking reelection under the All Progressives Congress (APC).

The same claim also appeared here and here. (Note: See other instances of the claim at the end of this report).

But is this front page genuine? We checked.

Graphic is fabricated

Africa Check found no Nigerian newspaper, print or online, called "The Daily Tribune".

We also found no credible media reports or statements from the presidency or the APC supporting any of the three promises attributed to Tinubu.

The graphic contains inconsistent fonts and layout, raising further doubts about its authenticity.

Tinubu's administration has consistently rejected calls to reinstate the petrol subsidy. In May 2026, finance minister Taiwo Oyedele said the government would not bring back the subsidy because it created economic distortions.

In August 2026, Tinubu defended his administration's decision to remove the subsidy, describing an opponent's subsidy proposal as "serious ignorance" of the economy.

There is no credible evidence Tinubu made any of the promises attributed to him. The claim is false

World.title: FedEx cargo jet overshoots runway at Miami International Airport and stops just short of busy road
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop at Miami International Airport Wednesday evening due to a disabled FedEx aircraft after it overshot the runway, disrupting flights amid the busy Thanksgiving holiday travel rush.

Video from the scene shows a large FedEx cargo jet sitting near a fence that runs next to a busy road. The airport confirmed the aircraft overran Runway 26R, prompting all runways to close except for Runway 9R. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue responded to the airport and reported no injuries.

The incident comes nearly three months after a Prime Air cargo jet overran Runway 30 at Miami International Airport, killing five people.

FAA ISSUES GROUND DELAY AT CHICAGO O'HARE DUE TO 'EQUIPMENT OUTAGE'

In a statement provided to Fox News Digital shortly before 10 p.m., the FAA said flights would be "resuming shortly" at the airport.

The FAA said FedEx Flight 910, a McDonnell Douglas MD-11 arriving from Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis, Tennessee, ran off the runway after landing in Miami.

No injuries have been reported, according to the agency.

The FAA is investigating the incident.

FedEx confirmed the incident in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying the plane's crew was safe.

"FedEx Flight 910 from Memphis to Miami experienced an issue upon landing Wednesday evening at Miami International Airport," a spokesperson said. "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries."

FedEx added that it was coordinating with investigators.

According to an advisory issued by the FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center, the ground stop took effect at 8:16 p.m.

In its advisory, the FAA said a disabled aircraft caused the ground stop and indicated a medium probability that the restrictions could be extended.

The FAA said the pause was scheduled to remain in place until 9:45 p.m.

WORST AIRPORTS FOR THANKSGIVING TRAVEL CHAOS RANKED AS MAJOR US HUBS TOP LIST

According to an updated FAA advisory, Miami International Airport was experiencing average delays of 47 minutes, with maximum delays reaching two hours on Wednesday evening.

The airport encouraged passengers to check directly with their airlines for flight updates before heading to the airport.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Miami International Airport and the FAA for comment.

World.title: USC suspends entire marching band from UCLA game over crude sign prank on Bruins campus
World.content:
USC pulled its marching band from Saturday's rivalry game at the Rose Bowl following a late-night campus prank at UCLA.

Ahead of the Big Ten matchup between No. 15 USC and No. 9 UCLA, officials barred the Trojan Marching Band from its pregame and halftime shows after members allegedly vandalized signage at the Wasserman Football Center.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The incident capped off a spirited Tuesday night in Los Angeles.

An hour after the latest College Football Playoff rankings dropped, USC held its annual Conquest pep rally featuring a mock fight between the USC and UCLA mascots. The marching band performed and several USC players attended. Head coach Lincoln Riley did not make an appearance.

ARMY CADETS SNEAK INTO NAVY'S STADIUM TO LEAVE A SPECIAL MESSAGE IN THE UPPER DECK

Later that night, according to UCLA's Daily Bruin, band members allegedly crossed town and removed letters from the Wasserman Football Center's exterior sign to spell "ass Football Center."

The vandalism left the facility temporarily branded as the "ASS Football Center." USC President Beong-Soo Kim responded Wednesday with a formal apology to UCLA.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL CORPORATE OVERLORDS RUIN ANOTHER CLASSIC RIVALRY GAME WITH STUPID NEW NAME

"This morning, we learned that a portion of UCLA's campus had been vandalized by individual students belonging to the Trojan Marching Band. This conduct runs contrary to USC's values and is unacceptable," Kim wrote in a statement to the Trojan community.

"We are cooperating fully with law enforcement and an investigation is underway. Appropriate interim actions will be or have already been taken, and any student ultimately found responsible will be subject to discipline under university policy."

The move will sideline hundreds of student musicians for the actions of a few. Kim added that the decision was made jointly with band leadership.

"We want to express our deepest apologies to the entire UCLA community. Our rivalry is one of the great traditions in college athletics, and it has always rested on mutual respect. What happened on UCLA's campus last night has no place in this tradition," Kim wrote.

World.title: Netanyahu declares corruption trial has 'fallen apart' after judges question key charges
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The decade-long legal battle against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suffered a major blow Wednesday after judges cast doubt on key corruption charges, prompting the Israeli leader to declare that his trial had "fallen apart" and demand an immediate end to the proceedings.

A three-judge panel at the Jerusalem District Court suggested that Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara consider dropping the most serious case against Netanyahu, questioned whether a criminal offense occurred in a second case and recommended resolving a third through a plea deal.

"Today, the trial fell apart," Netanyahu said in an evening address following the proceedings, according to The Times of Israel.

FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY

"Ten years ago, I said, ‘There will be nothing because there was nothing.’ But it took 10 years for this truth to be revealed to everyone," he said.

"Citizens of Israel, this trial must end immediately. And what also needs to end immediately is what came out of it — the hatred, the incitement, the division."

The court's intervention dealt a major setback to prosecutors more than six years after Netanyahu's trial began and roughly a decade after authorities launched the initial probe into him.

Judges had summoned Baharav-Miara to court Wednesday amid concerns over the strength of the prosecution's evidence and whether continuing the cases served the public interest.

"We’re now at a crossroad and need to rechart a new path," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told the attorney general, according to The New York Sun.

"Public interest dictates a need to rethink."

NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'

She and her colleagues, Judges Moshe Bar-Am and Oded Shaham, stressed that their comments were preliminary, did not constitute a verdict and applied only to Netanyahu because they still had to hear the other defendants’ testimony, The Jerusalem Post reported.

Baharav-Miara signaled that prosecutors would review the judges' recommendations and weigh their options.

Netanyahu faces charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust stemming from three corruption investigations.

Prosecutors announced the charges in November 2019 and formally filed the indictment in January 2020, and Netanyahu consistently denied wrongdoing.

The most serious charge, Case 4000, centers on allegations that Netanyahu granted regulatory favors to Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq in exchange for favorable coverage on the Walla news website, which was then controlled by businessman Shaul Elovitch.

Judges questioned whether prosecutors presented sufficient evidence to secure a conviction. In Case 2000, prosecutors also allege Netanyahu negotiated for favorable coverage from Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper publisher Arnon Mozes in exchange for legislation to weaken rival newspaper Israel Hayom.

TRUMP WANTS LARGEST-EVER ISRAELI HEAVY BOMB TRANSFER — BUT PROPOSAL HAS CONGRESS PREPARING FOR $2.8B FIGHT

The proposed deal never materialized, and judges questioned whether a criminal offense had happened.

Case 1000 centers on allegations that Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, received almost $300,000 in gifts from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer.

Judges suggested resolving that case through an agreement. Zion Amir, an attorney who previously represented Netanyahu in the proceedings, rejected the prospect of a settlement.

In his address Wednesday, Netanyahu also accused investigators of pressuring his political associates to testify against him and described the toll the investigations had taken on his family.

"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my wife and my sons," he said.

"Of delusional interrogations. Of character assassination. Of grave incitement that wounds the soul. Who will give us back those 10 years?"

Netanyahu, who requested a presidential pardon in November 2025 without admitting guilt, also called on his political opponents to set aside their differences and form a unity government.

"The boycotts must end, and now," Netanyahu said.

"I know what enormous and immediate dangers the State of Israel faces. There is only one way to deal with them. To unite in order to deal with them. We must unite to secure the future of Israel — no less than that, and immediately."

World.title: Judge blocks FCC review of ABC station licenses for now
World.content:
The Walt Disney Co. secured a temporary restraining order Wednesday blocking the Federal Communications Commission from moving forward with an unusually early review of ABC’s broadcast-station licenses, which the media company has called an attack on free speech by the Trump administration.

U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan’s decision is the latest turn in the legal battle between Disney and the FCC, the federal agency that regulates the broadcast airwaves. Disney filed a lawsuit against the FCC in August, calling the early license review an “existential threat” to the First Amendment.

The FCC “wants to stop, censor [and] control” what ABC can broadcast, Disney lawyer Beth Wilkinson told AliKhan at a hearing on Oct. 6. Wilkinson characterized FCC Chairman Brendan Carr’s actions as a series of “unending threats and retaliation.”

The FCC’s lawyers argued at the hearing that the U.S. District Court does not have jurisdiction in the matter, accusing ABC of trying to circumvent the federal regulatory process.

In her order Wednesday, the judge wrote that she concluded Disney was “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim” against the FCC.

The order blocks the agency “from taking any continuing or further action against Plaintiffs in relation to the early license renewal proceedings before the Federal Communications Commission.”

She also denied a request by the FCC to dismiss Disney’s lawsuits against the agency.

“This is not a close case,” AliKhan wrote, adding that the ABC stations “have a weighty interest” in vindicating their right to free speech without retaliation.

“Chairman Carr has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders,” AliKhan wrote. The judge’s opinion and order referenced multiple social media posts by Trump in which he was critical of ABC. “Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now.”

In response to a request for comment, an FCC spokesperson said: “While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear.

“The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations,” the agency spokesperson added.

In a statement, an ABC News spokesperson cheered the temporary restraining order as an “important victory for the First Amendment.”

The courtroom confrontation stems from the FCC’s April 28 order directing Disney’s eight owned-and-operated TV stations to file their broadcast license renewals ahead of schedule. The licenses were not due to come up for renewal until 2028 at the earliest.

Carr has said that order was tied to the agency’s investigation into Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices. It came a day after Trump called on ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he had made about first lady Melania Trump.

AliKhan addressed the sequence of events following Kimmel’s joke, writing that “against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr’s call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.”

The FCC is also reviewing whether ABC’s “The View” broke a requirement that broadcast stations give equal time to political candidates for the same office. Disney has argued that the talk show qualifies as a “bona fide news” program, meaning it is exempt from the equal-time rule.

In a phone interview with NBC News after Disney filed suit, Carr said he believed Disney’s challenge to the FCC’s order was a “meritless case.” In remarks at the agency’s open commission meeting last week, Carr said the suit was filed “in the wrong court” at “the wrong time.”

ABC Owned Television Stations, a division of Disney Entertainment Television, operates stations in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, Houston, San Francisco, the Raleigh-Durham area, and Fresno, California.

Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, said in a statement that AliKhan’s decision “shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights.”

“Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I’ve said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side,” Gomez added.

World.title: A rising political star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
World.content:
He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.

The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.

Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.

He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.

But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.

“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.

Xi’s pursuit of loyalty

Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”

Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.

Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.

In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.

By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.

Chen Jining and Sen. Chuck Schumer in Shanghai in 2023. Aly Song / AFP via Getty

Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.

“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.

The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.

“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.

“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping, right, and Zhang Shengmin, second left, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing in March. Kevin Frayer / Getty ]

The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.

Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.

From London to Shanghai

Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.

After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.

Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography.

He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring.

The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest, a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.

The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.

World.title: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine war, new estimate suggests
World.content:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine, according to a new projection based on leaked official data, an estimate that sheds new light on the staggering cost of President Vladimir Putin’s war.

The grim assessment comes more than 4½ years after the Kremlin’s invasion of its neighbor, an all-out war that has consumed Russian society. The death toll has been mounting with each painstaking ground assault, with no end to the conflict in sight despite pressure from President Donald Trump for Kyiv to make a deal.

The leak from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat — released by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers earlier this month — reveals that at least 490,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in Ukraine based on registered deaths as of the end of September. That’s according to breakdowns by a range of independent media, including the BBC and others, that were published this week. But one exiled Russian media outlet, Meduza, also used the leaked mortality data to project the total number of military deaths, including those that have not yet been recorded.

Meduza estimates that number to be 720,000.

NBC News did not have access to the leaked data and could not authenticate it or independently confirm these numbers.

Neither Moscow nor Kyiv provide regular updates on their battlefield losses.

Mediazona, along with the BBC Russian Service and a team of volunteers, has been compiling a separate named list of Russian war dead using open-source data for years, given the difficulty of gauging the true impact of the war on Russian society.

In its analysis, Mediazona said it arrived at the 490,000 war dead number from the 29.7 million records it obtained from the hackers that covered nearly all death registrations in Russia from early 2021 through September this year, based mainly on records with an “explicit military cause of death” and court rulings declaring people dead.

The leaked data was cross-checked against Mediazona’s own named list and matched 95% of the records, as well as the publicly accessible national Probate Registry, a database of inheritance cases, and Rosstat’s own official mortality statistics, the outlet said.

Mediazona said it also checked against possible data tempering and fake military death injections by cross-referencing a unique vital record number that every death registration carries, and court rulings, which often cite death record numbers.

“We are confident that this data is genuine,” the outlet said, adding that fabricating a dataset of this scale from scratch would be “impossible” especially as it checks out against official registries.

The hackers shared leaked data with a number of other exiled Russian media outlets and the BBC, who all arrived at a figure close to the 490,000 reported by Mediazona. A similar estimate of half a million Russian troops killed was also shared by a senior British defense official in September.

Before the new analysis of the data in the Rosstat leak, the verified named list of Russia’s war dead compiled by Mediazona and the BBC stood at just over 289,000. It was based on obituaries, local news and official registries, and was the only publicly available database containing the fallen soldiers’ names.

The Russian Defense Ministry has not officially updated its death toll in Ukraine since the early months of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said it stood at nearly 6,000.

Mediazona warned that due to a considerable lag in military death registrations, Rosstat may not yet have finished capturing deaths from 2025. “That means the leaked records through late September — however authentic and reliable they are — still fall short of the true death toll,” it said.

World.title: Trump owned millions in Nvidia stock as he pressed for Jensen Huang's reinstatement
World.content:
President Trump holds tens of millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, giving him a personal stake in the company's stock market roller coaster ride over the past two weeks, financial disclosure documents show.

Mr. Trump stood to lose large sums with CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt departure, and stood to profit handsomely after he successfully pressed the chip developer's board to reinstate Huang. Nvidia stock surged more than 30% when Huang returned to the company on Monday, reversing a weekslong slide.

Huang resigned two weeks ago over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China, and another alleged affair with a subordinate. Mr. Trump said Monday he personally spoke with Nvidia's board and "convinced them" to rehire Huang, offering an "assurance" that there was no national security threat.

Mr. Trump held between $13 million and $58 million in Nvidia stock in his investment accounts as of the end of 2025, according to financial disclosures filed with the Office of Government Ethics. He bought or sold the company's stock in more than 100 transactions that were worth between $27 million and nearly $98 million between January 2025 and September 2026.

The value of the president's Nvidia shares increased anywhere from $1.3 million to $14.8 million on Monday, before paring back some of those gains when Nvidia's share price ticked down Tuesday. The range is so large because it isn't clear how many shares of Nvidia the president currently owns, but it can be roughly estimated based on his sales and purchases this year.

"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions," a White House spokesman told CBS News Tuesday, adding that his investments mirror indexes like the Schwab 1000. "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."

In addition to the president, several of his appointees to positions in the State, Commerce and Treasury departments as well as the IRS reported millions in Nvidia stock in their investment portfolios. Many have since sold their holdings.

Forbes estimates Mr. Trump's net worth at more than $6 billion, making Nvidia a small part of his total wealth. And Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable public companies, at more than $3.7 trillion, so many investors hold shares in the tech giant.

Still, some ethics experts questioned Mr. Trump's large stake in Nvidia, especially after he intervened to boost the company's fortunes.

"This goes beyond a conflict of interest," said Kathleen Clark, a law professor and expert on government ethics at Washington University in St. Louis. "He is squarely, explicitly using his power as president to benefit himself financially. He has prioritized his finances over the security of the nation."

Donald Sherman, president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit government watchdog, told CBS News that Mr. Trump's "continued ownership of stock in this company is the clearest example of how the president's personal financial interest makes everything he does suspect."

Mr. Trump's personal investments have drawn controversy in the past, including his stakes in publicly traded energy companies, firms that have business with the government and his family's cryptocurrency firm. He has denied any conflict of interest.

Some critics called for legal reforms to prohibit the president and members of Congress from buying and selling stocks while they hold office. Elected officials are generally allowed to trade individual stocks, though lawmakers from both parties have called for the practice to be banned.

Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and former chief ethics attorney for the White House between 2005 and 2007, said he has long argued for changes to the federal conflict of interest law that prohibits government employees from participating in matters that result in their personal enrichment while in office. That current law does not apply to the president, vice president or members of Congress, he said.

"We need a prohibition on this right away," he said, adding that the new Congress may take up the cause in January.

Painter called Mr. Trump's intervention with the Nvidia board "a huge conflict of interest" and overreach of government power.

"It's not the job of the government to call up and say who the CEO of a company should be," he told CBS News.

The president has defended his decision to intervene, saying on CNBC that "we have to protect our geniuses" and arguing that Nvidia — as the world's leading designer of advanced chips — plays a key role in maintaining the U.S.' lead over China in AI technology.

Mr. Trump has also frequently pointed to the performance of the stock market as a barometer of his success as president. Shortly after Huang was reinstated, Mr. Trump told The Wall Street Journal the "response from the market has been very positive," and "that really shows the decision was right."

Beyond Mr. Trump, numerous political appointees held Nvidia stock. Some divested themselves of their holdings after they were appointed to government positions, federal filings show.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin owned between $250,000 and $500,000 in Nvidia stock in March 2026, and sold $500,000 to $1 million in shares of the tech company in June of this year, his financial disclosures show.

"As Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin acts to ensure full compliance with all ethics and conflict of interest rules," said a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security.

In the Commerce Department, where Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing scrutiny over whether he has done enough to crack down on highly sensitive AI chip sales to China, a number of senior advisers last year reported selling large positions in Nvidia.

Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm that was previously run by Lutnick and is now controlled by his sons, reported holding roughly 1 million shares of Nvidia for its clients as of Sept. 30, worth around $228 million at the time. Those shares were worth just over $150 million at Tuesday's price. None of Lutnick's personal financial disclosures filed by the federal government mention Nvidia holdings or transactions.

In the State Department, some of Mr. Trump's diplomatic appointees had Nvidia holdings.

Charles Kushner, the U.S. ambassador to France and father of Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, reported Nvidia holdings totaling between $1.5 million and $6 million, according to public disclosures filed January 2025.

U.S. Ambassador to Costa Rica Melinda Hildebrand reported Nvidia holdings between $5 million and $25 million, her April 2025 disclosures show. The Texas billionaire, who was a major Trump campaign fundraiser, sold the stock in November of that same year, filings show.

Warren Stephens, another major Trump donor and ambassador to the United Kingdom, reported Nvidia holdings between $750,000 and $1.5 million, according to his January 2025 disclosures. He sold those shares in July and August 2025, a few months after he was sworn in as ambassador.

In the Treasury Department, when she was nominated to be under secretary for International Affairs, Erin Browne held Nvidia shares totaling between $250,000 and $500,000, her disclosures from January show. Browne sold the stock before her confirmation in August, filings show.

Todd Newnam, who was appointed chief financial officer of the IRS in January, holds between $115,000 and $250,000 in Nvidia stock, according to his financial disclosure, filed in April of last year. Newnam, a former CEO of a tech company, was part of the Department of Government Efficiency team that sought to streamline government spending and cut the federal workforce.

"All OGE (Office of Government Ethics) 278 filers are required to disclose any equity positions they hold and are advised of their recusal obligations in accordance with the ethics rules," an IRS spokesperson said Tuesday, referring to the financial disclosure required by members of the executive branch of the federal government.

Many other officials could be indirectly exposed to Nvidia stock if they invested in mutual funds or similar assets. For example, Vice President JD Vance reported $1 million to $5 million in a fund that tracks the S&P 500 — and Nvidia is one of that index's largest components.

World.title: Army detonates toxic explosives at Iowa plant despite concerns
World.content:
The U.S. Army detonated a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning, following community outcry and a legal fight over concerns of a possible dust plume containing toxic lead particles spreading after the blast.

Five tons of unstable explosive material, containing the highly sensitive compound lead azide, were blown up in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, which is a small community of about 350 people, located four hours west of Chicago by car.

As scheduled, the detonation took place at 9 a.m. local time. A few loud pops rang out in livestream footage of the explosion published by The Associated Press, followed by a faint smoke cloud that rose up above the rooftop of the Armed Forces Reserve Center building that separated its cameras from the detonation site.

Fifteen minutes after it happened, the Environmental Protection Agency reported that zero lead was detected in the air by four monitoring stations in the area. Those sensors continued to show the same readings two hours later, according to the EPA.

The Army said in a follow-up social media post Wednesday evening that the Federal Emergency Management Agency had given an "all clear" around the plant. The Army also added that maps from the Pentagon's Defense Threat Reduction Agency indicated "ZERO airborne lead detection" from the detonation. FEMA said in a separate statement Wednesday night that its air monitoring results indicated there was "no detectable lead."

Army Maj. Gen. Eric P. Shirley, the commander of the operation, described the detonation as "tremendously successful" at a news conference Wednesday.

"I believe absolutely that we reduced, as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and the safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa," he said.

Rob Cekada, the director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, added that the operation went "100% as planned," with the blast driving the explosion into the ground and minimizing the amount of lead dispersed into the atmosphere, as designed.

Debris flies into the air after the Army detonated several tons of highly volatile, degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 25, 2026. Scott Olson/Getty Images

"The explosion exceeded all expectations," a senior administration official told CBS News. "Maximum mitigation efforts achieved."

President Trump echoed that assessment in a social media post after the detonation, writing that "early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations." An Army official told CBS News the detonation went "much better than projected," while current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds called it "successful."

"We remain in close contact with authorities on the ground, while state agencies continue to monitor incoming data from the State Emergency Operations Center," Reynolds said. "We will keep Iowans informed as details become available."

The Middletown plant housed about 68 barrels or roughly 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the explosives degraded over about 20 years in storage, giving way to a process called recrystallization that made the material more susceptible to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.

The Army had pushed to carry out the controlled detonation because of the public safety risks associated with the cache possibly blowing up on its own. But environmental groups and local residents attempted to block its plans, fearing the health and agricultural consequences of a toxic plume of lead dust that could disperse across the region after the blast.

The Army said it had taken steps to barricade the concrete bunkers holding the munitions and absorb the toxic dust, including with aqueous foam, which is used to extinguish fuel fires, environmental officials have said.

"Precise deployment of aqueous foam blocks, two walls of four 16,000-gallon water tanks, and gel blocks adjacent to the bunkers will absorb thermal energy and reduce airborne particulate emissions directly at the blast source," the Army said in a statement.

Officials had warned that a plume could spread over parts of southeastern Iowa and northeastern Missouri, potentially threatening homes, playgrounds, farmlands and other spaces.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said after the explosion that reports from federal and state officials in Iowa indicated it was "well-contained."

"Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained," Kehoe said on social media.

Legal challenge questioned detonation

The detonation was postponed last week after environmental groups filed a lawsuit challenging the emergency permit the EPA had granted the Army to authorize it. The groups argued the agency had not provided residents of the area with adequate notice of its plans or evidence showing the detonation was the best course of action from a health and safety perspective.

But the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals' initial ruling blocking the detonation was lifted Monday. The court acknowledged "the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation," but ultimately found the risk of an uncontrolled explosion more harmful.

A plume rises after the U.S. Army detonated a stockpile of lead azide at its Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Austin Johnson

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said at a Tuesday news conference that plans would move forward as falling temperatures caused the explosives to become more and more volatile, increasing the chances of a spontaneous explosion. Telle said the weather forecast Wednesday was "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

"Inaction is no longer an option," Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."

Mr. Trump had said earlier this week that the Army would not move ahead with the detonation without the court's affirmative ruling and the approval of Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. However, Sand was not required to weigh in and hasn't officially taken office.

World.title: Maps show where Thanksgiving storms could disrupt holiday
World.content:
Various types of severe weather are expected to impact large stretches of the United States this week, potentially disrupting Thanksgiving plans and hampering travel for Americans along both coasts and into the middle of the country.

A storm developing Wednesday over Florida threatened to bring flooding to southeastern states before quickly traveling up the coast and moving into the Northeast in time for Thanksgiving. Forecasts showed the storm could generate high winds and heavy rain across the region, while areas in the Midwest, including St. Louis, could see snow around the holiday.

CBS News

In New York City, organizers of the iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade announced the parade is being postponed until Saturday due to the coming storm. It's the first time in the parade's 100-year history that it's been postponed, although it was not held at all from 1942 to 1944 because of World War II. In 1971, the balloons were grounded due to strong winds, but the parade still went on.

While the city isn't expected to get excessive rain, a relatively rare High Wind Warning was issued, and wind gusts could reach 60 mph.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Wednesday night declared a state of emergency for New York City, along with Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties.

"We're expecting heavy rain and strong winds that could create dangerous travel conditions," she wrote on social media.

And in a travel advisory, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani stated that forecasts showed the worst of the storm would likely hit the city beginning Thursday afternoon into the late Thursday night.

CBS News

More than 80 million people were under alerts Wednesday as the National Weather Service warned of powerful wind gusts, potentially as intense as 70 mph, that could impact a massive stretch of the East Coast, from South Carolina up to Massachusetts.

CBS News

In addition to New York, other major cities like Boston, Philadelphia and Washington, D.C., would likely receive chilly rainfall on Thanksgiving, but forecasters expected most metropolitan hubs to be spared from the highest amounts. The weather service did note a flash-flooding threat impacting the Southeast on Wednesday could shift toward New York City by Thursday.

CBS News

Up to 5 inches of rain could fall in other places, especially in southeastern states like Florida and the Carolinas. As the storm continues to develop, those areas could also face damaging winds, tornadoes and, potentially, waterspouts, forecasters said. The storm system already brought more than half a foot of rain to Miami, causing flooding in South Florida.

Interior portions of the eastern U.S. and some spots in the Midwest could receive their first measurable snowfall of the season around Thanksgiving. The weather service issued several winter storm warnings and winter weather advisories for parts of Illinois and Missouri, including St. Louis, through Thursday evening, as sections of both states brace for up to 6 inches, or even 9 inches in certain areas, of snow.

CBS News

"Roads, especially bridges and overpasses, will likely become slick and hazardous. The weight of snow on tree limbs may down power lines and could cause sporadic power outages," the weather service in St. Louis wrote in a Wednesday advisory, which recommended that people delay travel completely, if possible.

World.title: Judge temporarily blocks FCC from reviewing ABC's licenses
World.content:
A federal judge blocked the Federal Communications Commission from moving forward with an early review of ABC's broadcast licenses Wednesday, a move the network argues is an attempt by the Trump administration to punish speech it does not like.

In a 45-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan found ABC is likely to succeed in showing the FCC's license review was retaliatory. Her preliminary injunction bars the FCC from "taking any continuing or further action against [ABC] in relation to the early license renewal proceedings" while the network's lawsuit against the agency works its way through the courts.

The judge pointed to at least 11 different examples of President Trump publicly urging the FCC to strip ABC of its licenses in recent years — an action the president argues is necessary because the network's news coverage or late-night shows are unfair to him.

AliKhan also said FCC Chair Brendan Carr — who frequently echoes Mr. Trump's criticism of media outlets — "has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders."

"Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," the judge wrote.

She said the question of whether ABC's interest in a preliminary injunction outweighed the federal government's interests was "not a close case." She did not agree to ABC's request for a broader ban on "taking any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten Plaintiffs with sanctions in an effort to alter their exercise of editorial discretion."

An ABC News spokesperson said: "Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration."

An FCC spokesperson called the decision to grant ABC's motion "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law—as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear," and said the agency "looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter."

Earlier this year, the FCC ordered ABC to file early license renewal applications for the eight local television stations it owns and operates, saying it was investigating "possible violations" of the Communications Act of 1934 and the agency's prohibition on unlawful discrimination. The licenses originally weren't scheduled for renewal until 2028 to 2031.

ABC sued over the move, calling it "blatant retaliation" in violation of the First Amendment and arguing the FCC's investigation into discrimination was a pretext.

"Each day, Plaintiffs (and every other broadcaster observing the Commission's actions) face a choice between exercising independent editorial judgment or risking the loss of valuable broadcast licenses—precisely the type of choice that chills protected First Amendment activity and cannot be remedied after the fact," the network and Disney wrote in a filing.

At one point during a court hearing last month, Disney attorney Beth Wilkinson invoked the French Revolution, saying the FCC's review was forcing the company to sit with its "head on a guillotine" while it awaits a decision about the licenses.

The FCC has denied that it is seeking to punish ABC for its speech. Government lawyers say the agency has been investigating the broadcaster since last year over its compliance with anti-employment discrimination rules, alleging its responses to requests for information have been insufficient, leading the FCC to push for early license renewal.

"The commission decided to look for information that it needed by calling for early renewal of plaintiffs' broadcast license," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remme said in last month's court hearing before AliKhan.

AliKhan appeared skeptical of the government's arguments in Wednesday's ruling. At one point, she noted that the FCC took action shortly after late-night ABC host Jimmy Kimmel joked that first lady Melania Trump had "the glow of an expectant widow."

She said "it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel's skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings."

The Trump administration has often tangled with ABC and other outlets. Last year, following another controversial joke by Kimmel, Carr did not rule out punishing the network, saying on a podcast: "We can do this the easy way or the hard way."

More broadly, Carr has suggested networks could lose their licenses for coverage of the Iran war, and Mr. Trump called for licenses to be revoked when some networks opted out of carrying a primetime speech in July. The FCC has also warned daytime and late-night talk shows that they must provide equal time to political candidates — a rule that historically hasn't applied to them. Separately, the administration has sought to restrict some outlets' access to the White House.

World.title: A look at the probes involving Nvidia, Jensen Huang and Megaspeed
World.content:
Washington — Revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset have put the leading AI company under a microscope, as lawmakers and states question whether Nvidia skirted federal export rules that aim to stop its most advanced chips from going to China.

While Huang initially resigned his post amid scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, Nvidia's board of directors announced Monday that it reinstated Huang as president and CEO.

News of Huang's return to Nvidia sent shockwaves through the business and political worlds, even as President Trump said he had spoken to the board and "convinced them" to bring Huang back. The president told CNBC in an interview that his administration gave Nvidia "assurances" that Huang is not a threat to national security.

The company, meanwhile, said it received "input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

Still, investigations by at least one state and Congress are unlikely to be derailed by Huang's dramatic return to Nvidia.

California Department of Justice

California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia last week following revelations of Huang's affair with the woman who is alleged to have ties to China's Ministry of State Security.

Bonta, a Democrat, said the state's Department of Justice is seeking information from Nvidia about whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether the company misled investors and the public.

"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," he said in a statement. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law."

Bonta said the information his office receives from Nvidia will help determine whether the company broke state law.

Congressional probes

Numerous congressional committees were readying investigations into Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy, and his reinstatement as CEO did not diminish lawmakers' appetite for more information about Huang's actions and whether his company's chips were diverted to China.

Huang is set to answer questions behind closed doors from lawmakers on three House panels, the Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select Committee, on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, will appear before the committees on Dec. 2.

The Senate Banking Committee will then hold a public hearing with Huang on Dec. 3.

Democrats, who will take control of the House and Senate in January, say they intend to launch investigations into Nvidia and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose agency oversees government export controls on sensitive technology.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to serve as House speaker in the next Congress, denounced the decision by Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang as "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible."

"Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce," he said in a statement Monday.

Senate Democrats have also pledged to act.

"Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he's learned nothing from his resounding election defeat," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X. "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain."

Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is poised to take the helm of the Senate Banking Committee in January, said Nvidia officials and the Trump administration will have to answer questions from lawmakers.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," she said in a statement. "The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."

House and Senate Democrats have also demanded that the president and his administration provide information about their role in Huang's reinstatement.

"President Trump has acknowledged personally intervening on Huang's behalf, and Nvidia has acknowledged that it received 'input from senior levels of the United States government' in reaching its decision," a group of five Democratic senators said in a joint statement. "The American people deserve to know why the president intervened in this extraordinary manner, whether serious counterintelligence or national security concerns were disregarded, and whose interests this intervention was intended to serve."

The senators are: Warren, Chris Coons of Delaware, Ron Wyden of Oregon, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Maria Cantwell of Washington.

Justice Department

The Justice Department and Commerce Department said in a joint statement earlier this month that the federal government had been investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based computing company that is a Nvidia client, since 2024.

The Commerce Department sought records from Nvidia in May 2025 about direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed and placed the Singaporean company on its "no sell" list that June.

Agents with the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, working with Singaporean law enforcement, conducted an on-site, in-person check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed Alice Huang, the Commerce and Justice Departments said in their statement. After that action, the Justice Department took the lead in the criminal probe into Megaspeed.

Nvidia has received a subpoena as a witness from the Department of Justice in relation to its investigation into Megaspeed and export controls, a source directly familiar with the situation told CBS News.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025. China has denied allegations that she is a spy.

Mr. Trump told reporters earlier this month that the FBI was "looking into" Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who is of no relation. A Justice Department official said Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche spoke with Mr. Trump about Jensen Huang and Nvidia over the weekend, and said "the DOJ has no evidence of any wrongdoing" by either Huang or his company.

At a press conference Tuesday, the attorney general said the Justice Department did not have any information showing Huang committed criminal acts, and if he had, Blanche "would have certainly told the president."

Reporters pressed Blanche on how he and the Justice Department had made that determination if there was no investigation into Alice Huang or potential violations of federal export control laws by Nvidia. He dodged questions on the topic. Still, the attorney general referred to Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen."

Blanche said that "looking into it" does not mean there was an investigation into the Nvidia CEO and his alleged mistress, or the company itself.

The attorney general also said there was a "collective consensus" to conclude there was no national security risk posed by Huang.

Securities and Exchange Commission

The Securities and Exchange Commission is conducting its own civil investigation into Nvidia, the Wall Street Journal reported last week. Among the matters that the SEC will look into is whether the company's disclosures misled investors, sources told the Journal.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 11 that Nvidia altered its reporting methods for international chip sales and stopped reporting revenue tied to Singapore on financial disclosures last year.

Reuters said Friday that the SEC is examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. It's unclear when the agency began its investigation.

The SEC declined to comment.

Huang resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12, and the board said Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, would serve as interim CEO. During an earnings call on Nov. 17, Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said it "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Kress, too, told CNBC on Nov. 17 that the "board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen."

Less than a week later, on Nov. 23, the board reinstated him.

Internal Nvidia probe

After the New York Times reported that Huang was the target of a potential Chinese intelligence operation, Nvidia's board announced earlier this month that it would be launching an independent investigation into the allegations and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to help with the probe.

After announcing that Huang would return to Nvidia as president and CEO, the board said the investigation "will proceed to conclusion."

"Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it," the board said.
