Participation is entirely voluntary, and all responses will be anonymous and used exclusively for this tax review

The Falkland Islands Government has commissioned Alma Economics to undertake an independent review of the Falkland Islands tax system.

The Falkland Islands Government has commissioned Alma Economics to undertake an independent review of the Falkland Islands tax system.

The review will cover:

Policy: what taxes people and businesses pay in different circumstances

Administration: how the tax system works in practice

Legislation: the legal framework that translates tax policy into enforceable rules and aims to assess whether the current system remains fit for purpose, and/or identify how it could be improved.

As part of the review, Alma Economics wishes to collect residents' views on the current tax system and invites residents to complete a short survey. Participation is entirely voluntary, and all responses will be anonymous and used exclusively for this tax review.

To facilitate IP tracking, participants are encouraged not to use a VPN while completing the survey.

The survey is now open, and will remain live until 4:30pm local time on Friday 11 December.

World.title: CIA and US intelligence office suffer intrusion exposing unclassified information
World.content:
CIA and US intelligence office suffer intrusion exposing unclassified information

25th Wednesday, November 2026 - 01:08 UTC Full article

The CIA headquarters seal in Langley, Virginia

The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a computer intrusion that exposed unclassified information from an open-source intelligence analysis system, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Unlike the system outages of recent weeks, attributed to technical failures, this is a security breach.

The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a computer intrusion that exposed unclassified information from an open-source intelligence analysis system, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Unlike the system outages of recent weeks, attributed to technical failures, this is a security breach.

The intrusion affected a network analysts use to draw intelligence from public, unclassified material such as social media, satellite imagery and commercial databases, according to US officials and people familiar with the incident cited by the newspaper and by Reuters. It is unclear what information was compromised or how the intrusion occurred, and data from other federal agencies was probably also exposed. Those responsible have not been identified.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there had been “no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems”. The CIA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The incident adds to a series of security breaches at federal bodies: according to Reuters, one has recently been reported at the Department of Agriculture and two at the FBI, one of them at its National Crime Information Center, while the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security have also been affected by cyber incidents.

It also coincides with a string of technology failures that authorities attributed to technical causes: the global Microsoft outage on November 12; the nationwide ground stop of all US flights for about four and a half hours on November 13, which the government blamed on outdated telecommunications equipment; and the outage of the National Security Agency's classified internal network on November 17, which the agency attributed to routine maintenance.

According to Uruguay's El País, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence that the failures are linked or that the country is under a systemic attack.

World.title: The Sheinbaum administration earns praise from the UN for its work to prevent violence against women
World.content:
As President Sheinbaum opened her daily press conference on Wednesday with a shout-out to the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, her administration received praise from the United Nations for its efforts in protecting girls and women.

United Nations Women Representative in Mexico Eleonora Bentacur González praised the government’s reforms and initiatives, such as the creation of more than 1,000 LIBRE centers — free community spaces for women, telephone hotlines, legal services and the distribution of women’s rights booklets.

“In a global context of setbacks in gender equality, these measures are especially relevant,” Bentacur González said. “Given its political, economic, and cultural standing, Mexico has a unique capacity to exercise leadership in Latin America and in multilateral forums.”

Sheinbaum, in turn, announced the launch of several strategies aimed at tackling violence against women, including a 16-day activism campaign, a guide to combating digital violence and a campaign focused on men.

She also announced plans to present a bill on Thursday focused on family justice and designed to guarantee the protection of women’s rights.

Minister of Women’s Affairs Laura Itzel Castillo detailed the launch of the UN’s UNiTE campaign, also known as the Orange Campaign, which will include 16 days of activism against gender-based violence. This year’s campaign has three main pillars: strengthening access to justice, guaranteeing protection and comprehensive care for survivors and promoting accountability for perpetrators of violence, both in physical and digital spaces.

In Mexico, the 16-day activism plan includes:

November 25: Launch of the campaign

November 26: Certification of Justice Centers for Women

November 27: Forum: Men in the Prevention of Violence

November 28: Inauguration of the Mobile Justice Center in Baja California

November 29: Children’s Day of Community Care

November 30: National System and Xicoténcatl Agreement

December 1: Meeting with Specialized Prosecutor’s Offices

December 2: Panel on Digital Violence and Access to Justice

December 3: National Meeting of Shelters

December 4: Day of Action: “Because It’s Our Responsibility to Protect Them.”

December 5: Inauguration of the Mobile Justice Center in Oaxaca

According to Itzel Castillo, one of the government’s new strategies for tackling gender violence is the digital guide, which is aimed at preventing, identifying and addressing online attacks, with sections directed towards girls, boys, adolescents, adult women and older women, as well as mothers, fathers and caregivers.

She said that the government had worked with major platforms, such as Google, Meta and TikTok, to develop the guide, which is now available for free download.

To date, 26 states have already approved Federal Penal Code reforms with a focus on sexual offenses, according to Itzel Castillo. She emphasized that such reforms have helped reduce femicides by just over 5%.

With reports from Infobae, Enfoque Noticias and Quadratín

World.title: Business leaders: 15% minimum wage hike would cost jobs
World.content:
The presidents of two of Mexico’s leading business groups have rejected the 15% minimum wage increase proposed for 2027 by union representatives.

A 15% increase in the minimum wage — currently 315.04 pesos (about US $16) per day in most of the country after a 13% increase on Jan. 1 — would pose “a risk” to businesses and jobs, according to José Medina Mora, president of the Business Coordinating Council (CCE), an umbrella organization made up of 14 Mexican business groups.

“What it would cause is a loss of jobs,” Medina Mora said Monday at an event in Mexico City organized by Mexico’s Confederation of Industrial Chambers (Concamin).

“We have to look after employment. We’ve become an expensive country for businesses,” he said.

Medina Mora asserted that 60,000 jobs have been lost in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, due to the increase in the minimum wage in the northern border region. The minimum wage there is 440.87 pesos (US $22.50) per day after a 5% increase on Jan. 1.

The CCE chief said that the private sector will propose a single-digit minimum wage increase for 2027 — one of around 6% in most of the country. He said that his proposal for the northern border region is an increase in line with annual inflation, which was just below 4% in the first half of November.

The National Minimum Wage Commission (Conasami) decides the increase after weighing proposals from business, union and government representatives. The annual increase is usually announced in early December before it takes effect on Jan. 1.

The president of Concamin, Alejandro Malagón, also opposes the increase proposed by el sector obrero, as organized labor is commonly known in Mexico.

“[A] double-digit [increase], no,” he said Monday.

“We can’t take it, … it would put too much strain on the situation,” Malagón said, asserting that an increase in the minimum wage of 10% or more would place the survival of businesses at risk.

He also warned of possible job losses and of businesses being unable to pay their bills.

Mexico’s minimum wage has increased significantly during the presidencies of Andrés Manuel López Obrador (2018-24) and Claudia Sheinbaum. In nominal terms, it has risen 256.5% since 2018, when it was 88.36 pesos a day.

In her second annual report to the nation on Sept. 1, Sheinbaum said that the monthly minimum wage has increased “154% in real terms” since 2018 to reach 9,582 pesos (US $490) in 2026.

She asserted in May that Mexico is experiencing a “labor spring” under Morena party governments due to significant annual increases in the minimum wage and the approval of several worker-friendly laws in recent years, including those that doubled paid vacation time and set in motion a phased reduction of the workweek to 40 hours.

Medina Mora: A Mexico-US trade deal could be announced next month

At the Concamin event on Monday, Medina Mora also said that a trade deal between Mexico and the United States could be announced at the upcoming G20 Leaders’ Summit, which will be held at the Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida on Dec. 14 and 15.

Both Sheinbaum and U.S. President Donald Trump said last month that a deal was “very close,” and Trump reiterated that view last Friday.

Mexico and the United States have been seeking to resolve a range of trade-related issues following the U.S. government’s decision in July not to renew the USMCA free trade pact for an additional 16 years to 2042. Trump is particularly concerned about the United States’ large trade deficit with Mexico, while the Mexican government is pushing for a reduction of U.S. tariffs that currently apply to Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

After a meeting with Trump on the sidelines of the APEC Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, last week, Sheinbaum said that bilateral trade negotiations are “very far along.”

For his part, Medina Mora said that Mexico’s negotiations with the U.S. aimed at securing a reduction in the United States’ Section 232 tariffs — which apply to steel, aluminum and vehicles from many countries — are “advanced.”

He said that the Section 232 tariffs — imposed on national security grounds — violate the USMCA and other trade agreements, adding that their implementation last year marked the commencement of a “new era” in international trade.

“We came from an era of free trade agreements and we began an era of international agreements with tariffs,” he said.

“It’s a new global geopolitical reality,” Medina Mora said.

His remarks came after Trump said last Friday that the United States and Mexico were getting “close to a deal.”

⚡️TRUMP AHORA: MEXICO

– Tuve una reunión con Sheinbaum

– ⁠Estamos acercándonos a un acuerdo con México (USMCA)

– ⁠México tiene un superávit (comercial con EUA), no voy a permitirlo

– ⁠Estamos trabajando con la presidenta, los cárteles controlan México FENTANILO

– ⁠El fentanilo que entra a EUA ha caído 97% — Ariel Moutsatsos (@arielmou) November 20, 2026



He asserted that the bilateral trade relationship had been “allowed to get out of hand,” saying that Mexico has a “tremendous surplus with the United States.”

“I said, Claudia, we can’t [let] you have a surplus,” Trump said, referring to his conversation with Sheinbaum in China.

“We’re not going to let that happen. So we’re working with her and we’re working with her on the cartels because the cartels are running Mexico — I told her that,” he said.

“And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico, they’re our neighbor,” Trump said.

Just hours later, Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro,” who was one of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 10 most-wanted fugitives. The Friday night military operation in Guasave, Sinaloa, was informed by U.S. intelligence, Mexican authorities said.

With reports from Imagen Radio, Expansión and El Economista

World.title: A new Museum of Ritual Art in Indigenous Cultures is set to open in Oaxaca
World.content:
A museum projected to open in the city of Oaxaca before Dec. 1 will bring together about 4,000 masks, textiles and other objects from Mexico and more than 30 other countries in a former governor’s residence.

The Museum of Ritual Art in Indigenous Cultures — also called the Museo de las Máscaras, or Mask Museum — will house the collection of Oaxacan researcher René Bustamante in five galleries, with plans also calling for a restoration workshop, library and cafeteria.

It is separate from the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca, run by the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) in the former Santo Domingo convent, and the Oaxaca Textile Museum, run by the Alfredo Harp Helú Oaxaca Foundation.

State officials presented the new museum last week without formally inaugurating or opening it. In August, Gov. Salomón Jara had announced an October opening, but donation paperwork reportedly delayed things.

Officials have since switched to a late November opening without offering any specifics.

The state invested some 98.4 million pesos (about US $5 million) in the museum, according to reports. It covers converting the former governor’s residence into a museum, not the purchase of Bustamante’s donated collection.

The pieces will be installed gradually; officials did not announce admission prices or a director at the presentation.

Bustamante, 75, began documenting dances in Oaxaca some 53 years ago. His research initially focused on dancers’ textiles before expanding to masks and their ritual significance.

The collection will show how communities use masks to represent animals, ancestors, spirits and natural forces, preserving memories and conveying their histories through dance.

The collection includes historic pieces, among them a fishermen’s dance mask from coastal Oaxaca reported to be more than 170 years old.

The museum’s five galleries will focus on Mexico, Guatemala, Africa, Oceania and the wider world.

Other Mexican institutions devoted to masks include the National Mask Museum (Museo Nacional de la Máscara) in San Luis Potosí and the San Miguel Mask Museum (also known as Another Face of Mexico, or La Otra Cara de México) in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato.

The latter is a private museum opened by an American, Bill LeVasseur, and his wife, Heidi, in 2006. It includes more than 500 masks, compared to about 1,300 at the National Mask Museum; the new museum should have at least 700 masks, based on a 2023 mask exhibition from Bustamante’s collection.

Bustamante has no university degree and calls himself a self-taught anthropologist. As a student in 1973, he traveled to Oaxaca’s Costa Chica to study textile symbolism and instead became captivated by the region’s dance traditions. He has since documented more than 80 dance themes.

With reports from El Universal, Oaxaca Media and El Heraldo de México Oaxaca

World.title: Job creation slows and unemployment ticks up in Mexico’s third quarter
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico added 122,348 jobs in the third quarter of 2026, according to official data, down from 487,434 in the second quarter.

The slower pace of job creation coincided with a slowdown in quarter-over-quarter economic growth. Mexico’s economy grew 0.9% on a sequential basis in the third quarter, compared to 1.4% in Q2.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported on Wednesday that 60,162,442 (60.16 million) people were in jobs in the third quarter, up from 60.04 million in the second quarter.

The total number of people in jobs was 628,993 higher in the third quarter than a year earlier.

Overall, the number of women in jobs increased by 157,009 between the second and third quarters, while the number of employed men fell by 34,661.

INEGI also reported on Wednesday that Mexico’s unemployment rate was 2.9% in Q3, up from 2.7% in the previous quarter. That’s the highest rate of any quarter since Q3 of 2024. Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, said that the higher unemployment rate and the high level of employment informality were signs of a “weak” labor market.

Mexico’s employment informality rate — the percentage of total workers employed in the informal sector of the economy — was 55% in Q3, down from 55.1% in Q2.

The newspaper El Economista reported that 78% of the jobs added in the third quarter were formal sector positions, causing the informality rate to decline slightly.

Of the more than 60.1 million people in jobs in the third quarter, 6.9% were underemployed, down from 7.1% in Q2.

Which sectors added the most jobs over the past year?

According to INEGI’s data, 722,566 jobs were added in Mexico’s tertiary or services sector in the 12 months to the end of September. The secondary sector added 179,297 positions in the same period, while the primary sector shed 270,633 jobs.

The industries that added the most jobs between the end of Q3 2025 and the end of Q3 2026 were:

Diverse services: 337,440

Construction: 166,384

Government and international organizations: 152,750

Professional, financial and corporate services: 150,431

Restaurants and accommodation services: 112,475

Social services: 55,599

Manufacturing: 20,799

The composition of Mexico’s workforce

Mexico’s economically active population (PEA) — the number of people in jobs and looking for work — numbers 61.96 million, according to INEGI’s third-quarter data.

The percentage of economically active people who currently hold a paid job (i.e., not seeking employment) is 97% (35.3 million men and 24.9 million women).

Of the 60.16 million people in jobs, 64.3% (38.71 million) work in the tertiary sector, 24.7% (14.85 million) work in the secondary sector and 10.3% (6.19 million) work in the primary sector.

The informal sector workforce is made up of 33.11 million people, or 55% of all workers.

Around 68.4% (41.14 million) of all workers are employees, while 6.2% (3.67 million) are employers.

Around 22% (13.33 million) of employed people work for themselves and have no paid staff. The number of independent, self-employed workers increased by more than 386,000 in the 12 months to the end of September.

Just over 3.2% (1.94 million) of workers are unpaid, according to INEGI’s latest employment data.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: A ‘unique’ human skeleton found during AIFA airport construction may date back 13,000 years
World.content:
A male human skeleton unearthed in 2021 during construction of the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA) outside Mexico City has now been confirmed by the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to date back at least 11,700 years, making it one of the 23 oldest human skeletons found in the Basin of Mexico.

Foreign laboratories determined the age of the find by focusing mainly on the third molar. Isotopic Aging Inc., in Belgium, examined collagen and determined an age of between 12,987 and 13, 087 years before the present. The University of Georgia, in the United States, studied bioapatite — a non-organic substance in human bones and teeth — to come up with an age of between 11,700 and 12,050 years.

“Yotzin is one of the oldest human remains known to us from the Basin of Mexico,” said Culture Minister Claudia Curiel de Icaza, using the skeleton’s nickname from a Náhuatl word for “unique.” “Its dating brings us closer to a period in our history for which very little evidence exists, and it opens up new possibilities for investigating how those populations lived and where they came from.”

Three other human skeletons were found during the AIFA’s construction work, but according to INAH anthropologist Arturo Talavera González, Yotzin’s features are unique, as his nickname implies. He measures 1.75 meters tall and features high bone mass and a “tremendously robust” skeleton, showing characteristics of a hunter used to long-distance walking and combat.

As Yotzin’s teeth were examined, tooth wear was confirmed but there were no cavities. That absence reflects the fact that pre-ceramic hunter-gatherers did not consume sugars or simple carbohydrates. As Talavera explains it, instead they chewed many roots and tough barks, and used their teeth as a “third hand” for cutting and crushing, which accounts for the wear on its teeth.

Yotzin was discovered by archaeologist Israel Peña in the northwestern sector of AIFA, in sediments associated with ancient marshy environments and the remains of Late Pleistocene fauna – primarily mammoths and camels. Initially, Peña assumed they belonged to a camel. But as the excavation expanded, he identified them as human.

INAH expects to have the results of a genomic study from the University of Burgos, Spain, available during the first quarter of 2027. It should clarify the individual’s ancestry and provide information about the ancient populations of the Basin of Mexico, a geological region comprising four valleys, including the Valley of Mexico.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico’s new Animal Welfare Law officially reclassifies Mexico City roof dogs as municipal early-warning infrastructure
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Congress has formally approved the General Law on Animal Welfare, Care and Protection, landmark legislation that legally recognizes domestic animals as sentient beings while carefully preserving the constitutional right of second-story concrete roofs in the capital to serve as unregulated canine surveillance towers.

The sweeping reform, which amends five separate federal statutes and awaits publication in the Official Gazette, mandates that pet owners provide constant access to drinking water, suitable nutrition and shelter from harsh weather. However, legislative aides confirmed that the statute includes a critical semantic carve-out classifying a three-by-four-meter slab of sun-baked mortar in Colonia Narvarte or Santa María la Ribera as “an elevated, open-air security perimeter with panoramic street visibility.”

Under the new framework, failing to meet basic standards of pet care can result in administrative detention of up to 36 hours and steep fines. Yet legal analysts noted that the law’s enforcement mechanisms in Mexico City rely heavily on whether a territorial chihuahua barking at a passing tamales oaxaqueños loudspeaker at 3:14 a.m. constitutes “emotional distress” or “performing essential municipal infrastructure duties.”

“We are thrilled to align Mexico with the highest international standards of animal sentience,” said Hilario Padilla, a policy adviser to the Senate’s Joint Committee on Urban Ecology and Elevated Guard Dogs. “At the same time, we had to respect capital realities. If you take Solovino off a third-floor roof in Iztapalapa, who is going to alert a four-block radius that a gas truck or camote vendor has entered the neighborhood?”

The bill also cracks down on unregulated pet sales on social media platforms and prohibits aesthetic mutilations, though it stops short of defining whether an overturned plastic laundry tub wedged next to a tinaco water tank qualifies as “adequate protection from the elements.” Across Mexico City boroughs from Coyoacán to Azcapotzalco, residents reported that their local roof dogs had already reviewed the legislation and found it entirely satisfactory, largely because nobody climbed the staircase to tell them about it.

Lawmakers indicated that a follow-up subcommittee will convene next spring to determine whether a piece of corrugated fiberglass weighted down by a cinder block meets the federal definition of a “clean and safe environment,” provided the dog is left with at least some shade between noon and 4 p.m.

World.title: Sheinbaum marks Day Against Violence Toward Women, questions US over unfulfilled extraditions: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

👩🏽 Sheinbaum marks International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women: The president noted the date at the start of her press conference. She noted Mexico has sent “94 criminals” to the United States, while “a lot” of its extradition requests, including ones related to the Ayotzinapa case, haven’t been granted. 💼 Sheinbaum’s husband didn’t go to China due to work commitments: Asked why Jesús María Tarriba Unger didn’t accompany her to the APEC Leaders’ Meeting last week, the president said he has his own job at the Bank of Mexico. She noted he often joins her on weekend working trips within Mexico.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At the start of her press conference, President Sheinbaum noted that today is the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.

Minister for Women Laura Itzel Castillo announced that Mexico would once again take part in the United Nations’ 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence campaign, which starts today.

Among the other notable issues discussed at today’s mañanera were the dispute between coffee growers in Chiapas and the Swiss multinational Nestlé, and the release of Inés Gómez Mont, a former Mexican television host, from immigration detention in the United States.

Gómez, who was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Oct. 30 for overstaying her U.S. visa, is wanted in Mexico for alleged tax fraud and embezzlement. On Monday, she was released from ICE custody and removed from the United States, according to a Department of Homeland Security statement sent to the newspaper El Universal.

Sheinbaum sides with coffee growers in dispute with Nestlé

A reporter noted that coffee producers in Chiapas protested against the low prices they are paid by Nestlé to grow coffee beans for Nescafé. The producers say they receive 43 pesos (US $2.20) per kilogram and are pushing for 60 pesos. The reporter asked the president whether federal authorities would speak with the coffee producers and governor of Chiapas about the issue. She also asked whether the government could provide additional incentives to coffee growers through the Alimentación para el Bienestar (Food for Well-being) program.

“I agree with the campesinos, with the coffee growers,” Sheinbaum said.

“Nestlé has to pay what it has to pay for a kilo of coffee,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that coffee producers say that Nestlé sells coffee for 580 pesos per kilo, but only pays 43 pesos for a kilo of beans.

“I think what they’re asking is for them to buy [a kilo of coffee beans] for between 50 and 60 pesos. We completely agree with what they’re requesting,” she said.

Sheinbaum said she had instructed the minister of agriculture to “support” the coffee growers in Chiapas in their negotiations with Nestlé.

“It cannot be that the international market sets the price of coffee for coffee growers through intermediaries … and that the price of Nescafé doesn’t come down,” she said.

“The coffee growers are right and we’re going to support them,” Sheinbaum said.

“And Nestlé has to pay [a fair price] and has to buy directly from the producers,” she added.

Sheinbaum questions why the US didn’t extradite Inés Gómez Mont to Mexico

Sheinbaum said that the release of Gómez Mont from ICE custody and her removal from the United States — but not to Mexico — is a “very important issue” in Mexico’s relationship with the U.S.

She noted that Gómez Mont was the subject of an Interpol Red Notice because a warrant for her arrest was issued in Mexico.

But the Red Notice — a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action — was “withdrawn” around a month ago, Sheinbaum said.

“So we have a very relevant complaint with Interpol. Why was this Red Notice withdrawn?” she said.

Sheinbaum said that Gómez Mont entered the United States on her Spanish passport and was consequently deported to Spain.

She questioned why U.S. authorities didn’t send her to Mexico given that “they know” there is an outstanding warrant for her arrest here.

“What we ask for in the relationship, as we have always said, is reciprocity,” Sheinbaum said, noting that her government has sent “94 criminals” — including a number of high-profile cartel figures — to the United States.

She said that “a lot” of Mexico’s extradition requests to the United States haven’t been granted, including ones for suspects in the infamous Ayotzinapa case involving the abduction and presumed murder of 43 students in Guerrero in 2014.

After reiterating that Gómez Mont’s case is an “important” issue in the Mexico-U.S. relationship, Sheinbaum said her government would send a diplomatic note to its U.S. counterpart.

She added that her administration has submitted a request to the government of Spain for Gómez Mont’s extradition to Mexico.

“We already requested it. But we’re interested in knowing why the Red Notice was withdrawn … because there is ample proof that she dedicated herself to fake invoices,” Sheinbaum said.

“So why wasn’t she extradited to Mexico?”

Sheinbaum explains why her husband didn’t accompany her to China

Asked why her husband, Jesús María Tarriba Unger, didn’t accompany her to China last week for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting, Sheinbaum explained that he had work commitments.

“My husband works,” she said before breaking into a hearty laugh.

“As you know, he works at the Bank of Mexico,” Sheinbaum said, referring to Tarriba’s employment at the central bank as a financial risk specialist.

“He goes to work every day. … That’s why he didn’t go with me,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that Tarriba does often accompany her on her weekend working trips to different parts of Mexico.

“But on this occasion, well, he also has his job,” she said.

World.title: MND Local BCS: Enjoying film and food festivals in Los Cabos, plus a guide to whale watching season
World.content:
Celebrities were synonymous with Los Cabos long before that moniker — a reference to the shared word for “cape” in both Cabo San Lucas and San José del Cabo — was officially coined for the newly minted municipality in 1981. When tourism began in the area in the late 1950s, celebrities were among the first guests at local hotels, including movie stars like John Wayne and Bing Crosby.

It’s not surprising, really, when you consider that Los Angeles has always been Los Cabos’ primary market for international arrivals, or that before the first scheduled flight from Los Angeles to La Paz was inaugurated in 1962, one needed either a boat or a private plane to reach Los Cabos’ early hotels.

But even as Los Cabos became more accessible in subsequent decades, celebrities continued to be among the destination’s most loyal visitors, a trend that has continued into the present.

However, it is only since 2012 that Hollywood A-listers have come to Los Cabos not just for pleasure, but also for business.

The Los Cabos International Film Festival returns in December

Numerous stars have walked the red carpet for opening night at the Los Cabos International Film Festival, or appeared to receive awards or talk up their latest films, including actors Monica Bellucci, Robert De Niro, Matt Dillon, Adam Driver, Gael García Bernal, Daniel Giménez Cacho, Nicole Kidman, Jared Leto, Diego Luna, Virginia Madsen, Ewan McGregor, Liam Neeson and Reese Witherspoon, and directors such as Terry Gilliam, Spike Lee and Oliver Stone.

Despite the movie star glamor, the festival is perhaps best known internationally as an industry platform that brings together filmmakers from the U.S., Canada and Mexico for behind-the-scenes dealmaking, and as a support network for Mexican filmmakers through its Gabriel Figueroa Film Fund (named for the acclaimed Mexican cinematographer). Locally, however, it’s the screenings that are the festival’s most beloved feature, including, through the years, the Mexican premieres for films like “Jackie” and “The Killing of a Sacred Deer.”

Screenings

For those planning to be in Los Cabos from Dec. 9-13, the scheduled dates for the 14th edition of the Los Cabos International Film Festival, headline screenings include “Elsinore,” a film starring Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman and “Mobland” villain Johnny Flynn, which will open the festival with an outdoor showing at the Puerto Los Cabos Marina.

Visit the festival’s website for a complete listing of screenings and events, including a Dec. 10 tribute to Dolores Heredia presented by fellow Mexican actor José María Yazpik. Like the majority of screenings, this retrospective will take place at Cinépolis in San José del Cabo, with tickets available to the public. The closing night outdoor screening, meanwhile, will be free in Plaza Mijares in San José del Cabo, although the film has yet to be announced.

Dates: Dec. 9-13

Location: Cinépolis, Mauricio Castro 1738, Campo de Golf Fonatur, 23400 San José del Cabo, B.C.S.

Cost: Not yet announced

Whale watching season approaching in Los Cabos

You don’t need to take a cruise to see whales in Los Cabos, as transiting cetaceans can be seen from virtually every coastal vantage during winter months. However, boat tours, particularly aboard high-speed inflatable Zodiacs, do offer the most intimate encounters once the season officially starts on Dec. 15, although “intimate” is relative, since regulations prevent boats from getting closer to whales than 60 to 80 meters (depending on the size of the boat).

For the benefit of first-time visitors, whale watching season essentially heralds the arrival of 5,000 or so whales, which have migrated from summer feeding grounds in the Arctic to their winter breeding grounds around Baja California Sur. Numerous whales make this annual journey, including gray and humpback whales, as well as blue, bryde, fin, minke, orca and sei species.

Gray whales are the main attractions in Magdalena Bay and the San Ignacio and Ojo de Liebre lagoons within the El Vizcaíno Biosphere Reserve, while in Los Cabos, transiting humpbacks, known for their spectacular breaching behavior, are typically the stars of local tours.

The season runs through April 15.

Foodie fest Sabor a Cabo returns

Sabor a Cabo was firmly established as the premier food festival in Los Cabos, at least before the COVID-19 pandemic, when the annual eat, drink and be merry fête featuring gourmet fare from international chefs and more than 50 local restaurants drew thousands of attendees, as well as a wealth of world-class musical talent, from Lila Downs to Earth, Wind and Fire.

This decade, though, the event sponsored by CANIRAC Los Cabos, the local restaurant association, suffered a long absence from annual event calendars during a three-year hiatus from 2020 to 2022 — although Sabor a Cabo Rural, a smaller gastronomic get-together held each spring in organic farm-to-table farming community Miraflores, has been more consistently scheduled.

The 18th edition of the main event, themed “La Verbena Sibarita” (“The Sybarite’s Fair”), should help restore Sabor a Cabo to its former prestige, particularly if organizers reach their targeted attendance of 3,500 on Dec. 5 at EDEA Venue, just outside Cabo San Lucas.

What to expect for the 2026 edition

The food and wine attractions will be abundant, highlighted by fare from 45 restaurants and a wine garden focused on Mexican vintners, with over 40 represented (many from Baja California’s Valle de Guadalupe). A producer’s market will also be held this year, along with a mixology garden; a chef’s plaza showcasing classes and presentations; a sybarite’s market spotlighting artisanal cheeses, chocolates and other gourmet goods; and “streets” focused on everything from seafood and tacos to coffee and desserts. The musical headliner is La Única Internacional Sonora Santanera.

Date: Dec. 5, 5 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Location: EDEA Venue, behind Viveros de la Baja, Puente Salto Seco, El Arenal, 23460 Cabo San Lucas, B.C.S.

Cost: General admission tickets are 3,250 pesos; VIP tickets are 5,600 pesos

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Venezuela Signs Power Deals With Siemens
World.content:
Venezuela has signed the first steps of a deal with a German group to rebuild its failing power system, but no price or timetable has been given.

Venezuela’s lights have been failing for more than a decade, and on Wednesday its government called in Siemens Energy, the German power-equipment maker, to help fix them. Two agreements were signed in Caracas on Nov. 25, 2026, and word of them was out by 6:45 p.m. ET (7:45 p.m. Caracas).

The deals add a new strand to the Venezuela US tensions between Caracas and Washington, because Acting President Delcy Rodríguez, who leads Venezuela’s interim government, says eased sanctions made them possible. They also follow a new electricity law meant to lure private and foreign money into a state-run sector.

Key Facts What: Venezuela and Siemens Energy signed two start-up accords to repair the power grid.

Who: Acting President Delcy Rodríguez and Siemens Energy CEO Christian Bruch led the ceremony.

When and where: Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026, in Caracas; exact time not reported.

The numbers: No contract value, financing or deadline has been disclosed.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, a prediction market, gives Rodríguez 4.4% odds of being out by Dec. 31 (8:13 p.m. ET).

Two Accords, Signed in One Ceremony

The first accord covers the electricity that powers oil operations. Héctor Andrés Obregón, president of the state oil company PDVSA, signed it with Christian Bruch, Siemens Energy’s president and global chief executive.

The second covers repair and maintenance of the national grid. Rolando Alcalá, the electric energy minister, signed it with Bruch, according to the state news agency AVN, which carried the government’s account.

Rodríguez led the ceremony, with Paula Henao, the hydrocarbons minister, and Juan Fernández, head of the state utility Corpoelec, among those present. Venezuelan officials describe both as the start of strategic alliances, built on technical support and technological modernisation.

Why Sanctions Sit at the Centre

“In Siemens’ case we could not get access because of sanctions, and today we are making it possible,” Rodríguez said at the signing, in a translation of her Spanish. She said the restrictions had blocked parts and equipment for more than a decade and were eased this year.

She added that much of the country’s thermoelectric fleet, its gas- and fuel-burning power stations, relies on Siemens equipment, and that work would start immediately. Rodríguez also said the effort began two years ago and credited diplomatic relations with Germany and other European countries.

She called grid recovery decisive for the government’s Venezuela Renace economic plan.

A Grid Law and a Decade of Blackouts

The signing came two weeks after parliament, which the governing chavista movement (supporters of the late president Hugo Chávez) controls, passed a reform of the electricity law on Nov. 10. It lets the state operator, mixed companies and authorised private firms generate power, with private concessions of up to 25 years.

Venezuela has had an electricity crisis for more than a decade, and blackouts have grown worse over the past year, sparking protests in several states. The opposition and experts blame corruption and poor maintenance, while the government points to sanctions, weather and alleged sabotage.

Chávez nationalised the sector in 2007. For the wider backdrop, see our Venezuela geopolitics explainer.

What Prediction Markets Say

No market covers the Siemens deal itself. On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, traders put the chance of Rodríguez being out as Venezuela’s leader by Dec. 31 at 4.4%, with US$663,618 traded at 8:13 p.m. ET on Nov. 25.

What It Means for US Readers

A German industrial group is returning to Venezuela’s energy sector, and the Venezuelan government says sanctions relief allowed it. Reliable oil-field power would be the likeliest winner if the work is delivered, because the first accord targets the electricity that PDVSA’s fields depend on.

The risk is delay. With no price, financing or deadline made public, the next signal to watch is whether Siemens Energy or Washington confirms any licence or timetable.

What Is Not Known

No contract values, financing or timelines have been given, and it is unclear whether the start-up records are binding contracts. Siemens Energy’s own statement was not found, and neither side has said which US licences or other measures allow the work.

The exact time of the signing was not reported. We found no reaction yet from the opposition, outside experts, the US government or Germany.

World.title: Corn Rises 1.29% and Soybeans 0.35% as Wheat Slips | Grains Wrap, Nov 25
World.content:
Grain funds bounced after weeks of losses, but corn is still 15.1% below its September peak and wheat 23.9% below its August high.

Think of the grain market as a three-lane road. On Wednesday, November 25, 2026, corn and soybeans moved forward while wheat drifted back.

The soybean-tracking fund added 0.35% and corn +1.29%, while the wheat-tracking fund lost 0.23%.

Key Facts Corn led: the corn fund rose 1.29% to US$17.22, a third straight gain, 15.1% below its September peak.

the corn fund rose 1.29% to US$17.22, a third straight gain, 15.1% below its September peak. Soybeans: the soybean fund rose 0.35% to US$25.98, a fourth straight gain.

the soybean fund rose 0.35% to US$25.98, a fourth straight gain. Wheat: the wheat fund fell 0.23% to US$21.30 and is 23.9% below its 28 August high of 28.00.

the wheat fund fell 0.23% to US$21.30 and is 23.9% below its 28 August high of 28.00. Risk mood: the VIX fear gauge rose 7.32% to 28.29, yet grains still gained.

the VIX fear gauge rose 7.32% to 28.29, yet grains still gained. Funds, not grain: these funds track futures contracts, not the price a farmer receives.

Grains — the daily wrap.

Today’s Focus Corn and soybeans rose on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, while wheat slipped, and the split tells you where the money believes demand is. No single trigger is confirmed. Corn’s gain was the sharpest. The corn-tracking fund closed at US$17.22, up +1.29%. The bounce is small against the fall behind it. Over 60 sessions the soybean fund is down 6.5%, corn down 15.1% and wheat down 23.9%, so this looks like a pause in a long retreat. China’s choice of Brazilian over American soybeans and the size of Brazil’s coming harvest are the two forces that decide whether this bounce lasts.

01 The session in one read

No single driver is confirmed. For a reader outside the trade, the point is that grain prices are increasingly shaped far from Chicago, in Beijing and Brazil’s farm belt.

02 The board

The soybean fund closed at US$25.98 and the corn fund at US$17.22. Both are proxies: they follow futures contracts, not the price a farmer receives.

The wheat fund finished at US$21.30. Corn’s 5-session gain of 2.01% and soybeans’ 1.56% show the rebound has some depth; wheat’s 0.57% five-day gain is thin and has just reversed.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest: China’s tariff stance. Beijing keeps an extra 10% retaliatory tariff on American soybeans, so its crushers buy South American beans. Confidence: medium.

Second: position-covering. After weeks of losses, traders who had bet on lower prices may have bought back contracts, which magnifies a rise. Confidence: low to medium.

Third: wheat slipped 0.23% with no confirmed trigger. Confidence: low.

The usual drivers were mixed. The dollar index eased 0.11% to 103.70 and the 10-year Treasury yield fell 7 basis points to 4.86%, which helps dollar-priced grain a little. But the S&P 500 fell 0.25% and the VIX rose, so risk appetite was not the driver, while oil’s 3.29% jump in the USO fund hints at support through fuel and biofuel demand.

04 The trend behind it

The soybean fund is 7.7% below its 10 September high of 28.14 and 19.7% above its 13 January low of 21.71.

Corn is 4.6% above its 29 June low of 16.47 but 15.1% below its September peak. Wheat has fallen furthest, 23.9% from its August high, and is 7.1% above its 17 December 2025 low of 19.88.

This is a continuation of a late-summer to autumn retreat, with a relief bounce on top. It is not yet a new phase.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil gains most from China’s preference. Conab, the national crop agency, puts the 2026/27 soybean crop at about 181.6 million tonnes, while the US Department of Agriculture sees 186 million, and each extra tonne goes to a hungry Chinese buyer.

The catch is price. A record harvest pushes prices down, so Brazilian farmers earn more in volume but less per bag, and a weaker real helps them only if the dollar price holds.

Argentina, the third big exporter of soy products, faces the same pressure on prices from Brazil’s supply. Wheat’s 23.9% slide from its peak squeezes Argentine growers, while importers such as Mexico and Peru enjoy cheaper bread flour and feed.

06 The names to watch

Watch the three trackers: the soybean fund, the corn fund and the wheat fund. They follow the contracts that farmers, flour millers and feed makers use to lock in prices.

Outside the funds, Conab’s monthly crop surveys and the US Department of Agriculture’s Brazil estimates move the market. A cut to Brazil’s expected harvest would be the surprise that matters.

07 What would end it

For soybeans, 28.14 is the ceiling and 21.71 the floor; for corn, 20.29 and 16.47; for wheat, 28.00 and 19.88. Corn at 17.22 is still much closer to its floor than its ceiling.

A weather scare in Brazil or Argentina, or a confirmed Chinese buying spree, would lift prices. A smooth Brazilian planting season and an end to the tariff dispute would push them down.

The honest answer is that the bounce can run a few more sessions, but without a supply shock the broader slide is more likely to resume.

08 What to watch

China purchases: Chinese buying of Brazilian beans: the 10% tariff on US soybeans is the reason to watch it.

Chinese buying of Brazilian beans: the 10% tariff on US soybeans is the reason to watch it. Conab and USDA estimates: Any revision to Brazil’s expected record crop of about 181.6 to 186 million tonnes.

Any revision to Brazil’s expected record crop of about 181.6 to 186 million tonnes. Wheat support: The 19.88 low in the wheat fund, 6.7% below Wednesday’s level, is the next big test.

The 19.88 low in the wheat fund, 6.7% below Wednesday’s level, is the next big test. Dollar and yields: A dollar index near 103.70 and a 10-year yield at 4.86% both ease pressure on dollar-priced grain.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did corn and soybeans rise on Wednesday, November 25, 2026?

No single trigger is confirmed: the corn and soybean funds rose after weeks of losses, while the wheat fund slipped 0.23%.

Why does Brazil matter for grain prices?

It is the world’s biggest soybean exporter, and China is its largest buyer.

Are these prices the grain itself?

No. They are funds that track futures contracts, so they follow the market but are not the price a farmer or buyer pays.

Will the rally last?

Probably only briefly: all three funds sit well below their summer peaks, and Brazil’s expected record crop caps the upside.

Oil — the daily wrap.

Key Facts Oil fund: USO, which tracks US crude futures, rose 3.29% to US$139.89, a second straight gain.

USO, which tracks US crude futures, rose 3.29% to US$139.89, a second straight gain. Still down: the fund is 17.5% below its 23 October peak and down 16.02% in 20 sessions.

No single trigger is confirmed. US government data showed crude stocks rising, which is mildly bearish, yet the fund still gained 3.29% (US Energy Information Administration, week to 20 November). What matters today. Oil bounced from a deep fall without a confirmed reason, so the move looks like short-term buying after a month of losses. 03 Why it moved

First and heaviest: a bounce after a long fall. The fund is down 16.02% over 20 sessions, so even a calm day invited buyers. Confidence: medium.

Second: the usual drivers did not help. The dollar index was 103.70, down 0.11%, and the 10-year US Treasury yield eased by 7 basis points to 4.86%, which usually supports oil modestly. Against that, the S&P 500 slipped 0.25% to 7,183 and the VIX fear gauge rose 7.32% to 28.29 (RT, 25 November close).

Third: US stocks of crude rose. The US Energy Information Administration (eia.gov) reported commercial crude stocks of 418.9 million barrels in the week to 20 November, up 1.1 million. Those are reasons for caution, so some of Wednesday’s gain is likely short-covering rather than new belief in higher prices. Confidence: low to medium.

04 The trend behind it

The fund has lost 16.02% over 20 sessions, and sits 111.4% above its 12-month low of 66.17 set on 16 December 2025. It is a long way up from there and a long way down from October.

This looks like a continuation of the correction, not a new phase. Petrobras is a clearer picture of the damage than the fund itself.

Our own history since 2007 offers a sober reference. After 33 earlier falls of this size, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 16 cases, or 48%, with a median change of -1.3% and a worst case of -32.4%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Latin America splits on oil. Exporters such as Brazil, Colombia and Argentina earn less per barrel, while importers and drivers gain from cheaper fuel.

On Wednesday the region’s oil shares rose with crude, apart from Argentina’s YPF (RT, 25 November close).

06 The names to watch

Petrobras is up 2.43% on the day but 27.14% lower over 20 sessions and 38.6% below its 26.16 peak of 23 October. Its low of 11.54 on 7 January is the floor investors will watch.

Ecopetrol is 3.09% higher on the day, 27.0% below its 18.26 high of 15 September and 44.7% above its 12-month low of 9.21. YPF, down 0.82% in a rising market, moves more on Argentine politics and its own drilling than on oil’s daily swings.

07 What would end it

On the chart, the fund’s nearest support is the round 130 area, then the 12-month low of 66.17; resistance is the 23 October high of 169.53. The next US crude stock report from the Energy Information Administration is the next hard check.

The honest answer is that the fall can pause but not yet end. It stops only if buyers keep returning and crude stocks stop rising.

08 What to watch

US crude stocks: The next weekly report shows whether the 1.1 million barrel build was a one-off.

The next weekly report shows whether the 1.1 million barrel build was a one-off. The 130 area: A close back below it would suggest Wednesday’s bounce failed.

A close back below it would suggest Wednesday’s bounce failed. Petrobras support: The 12-month low of 11.54 is the floor to watch if crude slips again.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did oil rise on 25 November?

No single trigger is confirmed. The US oil fund gained 3.29% after a month of losses, even though US crude stocks rose 1.1 million barrels.

Does USO show the oil price?

No. USO is a US fund that tracks West Texas Intermediate crude, so its price is a proxy, not the oil price itself.

Who benefits from cheaper oil in Latin America?

Importers and drivers gain, while exporters such as Brazil, Colombia and Argentina earn less per barrel.

Is this the bottom?

Not confirmed. Our history shows moves this large were followed by gains only 48% of the time, so treat Wednesday as a bounce, not a turn.

CSN, the Brazilian group whose New York shares had fallen to a 12-month low on 20 November, jumped hardest. The likeliest cause is bargain-hunting after a brutal fall. What matters today. Latin American steel shares bounced together after weeks of selling, but nothing confirms that the slide has ended. 01 The session in one read

For a foreign reader, the point is that the rally came from low prices, not from confirmed news.

02 The board

The most violent move belonged to CSN, whose American depositary receipts (dollar-traded certificates of its Brazilian shares) rose +6.31% to US$0.5422. Gerdau added +4.68% to US$4.47 and Ternium +3.21% to US$48.84.

The SLX fund, which holds steel producers worldwide, rose only +1.34% to US$90.42. Latin American names outran the global group, a sign of rebound buying in beaten-down shares.

03 Why it moved

First, and with the most weight, was an oversold bounce. CSN had dropped 32.23% in 20 sessions and 52.0% in 60, so even a calm day invited buyers (confidence: medium-high).

Second, the wider markets gave mixed signals. The 10-year US Treasury yield eased 7 basis points to 4.86% and the dollar index slipped 0.11% to 103.70, which usually helps emerging-market shares, yet the S&P 500 fell 0.25% and the VIX fear gauge rose 7.32% to 28.29.

Oil also gained 3.29% in the USO fund, which can lift Latin American sentiment broadly. We rate the cross-asset link as weak: the bounce was driven mostly by company and sector factors, with about medium confidence overall.

04 The trend behind it

The picture is still one of decline. The SLX fund is 20.4% below its 2 June high, down 16.5% over 60 sessions and 2.08% lower over five, though 13.4% above its 12-month low of 25 November 2025.

Gerdau is better placed, 37.1% above its March low.

This is a continuation, not a new phase. Rebounds of one or two days have not yet changed the direction of the 20- and 60-session trends.

05 What it means for Latin America

Steel prices feed into construction costs and factory jobs in Brazil and Mexico, so a weak sector weighs on both economies. We could not confirm today’s import figures, tariff changes or trade talks, so we print none.

For investors in São Paulo or Mexico City, the lesson is that steel shares can swing sharply on small news. CSN’s American depositary receipts (dollar-traded certificates of its Brazilian shares) trade below US$1, so percentage moves look large.

06 The names to watch

CSN is the most fragile: its shares sit just above the 12-month low, and in our own history such falls have often continued. Gerdau is the Brazilian bellwether and has risen three days in a row.

Ternium, the Mexican producer, is the steadiest of the three on the day, up 3.21%. We found no fresh data on Usiminas, a Brazilian steelmaker, so we leave it out rather than guess.

07 What would end it

For the SLX fund, the nearest support is the 12-month low of 79.77, set a year ago, and the nearest resistance is the 2 June high of 113.57. For CSN, support is the 20 November low of 0.51 and for Gerdau the 20 October high of 5.24 is the ceiling.

Our own price history offers a sober check. The SLX fund fell 10.9% in 20 sessions, and in 52 earlier cases of a move this large it was higher 20 sessions later in 27 (52%), with a median gain of 1.3% and a worst case of 35.0% lower. CSN fell 32.2% in 20 sessions; in 17 earlier cases it was higher 20 sessions later in only 7 (41%), with a median of 2.8% lower and a worst case of 45.5% lower. History is not a forecast.

The decline would end only if selling pressure in the global steel sector eased. Nothing confirms that yet.

08 What to watch

CSN’s low: A close below the 20 November low would extend the slide.

A close below the 20 November low would extend the slide. Gerdau’s ceiling: A close above the 20 October high of 5.24 would show the rebound has legs.

A close above the 20 October high of 5.24 would show the rebound has legs. The SLX fund: Its 12-month low of 79.77 is the line below which the global slide would deepen.

SLX is an exchange-traded fund, a basket of shares that trades like one stock, holding steel producers around the world.

Is this a buying signal?

Not by itself. In our own history, the SLX fund was higher 20 sessions later in 52% of comparable cases, and CSN in only 41%. Past results are not a forecast.

03 Why it moved

First, in our reading: falling yields. The US 10-year yield dropped 7 basis points on the day and 22 basis points over five sessions, and the dollar index slipped 0.11% to 103.70, which makes metals priced in dollars cheaper for foreign buyers. Confidence: medium-high.

The signals conflict. The S&P 500 fell 0.25% to 7,183 and the VIX rose 7.32% to 28.29, so this was not a day of broad risk appetite. The gold fund fell 4.03% over five sessions as strong US data fed bets on higher interest rates (RT economic calendar, 25 November), and that weighs on Buenaventura.

We found no single zinc headline behind the day’s jump. Our best reading, at low-to-medium confidence, is bargain-hunting after a 20.6% fall in 60 sessions, with oil’s 3.29% rise adding support for energy-linked metals.

04 The trend behind it

Nexa’s 12-month range runs from 6.50 on 25 November 2025 to 16.72 on 6 May 2026. It now sits 60.3% above the low but 37.7% below the high, so it is roughly where a long retreat has taken it, not at a final low.

Buenaventura is in a harsher phase: 53.5% below its 27 February high of 43.67. This is a continuation, not a new phase, because the yield relief of the past week has not yet reversed either chart.

05 What it means for Latin America

Peru feels this most. It hosts Nexa’s Cerro Pasco, Cerro Lindo and Atacocha mines and Buenaventura’s gold and silver operations, so falling share prices mirror pressure on mining royalties, local jobs and the sol economy.

Mexico and Bolivia are also major zinc producers, but we have no figures on their output today.

06 The names to watch

Nexa is the cleaner zinc proxy.

Buenaventura is a weaker zinc signal because gold and silver dominate its revenue. Its history is sobering: after six earlier falls this large it was higher 20 sessions later in only 1 of 6 cases, or 17%.

Our records since 2017 show Nexa was higher after 20 sessions in 20 of 41 comparable falls, with a median move of -3.1% and a worst case of -57.0%. Buenaventura’s median in the earlier cases was -10.3%, with a worst of -28.1%. History is not a forecast, but it says a rebound is a coin toss, not a given.

07 What would end it

For Nexa, the round number of 10 is the first support and the 20-session slide shows how easily it can give way. The 12-month low of 6.50 is the deeper floor, and resistance lies far above at the 16.72 peak.

For Buenaventura, the line is the 19.61 low set on 20 November, with 20 as the round number just above the close. A fall through it would open the way to fresh lows.

The next catalyst is the next US inflation data, which drove gold’s slide. The honest answer to whether the slide stops: only if yields keep falling and fear stops rising, and Wednesday did not prove either.

08 What to watch

US yields: Whether the 10-year yield keeps falling from 4.86%; it is the cleanest driver for both miners.

Whether the 10-year yield keeps falling from 4.86%; it is the cleanest driver for both miners. Fear gauge: The VIX at 28.29 has risen 15.19% in five sessions; a calm-down would help miners.

The VIX at 28.29 has risen 15.19% in five sessions; a calm-down would help miners. Buenaventura floor: A close under the 19.61 low of 20 November would signal fresh weakness.

Why did zinc miners rise on Wednesday, November 25, 2026?

Lower US bond yields and a softer dollar helped, and the shares were also oversold after a 20.6% fall in 60 sessions for Nexa.

Is Nexa Resources a direct measure of zinc?

No. It is a leading producer whose shares track zinc, so it reflects the metal but also mine disruptions and company news.

Why does gold matter for Buenaventura?

Buenaventura earns much of its revenue from gold and silver, so a weak gold fund, down 4.03% over five sessions, pulls its shares lower.

Does history say the rebound will last?

Not reliably. After 41 earlier falls this large, Nexa was higher 20 sessions later in 49% of cases, and past patterns are not a forecast.

World.content:
Brazil's biggest miner bounced but is still 44.9% below its April high; Rio Tinto rose 1.90% and CSN Mineração fell 3.24% on the day.

Vale’s New York shares rose on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, ending a slide that had pushed them to 9.37 on 24 November. That was the lowest close in 12 months.

The rebound was modest against the scale of the fall. Vale is still 44.9% below its 12-month high of 17.82, reached on 20 April.

Key Facts Vale rebound: its New York shares rose 4.70% to US$9.81, a day after a 12-month low of 9.37.

Iron Ore — the daily wrap.

Today’s Focus Vale, the Brazilian miner that is one of the world’s two biggest iron ore exporters, bounced on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. Its New York shares rose after a brutal run that took them to a 12-month low the day before. The bounce looks like bargain-hunting, not a change of mood. Iron ore is the red rock that is melted into steel, and China buys most of it. Chinese crude steel output in October was 70.83 million tonnes, down 1.6% from a year earlier (China’s statistics bureau, via SteelOrbis), so mills are taking less ore. Vale’s shares are still 14.47% down over 20 sessions. Iron ore demand comes from China’s steel mills, and until they buy more, Brazil’s biggest exporter has no firm floor.

01 The session in one read

02 The board

Vale closed at US$9.81, up 4.70%. That was its first daily gain after a long run of losses, and it sits 5 sessions down 2.29%, so the week is still negative.

Rio Tinto rose 1.90% to US$74.58, while CSN Mineração, a Brazilian producer listed in São Paulo, fell 3.24% to R$4.78. That was its third straight fall.

Miners did not move together, which suggests investors were picking stocks, not buying the whole sector.

03 Why it moved

The first and heaviest cause is weak Chinese demand. China makes more than half of the world’s steel.

The second cause is the wider market mood. The VIX fear gauge rose 7.32% to 28.29 and the S&P 500 slipped 0.25% to 7,183 (RT, 25 November close), which hurts risk-sensitive stocks such as miners.

The usual drivers did not explain the bounce. The dollar index eased 0.11% to 103.70 and the 10-year US Treasury yield fell 7 basis points to 4.86%, which usually helps commodities, so those were a mild tailwind at most.

Our best reading, with medium confidence, is that the rise was investors covering bets against Vale after a stretch of selling that had gone too far.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. Vale has lost 35.1% in 60 sessions and 14.47% in 20, and its low of 9.37 was only a day old when the bounce came.

Rio Tinto tells the same story. It is 33.4% below its 12-month high of 112.04, set on 13 May, and has lost 26.8% in 60 sessions.

Our price history adds a cautionary note. Vale’s shares have fallen at least as hard as they did over the last 20 sessions in 52 earlier cases since 2007.

In 25 of those 52 cases, or 48%, the price was higher 20 sessions later, with a median move of -2.3%, a worst case of -37.7% and a best case of +31.9%. History is not a forecast, but it says that a drop this size gives no reliable signal that the worst is over.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil feels this most. Iron ore is one of its largest exports, and Vale is its biggest mining company, so lower prices mean less tax revenue, weaker export earnings and a softer real.

For Brazilian investors, CSN Mineração is the clearest local proxy. It sits 31.6% below its 12-month high of 6.99, reached on 10 September, and 17.2% above its low of 4.08 on 19 May.

Chile and Peru are less exposed, as copper matters more to them. A broad slump in Chinese steel, however, tends to drag down all industrial metals and the budgets that depend on them.

06 The names to watch

Rio Tinto is the global comparison. Its 12-month low of 71.07 was set on 25 November 2025, so the shares sit 4.9% above it a year later.

CSN Mineração is the more fragile name, as a smaller producer with less room to absorb falling prices.

07 What would end it

The first signal is on the chart. If Vale closes below 9.37, the 12-month low, the slide is unbroken; a climb back towards 11 would suggest the bottom is in.

The second is Chinese output. The next Chinese steel output figures will show whether mills are starting to restock.

The third is policy. Only a new stimulus push for Chinese construction and infrastructure would lift demand quickly.

The honest answer is that this probably does not stop until Chinese mills turn profitable again.

08 What to watch

Chinese steel output: The next monthly figures show whether mills keep cutting.

The next monthly figures show whether mills keep cutting. Vale’s 12-month low: A close below 9.37 would confirm the slide; a hold above it would support the rebound.

A close below 9.37 would confirm the slide; a hold above it would support the rebound. China stimulus: Any support for property or infrastructure would be the quickest route to higher ore prices.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Vale’s share price track iron ore?

Iron ore is Vale’s main product, so when the price of the rock falls, the company’s profits and its share price fall too. That is why its shares serve as a stand-in for the ore itself.

Why does China matter so much?

China is the world’s largest steel producer and the biggest buyer of iron ore. When its mills cut output, demand for ore falls everywhere.

Is Wednesday’s rebound the bottom?

Not yet. The bounce came a day after a 12-month low, and Chinese steel demand has not improved.

How does this affect ordinary Brazilians?

Lower ore prices cut export earnings and tax revenue, and can weaken the real, which raises the cost of imports and foreign travel.

World.title: Lithium Fund Falls 1.55% as Miners Bounce | Lithium Wrap, Nov 25
World.content:
Lithium miners sit 42.3% below their May high; Albemarle and Chile's SQM bounced on Wednesday while the broader LIT fund slipped.

Lithium — the daily wrap.

Key Facts LIT fund: closed at US$52.86 (-1.55%), 42.3% below its 11 May high of 91.62.

closed at US$52.86 (-1.55%), 42.3% below its 11 May high of 91.62. Near the floor: the fund is 1.7% above its 12-month low of 51.98, struck on 20 November.

LIT is down 15.68% over 20 sessions and 29.2% over 60. Producers bounced: Albemarle rose 1.08% to US$81.50 and Chile’s SQM 2.05% to US$47.84.

Albemarle rose 1.08% to US$81.50 and Chile’s SQM 2.05% to US$47.84. History: after 12 earlier falls this large, LIT was higher 20 sessions later in 10; not a forecast.

Today’s Focus Lithium, the light metal at the heart of electric-car batteries, is having its worst stretch in years. The lithium-miners fund LIT closed Wednesday at US$52.86, down 1.55% on the day and 42.3% below its 11 May peak. The main cause is oversupply. China, which refines most of the world’s lithium, has seen carbonate prices drop to their lowest this year as stocks pile up and demand cools. SQM, Chile’s lithium giant, confirmed the pain on 17 November by warning that fourth-quarter prices could be substantially lower. Assessment — Glut-driven slump, with bounce risk MEDIUM The weight of evidence says this is a supply-and-demand reset, not a one-day scare: prices are falling because producers made more metal than batteries are absorbing. The producers’ shares bounced on Wednesday because they have already fallen so far, but a lasting recovery needs Chinese carbonate prices to stabilise, which is the variable to watch.

03 Why it moved

First cause, high confidence: a glut. Chinese lithium carbonate fell to a new low for 2026, according to the data provider Mysteel (analysis of November), and new supply keeps arriving.

Second cause, high confidence: the producers themselves are warning. SQM said on 17 November that fourth-quarter prices could be substantially lower than in the third quarter.

Third cause, medium confidence: a nervous market. The VIX fear gauge rose 7.32% to 28.29 and the S&P 500 slipped 0.25% to 7,183, so investors were trimming risk, while falling gold added to a cautious mood across commodities.

The usual drivers did not explain the day. The dollar index eased 0.11% to 103.70 and the 10-year US Treasury yield fell 7 basis points to 4.86%, which normally helps miners.

Our best reading, with medium confidence, is that lithium’s own glut outweighed any macro relief, while the producers’ bounce was bargain-hunting near lows rather than good news.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. LIT has fallen 29.2% over 60 sessions and has now closed lower two sessions in a row.

The 12-month high of 91.62 on 11 May feels distant, and the fund is hugging its 12-month low of 51.98. Over 60 sessions Albemarle has lost 39.9% and SQM 40.6%, showing the producers have suffered even more than the basket.

Our own price history since 2010 adds a counterweight. After 12 earlier falls of at least this size in LIT, it was higher 20 sessions later in 10 cases (83%), with a median gain of 9.7% and a worst loss of 9.4%.

For Albemarle the record is a coin toss: higher in 22 of 41 cases (54%), median +2.1%, worst -29.7%. For SQM it is better: higher in 25 of 35 cases (71%), median +8.8%, worst -27.5%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile is most exposed. SQM runs the Salar de Atacama, a brine field in Chile’s Atacama Desert, and its Novandino venture with state copper miner Codelco ties the metal to public finances and royalty income.

Lower prices cut export earnings and tax take for Santiago, even if volumes hold. Argentina, whose brine projects are expanding, faces a tougher case for new investment, while Bolivia, with huge but little-developed reserves, has less reason to hurry.

For investors in Sao Paulo, Mexico City or Lima, the lesson is that a boom commodity can lose its glow fast. SQM is 49.8% below its April high, a reminder that Latin American resource stocks swing with Chinese demand.

06 The names to watch

Albemarle is the largest US producer and a bellwether for the whole sector. A close below its 20 November low of 79.70 would signal fresh selling.

SQM matters most for Chile. Its 24 November low of 46.88 is the level to guard, and any update on fourth-quarter pricing would move the shares.

LIT is the broad gauge. Its 12-month low of 51.98 is the line that, if broken, would confirm the slide is still running.

07 What would end it

Support sits at the LIT low of 51.98 and, for the producers, at 79.70 (Albemarle) and 46.88 (SQM). Resistance is far away: the peaks of 91.62, 215.62 and 95.31 are not realistic near-term targets.

A new test arrives on 26 November, when China’s Guangzhou Futures Exchange launches lithium hydroxide futures, with options following on 27 November. Deeper trading could help price discovery and, over time, calmer markets.

The honest answer to whether it stops: not until Chinese stocks drain or producers cut output. Price rebounds without that are likely to be short-lived.

08 What to watch

Chinese carbonate price: Whether it stabilises after its fall to a 2026 low decides whether the miners can recover.

Whether it stabilises after its fall to a 2026 low decides whether the miners can recover. Guangzhou launches: Lithium hydroxide futures begin on 26 November and options on 27 November, adding new price signals.

Lithium hydroxide futures begin on 26 November and options on 27 November, adding new price signals. SQM guidance: Any figure on fourth-quarter prices after its warning of 17 November would reset expectations.

Any figure on fourth-quarter prices after its warning of 17 November would reset expectations. Support levels: LIT’s 12-month low of 51.98 and Albemarle’s 79.70 are the lines the sellers must break.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is lithium falling?

Producers made more lithium than battery makers needed, so stocks piled up, especially in China, and prices dropped to a new low for 2026.

Is LIT the price of lithium?

No. LIT is a fund holding lithium-mining and related shares, so it tracks the industry, not the metal’s spot price.

Why did Albemarle and SQM rise while LIT fell?

Both had slid to lows, and buyers stepped in after steep losses; the wider basket still fell 1.55%.

Is the slump over?

Not yet. Our history shows a rebound after most large falls, but it is not a forecast, and a lasting recovery needs the glut to clear.

World.title: Copper Fund Edges Up 0.03% After a 19.39% Slide | Copper Wrap, Nov 25
World.content:
Miners bounced as Southern Copper gained 3.03% and Freeport-McMoRan 1.72%, but the copper fund is only 4.3% above its 12-month low.

Copper stood still on Wednesday while the shares of its producers jumped. That gap is the story: the metal’s price drifted, but investors in mining companies decided that the sell-off had gone far enough for a day.

The CPER fund rose +0.03%, Southern Copper +3.03% and Freeport-McMoRan +1.72%. A fund tracks futures, which are contracts to buy copper at a set future date, so it can differ from the spot price that factories actually pay.

Key Facts Copper fund: CPER, a copper futures fund, is down 19.39% in 20 sessions, 21.5% below its September peak.

CPER, a copper futures fund, is down 19.39% in 20 sessions, 21.5% below its September peak. Wednesday: the fund edged up 0.03% to US$32.51, its first rise after a 4.66% drop over five sessions.

the fund edged up 0.03% to US$32.51, its first rise after a 4.66% drop over five sessions. Miners bounced: Southern Copper rose 3.03% to US$140.99 and Freeport-McMoRan 1.72% to US$48.55.

Southern Copper rose 3.03% to US$140.99 and Freeport-McMoRan 1.72% to US$48.55. Macro pressure: US growth and inflation beat forecasts; the gold fund GLD is down 4.03% in five sessions.

Today’s Focus Copper, the metal in power cables, electric cars and air conditioners, has lost almost a fifth of its value in a month. The CPER fund, which follows copper futures contracts rather than the metal’s spot price, closed Wednesday, November 25, 2026 at US$32.51, up only +0.03%. The sell-off has been driven less by copper’s own story than by the wider mood. Strong US data has strengthened bets that interest rates will rise (RT economic calendar, 25 November), and that has weighed on anything tied to global growth. Chile, the world’s largest producer, and Peru, also among the top three, feel this directly through their mining revenues and currencies.
