01 The session in one read

Assessment — Oversold, but not yet turning MEDIUM Wednesday looks like a pause inside a downtrend rather than a reversal, because the fund barely moved while fear gauges rose. The miners’ bounce shows buyers are testing the water, yet the macro pressure of rate fears is unresolved. The variable to watch is whether the copper fund holds above its 12-month low of 31.18.

Copper — the daily wrap.

02 The board

Read the board as a split screen. The metal’s proxy is flat, while the two best-known copper miners in the United States, both with large mines in Latin America, rebounded sharply after steep falls.

A rebound this size after such losses usually reflects bargain hunting and investors closing bets against the shares. It rarely marks a lasting low by itself.

03 Why it moved

First, and heaviest, is the macro squeeze. US third-quarter growth of 4.3% against 3.5% expected and core PCE inflation of 3.3% against 3.2% (RT economic calendar, 25 November) reinforced bets that US interest rates will rise, and higher rates slow factories, the biggest buyers of copper. Gold tells the same tale, with the GLD fund down 4.03% in five sessions, so this is a broad retreat from raw materials and not a copper quirk. Confidence: medium-high.

Second, China, the buyer of roughly half the world’s copper. We found no fresh Chinese demand data for the day, so we cannot say whether factory caution there added to the pressure. Confidence: low.

The usual drivers did not fully explain Wednesday. The dollar index slipped -0.11% to 103.70 and the 10-year US Treasury yield fell 7 basis points to 4.86%, both normally helpful for copper, yet the metal only managed a flat close. The S&P 500 fell -0.25% to 7,183 and the VIX fear gauge rose +7.32% to 28.29, so nervousness outweighed the easier dollar and yields. Oil, via the USO fund, rose +3.29%.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. The copper fund is down 4.66% over five sessions, 19.39% over 20 and 16.8% over 60, and it sits 21.5% below its 12-month high of 41.43 reached on 22 September.

The miners have fallen further because they magnify the metal’s moves. Southern Copper is 35.1% below its 25 August high of 217.40, and Freeport-McMoRan is 39.2% below its high of 79.91 set the same day.

Our own archive since 2007 offers a modest comfort for Southern Copper. After 8 earlier falls at least as large as its 26.52% drop in 20 sessions, the shares were higher 20 sessions later in 5 of 8 cases (62%), with a median gain of 8.5% and a worst case of a 47.4% further fall.

For Freeport, the odds were a coin toss. After 14 earlier falls at least as large as its 27.10% drop, it was higher in 7 of 14 cases (50%), with a median move of -2.1% and a worst case of -61.0%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile and Peru live and die by copper. Lower prices shrink the tax and royalty income their governments collect, and they tend to weigh on the Chilean peso and the Peruvian sol, which makes imports and foreign holidays costlier for locals.

Southern Copper, with major operations in Peru and Mexico, is the most direct listed stake, and its 20-session fall of 26.52% shows how much market value has gone.

For visitors, a weaker currency can stretch a travel budget, but the reason is a slowdown in mining income, which is not good news for local jobs.

06 The names to watch

Southern Copper at US$140.99 is 13.8% above its 12-month low of 123.95, which is the level bulls need to protect. Freeport-McMoRan at US$48.55 is 18.2% above its low of 41.07.

The US Geological Survey’s annual mineral summary still ranks Chile first by a wide margin, a reminder that supply is concentrated in a few vulnerable countries. That concentration is why any strike, flood or political shock in Chile or Peru can move prices quickly, in either direction.

07 What would end it

The nearest support is the copper fund’s 12-month low of 31.18, only 4.1% below Wednesday’s close. The next resistance is far above, at the 22 September high of 41.43, about 27% higher, so recovery would need to come in stages.

What would change the picture is a calming of rate-hike fears, shown by steadier US inflation data and lower Treasury yields. Firmer Chinese factory orders would confirm it. Until then, the honest answer is that the slide is slowing but has not stopped.

08 What to watch

US inflation data: Hotter readings would raise rate expectations again and press on copper and gold.

Hotter readings would raise rate expectations again and press on copper and gold. The 31.18 floor: A close below the copper fund’s 12-month low would signal a new leg down.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is copper falling?

Mainly because strong US data has lifted bets on higher interest rates, which pushes investors out of growth-linked commodities.

Does CPER show the actual copper price?

No. It tracks copper futures contracts, so it can differ from the spot price paid for physical metal.

Which countries are most exposed?

Chile, the world’s largest producer, and Peru, also among the top three, depend heavily on copper for exports and government revenue.

Is this a buying opportunity?

Our archive shows Southern Copper was higher 20 sessions later in 5 of 8 comparable falls, but it also fell a further 47.4% in the worst case, so history is not a forecast.

World.title: Costa Rica Sloth Rope Bridges Reach 410 With 22,000 Crossings
World.content:
Costa Rica’s sloth rope bridges are drawing international attention, with The Associated Press publishing a feature yesterday on the conservationists and caretakers working to keep the sloths in the trees. The story begins behind a beachfront hotel in Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, where a small crew strings rope from one trunk to the next. To a passing tourist it looks like little more than a clothesline. To a sloth it can be the difference between staying safely in the canopy and coming down to the ground, where dogs, cars and power lines are waiting.

The work is led by The Sloth Conservation Foundation, founded by British zoologist Rebecca Cliffe, who has spent close to 20 years studying the animals on Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean coast. Her team has now installed roughly 410 rope bridges, most of them in places where roads, houses and hotels have opened gaps in the forest.

The design is deliberately simple, usually a single line. Cliffe says that for animals built to live in the trees that is enough, giving them a way over a gap they could not otherwise cross. Unlike monkeys, sloths cannot jump. Cliffe has a name for the problem, microfragmentation. A break of just 2 or 3 meters (about 7 to 10 feet) between neighboring treetops can force a sloth to look for another route, and the other route is often the ground or an electrical cable.

Making matters harder, sloths tend to stick to the paths they learned when young, even after the landscape around them has changed. Cliffe began experimenting with bridges nearly two decades ago after working at the Sloth Sanctuary of Costa Rica in Penshurst, where she kept seeing animals brought in after dog attacks, collisions with vehicles and electrocutions. With almost no funding, she started hanging single ropes.

Cameras mounted on some of the bridges have since recorded more than 22,000 wildlife crossings, and sloths are not the only users. Today the team responds to sightings at hotels and private properties, plants trees and works with neighbors to reconnect their lots. The ropes are not permanent. Tropical sun and rain wear them out in four or five years, and they have to be replaced.

The paradox is that Costa Rica is a celebrated reforestation success. A 2023 OECD report put forest cover at 59 percent of the national territory, up from about 21 percent in 1987. But geographer Carlos Morera Beita of the National University points out that much of that regrowth took place on old pastureland, in a countryside still divided up by farming. Sloths have proven more adaptable than scientists once believed, getting around through pastures with scattered trees, living fences and vegetation along rivers.

Those links matter, he says, because an isolated sloth has a hard time finding food, shelter and a mate. In his view bridges fix specific choke points, but lasting protection depends on keeping existing forest standing, restoring biological corridors and stopping further fragmentation. Back at the Sloth Sanctuary, founder Judy Avey-Arroyo cares for the animals that cannot go home.

Her work began when she and her husband took in an orphan named Buttercup, and today the sanctuary houses sloths with severe injuries or disabilities along with babies whose mothers were killed by cars, dogs or power lines. The smallest are raised in incubators and fed milk, while older juveniles move on to leaves, time outdoors and climbing practice. Avey-Arroyo says a mother cannot really be replaced.

A young sloth spends about a year learning which leaves are safe, which plants to avoid, how to move through the forest and even how to deal with parasites, and orphans that miss those lessons can struggle in the wild even when they look healthy. Accepting that some of her animals will never return to the forest, she says, is the hardest part of the job.

Climate change adds another layer. Small patches of forest heat up and dry out faster than continuous forest, and sloths control their body temperature by moving between sun and shade. Cliffe says extreme heat can drain their limited energy reserves while cold can interfere with digestion, so her group is planting shade trees alongside the bridges.

Scientists still lack reliable estimates of how many sloths Costa Rica has or whether their numbers are rising or falling. Cliffe’s team is testing thermal imaging drones, trained detection dogs and field surveys to find out. Two rescue centers in the region take in around three sloths a day, but without historical data no one can say whether that figure is climbing. Costa Rican conservation groups have separately backed a U.S. bill to ban sloth imports.

The idea is spreading beyond the Caribbean. On the southern Pacific coast, Alturas Wildlife Rescue Center and the state utility ICE are installing eight rope crossings along the coastal highway between Dominical and Uvita to cut down on wildlife being hit by traffic or electrocuted. Four were in place by late September.

The best outcome, Cliffe told the AP, would be for the bridges to become unnecessary once the trees grow close enough for sloths to move freely on their own. Until then she believes their future rests on many small acts, a tree planted here and a rope hung there. She calls it “the cumulative power of many individual actions” and says that is what keeps her hopeful.

World.title: Expect Two Weeks of Night Lane Closures on Costa Rica’s Route 1 Near Naranjo
World.content:
If you drive Costa Rica’s Route 1 at night, expect lane closures and a short detour near Naranjo for the next two weeks. Crews are demolishing the former Naranjo toll station on the Bernardo Soto Highway. Work runs from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. and started today. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) and the National Road Council (CONAVI) expect it to take about two weeks, with partial lane closures while crews are on site.

If you are heading from San Ramón toward Alajuela, you will be moved onto a temporary lane that runs alongside the old toll station. That is the direction drivers take toward San José and Juan Santamaría International Airport, so it affects night trips in from Guanacaste, San Carlos and the western Central Valley.

The overnight schedule keeps the work out of rush hour, but you should still leave extra time, especially if you have a late-evening or early-morning flight. Slow down as you approach the work zone, follow the temporary signs and do what the crews on site tell you. They will be working next to moving traffic in the dark.

The Naranjo station has not charged a toll since September 1, 2025. Authorities suspended collection that day at Naranjo and at Río Segundo de Alajuela, citing constant backups at Río Segundo and changes tied to the highway project at Naranjo. The booths stayed in place after the toll ended.

In April 2026, then-President Rodrigo Chaves ordered both toll stations removed, calling the unused structures an unnecessary obstacle for drivers. Crews began demolishing the Río Segundo booths in late April. The Naranjo structures stood until this week. Transportation authorities say taking down the Naranjo station is part of the San José to San Ramón highway expansion. Removing the abandoned booths clears an obstacle from the road, improves safety and ends vandalism at the unused site.

World.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia Arrives in Spain After Leaving the United States Voluntarily
World.content:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid today, after departing the United States the previous night on a commercial flight. The 31-year-old Salvadoran national left Washington Dulles International Airport on a United Airlines flight with his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, a U.S. citizen, and other family members and legal representatives.

His departure ends a 20-month legal fight that began when U.S. immigration authorities deported him to El Salvador in March 2025. That removal violated a 2019 immigration judge’s order barring his return to El Salvador because a gang had threatened him and his family over their pupusa business. Officials later described the 2025 deportation as an administrative error. Abrego Garcia was held for a period at the Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), before courts ordered the U.S. government to facilitate his return.

He came back to the United States in June 2025. Federal prosecutors then charged him with human smuggling in connection with a 2022 traffic stop. A federal judge in Tennessee dismissed those charges earlier in 2026, finding the prosecution vindictive. The Justice Department appealed the dismissal. While that appeal continued, the Department of Homeland Security sought to remove him to one of several African countries, including Liberia. Abrego Garcia and his lawyers had indicated a preference for Costa Rica in earlier stages of the case.

U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who oversaw the Maryland immigration proceedings, signed an order on November 20 that set a Tuesday deadline for his unimpeded departure to any country willing to accept him. The order required the removal of the GPS ankle monitor he had worn for months and lifted other barriers to his exit. The case was dismissed after he left. Abrego Garcia paid for his own flight. Department of Homeland Security officials confirmed the departure and stated he received no incentives.

At Madrid’s Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport, Abrego Garcia raised a fist as he entered a vehicle. He did not speak to reporters on the ground. Hours later, in a virtual press conference conducted in Spanish, he said he was leaving happy and with his freedom. “This time I am leaving with my freedom, and not the way they took me out before, practically inhumanely,” he stated. He added that the government does not decide where his story continues and that his family and he will decide their future. He also said he is no longer afraid to face a government.

His attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described the move as a temporary departure. Sandoval-Moshenberg said Abrego Garcia entered Spain as a tourist on his Salvadoran passport. Salvadoran citizens can enter Spain for short stays without a visa, typically up to 90 days. The lawyer noted that Abrego Garcia, as the husband of a U.S. citizen and father of a U.S. citizen child, has pathways that could allow him to return as a lawful permanent resident, though those would require State Department waivers that the current administration is not expected to grant. Sandoval-Moshenberg said Abrego Garcia plans to speak at events in Spain and other countries at the invitation of organizations and research institutes.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the department was delighted that Abrego Garcia had self-deported to Spain. In a statement, Mullin described him as a human trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator and said he would no longer be able to terrorize Americans.

A Department of Homeland Security post stated that Abrego Garcia departed pursuant to a removal order, paid for his own flight, received no incentives, and will never be allowed back into the United States. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis called the departure good riddance and criticized Spain’s immigration policies.

Abrego Garcia has never been convicted of a crime. He has repeatedly denied gang membership. Allegations of domestic violence against his wife were raised in the past; a protective order sought in 2021 was later dropped. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen said Abrego Garcia left as a free man traveling to a country of his choice and was relieved that the administration’s efforts to leave him in a Salvadoran prison had not succeeded.

Abrego Garcia lived in Maryland for years with his family before the 2025 arrest. His case drew national attention after the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate his return from El Salvador and after repeated court findings that the administration had acted in bad faith on aspects of the litigation. As of today, he remains in Spain on a short-term tourist basis while he and his family determine next steps. The removal order recorded by U.S. authorities generally bars reentry for 10 years under federal law, though his lawyers have pointed to existing family-based pathways that could be pursued under a future administration.

World.title: Half of Costa Ricans Now Rate the Economy as Bad, Up From 43% in September
World.content:
Just over half of Costa Ricans now describe the country’s economy as bad or very bad, a majority for the first time in this year’s surveys by the University of Costa Rica’s Center for Research and Political Studies (CIEP). President Laura Fernández, however, keeps the approval of six in 10 people.

In the new survey, released today, 51% rated the national economy as bad or very bad. That is up from 43% in September and 35% earlier this year. The share who call the economy good fell to 28%, down from 37% in September.

The president’s own standing has held up far better as sixty percent of respondents gave Fernández’s performance a positive rating, 25% a negative one and 15% neither. Her positive rating slipped four points from the 64% recorded in the CIEP’s September poll, a change only slightly larger than the survey’s margin of error.

For comparison, the CIEP said her predecessor, Rodrigo Chaves, had 68% favorable and 14% unfavorable ratings at the same point in his term. Insecurity remains the country’s top concern by a wide margin, named by close to 40% of respondents as the main problem facing Costa Rica. Corruption ranked second, followed by poor government management, the cost of living and drug trafficking.

Asked about safety over the past 12 months, 45% said it had worsened and 35% said it had improved, close to the September reading. The findings come as Costa Rica grapples with an expanding criminal economy that the latest State of the Nation report described as the country’s third economy.

The CIEP interviewed 1,000 people between Oct. 28 and Nov. 3, with a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points. Fieldwork closed before the killing of journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri, so the results do not capture any public reaction to that case. The survey also tested support for a ruling party proposal that would allow consecutive presidential reelection.

Fifty-two percent opposed immediate reelection, 41% supported it and 7% took neither side. According to the CIEP, rejection rises the worse a respondent’s opinion of the government, reaching about nine in 10 among those who rate it negatively. Respondents also described a more divided country.

Seven in 10 said the current political situation is splitting Costa Rica, while 24% said society is coming together. Sixty-four percent said insults in public life have increased under the current government, against 10% who said they have decreased. Despite that, most Costa Ricans do not place themselves in either political camp. Three-quarters identified as neither supporters nor opponents of the movement built around Chaves, with 13% describing themselves as chavista and 12% as antichavista.

Few people have taken to the streets. Only 9% said they had joined a protest in the past year. But 57% said they would be willing to protest peacefully if the authorities made a decision they strongly opposed, including 35% who said they would be very willing. Thirty-one percent said they would not protest under any circumstances.

The gloomier view of the economy arrives in a year when the dollar has repeatedly hit record lows against the local currency, squeezing exporters, tourism businesses and anyone whose income or savings are held in dollars.

The results point to a president whose personal popularity has so far outlasted public confidence in the economy. Whether that gap narrows or widens will likely shape the political climate heading into 2027, as the government presses ahead with its legislative agenda and a budget fight with the courts and universities.

World.title: Costa Rica Urban Bee Survey Finds 128 Species in Belén
World.content:
Costa Rica’s biodiversity is not confined to just its national parks and tropical rainforests. A scientific inventory in Belén, Heredia, has shown that even highly urbanized communities can harbor a remarkable diversity of native bees. Researchers documented 128 bee species belonging to 49 genera, coming from 3,178 records. The results highlight the ecological importance of urban gardens, parks, and other green spaces, and follow a separate survey that added 60 new species records in urban Heredia.

The findings are featured in a new book, “Plantas y abejas del cantón de Belén” (Plants and Bees of Belén), presented by the Municipality of Belén. The free publication aims to encourage residents, businesses, educational institutions, and gardening enthusiasts to take part in pollinator conservation.

Biologist Daniela Azofeifa and entomologist Manuel Zumbado led the development of the publication, with contributions from parataxonomist Enia Navarro and ethnobotanist Agustín Contreras. The research draws on fieldwork conducted between February and June 2025 across 22 locations in Belén’s three districts, San Antonio, La Ribera, and La Asunción. Previously collected scientific records were also incorporated.

Bees are an exceptionally diverse group of insects that play an essential role in plant reproduction, ecosystem stability, and agricultural production. Protecting them does not necessarily require large areas of land or specialized scientific knowledge. Something as simple as allowing certain plants to flower rather than removing them can provide valuable food for pollinators. The guide encourages residents to select native vegetation with different flowering seasons, so bees have access to food throughout the year.

It also recommends reducing intensive garden maintenance and where it is safe to do so, leaving natural materials such as fallen leaves and dead branches in place, since these can provide nesting sites. Avoiding synthetic pesticides and herbicides is another important conservation measure.

Belén officially declared itself a bee-friendly area in 2021. Since then, local authorities have promoted environmental education, native beekeeping, and the creation of green spaces that support pollinators. The municipality is also encouraging private companies and community organizations to take part through a pilot recognition program that promotes environmentally responsible gardening practices.

Residents interested in contributing to scientific knowledge can document their observations through Naturalista Costa Rica, part of the international citizen science platform iNaturalist. The book is available in Spanish as a free PDF download.

World.title: Solana Sierra and Nadia Podoroska Advance at Argentina Open
World.content:
Argentine tennis players Solana Sierra and Nadia Podoroska advanced to the second round of the WTA 125 Argentina Open on Tuesday, giving home fans two reasons to celebrate as the women’s professional tennis season draws to a close. Sierra, the tournament’s top seed and Argentina’s highest-ranked female player, overcame a difficult start against Andorra’s Victoria Jiménez Kasintseva.

After losing the opening set 6-1, Sierra won the second in a tiebreak before her opponent retired with an injury while trailing 2-0 in the deciding set. The match lasted two hours and seven minutes, with Sierra advancing by a score of 1-6, 7-6(1), 2-0. She will face France’s Carole Monnet in the second round.

Podoroska, meanwhile, delivered a convincing performance against Spain’s Leyre Romero Gormaz. The former French Open semifinalist won a closely contested opening set before dominating the second to secure a 7-6(4), 6-0 victory. For Podoroska, the result represents another encouraging step in her return to competitive tennis following an extended absence caused by injuries. The 29-year-old, who once reached No. 36 in the world, is working her way back up the WTA rankings after spending more than a year away from competition.

She will face either María Lourdes Carlé or Sol Larraya Guidi in the second round, guaranteeing Argentina at least one representative in the quarterfinals. Argentina’s Julia Riera also remains in contention after defeating Greece’s Despina Papamichail 6-2, 7-5 on Monday. Her next opponent is Turkey’s Ipek Oz.

Not all the local players enjoyed the same success. Victoria Bosio, Luna María Cinalli and Lourdes Ayala were eliminated in their opening matches. Sierra and Podoroska have been responsible for two of Argentina’s most notable women’s tennis achievements in recent years. Podoroska reached the Roland Garros semifinals as a qualifier in 2020, while Sierra made history in 2025 by becoming the first women’s singles lucky loser to reach the fourth round at

The Argentina Open, played on outdoor clay at the Tenis Club Argentino in Buenos Aires, offers $115,000 in total financial commitment and features a 32-player singles draw. Part of the WTA 125 calendar since 2021, the tournament provides South American players with a valuable opportunity to earn ranking points closer to home before preparations begin for the 2027 season and the Australian Open in January.

The tournament runs through Sunday, November 29.

World.title: Your Guide to Puriscal’s Chicharrón Fair as It Opens Friday
World.content:
If you want to taste the chicharrón many Costa Ricans call the best in the country, your window opens Friday. The Feria del Chicharrón in Santiago de Puriscal, a hill town about an hour west of San José, runs from Nov. 27 through Monday, Dec. 7. The fair takes over the Parque del Agricultor in the center of town with food stands, live music and family activities. Entry has traditionally been free, so you only pay for what you eat and drink.

Puriscal earned its reputation the slow way. Local butchers and home cooks have made Costa Rica’s favorite fried pork, along with chorizo and salchichón, for generations, and many families still guard recipes handed down for more than a century. The fair has run almost every year since 1999, pausing only during the pandemic.

Forget the bagged pork rinds sold in supermarkets. The chicharrón here is meaty, with chunks of pork belly fried with the fat still attached until the outside crackles and the inside stays tender. Locals call this style chicharrón de panzada, and it is what most stands are known for.

It usually comes with fried yuca, tortillas and a wedge of lime. Some stands add chimichurri, the Costa Rican tomato-and-onion salsa similar to pico de gallo. Save room for the local chorizo and salchichón, and for traditional dishes such as tamal de maíz and pozol that have turned up at past editions.

Vendors start frying in the morning. Go in late morning or early afternoon if you want pork fresh from the pan and shorter lines. By evening, the crowd shifts toward the main stage. The program is built for families. Past editions have included children’s shows, a mechanical bull for kids, a pet pageant, a beach volleyball tournament, a horse parade and concerts by national artists. Mornings lean toward sports and recreation, while afternoons and evenings bring music, comedy and cultural performances.

The main event for many visitors is the Mejor Chicharrón contest, where local producers put their best batch in front of judges who score it on flavor and texture. At last year’s Puriscal chicharrón festival, it was held on the final Sunday. The full schedule, including the date of this year’s contest, is posted on the fair’s official Facebook page. It can change from day to day, so check it before you leave home.

Driving from San José takes about an hour. Expect heavier traffic on Friday evenings and Sunday afternoons and arrive before lunch on weekends if you want a parking spot close to the park. If you would rather not drive, Comtrasuli buses connect San José and Puriscal from a terminal near the Coca-Cola market. Staying for the evening concerts? Check the time of the last bus back before you go.

Bring cash. Many stands are small family operations that may not take cards, and SINPE Móvil transfers only work if you have a Costa Rican bank account. Pack a light layer too, because December days in the Central Valley are usually sunny but evenings can turn cool and breezy. Portions are generous, so a group can share a few plates and try more. If you want to make a day of it, La Cangreja National Park is in the same canton and makes a good morning hike before lunch at the fair. Check its opening hours before you go.

For Puriscal, the fair is more than a food festival. It traditionally opens the town’s Christmas season with the lighting of the town tree, and it gives small producers a place to sell directly to the public. One plate of chicharrón de panzada usually explains why people keep making the drive each December.

World.title: Turtle Season Is On in Guanacaste and Playa Grande Now Closes at 5 p.m.
World.content:
If you are heading to Playa Grande before March, plan to be off the sand by 5 p.m. Leatherback nesting season is under way at Las Baulas National Marine Park, and the beach closes an hour earlier than usual so the turtles can come ashore undisturbed. The season runs from October through February, according to the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC). The park was created to protect leatherbacks on three nesting beaches near Tamarindo: Playa Grande, Ventanas and Langosta.

Leatherbacks are critically endangered worldwide. They nest at night, which is the reason for the early closing. Lights, noise and people on the sand can send a female back to the water before she lays her eggs. Do not expect to find one on your own, and do not walk the beach after dark to look. Few leatherbacks reach these beaches now. Ask the park office whether guided night visits are operating this season before you pay anyone for a tour.

Farther south, Ostional National Wildlife Refuge offers a different sight. Olive ridley turtles nest there in mass arrivals known as arribadas, when thousands come ashore at once along 7 kilometers (4.3 miles) of beach. SINAC says the arrivals happen throughout the year. Arribadas tend to cluster around the moon’s last quarter. Tuesday’s moon is full, which puts the next last quarter around Dec. 1. Treat that as a window and not a date, because the turtles keep their own schedule.

One of this year’s largest arrivals came in early September. SINAC specialists warned at the time that the heat brought by El Niño could affect nesting. Hatchlings normally emerge about 50 days after the eggs are laid. If you go, get a certified local guide, keep your distance and leave flash and white lights off. The eggs are protected by law. In September, authorities detained two people carrying 125 olive ridley eggs taken illegally from the refuge.

Both sites are part of the public protected area system and the rules apply to everyone on the beach during nesting season.

World.title: Robert Arnold beats second murder charge in five months but remains behind bars on robbery charge
World.content:
Robert Arnold beats second murder charge in five months but remains behind bars on robbery charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Robert Emmanuel Arnold, 24, was acquitted of murder on Wednesday after High Court Justice Candace Nanton found that the prosecution failed to reliably establish that he was the gunman who shot and killed 32-year-old Cruz Magana during a home invasion in the Fresh Pond area of Burrell Boom Village on June 3, 2024.

Arnold’s acquittal marks the second murder case against him to end without a conviction in five months. However, he remains behind bars due to an outstanding robbery charge before the lower court.

The prosecution alleged that two armed men entered the Magana family home demanding money before Cruz Magana was fatally shot. His sister, Theresa Magana, fled the house and heard gunshots as she ran for safety.

The Crown’s case rested primarily on Theresa Magana’s identification of Arnold as the gunman.

In delivering her verdict, Justice Nanton highlighted several inconsistencies and deficiencies in the identification evidence, including poor lighting, the witness’s brief opportunity to observe the gunman and conflicting descriptions of his physical features.

While Theresa testified during the trial that the gunman had big eyes, she had described him as having small eyes in her original statement to police in 2024.

Justice Nanton also expressed concern that Theresa had seen a photograph of Arnold on television in connection with a separate murder before participating in a police group identification exercise. The judge noted the possibility that this exposure could have influenced her subsequent identification, although she made no definitive finding that the witness’s evidence had been contaminated.

Further concerns surrounded the identification exercise itself, which was conducted outside the Belize City Magistrate’s Court as prisoners exited a prison bus. The court was not provided with sufficient information to determine whether the other participants shared similar physical characteristics with Arnold.

The presence of the investigating officer inside the vehicle from which Theresa identified Arnold was also deemed particularly concerning by the judge, who described it as a departure from proper procedure.

Additionally, Cruz Magana’s mother, Lorena Magana, participated in the identification exercise but was unable to identify Arnold as the gunman, leaving the prosecution without independent corroboration of its principal witness’s identification.

Arnold, meanwhile, gave sworn testimony that he was at home at the time of the murder. His girlfriend also testified, corroborating his alibi.

Justice Nanton concluded that the cumulative effect of the deficiencies in the identification evidence left her unable to determine beyond a reasonable doubt that Arnold was responsible for Magana’s murder.

While acknowledging the tragic loss suffered by the Magana family, the judge emphasized that the court’s responsibility was to determine whether the prosecution had proven its case against the accused.

Arnold’s trial, conducted without a jury, began on October 19 and concluded on October 22, 2026.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Arnold was charged in July 2024 with both murder and robbery in connection with the Fresh Pond incident. The robbery allegations involved $2,500 in cash and a Samsung A21 cellphone.

On June 24, 2026, Arnold and Travis Jamaal Herbert saw their murder case concerning the killing of Elwin Rudolph Lewis, otherwise known as “Bobo Youth,” discontinued after the prosecution’s principal witness could not be located to testify. The two men had been awaiting trial for the murder since 2024.

Arnold also previously received a four-year prison sentence for robbery, which was upheld by Justice Nanton in February 2026 after he unsuccessfully appealed his conviction and sentence.

World.title: Lloyd Parchue granted $6,000 bail after three months on remand for firearm and ammunition charges
World.content:
Lloyd Parchue granted $6,000 bail after three months on remand for firearm and ammunition charges

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Lloyd Parchue is out on bail after spending exactly three months on remand at the Belize Central Prison following an alleged firearm and ammunition bust in Belize City.

Parchue appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in Court #1 of the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, where he applied for bail on the grounds that he had spent three months behind bars.

The prosecution raised no objection to bail but requested that stringent conditions be imposed.

The Chief Magistrate granted Parchue bail in the sum of $6,000 with two sureties in the same amount, which he managed to meet by 12:30 p.m.

As part of his bail conditions, Parchue must report to the Raccoon Street Police Station twice a week, on Tuesdays and Fridays, and attend all scheduled court hearings. Failure to comply could result in his bail being revoked.

Parchue was initially arraigned on August 24, 2026, on charges of keeping an unlicensed firearm and keeping unlicensed ammunition. He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded to prison.

According to police, at approximately 3:40 a.m. on Sunday, August 23, members of the GI3 Unit were conducting mobile patrols near the intersection of Flamboyant Street and Croton Lane when their attention was drawn to a white SUV traveling at high speed.

Police intercepted the vehicle on Croton Lane and instructed Parchue, who was driving, to exit the SUV.

Although Parchue reportedly told officers that he had nothing illegal to declare, a subsequent search of the vehicle allegedly led to the discovery of a 9mm pistol and eight live rounds of ammunition behind the glove compartment.

Parchue was subsequently escorted to the Queen Street Police Station and charged.

He is scheduled to return to court on December 17, 2026.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Parchue, 33, a former security guard, had requested a sentencing indication during his initial arraignment. He was informed that he would face four years and one month in prison if he pleaded guilty to both charges, with the sentences running concurrently.

Parchue rejected the proposed sentence and opted to maintain his innocence. His case remains pending before the court.

World.title: Man with 12 drug convictions narrowly avoids jail after paying $1,775 in outstanding court fines
World.content:
Man with 12 drug convictions narrowly avoids jail after paying $1,775 in outstanding court fines

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 35-year-old Vernon Street resident narrowly avoided prison on Tuesday after picking up his 12th drug-related conviction, this time for possession of 27.29 grams of marijuana.

Cassian Albert Young appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 of the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to a single charge of possession of controlled drugs.

However, Young’s extensive criminal record, which revealed 11 previous drug-related convictions dating back to 2019, proved to be a significant aggravating factor in determining his sentence. His most recent conviction before Tuesday was in May 2025.

The Senior Magistrate indicated that she was inclined to impose a custodial sentence, explaining that it was not the relatively small quantity of marijuana involved in the latest offense but rather Young’s repeated convictions that concerned the court.

The Magistrate noted that the principles of sentencing, including deterrence and rehabilitation, appeared to have had little effect on Young.

Nevertheless, the court opted against imprisonment, imposing a fine of $200 plus $5 in court costs, payable by December 31, 2026, in default of three months imprisonment.

Before Young could walk free, however, the Magistrate ordered him to immediately settle $1,775 in outstanding fines from previous convictions.

Young, the father of a three-year-old child, managed to pay the entire outstanding amount before the close of court business, avoiding imprisonment.

According to police, Young was walking along Mosul Street at approximately 9:30 a.m. on Monday, November 23, when he changed direction upon spotting a police mobile patrol, arousing the officers’ suspicion.

Police stopped and searched Young, discovering a yellow plastic bag containing marijuana in his right hand. The marijuana subsequently weighed in at 27.29 grams.

Young was escorted to the police station and formally charged.

The quantity of marijuana found in Young’s possession exceeded the 10-gram threshold established under Belize’s Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Act of 2017 by 17.29 grams.

World.title: Homeless man reportedly causing naked disturbance near 7th Day Adventist School in broad daylight is fully clothed by the time police arrive but busted with crack pipe; denied bail because he has no fixed address
World.content:
Homeless man reportedly causing naked disturbance near 7th Day Adventist School in broad daylight is fully clothed by the time police arrive but busted with crack pipe; denied bail because he has no fixed address

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A homeless man who was reportedly causing a disturbance while naked near the Seventh-day Adventist School in Belize City in broad daylight was fully clothed by the time police arrived, but a subsequent search allegedly revealed that he was in possession of a pipe used for smoking controlled drugs.

The man, 32-year-old Kevin Clever Thomas, is now behind bars, not because of the reported public nudity, but because he was charged with possession of the pipe and could not provide the court with a fixed address to qualify for bail.

According to police, at approximately 1:10 p.m. on Monday, November 16, 2026, officers conducting mobile patrols received a report via police radio of a nude man causing a disturbance near the school.

Upon arriving in the area, however, officers encountered Thomas fully dressed in long blue pants and a long-sleeved grey shirt.

Thomas produced a valid Social Security card and explained to the officers that he was homeless, unemployed and was preparing to go sell some bottles.

Police subsequently conducted a search of Thomas, during which a small black metal pipe allegedly fell from his hands.

Thomas was arrested and charged with a single count of possession of utensils used for smoking controlled drugs.

When he appeared before a Senior Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, November 23, Thomas pleaded not guilty to the charge.

However, because he was unable to provide the court with a fixed address, the Senior Magistrate denied him bail.

Thomas, who was not charged with any offense relating to the reported public nudity, was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until January 28, 2027.

World.title: Convicted cop Dexter Diego, serving 21 years for sexual abuse of minor, back in court for alleged rape of another child
World.content:
Convicted cop Dexter Diego, serving 21 years for sexual abuse of minor, back in court for alleged rape of another child

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Former police officer Dexter Diego, who is serving more than 21 years in prison for sexually abusing a minor, was back before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday in connection with a separate case involving another young girl.

Diego appeared before the Senior Magistrate in Court #2, where his preliminary inquiry into four counts of rape of a child was adjourned until Friday, November 27, 2026.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Diego was arraigned on the additional charges on May 4, 2026, for the alleged rape of a 10-year-old girl while he was out on bail for sexual offenses involving another minor.

Just three weeks ago, Diego was sentenced to 21 years, eight months and seven days in prison by High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim after pleading guilty to four counts of unlawful sexual intercourse involving a girl who was 13 years old when the abuse began.

Diego received sentences of five years and seven days on each of the remaining three counts, all of which were ordered to run concurrently with the longer sentence.

In determining his punishment, Justice Pilgrim considered Diego’s abuse of his position as a police officer and the serious psychological harm inflicted upon his victim.

Diego had changed his pleas from not guilty to guilty on July 27, 2026, sparing the child from having to testify against him at trial.

While already serving his lengthy prison sentence, Diego must now answer to four additional charges involving a separate alleged victim. Those charges remain pending before the court.

World.title: 60-year-old Ladyville man sentenced to three months in prison after being busted in abandoned house with crack pipe
World.content:
60-year-old Ladyville man sentenced to three months in prison after being busted in abandoned house with crack pipe

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 60-year-old Ladyville resident is serving three months behind bars after pleading guilty to possession of a crack pipe in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court.

Edward Quilter appeared unrepresented before the sitting Magistrate in Court #3 on Monday, where he pleaded guilty to a single charge of possession of utensils used for smoking controlled drugs.

Given his previous convictions for similar drug-related offenses, the Magistrate imposed a custodial sentence of three months imprisonment, effective immediately.

According to police, at approximately 8:30 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, officers were conducting searches on Simon Lamb Street in Belize City when they entered an abandoned house.

Inside, police observed Quilter sitting with a silver-colored object in his mouth. The officer retrieved the object, which contained a wire mesh and was identified as a crack pipe.

Quilter was subsequently escorted to the Queen Street Police Station, where he was formally arrested and charged.

This is not Quilter’s first conviction for possession of a crack pipe. Previous media reports dating back to June 2017 indicate that he pleaded guilty to a similar offense.

Quilter is now serving his three-month sentence at the Belize Central Prison.

World.title: ‘I am an entertainer’: ‘Aunty’ Kyra Young on suicide watch following threat to kill herself after Judge revokes bail in cybercrime case
World.content:
‘I am an entertainer’: ‘Aunty’ Kyra Young on suicide watch following threat to kill herself after Judge revokes bail in cybercrime case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belizean social media personality “Aunty” Kyra Young is expected to be placed on suicide watch at the Belize Central Prison after reportedly threatening to take her own life following the revocation of her bail in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday.

Young stated she would kill herself in the presence of a police officer while awaiting transportation to prison in the court’s detention area.

Breaking Belize News understands that prison authorities are to be notified of the incident so that appropriate safety precautions can be implemented.

Young, who had been out on bail of $3,000, appeared before the Chief Magistrate after the prosecution received information that she had allegedly violated the conditions of her bail by threatening her former common-law husband during a matter at the Belize Family Court on Monday.

The man reportedly recorded the incident.

Under the conditions of her bail, Young was prohibited from interfering with her ex or members of his family, either directly or indirectly, including through social media.

During Wednesday’s bail revocation hearing, Young maintained that she had done nothing wrong, telling the Chief Magistrate, “I am a platform entertainer.”

Nevertheless, the Chief Magistrate revoked her bail and remanded her to the Belize Central Prison until December 4, 2026, when her cybercrime trial is scheduled to commence.

Young was initially charged on January 29, 2026, with using a computer system to coerce, harass or intimidate a person under Belize’s Cybercrime Act.

The charge arose from a report made by her ex, who alleged that Young had threatened him and members of his family in a video circulated on social media.

This is not Young’s first encounter with the criminal justice system. As previously reported by Breaking Belize News in April 2024, Young, then 27, was charged with drug trafficking after police allegedly discovered 153 grams of marijuana inside a sofa at her Belize City residence. She pleaded not guilty and was granted bail of $1,500.

Outside of her social media activities, Young represented South Africa in the ninth annual Miss Afrikan Queen pageant at the Bliss Centre for the Performing Arts in April 2023, where she placed second runner-up.

In May 2024, Young was also interviewed by Channel 5 after posting a video on social media highlighting residents’ concerns about a large crocodile in the Belama Phase Three area.

“Aunty” Kyra Young will spend nine days on remand before returning to court for the commencement of her cybercrime trial.

World.title: Belize Defence Force hosts U.S. Ambassador and U.S. Southcom Commander
World.content:
Belize Defence Force hosts U.S. Ambassador and U.S. Southcom Commander

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Belize Defence Force (BDF) hosted a special visit by the United States Ambassador to Belize, Andre Bauer, and the Commander of the United States Southern Command, General Francis L. Donovan.

The United States officials were received at Price Barracks with a welcoming parade, reflecting the military honors and formal protocol of the Belize Defence Force.

The senior United States officials held a meeting with Minister of National Security, Energy and Ports Michel Chebat; Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of National Security, Francis Usher (Maj. Rtd.); Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of Public Utilities, Energy and Logistics, Dr. Leroy Almendarez; Chief of Defence Staff in the Ministry of National Security, Major General Asariel Loria; Commander of the Belize Defence Force, Brigadier General Anthony Velasquez; and Commandant of the Belize Coast Guard, Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis.

The meeting provided an important opportunity for senior United States and Belizean officials to discuss bilateral military affairs, strengthen existing cooperation, and explore opportunities for continued engagement between both nations.

The BDF says that this highlights the enduring partnership between Belize and the United States and their shared commitment to fostering collaboration, mutual understanding, and regional security.

World.title: Kyle Butler, Vauxhall High part ways
World.content:
Vauxhall High School Head Coach Kyle Butler

Kyle Butler says his stint as head coach of Vauxhall High School’s football programme has come to an end after two seasons.

Butler made the announcement on social media, saying he was proud of what he had accomplished at the school, highlighting the team’s consistency in the Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competitions and his role in helping players secure professional contracts and college opportunities.

“Thank you, Vauxhall, for two seasons I’ll always be proud of. Together, we reached three quarter-finals and made one round-of-16 appearance,” Butler posted.

The development follows Vauxhall’s exit from the under-16 schoolboy football competition after their 3-2 win against Kingston College (KC) was reversed, handing KC a 3-0 victory, due to what ISSA said in a release were “irregularities”.

ISSA is yet to rule on the matter as the punishment could be severe seeing that allegations are that the school used two ineligible players in other players’ names.

Butler, in his announcement, identified player development and creating opportunities beyond schoolboy football as his biggest achievement.

“My biggest achievement was helping eight players sign professional contracts and opening doors to college for even more,” he said, while thanking the players for trusting him as their coach.

Butler explained that he had agreed to remain at Vauxhall for another season at the end of the previous campaign, but believes the time has now come to pursue a new challenge.

“At the end of last season, I agreed to stay at Vauxhall for one more year. My time at Vauxhall has now come to an end, and I’m proud of what we achieved together. Now I look forward to finding a new home,” he said.

The ambitious coach is now looking to take his experience in Jamaica to Europe, where he hopes to learn from some of the continent’s leading coaches and further his professional qualifications.

“I’m excited to take what I’ve learned in Jamaica overseas and learn from some of the best coaches in Europe. My ambition is to earn my UEFA Pro Licence, coach some of the biggest clubs in the world and one day lead Jamaica’s national team,” Butler said.

Despite his overseas ambitions, Butler made it clear that he has not closed the door on local schoolboy football, indicating that he would be willing to return to the competition when the right opportunity presents itself.

He also outlined the importance of loyalty, unity and mutual commitment in any future coaching appointment, insisting that success requires the backing of everyone involved in a programme.

“When I take on another programme, I want the board, the coaching staff and the players to know we can count on each other. That means celebrating the wins together and standing side by side when things get difficult, on and off the pitch,” he said.

— Howard Walker

World.title: PREDATOR!
World.content:
A 58-year-old Trelawny man who in 2022 dragged a 10-year-old girl into his house, raped her, and later falsely claimed that a relative had sent her to him so he could have sex with her, has been sentenced to 17 years behind bars after he pleaded guilty to the act. He had snatched the girl while she was on her way to fetch water from a spring.

The man, who already spent 10 years behind bars for incest with his own child, and who was also on the Trelawny police’s Most Wanted List for murder, was sentenced by Supreme Court Judge Justice Judith Pusey in the Portland Circuit Court on November 17 after pleading guilty.

In the matter prosecuted by Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Malike Kellier and Crown Counsel Nyron Wright, the child — who lived next door to the man — left her home one evening in June 2022 for the spring and “took a shortcut through his yard”. The man called out to her to “come here a little bit”. The child said she told him, “No, I am going to fill my water bottle,” at which point he jumped towards her, grabbed her by the arm, pulled her into his house and closed the door.

She said he then proceeded to touch her inappropriately and kiss her all over her face, except on her mouth. According to the child, she pushed him and kicked him, telling him to stop, but he ignored her protests and threw her on a bed while trying to remove her clothing.

She said he had partially penetrated her when a knock on the door by her grandmother, who began calling her name, interrupted him. According to the child, her violator told her not to answer or make a sound or he would “thump” her in her mouth. She obeyed.

The relentless grandmother, however, pushed the door down and entered the house, at which point the man replaced the child’s underwear before attempting to push the grandmother from the house.

He further told the child to continue on her journey, ordered her to “pretend” as if she was not in his house, and further threatened to kill her if she told anyone. The matter was reported to the police that same day. He was arrested a day later and subsequently charged with rape and sexual touching of a child.

During his arrest the man, who initially refused to divulge his name to cops, when cautioned declared, “Officer a di [name withheld] send her over deh fi mi [have sex] with her.”

The man later told probation aftercare officers that his marriage deteriorated after his wife accused him of inappropriate conduct with his daughter — for which he was prosecuted and found guilty. He had lived in the community for just under a year when he struck.

A probation aftercare officer who interviewed the convicted man ahead of his sentencing said he “appeared nervous and had a disposition of unease during his interview at the Horizon Adult Remand and Correctional Centre” and that “he struggled to speak definitively about the circumstances surrounding the offences for which he was charged”. According to the officer, he admitted to touching the child on her private parts and kissing her all over her face but “vehemently denied raping her”.

According to the officer, the man expressed regret about his actions but claimed that he was “unable to resist the advances” of the child who, he claimed, was “touching him in an affectionate way”. The official said when challenged about the child’s “cognitive ability to respond from an informed position, based on her age, he retracted his claim and expressed that he could not validate his actions”.

He further told his interviewer that while he recognised the experience may have been traumatic for the child and would cause her to struggle because of memories of that day, he could not see how it would affect her in other ways. Furthermore, he said while he was aware of the embarrassment his actions would cause to his family, and particularly his estranged spouse, he did not believe what he did would affect the wider community. The man has also been accused by community members of engaging in inappropriate conduct with other minors over the years.

In a report produced for the courts in February of this year, at which point the repeat offender had yet to plead guilty, a probation aftercare officer said if the man decided to take responsibility for his actions, a custodial sentence would be a “suitable means of punishment”.

Residents from the area, in the meantime, further described him as “brazen”, alleging that he was also involved in praedial larceny and was seen taking produce from the farms of others. Furthermore, the residents, who said they did not confront him out of fear for their own safety, described his actions as “troubling” to them while expressing “relief” at his departure from the area.

World.title: Precarious position
World.content:
Jonathan Bernard’s house that sits precariously on the hillside in Spring Mount, above a gaping breakaway.

SPRING MOUNT, St James — Faced with uncertainty about the structural integrity of his house, Spring Mount resident Jonathan Bernard is hoping Government will buy the property, even as uncertainty swirls around if and when repairs will be done to the massive breakaway which threatens the building.

Bernard’s house sits atop a hillside, offering him a bird’s-eye view of the collapsed roadway that has cut off vehicular traffic along the Spring Mount and Springfield corridor since last year’s Hurricane Melissa. There had been reports that the purchase of his house was being considered as part of efforts to fix the issue, and Bernard confirmed that discussions had taken place.

“Them come to me about it. The last time I spoke to them was in August and since then there hasn’t been any contact,” he told the Jamaica Observer during a recent visit to the community.

Bernard explained that the two-bedroom, one-bathroom dwelling had been his home for the past 17 years, but he was willing to sell.

“We had made some arrangements as it relates to that, but they haven’t come forward again,” he explained.

“We’ve tried to reach out to them but we can’t get a positive response as to what is happening,” he lamented.

The proposed purchase has become even more urgent because, just over two weeks ago, he received word that heavy equipment was being used to cut into the land on which his house stands. He said the intention was to create space for vehicles to pass.

“It has made the situation worse because I can’t access the place and is there I have all of my stuff. If I need to change my clothes, anything I need to do, that’s where I go because I don’t live anywhere else,” said a forlorn Bernard.

He told the Observer that after the Category 5 storm there had been some indication of danger as the house appeared to have tilted. However, he was still able to access the property then. Now, portions of the columns holding it up are increasingly being exposed as the surrounding soil continues to loosen.

“It wasn’t in danger but a this that them come do now cause the problem. I had my place, I would sleep there,” he said.

“Them just think that my thing has no value. Them want them road and that is the most important thing to them,” Bernard added.

He explained that he began building the house 17 years ago after landing a job at a call centre.

“Most of the material, a me carry them there, most of the blocks a me carry them up there,” he said.

“It’s not like I have money or whatever, it’s [from doing] a 9-5 I work,” he told the

Observer.

Bernard now farms for a living and he has put together a makeshift shelter while he awaits word on his precariously perched house.

“I have a hut in the bush so this is all I have,” he lamented.

Bernard said he has reached out to political representatives in the area and was told that efforts would be made to assist him.

“The councillor said them going to try build up a place where I can store my things, for now, and then he is going to talk to the member of parliament to see if I can get one of the social house them, something to that sort; but I need somewhere to live now,” he appealed.

Initial indications that nearby land would be bought and the Spring Mount breakaway repaired were dashed after the Government said it would be unwise to spend US$250,000 on a fix that likely would not last more than five years. The focus is now on repairing other routes.

World.title: Curtisay the Bessout turns dubplate job into a bouncy single
World.content:
Curtisay the Bessout .

Emerging dancehall artiste Curtisay was supposed to cut a dubplate and remix a track for Latin pop singer Natalie Q. Instead, the talented rhyme-spitter flipped the script and formulated a whole new song.

The producer, Psycho Pablo, loved the song so much it was released as a separate single, Back it Up Senorita, and he still recorded another verse for Natalie Q.

“All of that happened because of my philosophy of doing more than what is asked. I have a mindset centred on initiative, ownership, and value creation; I always try to go above and beyond,” Curtisay the Bessout said.

Released earlier this month, the song is already putting up impressive streaming numbers.

Curtisay the Bessout is excited about the early feedback. The record reflects the pulse of the streets, built for the dancers, with a Spanish lilt in Psycho Pablo’s instrumental and a chorus that tells you what to do with your waist.

As the sing progresses, the verses get more specific. Curtisay uses his lived experiences in the streets to pen songs about DMs, and the ‘genie wine’ to paint portraits with his music.

“Each line in this song is about someone and a real experience. My babymother, after all, is a dancer,” he said.

The first version was raunchier. Then Curtisay took it to Tuff Gong, where the association with Bob Marley made him think twice about just how far to push it. He dialled back the explicit lyrics and came away thinking the edit made the song easier to take abroad.

The studio changed his approach to the vocal, too. He spent years honing his craft to construct the right sound out of his voice. At Tuff Gong, he could relax and let the lower register do its job.

“All I had to do there was be myself,” he said.

When Curtisay drops into those deep tones he remembers Baby Cham passing his gate in a topless luxury car alongside the Topless Crew.

“Nuff Baby Cham influence is in my style,” he said.

He points to Sean Paul and Shaggy for a different lesson in delivery. Both showed him how far a Jamaican cadence can carry when listeners around the world can follow the words.

On Back It Up Senorita he deejayed with a Spanish touch inspired from the beat. The rest comes from nights out in the dancehall, where selectors, dancers, and the crowd let you know quickly whether a chorus works.

Curtisay has spent enough time in other people’s sessions to appreciate having his own voice out front. He contributed Stay With Me to Jah Cure’s Grammy-nominated album The Cure.

Working with Ahzee on Way You Whine, he recalled going through roughly 20 cuts before settling on lyrics. Curtisay usually likes to walk into the booth and leave with a finished song. Ahzee made him sit with the melodies first, a habit he took back to his own work. Writing for other artistes taught him a tougher lesson about what happens when the paperwork comes around.

These days he demands a substantial advance before taking on that kind of job.

For Back It Up Senorita, Curtisay wrote and performed, Psycho Pablo produced the instrumental, and Ramjam handled the mix.

Once it was time to make the video, Curtisay lined up the dancers, helped organise the shoot, and edited the footage after Driz N8 and Great Devoted Generation filmed it.

The artiste who turned a remix brief into his own single had apparently found a few more ways to make himself useful.

Now comes the litmus test: The walking gauntlet that is the essence of dancehall. He wants to see what dancers like Shelly Belly and others do with the chorus at Boom Sundays.

“I can’t wait to see what the reaction will be inna the dances…It’s going to be epic,” he said.

World.title: ‘TIME TO TALK!’
World.content:
Match officials (from left) Ojay Duhaney, Oshane Nation, Stephanie-Dale Yee-Sing, Okeito Nicholson, and Kemar Gayle receive tokens after officiating the Jamaica Premier League football final between champions Cavalier FC and Mount Pleasant Football Academy on May 19, 2024.

MONTEGO Bay United Chairman Yoni Epstein has called for an urgent meeting involving the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF), the Jamaica Football Referees Association (JFRA) and Jamaica Premier League clubs to resolve the dispute over outstanding payments to match officials and get the competition back on track.

Epstein says all parties have a responsibility to find a solution as the continued suspension of games is hurting the sport, its sponsors, supporters and players.

Last Sunday’s Jamaica Premier League games were postponed after referees withdrew their services over outstanding payments. The JFRA and Professional Football Jamaica Limited (PFJL) — organisers of the competition — were still uncertain up to yesterday about when the games would resume,

JFRA President Valdin Ledgister told the Jamaica Observer that the association was still awaiting more than $2 million promised by the JFF. Ledgister said that as of 1:45 pm on Tuesday, the outstanding amount had not reached their accounts.

The referees had received approximately $3.2 million from the PFJL but were still awaiting the balance, Ledgister said.

“The referees are not in a position to turn out for the games,” he said, adding that the outstanding money had reportedly been sent since Friday.

Ledgister said the dispute had not affected games in the Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competitions, as the referees were not owed any money for those matches.

“We are not owed anything from the ISSA games, and we have clear communication and arrangements with them,” he said.

PFJL Chief Executive Officer Owen Hill, however, says his organisation had fulfilled its responsibilities and was seeking clarification as to why the referees were still withholding their services.

In a letter to JFF General Secretary Gregory Daley dated November 23, Hill said the PFJL had advanced approximately $3.29 million between November 21 and 23 to the referees’ standard payment account, THE RA Limited, to settle the outstanding claims.

Hill said the payments were made without a formal invoice or the complete supporting documentation normally required, as the PFJL sought to prevent the disruption of the competition.

“The PFJL’s position is that all monies brought to its attention in connection with the current payment dispute have been advanced and settled accordingly, and that no further amounts have been formally established as outstanding in relation to the claims presented,” the letter stated.

Hill also questioned why the referees continued to withhold their services without providing an explanation or a reconciliation of any further amounts being claimed.

The PFJL chief executive said there were no new developments regarding the dispute and that the organisation was still awaiting word on when the next round of games would be played.

“We are yet to hear from the parties involved as to when the next scheduled round of games will be played,” Hill said. “The PFJL has a responsibility to its core stakeholders to protect their investment so we continue to seek a resolution.”

Epstein described the situation as a “real travesty” and says the parties need to put aside their differences and find a solution.

“I understand their concerns, and I think that we are all at fault. At the end of the day, the one thing that is suffering is the football. The sponsors, the supporters, the players trying to progress their careers are all suffering because of this situation,” he said.

Epstein says the clubs, JFF, and referees need to meet within the next 24 hours to understand the concerns and resolve the matter, whether in person or virtually.

“The referees feel disrespected, and as stakeholders we need to understand why, and we need to rectify this. Without them, the game cannot be played,” he said.

Epstein says the dispute is damaging the reputation of the JFF and the Jamaica Premier League while also hurting clubs, referees, players, fans and sponsors.

He is urging all parties to work together to find a solution and have the league back on the field by Sunday.

“There is nothing in life that is insurmountable, but we have to get into a room, and we have to get into a room fast in order to solve this situation to get football back on the field come this Sunday, no questions asked.”

World.title: BOJ moves to unlock farm credit in inflation fight
World.content:
Governor of the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) Brian Langrin addresses journalists during the central bank’s quarterly monetary policy press conference on Monday at its headquarters in downtown, Kingston. Looking on is Wayne Robinson, senior deputy governor of the BOJ.Garfield Robinson

BANK of Jamaica (BOJ) is proposing to halve the regulatory risk weights applied to loans for climate-resilient agricultural projects, seeking to draw more bank financing into a sector whose exposure to droughts and hurricanes has repeatedly fed food-price inflation.

The proposal would cover qualifying investments such as solar-powered drip irrigation, water storage, hurricane-resilient greenhouses, cold and dry storage facilities, farm roads, drainage and other post-harvest infrastructure.

Governor Brian Langrin said the measure is intended to strengthen domestic food production before another climate shock occurs, rather than relying mainly on interest rates to contain the inflationary fallout afterwards.

“Interest rates cannot prevent a drought, restore damaged crops, or repair a disrupted food supply chain.We must therefore look beyond interest rates and examine whether complementary measures can help to reduce the economy’s vulnerability to these shocks.” Langrin said during the BOJ’s monetary policy press briefing on Monday.

The proposal is still at an early stage. No framework has been agreed, and the measure remains subject to internal assessment, legal review and the required approvals. The central bank has also not yet held detailed discussions with deposit-taking institutions, although Langrin said they had been alerted to the initiative.

Under the proposal, a qualifying agricultural loan carrying a risk weight of 100 per cent could be assigned a 50 per cent weight. Reducing the risk weight would lower the amount of capital a bank must hold against the loan, giving financial institutions more room and an incentive to lend to approved projects.

Current risk weights on the loans range from 50 per cent to as much as 150 per cent.

Still, the BOJ is not proposing to relax the credit checks applied to borrowers. Eligible investments would have to be physical, independently verified assets with a clear resilience component, while the adjustment would be narrowly defined to ensure capital requirements continue to reflect the underlying credit risk.

Langrin acknowledged that the central bank would have to monitor whether financial institutions translate the regulatory benefit into increased lending on more favourable terms.

“We will have to watch: Do they in fact pass on these incentives to climate-resilient agricultural production? And they ought to, because now more loans in that area actually have a smaller charge on the capital,” he said during the question-and-answer segment.

The initiative comes amid renewed concern over the willingness of financial institutions to lend to agriculture and other productive sectors, particularly where borrowers lack the property or other readily marketable assets traditionally accepted as collateral.

Langrin said banks have historically preferred to lend against real estate and motor vehicles, which can be sold more easily if a borrower defaults, rather than assess businesses principally on their cash flow.

“They have to lend against cash flow,” he said, noting that farmers and other underserved borrowers may operate viable businesses without possessing the type of collateral banks typically demand.

The BOJ is examining how technology could allow financial institutions, with the borrower’s permission, to assess the cash flows of small and medium-sized businesses more efficiently. Langrin said this could reduce the cost of monitoring smaller borrowers and give banks greater confidence to lend based on the income generated by a business.

The agricultural initiative forms part of a broader attempt by the BOJ to expand its response to inflation beyond its traditional monetary policy tools. Food accounts for approximately one-third of Jamaica’s consumer price index, giving agricultural disruptions an outsized effect on the cost of living.

Research conducted by the central bank over a 25-year period found that global food-price shocks had a larger and more persistent effect on domestic inflation than comparable movements in oil and alumina prices.

Jamaica’s vulnerability has been reinforced by successive weather events, including hurricanes Beryl and Melissa and the intensifying El Niño conditions now affecting agricultural production.

Langrin said more resilient infrastructure could reduce crop losses, improve the reliability of domestic food supplies and lower the risk of agricultural loans becoming non-performing after a disaster. It could also strengthen farmers’ ability to supply the tourism industry, reducing some of the country’s dependence on food imports.

The governor argued that Jamaica’s agricultural sector has not been able to supply the tourism industry reliably and at sufficient scale, leaving the country exposed to both domestic crop failures and increases in international food prices.

“We would love for the industry to be able to supply the demand, especially from the tourism sector, but it simply cannot do so on a sustainable basis,” Langrin said.

“A large part of this impulse from food is from imported food. Prices have increased significantly abroad,” he added.

The BOJ has offered to convene a symposium involving government agencies, financial institutions and other stakeholders to examine the obstacles to agricultural financing and resilience. Langrin said several public agencies were already working in the area, but greater coordination was needed.

The proposed measure was unveiled as the BOJ increased its policy rate by 50 basis points to 6.50 per cent, its second consecutive increase of that size since September.

Annual inflation stood at 8.2 per cent in October, down from 8.6 per cent in September but above the BOJ’s target range of four to six per cent for a fifth consecutive month. The central bank now expects inflation to remain above target for most of the next four quarters and return sustainably to the range by late 2027, later than previously projected.

Food prices, transport costs and electricity rates were among the main contributors to the October out-turn. Business expectations for inflation 12 months ahead also rose to 8.3 per cent in September, from 7.3 per cent in July, increasing the risk that companies will adjust prices in anticipation of higher future costs.

The BOJ said the rate increases were intended to prevent those expectations from producing a self-reinforcing cycle of price increases. However, it believes the adjustments made to date should be sufficient to return inflation to target if current conditions do not deteriorate.

The proposed agricultural measure will take longer to produce results and is not expected to lower food prices immediately. Its objective is instead to reduce the severity of future supply shocks, which could lessen the need for the central bank to repeatedly use interest rates against inflation originating outside the financial system.

World.title: Fi Wi Land: The fight to save Jamaica’s dying lignum vitae
World.content:
A symbol of Jamaica’s natural beauty and national identity, the lignum vitae holds a special place in the island’s heritage. But despite its significance as Jamaica’s national flower, this treasured species is facing growing threats to its survival, raising concerns about the future of one of the country’s national symbols.

Renowned for its exceptionally hard and durable wood, the lignum vitae has faced years of overexploitation, habitat loss and land degradation, contributing to a decline in its population.

With the species subject to international trade restrictions under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), protecting and restoring its population is an important conservation priority.

In this week’s episode of Fi Wi Land, Environmental Officer for Flora at the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA), Ashleigh Sanderson, sheds light on the threats facing Jamaica’s national flower and the efforts being made to safeguard its future.

From population surveys revealing concerns about its decline to conservation action plans and environmental protection measures, discover how NEPA is working to preserve the lignum vitae and other threatened plant species across the island.

Catch the latest episode on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: From ‘Bulbie’ to ‘Blackman’, the evolution of the Klansman gang
World.content:
