The United States has designated the St Catherine-based Klansman gang as a transnational criminal organisation (TCO), a move that will bar purported members of the criminal group from entering the country.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness disclosed the development following a recent meeting with US Assistant Secretary of State for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura and members of his delegation, who were visiting Jamaica.

The TCO designation is a formal US government label placed on criminal groups that operate across international borders, and includes major criminal outfits and terrorist organisations such as the Sinaloa Cartel and Hezbollah.

During the 2000s and 2010s, the Klansman gang’s violent turf wars in Spanish Town, resulted in police crackdowns like Operation Kingfish, and the arrests and deaths of reputed figures such as Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett and Tesha Miller.

READ: US designates Jamaica’s Klansman Gang as transnational criminal organisation

ORIGINS OF KLANSMAN

Based in the southeastern parish of St Catherine, west of the capital Kingston, despite the name, the Jamaican gang has no connection to the Ku Klux Klan, an American white supremacist group whose members are called “Klansmen”. Anecdotal tales say the local gang was formed when young men met in a house in Dela Vega City and decided to become one ‘clan’, and set up an extortion racket in the Old Capital of Spanish Town.

The history of the Klansman gang is like a top ten Netflix movie: rival factions, secret burial sites, homicidal bosses.

The recent trials of dozens of members of the gang in Jamaica is shedding light on how criminal groups function on the island. At one time, police said the gang was raking in J$1.8 million weekly from extorting mainly business owners and transport operators. The gang also reportedly made money through targeted killings and weapons trafficking.

The gang’s status and organisation also helped rake in the cash. Its primary means of revenue, according to prosecutors, is extortion. One witness said that extortion payments from a section of the bus park in Spanish Town ranged from $80,000 to $100,000 a day.

One popular loan company, Torpedo, also paid up to $150,000 a month to a splinter faction of the gang, claimed one witness. The witness revealed that another organisation, which he refused to name due to security concerns as it includes “powerful individuals”, paid $200,000 a month.

Fifteen members of the One Don splinter faction of the gang, including leader Andre “Blackman” Bryan, were in March 2023 convicted under Jamaica’s anti-gang legislation. Meanwhile, 25 alleged members of the reputed Tesha Miller faction are now before the Supreme Court answering to 16 offences – including murder and robbery – allegedly committed over the span of five years between August 2017 and November 2022.

According to prosecutors and witnesses in the Klansman trial, the criminal outfit is now firmly a third-generation gang. The testimony of two former gang members stated that the Klansman reportedly had some 400 members within its different factions. The gang also had clearly defined roles, corrupt links with the police, international criminal connections and even allegedly carried out hits ordered by a celebrity musician.

Here are some of the generational figures that have defined the history of the Klansman, a firmly established third generation gang with tentacles in St Catherine, Clarendon and even Manchester.

BEFORE ‘BULBIE’: THE ‘PUPPY STRING’ CHAPTER

Derrick “Puppy String” Eccleston was an early leader of the Klansman, before Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett assumed control.

Eccleston was killed on May 12, 1993. His death marked a change in the gang’s leadership, with Bennett subsequently taking over.

Although some accounts alleged Bennett’s involvement in Eccleston’s killing, that allegation was never proven in court.

BALLAD OF ‘BULBIE’

Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett, the leader of the Klansman gang and Jamaica’s most-wanted man for over a decade, was fatally shot on October 30, 2005, during a joint police-military raid in Clarendon.

Bennett gradually built up a criminal empire through murder and extortion whose assets included 80 motor vehicles and heavy equipment used in construction and hauling industries throughout Jamaica.

Authorities believe he gained leadership through the murder of then leader Eccleston in 1993.

During the early 1990s, Bennett led the gang against their rivals, the One Order Gang, resulting in numerous gangland shootings and other violence in Spanish Town.

READ: From ‘Bubba’ to ‘Thickman’: The ill-fated leadership of the One Order Gang

He later established an elaborate extortion operation targeting local business, particularly taximen, in both the central and south central regions of St Catherine. He would later be connected to criminal activities in Old Harbour and Portmore, St Catherine and May Pen.

He was thought to have briefly fled from authorities in Kingston to Great Britain under a false identity in 2001.

In 2005, security forces under Operation Kingfish cornered the 43-year-old Bennett at a lavish, seven-bedroom hideout he had built in the secluded hillside district of Tanaky (near Rock River), Clarendon.

According to police reports, security forces came under gunfire as they approached the compound in the pre-dawn hours. In the ensuing gun battle, Bennett and his driver, identified only as Nathan, were killed.

Police recovered a .50-caliber Desert Eagle pistol from Bennett, a Ruger pistol from his driver, and a large cache of cash and jewelry. At the time of his death, his wealth—amassed through extortion, construction equipment, and heavy haulage—was estimated at over J$100 million.

News of Bennett’s death triggered immediate violent reprisal across Spanish Town. Gang members mounted roadblocks, burned effigies of then-National Security Minister Dr Peter Phillips, and launched a gun attack on the Spanish Town Police Station, injuring two officers.

Following his elaborate funeral in De La Vega City and burial in Goshen, Clarendon, leadership of the Klansman gang allegedly passed to Tesha Miller, a welder by profession.

THE RISE OF TESHA

Tesha Miller, who grew up in Spanish Town after being born in De la Vega City, gained national attention in 2005 when he was charged with four counts of murder and three counts of shooting, for which he received bail.

Miller however, allegedly absconded to the United States.

He is also known on the streets by the nickname “Rat” (sometimes spelled “Ratt”). He has allegedly also used the alias Marlon Andre Williams (or Marlon Williams) on travel documents during past immigration incidents in The Bahamas and Jamaica.

Authorities linked the organisation under his alleged leadership to widespread extortion networks targeting transport operators, bus terminals, and businesses across Spanish Town and St Catherine.

He became even more notorious, attracting national attention over the June 2008 killing of JUTC chairman Douglas Chambers outside the company’s Spanish Town depot. Sentenced in January 2020 to more than 38 years for being an accessory before and after the fact, Miller had those convictions overturned in March 2026 because of jury-selection errors. The Court of Appeal ordered a retrial.

His history also includes capture and deportation from The Bahamas, where he reportedly travelled under a false identity. He is separately standing trial alongside 24 co-accused on an anti-gang indictment concerning alleged offences across several parishes between 2017 and 2022. Miller maintains his innocence and denies leading a gang.

MILLER HAS A LONG RAP SHEET

On May 3, 2007, after being caught by US officials, he was deported to Jamaica and was slapped with a nine-month prison term for absconding bail.

On March 5, 2008, Miller was fined $100,000 for breaching his curfew order.

On July 7, 2008, a cell phone was allegedly found in Miller’s rectum during a search of his cell at Horizon Remand Centre after the device reportedly rang. Miller strongly refuted the claim.

On November 21, 2008, Director of Public Prosecutions Paula Llewellyn took the decision not to proceed with a triple-murder case against Miller, as the police were having difficulty locating the sole eyewitness in the matter. He had been charged with the murder of Orane Jackson, Jeffrey Johnson and Nicole Allen who were shot in Braeton, St Catherine, on January 14, 2005.

On March 25, 2009, Miller was back before the court, and was denied bail, as he awaited trial for the murder of Rohan Haughton, who was fatally shot on St John’s Road, Spanish Town in April 2004. The eyewitness in the case was reportedly shot dead in St Elizabeth in August 2008.

After being in custody for almost a year, Miller was found not guilty for the murder of Haughton on June 10, 2009 as the Crown offered no further evidence against him as there was nothing to link him to the offence.

On December 26, 2009, Miller was arrested while at the Boxing Day show, Sting, after he allegedly breached a curfew order imposed by the court.

On May 2010, Miller turned himself in to the police after being listed among 25 men wanted for allegedly being gang members and area leaders.

On June 2010, Miller was detained under a State of Emergency. October 15, 2010, Miller was taken into custody for questioning in relation to an upsurge of shootings and other crimes in the St Catherine North Police Division.

On December 21, 2010, Miller was charged with robbery with aggravation involving a motor car and illegal possession of a firearm. Not long after, his 23-year-old sister Renase James was shot and killed while she was a passenger in a taxi in Spanish Town, St Catherine, in December 2011.

On April 15, 2011, Miller was sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment for robbery with aggravation. He was also sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment for illegal possession of firearm with the sentences to run concurrently.

Miller’s conviction for illegal possession of a firearm and robbery with aggravation was quashed and his sentence set aside on March 22, 2013 by the Court of Appeal.

He left Jamaica for the United States of America in April 2013.

Five months later, he was arrested there and charged with illegal re-entry, having previously been deported, and for having an identification card in another person’s name. Miller was convicted of the offences and sentenced to two years and eight months in prison. He was subsequently deported in March 2016. While Miller was in custody in the US, two of his brothers were shot and killed in 2015.

On August 7, 2016, Miller was listed by the police as a person of interest with claims being he could assist with investigations into several murders recorded in Spanish Town and Portmore, St Catherine.

On April 4, 2017, Miller was deported from The Bahamas after illegally entering the country. Fifteen days later, Miller was fined the $100 maximum fine under the law after he pleaded guilty to making a false declaration to Jamaican immigration officials.

THE RISE OF ‘BLACKMAN’

The One Don gang, led by Andre “Blackman” Bryan, emerged as a breakaway faction of the Klansman following a power struggle with reputed leader Tesha Miller around 2017.

Prosecutors alleged that the faction carried out murders, extortion, arson and firearms offences across St Catherine between 2015 and 2019, particularly in Spanish Town and Jones Avenue.

In March 2023, Chief Justice Bryan Sykes convicted Bryan of leading a criminal organisation and facilitating serious offences in a landmark anti-gang trial. Fifteen of the 33 defendants were convicted. Bryan was subsequently sentenced in October 2023 to 39 years and six months in prison.

Bryan was allegedly once the top hitman for reputed Klansman boss, Tesha Miller. The split dates back to at least 2017, when Bryan appears to have rebelled against Miller and began killing his associates.

Bryan’s ability to operate freely was significantly enhanced in 2016 when both men were on trial for the 2008 murder of senior transport official Douglas Chambers. While prosecutors said Miller ordered the hit and Bryan was the gunman, Miller was sentenced to over 38 years in jail for being an accessory before and after the fact, and Bryan was exonerated. Miller’s conviction was subsequently overturned due to jury selection errors.

Witness testimony has painted Bryan as an incredibly violent individual who laughed upon learning targets had been killed. State witnesses said they were forced to join the gang out of fear for their lives.

During sentencing hearings in late September and early October 2023, Bryan addressed the court and openly acknowledged his leadership role, showing his sense of fearlessness and growing hubris.

World.title: Why Jean-Luc Mélenchon has it in for Germany
World.content:
The comments up the ante on Mélenchon’s long-standing defiance toward France’s neighbor, which he accuses of acting as a hegemon in Europe. His hostility toward Berlin — part longtime obsession, part political positioning — is one of the many ways the far-left leader clashes with his country’s establishment, which has traditionally worked closely with Berlin to shape the continent.

Unsurprisingly, his comments have riled many in Germany, given that the rearmament effort was a response to Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“Mélenchon paints a distorted picture of Germany and Franco-German relations,” said Roland Theis, a German lawmaker from the conservative Christian Democratic Union who chairs the Bundestag’s Franco-German Parliamentary Group and sits on its Defense Committee.

U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz during a work lunch as part of the G7 summit, in Evian on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Christian Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images

The leftist veteran is polling in second place ahead of next year’s presidential election, putting him within reach of a runoff against the far-right front-runner, Marine Le Pen. For some in Berlin, neither prospect is particularly reassuring.

“On security and European affairs, his political positions are at least as dangerous as Le Pen’s,” Theis said.

A critic of Berlin’s traditional positions on fiscal and European affairs, Mélenchon is the author of a 2015 book subtitled “The German Poison.”

World.title: How to watch the Spanish election like a pro
World.content:
What about the Senate?

Some 209 senators will also be elected directly by voters, with four coming from every province on the mainland and additional representatives elected on Spain’s islands and North African exclaves. Regional parliaments appoint the remaining senators.

The Senate is less powerful than the Congress, providing second readings of proposed legislation and territorial representation. The body has a reputation for being a dumping ground for sidelined party grandees and a refuge for politicians whom Spain’s political groups seek to shield from judicial investigations through parliamentary immunity.

However, its support is vital for constitutional reform, and the chamber has the power to appoint magistrates to the Constitutional Court. Although the Senate doesn’t normally get much attention during elections, right-wing parties are hoping to secure three-fifths of the seats this year, enough to push through appointments that could shift the Constitutional Court’s ideological balance without consulting the left.

In the hopes of gaining control of the chamber, the Socialists and the PP have both struck deals with like-minded parties to withdraw candidates from constituencies where they would run against each other.

What happens after election day?

Once all the votes are counted and seats in Congress are assigned, coalition negotiations and vote-whipping for investiture debates formally begin. This can take months and has become increasingly long-winded in recent years as Spanish politics has become more fragmented.

The process is, in theory, simple: The candidate who wishes to become prime minister meets with the king, who tasks them with forming a government. This candidate then presents themselves to the Congress for an investiture debate and vote, in which they need at least 176 votes from their peers to be elected.

World.title: This Riviera mayor wants to bring Javier Milei’s chainsaw politics to France
World.content:
“Lisnard is very different, very free,” said Geoffroy Boulard, a mayor and vice president of Lisnard’s New Energy party. “Some say he’s nothing but an online bubble, but there’s a surge of popular enthusiasm around him.”

Partly thanks to his stunts, the plain-speaking, athletic 57-year-old has become a social media phenomenon, with supporters posting AI-generated videos that portray him as a Marvel superhero, a World War I soldier or even a member of the Ghostbusters team.

Lisnard, a former member of the conservative Les Républicains party, openly praises Milei’s methods in Argentina. He argues that France needs its own “radical and cultural break” with the “infernal spiral” of debt, tax hikes and deteriorating public services.

POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts Lisnard at 11% in the first round, neck and neck with the center-right Edouard Philippe and the center-left Raphaël Glucksmann. Even Le Pen is under pressure to react to the emergence of a fresh face in the race, attacking him for failing to defend workers.

The Lisnard buzz is “a bubble,” said one of President Emmanuel Macron’s ministers who, like others quoted here, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But like Emmanuel Macron was at the beginning. We all laughed at him when he would lose his voice at his first political rallies.”

“Maybe the bubble will burst,” the minister added. “But it could also be the beginning of something.”

World.title: Tusk government ‘facing armageddon’ as European court resumes cases against Poland
World.content:
ND - NOVEMBER 7: Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk holds a press conference after a deadly shooting took place on November 7, 2026 in the Main Market Square of Krakow. | Omar Marques/Getty Images

The country faces millions of euros in potential compensation payments over its former nationalist government’s judicial overhaul.

Europe’s top human rights court resumed proceedings against Poland on Wednesday, putting fresh pressure on Prime Minister Donald Tusk to deliver on his promise to restore the independence of the country’s courts.

The European Court of Human Rights said it has around 1,600 cases pending over judicial changes introduced by Poland’s former nationalist Law and Justice government. It suspended proceedings in 2023 to give Warsaw time to restore judicial independence.

Tusk’s promise to restore the rule of law helped unlock billions in frozen EU funding following his return to power in 2023. But his efforts have been hampered by two successive PiS-backed presidents, most recently Karol Nawrocki.

World.title: “Les COP, c’est une blague” : les critiques enflent contre les sommets climatiques après l’échec à Antalya
World.content:
“Si nous parvenons à donner le meilleur de nous-mêmes, à nous organiser, au cours des douze prochains mois, la COP31 nous paraîtra rétrospectivement comme un moment cathartique de prise de conscience”, a positivé Rachel Kyte, envoyée spéciale du Royaume-Uni pour le climat, lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO, ajoutant que les pays devaient corriger le processus qui, ces dernières années, a peiné à produire des résultats.

Ceux appelant à une refonte du processus réclament une réforme du format COP, voire sa suppression pure et simple, sans que l’on ait réellement d’idées sur la manière de mettre en œuvre l’une ou l’autre de ces options. Reste que l’échec des organisateurs à négocier un accord final a libéré un flot de critiques.

Selon ses détracteurs, le processus actuel, dans lequel les pays pétroliers font obstacle aux initiatives visant à mentionner explicitement les énergies fossiles, n’est plus viable dans un monde qui se dirige à toute vitesse vers une aggravation des conditions climatiques.

“Nous avons tous été pris en otage par les producteurs de pétrole, mais aussi par les plus grands consommateurs de pétrole”, a pointé auprès de POLITICO le ministre panaméen du Climat, Juan Carlos Navarro.

La faute aux pays pétroliers, mais pas que

Ces négociations chaotiques en Turquie interviennent onze ans après que, pour la première fois, tous les pays se sont mis d’accord sur la nécessité de lutter contre le changement climatique en signant l’Accord de Paris. Depuis, des progrès poussifs ont laissé les pays à la traîne par rapport à leurs objectifs. Au point que l’ONU a annoncé le mois dernier qu’il n’y avait plus aucun espoir d’éviter un réchauffement de 1,5 °C.

L’échec de ce week-end contraste fortement avec les négociations de l’année dernière au Brésil, où les gouvernements étaient parvenus à un accord malgré les attaques à distance contre le processus du président Donald Trump, et sa décision de retirer les Etats-Unis de l’Accord de Paris.

World.title: Don’t ‘backslide’ on defense spending, senior US lawmaker tells Europe
World.content:
His comments come as EU leaders prepare to discuss the bloc’s next seven-year budget at a summit Thursday and Friday. The latest draft defense budget tabled by European Council President António Costa would see tens of billions cut from the European Commission’s earlier proposal, drawing the ire of some EU countries — though the total is still double the previous seven-year budget.

Boyle said he was “heartened” that all NATO allies were now spending more on defense than the alliance’s longstanding 2% of GDP target agreed at the 2014 Wales summit. “I’m glad that that is a floor and no longer considered a ceiling,” he said, while acknowledging that European governments face “similar budget constraints” to the U.S.

He said Europe building up its own defense industry after decades of relying on American weapons was a net positive for the NATO alliance, but warned against the bloc breaking that dependence too fast. EU countries are currently only spending about 15% of their defense procurement budgets on European-made equipment, despite calls from the Commission to raise this to at least half by 2030.

“Where it would become a negative is if suddenly there was a hard turn away from totally buying U.S. systems,” Boyle said. “That would be a mistake.”

World.title: From the track to the gallery: Dakar's autumn in the spotlight
World.content:
This November, Dakar hosted two exceptional events: the Youth Olympic Games, which ran until 13 November, and Dak'Art, the Dakar Biennale of contemporary African art, which runs from 19 November to 19 December. The Games were the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent, and the Biennale now brings together artists from across Africa and its diaspora. In this episode, we hear from participants in both events.

Advertising

Dakar, Senegal, hosted the Youth Olympic Games from 31 October to 13 November, a landmark event widely celebrated across the country.

It was the fourth edition of the Games for young athletes, but the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent.

Dancers form the word "Dakar" during the opening ceremony of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games at the Abdoulaye Wade Stadium in Diamniadio on 31 October, 2026. © AFP - SEYLLOU

In this episode, you'll hear from Kirsty Coventry, President of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), and from RFI English's sports journalist, Paul Myers. Both agree that it was a unique event, and they look ahead to the future of the Games in Africa.

As Senegal sets Youth Games medal record, Olympic hero calls for more investment

After sport, there's art

Then, just a few days after the Games closed, Dakar launched Dak'Art on 19 November. The Biennale runs until Saturday 19 December 2026 and features artists from across the continent and its diaspora.

The theme of this edition is "(Anti)fragility", which, according to the curator and organisers, refers to "the capacity to turn fragile situations into a space for invention and expressive power".

The main venue is the former Law Courts building, now the National Art Gallery.

Cultural exchanges beyond borders as African art gains global interest

"The project emphasises social and community bonds, co-creation, acts of care, and responses that allow the experience of shocks to be transformed into new possibilities," the curator said.

This year's artists include Nu Barreto from Guinea-Bissau, who won one of the main prizes, Ibrahima Cissé and Eva Diallo, both from Senegal, Chemu Ng'ok from Kenya, and Souad Abdelrasoul from Cairo, among many others.

Billboards advertising the Dakar Biennale 2026, the 16th Dakar Biennale of Contemporary African Art, the most important event of its kind on the continent, which showcases the best of African art and its diasporas through hundreds of cultural events combining painting, sculpture, and performance. © Patrick Meinhardt / AFP

Alpha Thiam, Senegal's Minister of Culture, Crafts and Tourism, said these events were "drawing on the philosophy of Senghor" and embracing "modernity without ever forsaking our authenticity".

In his view, the participants show that "contemporary African creation is not merely a superficial construct, but a genuine assertion of sovereignty", allowing Africans to build their future on their own terms.

In this episode, Souad Abdelrasoul, who had just arrived in Dakar for the opening, and her gallery manager, Menna Genedy, of the Misr Gallery in Cairo talked to RFI.

You'll also hear from the Senegalese storyteller, or griot, Bocar Niang, and his associate, the artist and philanthropist Amélie Mourgue d'Algue, of the French charity the Bureau of Invisible Hours (Bureau des heures invisibles).

Niang set up his own museum in his hometown of Tambacounda. The museum is dedicated to the culture of griots, the travelling musicians and storytellers who keep the tradition of oral history alive in parts of West Africa.

Beyond Senegal

Dakar is also a meeting point for artists from all over Africa, especially in the 'off 'programme.

The book, Made in Sierra Leone — Edition 02, will be unveiled during the fair for instance; it is the expanded second edition of the limited edition book by multidisciplinary artist Sahr Martin Kabba known as Sabanoh, from Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Made in Sierra Leone, Edition 02: by artist Sabanoh © Unx-art

Artist and curator Sarah Hachi-Duchene of Unx-art tells us in this episode how this publication extends Sabanoh's exploration of Sierra Leone’s contemporary visual language and cultural memory.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.
