The mayor of Warsaw has refused permission for opposition protests outside the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which was taken over last month by a group of government-backed judges, to continue. City hall, which is under the control of Poland’s main ruling party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), says that the demonstration threatens public safety. However, opposition figures have condemned the decision as “authoritarian” and one of the organisers of the protest has pledged to challenge it in court. Bum. Jest zakaz organizacji kolejnej manifestacji przed Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym.https://t.co/Ol8gQxC3A1 pic.twitter.com/bUqAkdojxe — Tomasz Skory (@TomaszSkory) November 25, 2026 On 30 October, a group of eight judges chosen this year by the government’s parliamentary majority – but five of whom opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in – effectively took control of the TK. They declared that the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, was suspended. Meanwhile, riot police surrounded the court and held back protesters, including Święczkowski himself. Since then, the demonstrators have maintained a constant presence outside the court, while Święczkowski has also periodically appeared. He and Nawrocki argue that the actions of the eight “usurper” judges are illegal and that Święczkowski remains chief justice. Given the ongoing demonstration in front of the court, the judges currently controlling the TK have used a separate entrance that leads in from the next-door chancellery of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. On Monday this week, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge who has declared herself acting head of the court, arranged a meeting with Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, and the commander of Warsaw police, Krzysztof Ogroński, to discuss the protest. She argued that, by preventing access to the tribunal, the demonstrators were “violating the constitutional and European standard of the right to a court”. On Wednesday morning, Warsaw city hall announced that Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of Tusk’s centrist KO party, had rejected a request for permission to continue the public assembly outside the TK from the end of November until January. ‼️ Rafał Trzaskowski zakazał zgromadzenia pod Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym! Protest trwa tam od września i dotyczy sporu o to, kto ma w TK zasiadać. W poniedziałek osoba podająca się za „Zastępującą Prezesa TK” zaprosiła ratusz i Policję, by „przywrócić” wstęp do Trybunału. Dwa… pic.twitter.com/a0EzqVzRDn — Magdalena Majkowska (@MagdaMajkowska) November 25, 2026 “While the freedom to organise and participate in peaceful assemblies constitutes a fundamental constitutional freedom, it is not unconditional,” wrote the municipal authorities. They noted that the current gathering outside the TK has been ongoing since 17 September (as protesters anticipated an attempted takeover of the court) and that the organisers had given assurances that they would not obstruct the roadway. In fact, tents, a television stage and other structures have blocked the road, wrote city hall. This “causes significant disruption for local residents” and “undoubtedly hinders emergency service vehicles, thereby threatening the life and health of residents”. The authorities also noted that, while the protests were initially peaceful, there had later been a number of “dangerous incidents”, including attempts to block vehicles from entering the TK and scuffles with police, which included throwing objects at officers, physical confrontations, verbal abuse and spitting. Such developments “have caused the gathering to lose its peaceful character”, wrote city hall. There are also “grounds to assume that the intention is, in effect, a long-term blockade of the entrance to the Constitutional Tribunal and the street itself”. One of the organisers of the protest, Adam Borowski, told Polsat News that it is a “lie” that they are preventing the TK from functioning properly. It is the judges “illegally occupying” the tribunal who are responsible, he said. Borowski announced that they would appeal against the city’s decision in court. They have 24 hours from the issuing of the decision in which to do so. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, meanwhile, declared that the decision to ban the protest was “authoritarianism in its purest form…trampling citizens’ constitutional rights”. Russia has “categorically denied” that the three missiles which struck Poland last week were Russian and has accused Warsaw of seeking to “stoke anti-Russian sentiment” around the incident. Its remarks came after Poland’s foreign ministry on Tuesday summoned Russia’s ambassador, Georgy Mikhno, to present him with a protest over the missiles. Today, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that expelling the ambassador is “one of the options” Poland could take, though it remains unlikely. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 24 listopada 2026 r. JE Pan Gieorgij Michno, Ambasador Federacji Rosyjskiej w Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej, został zaproszony do MSZ kraju przyjmującego, gdzie przekazano mu protest w ramach rzekomego „powiązania” naszego kraju z incydentami… pic.twitter.com/GUJB0RWZgt — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) November 24, 2026 On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeastern Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border, amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. On Sunday, Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. Subsequently, on Monday night this week, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine and spent a few minutes above Poland before turning back into Ukraine. On Tuesday, Mikhno was summoned to the Polish foreign ministry, which said it had presented him with “a very strong diplomatic note” regarding the missile strikes. Afterwards, Mikhno read a statement to the media saying that “Russia categorically rejects the accusations of involvement in the incidents”, which were being made based on “political judgements and unsubstantiated assumptions”. He also condemned what he said was “openly Russophobic rhetoric around the incident”, which suggests “a desire to exploit the situation to further stoke anti-Russian sentiment”. The ambassador claimed that “no convincing and verifiable evidence has been presented” to establish the origin of the missiles. He then refused to answer journalists’ questions before leaving. Russia has installed an exhibition titled “Ten Centuries of Polish Russophobia” outside a cemetery for thousands of Poles murdered by the Soviets in the 1940 Katyn massacre. It opened just before Poland marked its annual day of remembrances for victims https://t.co/HcfmeNrerB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026 Mikhno’s claims were immediately rejected by the Polish foreign ministry’s spokesman, Maciej Wewiór, who said that it was “beyond dispute” that the missiles were Russian and that Moscow “knows [this] perfectly well”. On Sunday, Polish prosecutors said that the remains of the missiles leave no doubt they are Russian, and added that preliminary findings even indicate which specific factory they were manufactured in and when. A number of Poland’s NATO allies, as well as the alliance’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, have also condemned Russia over the missile incident and expressed solidarity with Warsaw. NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week. Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026 On Wednesday morning, Sikorski was asked during an interview with Polskie Radio whether a “strong diplomatic note” was a strong enough response, given Russia’s repeated and continued hostile actions towards Poland. When it was put to the foreign minister that Poland should expel the Russian ambassador, Sikorski said that “this is one option” and “of course, it can be done”. However, he added that “we won’t pursue it yet” and noted that any such action would be met with an equivalent response from Moscow. In 2024 and 2025, Sikorski successively ordered Russia to close all of its consulates in Poland in response to Russian acts of sabotage. Moscow responded by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory. 🗣️ "Czy jest sens rozmawiania z ambasadorem Rosji? To symboliczny gest pokazania dezaprobaty. Liczą się sankcje i naciski gospodarcze. (…) Nie ma decyzji, by zerwać stosunki dyplomatyczne, ale one wiszą na cienkim włosku" Rzecznik rządu @adamSzlapka w rozmowie z @Piekarski_M… pic.twitter.com/JU9up9cm5N — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 25, 2026 On Monday morning, Polish government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVP that “relations [with Russia] are hanging by a thread”. He added that, while presenting a protest note to the Russian ambassador had been “a symbolic gesture of disapproval”, most important are “the sanctions and the pressure on Russia”. “I think [this pressure] is strong from the entire European Union…[but] we’ve had doubts from the United States regarding these sanctions in recent months,” said Szłapka. “Poland believes [the pressure] should be consistent and stronger…I hope the entire Western world will be very clear on this.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland and US sign defence technology cooperation agreement
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland and the United States have signed an agreement on defence research, development, testing and evaluation, concluding 17 years of negotiations and opening the way for deeper technological cooperation. The agreement establishes a framework for joint defence projects, as well as the exchange of technical data and expertise, giving Poland – which is already a major importer of US arms – a formal role in the development of American defence technologies for the first time. Under Secretary Emil Michael (@USWREMichael) and Mr. Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s Secretary of State at the Ministry of National Defence, signed the Agreement Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Poland for Defense Research,… pic.twitter.com/7EAgK3nD2i — Department of War CTO (@DoWCTO) November 23, 2026 The agreement was signed at the Pentagon by Poland’s deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk and US under secretary of war for research and engineering Emil Michael. According to the Department of War, the deal will help “turn research and development into validated military capabilities to jointly support US and Polish warfighters”. Tomczyk said the agreement would allow Polish universities, research institutes and companies to participate in joint research and development work on defence technology with US partners and would enable such technologies to be tailored more closely to the requirements of the Polish armed forces. During a briefing in Washington, Tomczyk admitted that the agreement had been negotiated for what he described as a “probably record-breaking” 17 years, but he noted a “significant acceleration in relations” between the US and Poland over the last six months. General Marcin Górka, who oversees innovation in the Polish armed forces and accompanied Tomczyk to the United States, likewise welcomed the agreement, which he said would “open the doors to American military laboratories for our scientists and engineers”. Górka also said the agreement would enable Poland and the United States to jointly develop anti-drone systems and advanced drones, with testing taking place in both countries. Poland is a major importer of US military hardware. Between 2021 and 2025, it was the biggest overall importer of arms in NATO, with around 44% of that equipment coming from the US, including F-35 fighter jets, Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence systems and HIMARS rocket launchers. But Poland has recently sought to move from being a client of the US defence industry to more of a partner. Earlier this month, Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed a declaration on expanding bilateral defence-industrial cooperation. Poland and the US have signed a statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation. Polish defence minister @KosiniakKamysz said his country would be "the US ambassador in the EU", including seeking EU funds for jointly produced equipment https://t.co/SKHrxTEKIW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2026 Last month, Poland was chosen as the location for a planned Patriot missile maintenance and servicing facility, the first of its kind outside the United States. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks. This year, Polish state defence group PGZ was chosen as the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles, while US defence giant Northrop Grumman and Polish arms manufacturer Niewiadów-PGM announced plans to jointly produce artillery shells in Poland. Poland is also seeking to host a new permanent US military base, with Tomczyk reiterating during his Washington visit that a decision is expected from the Trump administration in early December. NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week. Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026 The new agreement on defence technology was signed amid heightened tensions with Russia. On Friday, three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles struck separate locations in southeastern Poland, near the Ukrainian border. Tomczyk said the Polish delegation had briefed Pentagon officials on the missile strikes, which he described as a “provocation” by Russia. The Polish minister was also asked about US President Donald Trump last week calling Russia’s Vladimir Putin his “friend”. “One thing is certain: Vladimir Putin is not our friend; he is a threat to us,” replied Tomczyk. “This is the most important message that should come from Poland and resonate with the people of the United States.” Subsequently, on Monday night, a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine for a few minutes before turning back. World.title: Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated rights of migrants sent back to Belarus, finds European court
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled. However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders. That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation. 📽️ Watch a video explainer on the Grand Chamber cases concerning instrumentalisation of migration. 📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile. In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus. On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus. The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”. This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”. Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention. However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”. That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus. In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants. A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence. One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024 For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis. The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus. However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR. The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation. Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025 In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”. At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk. However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention. It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures. ⚖️ Grand Chamber cases ➡️ Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, European Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections. 🔗 Press release: https://t.co/nflEyCWKb1 — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In response to today’s ruling on Poland, the deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Maciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”. He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies. The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration. “In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC. Bardzo ważny i dobry dla nas wyrok Europejskiego Trybunału Praw Człowieka. Niezakwestionowano naszego modelu walki z nielegalną migracją. Trybunał odniósł się do instrumentalizacji jako sprzecznej z Konwencją i podkreślił prawo państ do obrony i ochrony swoich granic. — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) November 24, 2026 A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border. Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted. The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration. This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross. NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland in response to last week’s incident in which three Russian missiles struck Polish territory. Shortly after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone that entered from Ukraine. However, although the military was given authorisation to shoot the object down, they did not do so after the drone began to move back into Ukraine. Today, NATO Ambassadors met in the North Atlantic Council to discuss last week’s violations of Polish airspace. This was a dangerous incident and Russia bears full responsibility. NATO and Allied assets reacted quickly to the airspace violations, and the Supreme Allied Commander… — NATO Spokesperson (@NATOpress) November 23, 2026 On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeast Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine, and on Sunday Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. The missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before striking the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which were patrolling Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, received authorisation from NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre to fire upon the objects if certain conditions were met. However, the pilots were unable to confirm their identity in time due to poor weather conditions. On Monday, an extraordinary meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main decision-making body, took place to discuss the incident. Afterwards, deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski, who represented Poland at the meeting, announced that NATO had agreed to place an AWACS “at Poland’s disposal”. Later, NATO’s spokeswoman, Allison Hart, confirmed that “the Supreme Allied Commander Europe has authorised the forward deployment of a NATO AWACS aircraft” and is also “examining the deployment of additional assets as he continues to assess our deterrence and defence posture in Poland and elsewhere”. Poland has confirmed that the three objects which struck its territory last Friday were all Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. Preliminary findings indicate the missiles were recently manufactured at a plant in Dubna, Russia https://t.co/4N6k3eBUGN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 23, 2026 “This is a very serious capability that gives us enhanced situational awareness,” said Zalewski, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. “This is an immediate NATO response, and we are very happy about it.” “What I heard today is a great demonstration of the alliance’s unity with Poland in the face of Russian attacks,” he added. “It’s safe to say that the Russians have moved up the escalation ladder in their relations with NATO.This means…the need for an appropriate response.” Zalewski emphasised that “we’re not talking about offensive actions in any way, but about the ability to defend against all the attacks Russia is launching against NATO countries”. The aim is “not to escalate, but to…discourage Russia from attacks”. Wiceminister @ZalewskiPawel w Kwaterze Głównej #NATO: Do dyspozycji Polski będzie jeden samolot szybkiego ostrzegania #AWACS. To jest bardzo poważna zdolność, która daje nam pogłębioną świadomość sytuacyjną. I to jest natychmiastowa reakcja NATO. — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 23, 2026 On Monday night, after NATO had made its decision, Poland’s airspace was again violated, this time by a Russian drone that crossed the border from Ukraine. The operational command of Poland’s armed forces announced shortly before midnight that it had continuously tracked the object and granted authorisation to shoot it down. However, after the drone changed course and began to head east, back towards the border, a decision was made to refrain from engaging it, “taking into account the potential threat to civilians and the possible consequences of shooting down the object”, said operational command. W trakcie nocnego ataku Federacji Rosyjskiej na cele w zachodniej części Ukrainy, prowadzonego z wykorzystaniem środków napadu powietrznego, doszło do krótkotrwałego naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej przez rosyjski bezzałogowy statek powietrzny. W odpowiedzi na… pic.twitter.com/BhJN7UYg7m — Dowództwo Operacyjne RSZ (@DowOperSZ) November 23, 2026 According to a report by broadcaster RMF, based on unnamed sources, the vehicle was a jet-powered drone that flew 20 km into Poland and remained in Polish airspace for around nine minutes. Speaking to RMF on Tuesday morning, Zalewski said that “it is difficult to imagine that this was an accident; we assume it was an intentional action”. Russia has so far not commented on either its missiles hitting Poland last Friday nor the latest drone incursion. They are the latest in a series of airspace violations. In September this year, a Russian helicopter briefly crossed the border from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. In September 2025, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders in an unprecedented violation that prompted Poland to trigger NATO’s Article 4. The Netherlands will become the latest country to purchase Poland’s Piorun man-portable air-defence systems, which have been increasingly in demand following their successful use during Ukraine’s defence against Russia. On Monday, their Polish manufacturer, Mesko, which is part of state-owned defence group PGZ, signed an agreement adding the Netherlands to a list of countries that will buy Pioruns with funds from the European Union’s SAFE mechanism for financing defence spending. 🇵🇱🇳🇱⚡ HOLANDIA DOŁĄCZA DO DRUŻYNY PIORUNA! W @PGZ_MESKO_SA w Skarżysku-Kamiennej podpisano aneks do umowy ramowej, umożliwiający Holandii dołączenie do wspólnych zamówień zestawów PIORUN. ✍️ Dokument podpisali gen. dyw. Artur Kuptel, Szef @AgencjaUzbr, oraz Krzysztof Marwicki… pic.twitter.com/lVH0QgdD0t — Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa🇵🇱 (@PGZ_pl) November 23, 2026 Piorun (meaning “thunderbolt” in Polish) is a shoulder-mounted system that fires air-defence missiles capable of destroying aerial vehicles, such as helicopters, drones and low-flying planes, at short range. In 2022, Pioruns were among the large quantities of military equipment that Poland provided to Ukraine to help its eastern neighbour defend itself from Russia’s full-scale invasion. The systems have been successfully used to take down Russian aircraft. Since then, they have been in high demand, with Mesko receiving orders from the United States, Norway, Belgium and Sweden, as well as Ukraine itself. In August this year, Mesko signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.8 billion) agreement to supply further Piorun systems to Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia, with the deal financed through SAFE funds. Precise details were not revealed. However, the agreement was said to involve the supply of “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles, with over 80% of the equipment going to Poland’s own armed forces. Now Mesko has signed an addendum to that deal, adding the Netherlands to the list of countries that are jointly ordering Pioruns. Deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who has overseen Poland’s participation in the SAFE programme, said after attending Monday’s signing ceremony that the Netherlands would not be the last country to join the procurement of Pioruns. “We promised that the list of Mesko’s buyers from all over Europe would grow, and today we have living proof of that,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “And I can reveal a secret: it’s not over yet.” She noted that Mesko has stepped up its production volumes in response to demand. Last year, it could produce “several hundred” systems annually; that has now risen to 1,500, and is set to grow even further. Last week, PGZ and the state assets ministry signed an agreement to support Mesko’s expansion with around 370 million zloty from the state Capital Investment Fund (FIK). It will help bring production capacity to around 2,500 per year. 🗣️ "Obiecywaliśmy, że lista kupujących z całej Europy będzie się powiększać i mamy tego żywy dowód. A mogę zdradzić sekret, że to jeszcze nie koniec. Dzisiejsza umowa to umowa w ramach zakupów w mechanizmie SAFE"@magdasobkowiak o zestawach Piorun dla Holandii ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/sTxG5SwnbZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 23, 2026 Growing demand for Pioruns resulted in Mesko last year posting the best financial results in its 100-year history. The firm’s revenues of 2.3 billion zloty in 2025 were up 33% year-on-year. The EU’s SAFE programme is providing a total of €150 billion in loans at preferential rates for member states to use on defence-related spending. Poland, with around €44 billion, is the largest single recipient. While most SAFE purchases are conducted individually by member states, some are also carried out jointly. Such joint procurement can also involve certain non-EU countries, such as Norway. World.title: Public astronomical observatory opens in Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday. Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment. The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall. “Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening. “Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added. The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express. “The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper. “We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added. Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation. The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking. This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions. The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope. The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 The observatory also features a computer coordinating its measurements, a camera showing almost the entire sky, and a weather monitoring system. Observations will depend on atmospheric conditions and visibility. “Examples of how this telescope might be used include photographing the cosmos and conducting simple research, such as measuring changes in the brightness of stars and producing graphs illustrating these changes,” explained Ewa Konarzewska from Gocław Culture Terminal. Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last year, the country launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest-ever contract with the European Space Agency, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites. Meanwhile, 2025 also saw astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski become the second-ever Pole to travel into space, as part of an ESA mission to the International Space Station. Earlier this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new ESA centre focused on civil security and resilience, with the agency’s head declaring that “Poland has rapidly become one of the driving forces in Europe’s space sector”. World.title: Expedia to Acquire Czech Flight Booking Company Kiwi.com
World.content:
American travel company Expedia Group has agreed to acquire Czech flight booking platform Kiwi.com, bringing a change of ownership to the Brno-based business.

The transaction is expected to be completed by the middle of 2027, although the companies have not disclosed its value.

The acquisition will see the departure of Kiwi.com’s current majority shareholder, US investment fund General Atlantic, which has controlled the company since 2019. Co-founder Oliver Dlouhý, who holds a minority stake, is also expected to exit.



Expedia said the deal would strengthen its technology and expand its position in the European air travel market. Kiwi.com generated approximately €227 million in revenue last year, equivalent to around CZK 5.6 billion.

Expedia said the acquisition would give travelers access to a wider selection of flights and provide new opportunities for growth across its brands, including Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo.

Kiwi.com was founded in Brno in 2012 by Dlouhý and his business partners. The company became known internationally for its search technology, which allowed it to combine flights from airlines that did not necessarily have direct partnerships with the platform.

The company has since developed into an international flight retailer, focusing on technology, automation and artificial intelligence to improve its operations.

The acquisition comes after several years of restructuring at Kiwi.com, which faced financial difficulties following the decline in air travel during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The company reduced its workforce by more than 200 employees in 2024. Earlier this year, it announced plans to cut approximately 250 jobs from a workforce of around 700.

Expedia Group was founded in 1996 as a division of Microsoft. It operates an online travel platform offering bookings for flights, accommodation, car rentals and activities, as well as technology services for corporate partners.

World.title: Christmas Trees You Can Replant After the Holidays Are Available in Prague
World.content:
Residents of Prague and Brno can choose a living Christmas tree this year and give it a chance to grow in the forest after the holidays.

Both cities are offering small potted firs that can be planted in spring with the help of foresters.

In Prague, the Forests of the Capital City of Prague are running their Christmas fir project for the tenth consecutive year. The initiative, known as A Christmas Fir with a Future, allows people to buy a young silver fir for 150 CZK.

The trees, approximately 50 centimeters tall, have been grown in a forest nursery in Čimický háj. Unlike cut Christmas trees, they retain their roots and can continue growing after Christmas.



The organizers acknowledge that the firs may not look like traditional Christmas trees. Their branches are often irregular, and each tree has its own shape.

The project also aims to support the return of silver fir to Czech forests. The native species (Abies alba) became scarce during the 20th century, partly because of air pollution, forestry practices and excessive numbers of wild animals.

Where to buy a living Christmas tree in Prague

The potted firs are available at several locations, including the Ďáblice Garden Center, the Prales eco-center and forest lodges in Hostivař, Chuchle, Šárka, Běchovice, Kunratice and Čimice.

How to care for a potted Christmas tree

A living Christmas tree needs more attention than a cut one. It should remain outdoors in a cool place, such as a balcony or garden, for as long as possible before being brought inside.

The tree should be gradually acclimatized to the warmer indoor temperature. The room should ideally stay below 20 degrees Celsius, and the soil needs regular watering. Spraying the needles with water can also help.

After Christmas, the tree should be moved back to a cooler environment gradually.

Even with careful handling, survival is not guaranteed. According to the Masaryk Forest Křtiny School Forest Enterprise, around 60 percent of the Christmas firs planted in previous years have successfully taken root.

World.title: Higher Prices, Fuller Hotels: Prague Is Becoming a Luxury City Break
World.content:
Prague is strengthening its position as a high-end tourist destination, attracting visitors willing to spend more on accommodation and services.

The Czech capital has ranked ahead of Vienna and Berlin in an international tourism index, while demand for luxury hotels continues to rise.

More than 2.3 million tourists visited Prague between July and September 2026, representing a three percent increase compared with the same period last year.



The city received a score of 92.7 out of 100 in the Global Tourist Perception Index, compiled by Data Appeal and Mabrian Intelligence. Vienna scored 85.6, while Berlin received 78.4.

The ranking assessed several aspects of the visitor experience, including satisfaction with accommodation, safety and the variety of tourist attractions.

According to František Cipro, chairman of the board of Prague City Tourism, the results reflect a shift in the city’s tourism profile.

“Prague clearly demonstrates that it is no longer a budget tourist destination, nor does it wish to be one,” he said.

The trend is also reflected in visitor spending. During the first half of 2026, Prague welcomed more than 3.8 million tourists, a one percent increase year-on-year. However, Mastercard payment data showed that spending by visitors from selected foreign markets rose by 18 percent.

Tourists from China and South Korea recorded the most significant increases in spending.

Accommodation figures point in the same direction. Almost two-thirds of guests staying in Prague hotels choose four- or five-star properties.

In 2025, the average price of a hotel room in the capital stood at around CZK 3,000 per night. In central Prague, the average rose to approximately CZK 4,100, while luxury hotels charged around CZK 5,800.

Demand for higher-end accommodation has remained strong despite rising prices. In September 2026, luxury hotels recorded an occupancy rate of 83 percent, their highest September result in seven years.

Germany Remains the Largest Source Market

Tourism continued to grow during the first nine months of 2026, with Prague recording more than 6.1 million visitors, a two percent increase compared with the same period in 2025.

Germany remained the largest source market for international visitors during the third quarter.

Some other markets also recorded notable growth. Visitor numbers from Taiwan increased by 27 percent, followed by Israel at 26 percent and Ireland at 23 percent.

World.title: How to Choose a High School in the Czech Republic: Open Days and School Fairs
World.content:
Choosing a high school is an important decision for students and their families.

School websites and brochures can provide useful information, but visiting schools in person offers a much better idea of what studying there is actually like.

Open days and high school fairs are two ways to explore the available options, meet teachers and students, and find out which school might be the right fit.



This is the first article in our series on choosing a high school in the Czech Republic.

Visit Schools During Open Days

Open days give prospective students and their parents the opportunity to look around a school before applying.

High schools open their doors to visitors, allowing them to explore classrooms, workshops and laboratories, meet teachers and current students, and ask questions about studying there.

An open day can help families find out more about:

Study programmes: What courses and specialisations does the school offer?

Admission requirements: What are the conditions for applying, and how does the entrance examination work?

Future opportunities: What options are available after graduation, including further education and employment?

School environment: What is the atmosphere like, and would the school be a good fit for the student?

Open days take place throughout the school year, with many schools organising them ahead of the application period.

Dates vary from one institution to another, so check individual school websites or use the online overview of high school open days to find upcoming events.

Compare Schools at High School Fairs

High school fairs offer another opportunity to explore different institutions without having to visit each one separately.

In Prague, one of the main events is SCHOLA PRAGENSIS, where visitors can meet representatives of secondary schools from different regions.

You can visit META stand at Schola Pragensis, Prague’s high school fair, taking place from 26 to 28 November at the Prague Congress Centre

– stand number 245 on the 2nd floor.

The META team of professionals will help you explore the options and answer all your questions.

Students and parents can compare study programmes, ask questions about admission procedures and learn more about individual schools directly from their representatives.

These events are particularly useful for students who have not yet decided what they want to study or are still considering several different options. Meeting representatives from multiple schools in one place can help narrow down the choices.

If you live outside Prague, you can also find a high school fair in your region.

Use Worksheets to Help Make Your Decision

Comparing schools, admission requirements and study programmes can quickly become confusing, especially when several institutions are under consideration.

Free worksheets are available to help students organise information, compare their options and think about what they want from their future school.

You can download the worksheets here.

World.title: EF English Proficiency Index: Brno Speaks Better English Than Prague
World.content:
Prague has improved its English proficiency score, but it still trails Brno, according to the latest EF English Proficiency Index (EF EPI).

The Czech capital gained nine points over the past year, while Brno recorded a slight decline. Despite the contrasting trends, the South Moravian city remains ahead.



The Czech Republic ranked 24th out of 117 countries and regions in this year’s global index, published by education company EF Education First. Its score of 569 points represents a drop of 13 points and one place compared with the previous year.

The country remains in the high-proficiency category, although several neighboring states performed better. Austria ranked second worldwide with 613 points, followed by Germany in fourth place with 611. Slovakia came 11th with 594 points, while Poland ranked 15th with 587.

Slovakia’s performance is particularly notable. The country has gained 49 points since 2016, making it one of Europe’s most improved performers over the past decade. Although its score fell slightly compared with last year, it still leads the Czech Republic by 25 points.

Brno Maintains Its Lead Over Prague

Brno scored 613 points in this year’s assessment, placing it 28 points ahead of Prague, which recorded 585.

The gap between the two cities has narrowed, however. Prague improved from 576 points last year, while Brno fell from 620.

Brno’s result is particularly strong in an international comparison. Its score matches Austria’s, which ranked second among the countries included in the global index.

The regional figures also support Brno’s position. The South Moravian Region recorded 606 points, the highest score among Czech regions.

Sweden Takes First Place in Global Rankings

The Netherlands has lost its position at the top of the global English proficiency rankings, with Sweden taking first place this year with 615 points.

The Dutch finished fifth with 609 points. Austria, Denmark and Germany occupied the places between them, scoring 613, 612 and 611 points, respectively.

The survey was conducted through the Ipsos Instant Research application and focused on respondents’ self-assessments of their language abilities.

World.title: Massive Attack to Headline Colours of Ostrava in 2027
World.content:
British trip-hop pioneers Massive Attack will perform at Colours of Ostrava on July 22, 2027, organisers have confirmed.

The band will take the main stage at the four-day festival, which runs from July 21 to 24 at the former Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex in Ostrava.

The announcement marks Massive Attack’s return to the Czech Republic after a nine-year absence.

The Bristol-born group, formed in 1988, is regarded as one of the most influential acts in the development of trip-hop.

The band is best known for songs including Teardrop, Angel and Unfinished Sympathy. Its music combines electronic sounds with elements of hip-hop, soul and dub, creating a distinctive style that helped shape British music in the 1990s.

Massive Attack’s live performances also feature large-scale visual projections, often incorporating political and social commentary.

They join an already announced line-up for Colours of Ostrava 2027 that includes Robbie Williams, Ellie Goulding, Martin Garrix, 5 Seconds of Summer and David Kushner.

World.title: Leo Express Opens Prague–Munich Train Tickets From 49 CZK
World.content:
Leo Express has started selling tickets for its new Prague–Munich express service, which will replace České dráhy on the route from December 13.

The cheapest domestic fares currently available start at just 49 CZK for journeys between Prague and Plzeň.

The new service, known as Ex36, will be operated by Leo Express for five years after the company won a public tender. It will take over the route currently served by České dráhy’s Bavarian Express trains.



International tickets are not yet available. Although German stations already appear in the booking system, passengers can currently only book journeys within the Czech Republic. Leo Express says bookings for the full Prague–Munich route will open in the coming days.

The lowest advertised fare between Prague and Plzeň is 49 CZK. The same starting price applies to journeys as far as Domažlice. Business class tickets start at 199 CZK.

Prices will vary depending on demand and availability, so not all seats will be offered at the lowest fares. A second-class ticket between Prague and Plzeň will cost up to 236 CZK, equivalent to the standard OneTicket fare.

For comparison, České dráhy currently charges between 155 CZK and 235 CZK for the same journey, depending on the time of travel. Passengers can also use the cheaper Berounka express service by combining tickets from the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) and Plzeň Region Integrated Transport (IDPK) systems.

According to the booking system, most trains will have six carriages, including two business-class carriages. The operator will use former Deutsche Bahn carriages purchased by Spanish railway company Renfe and leased to Leo Express.

The trains will include both open-plan seating and traditional compartments. Eight services will run in each direction every day, matching the current timetable of České dráhy’s Bavarian Express.

World.title: Prague’s Abandoned Vyšehrad Station Begins Its Transformation Into Apartments
World.content:
Work has begun on the redevelopment of Prague’s historic Vyšehrad railway station, set to become part of a residential complex with 138 micro-apartments, shops and two new buildings.

Developer Karlin Port Real Estate, led by Milorad Mišković and his business partner Miki Goldshtein, began preparatory work at the end of October.

The company plans to start the main renovation and construction works in March 2027.



The developer acquired the station and surrounding land in early 2024 from Cyprus-based company Miquelira Limited, which has been linked to businessman František Savov. The deal followed months of negotiations and extensive checks, as the listed historic building was in a serious state of disrepair.

The plans include the restoration of the original station building and construction of two additional buildings. The development will offer 138 micro-apartments, around 50 underground parking spaces and up to 13 retail units on the ground floor.

The apartments will be sold rather than operated as rental accommodation. According to Mišković, they could appeal to students, young professionals, investors and families looking for temporary accommodation for children studying in Prague.

The developer also wants to improve the wider neighbourhood, including the streets connecting the station with Albertov and the Vltava riverfront.

More projects planned across Prague

Karlin Port Real Estate is also preparing other residential developments in the capital. In Hostivař, the company plans to start construction of the Výhledy Košík project in 2027. It will include 228 apartments and approximately 1,500 square metres of retail space.

The company is also exploring opportunities involving former railway properties and preparing to enter Prague 9, where it plans to focus on the redevelopment of former industrial sites.

Mišković said brownfield regeneration remains his main interest, although the company is now considering projects across Prague rather than concentrating exclusively on the city centre.

World.title: Daily cuteness: watch how Budapest Zoo’s Persian leopard cubs take their first steps
World.content:
Two Persian leopard cubs at Budapest Zoo are beginning to explore their surroundings after opening their eyes and attempting their first steps at around three weeks old.

Persian leopard cubs starting to explore their own

The young animals are being raised by their nine-year-old mother, Banu, in a quiet, protected indoor enclosure. She is caring for both cubs without human intervention, meaning zookeepers have not yet been able to examine them or establish their sex.

Visitors can currently catch glimpses of the family only through footage recorded by cameras inside the enclosure and shared on the zoo’s Facebook page. The zoo says the mother and her offspring need complete peace during this early stage, so neither visitors nor photographers are allowed near them.

Persian leopards are a subspecies of leopard (Panthera pardus tulliana). Like other leopards, their cubs are born blind, with their eyes usually opening at around one week of age. They generally begin trying to walk independently when they are two to three weeks old.

According to Blikk, the cubs are already showing signs of curiosity. While Banu gently carries one back to its resting place, the other may set off to investigate its surroundings.

Second litter for experienced breeding pair

The cubs’ father is Akhum, a ten-year-old leopard born in France. Banu was born in Jászberény and has family links to Budapest Zoo. The pair have now produced their second litter together.

As in the wild, only the mother takes responsibility for raising the cubs. Zoo spokesperson Zoltán Hanga explained that even weighing the newborns would require separating them from Banu, causing unnecessary stress.

Persian leopard cubs typically weigh between 500 and 750 grams at birth, but their exact weights will remain unknown until their first examination.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Meat introduced at around ten weeks

For now, the cubs feed exclusively on their mother’s milk. The nursing period for Persian leopards lasts approximately three months, although animals in zoos may continue suckling until they are around four months old. At about ten weeks, the cubs are expected to begin tasting solid food before gradually transitioning to a meat-based diet.

In the coming weeks, they should also become more confident at climbing and playing with one another. The zoo plans to introduce the cubs to visitors in December. Until then, their development can be followed through updates and videos on the institution’s social media channels.

World.title: Hungary could still reach EUR 1,000 minimum wage by 2028, despite missing another target
World.content:
Hungary is set to miss one of the key goals of its three-year wage agreement, as the gross minimum wage will not reach 50% of regular gross earnings next year. However, the country could still achieve another headline target: a minimum wage equivalent to EUR 1,000 by 2028.

Under an agreement reached last week by the government, employers and trade unions, the gross minimum wage will rise by 7.5% to HUF 347,000 (approximately EUR 930) in 2027. The guaranteed minimum wage, which applies to jobs requiring at least secondary education or vocational qualifications, will increase by 6.1% to HUF 396,000.

Minimum wage target falls short

The three-year wage agreement signed in 2024 originally envisaged minimum wage increases of 9% in 2025, 13% in 2026 and 14% in 2027.

However, economic conditions proved considerably less favourable than expected. The planned 13% increase for 2026 was reduced to 11%, while next year’s agreed rise is roughly half the originally planned 14%.

The agreement also aimed to bring the gross minimum wage to 50% of regular gross average earnings by 2027. Regular earnings exclude bonuses, rewards and 13th-month payments.

According to G7, the minimum wage represented 44% of regular gross average earnings in 2025. Although the full-year wage data for 2026 is not yet available, comparing the current minimum wage with the latest figure for regular gross average earnings, from September, gives a ratio of around 45%.

If you missed it: Official: Here’s how much minimum wage will be in Hungary in 2027

What could happen in 2027?

There are no specific forecasts for the growth of regular gross earnings. However, the Finance Ministry’s medium-term economic and budgetary programme for 2027–2030 projects average gross wage growth of 5.6% next year, while the National Bank of Hungary forecasts 5.8%.

If regular gross earnings increase by around 5% from their September level, the minimum wage would account for just over 46% of regular gross average earnings in 2027. Even if wages remained at September’s level, the ratio would approach 49%.

Jácint Hatvani, president of the LIGA Trade Unions, said the latest agreement had produced an unusual outcome: Hungary had met the expectation set by the EU minimum wage directive in terms of the net minimum wage, but not the gross minimum wage.

Is EUR 1,000 still within reach?

A separate political promise made in 2024 was for Hungary’s minimum wage to reach EUR 1,000 by 2028. Unlike the 50% target, this was not linked to an EU directive, but formed part of the previous government’s economic messaging.

The goal is still achievable, although it would require another substantial increase in 2028. A stronger forint would also help.

At the exchange rate prevailing recently, the new minimum wage of HUF 347,000 would be worth approximately EUR 930. By contrast, at the exchange rate of around HUF 350 to the euro seen in mid-June, the same wage would have been worth approximately EUR 990.

Reaching the EUR 1,000 threshold will therefore depend not only on future wage increases, but also on how the forint performs against the euro.

World.title: Peru and Hungary celebrate the voluntary restitution of 16 archaeological artifacts to Peru
World.content:
A special ceremony marking the voluntary restitution of sixteen archaeological artifacts belonging to Peru’s cultural heritage was held on November 25th 2026 at the Museum of Ethnography in Budapest, highlighting the strong bonds of friendship, mutual respect, and cultural cooperation between Peru and Hungary.

The artifacts, originally entrusted to the Museum of Ethnography by a private individual, were voluntarily returned to the Peruvian State through the Embassy of Peru in Hungary. This meaningful gesture represents an important contribution to the preservation and protection of Peru’s rich archaeological heritage and reflects a shared commitment to safeguarding cultural patrimony for future generations.

The sixteen artifacts, which include a ceramic plate and vessels, crucibles and a chisel, originate from pre-Hispanic cultures that flourished along Peru’s northern and southern coasts during three significant periods of Andean history: the Early Intermediate Period (200 BC–600 AD), the Middle Horizon (600–1000 AD), and the Late Intermediate Period (1000–1476 AD).

Photo: Dávid Demeter, Néprajzi Múzeum

Among the objects are pieces associated with the Nasca and Chimú civilizations, two remarkable cultures that made significant contributions to the artistic and cultural development of ancient Peru. The Nasca culture, which flourished along Peru’s southern coast during the Early Intermediate Period, is particularly renowned for its sophisticated ceramic traditions and artistic expressions, as well as for the Nasca lines. The Chimú civilization, which developed along the northern coast during the Late Intermediate Period, is recognized for its remarkable achievements in craftsmanship, architecture, and artistic production.

The ceremony brought together distinguished representatives of the diplomatic corps, senior Hungarian government officials, and prominent figures from Hungary’s cultural community. Among the attendees were Mr. Zsolt Sári, State Secretary at the Ministry of Social Affairs and Culture, Mr. Gábor Csaba, Deputy State Secretary for Cultural Diplomacy at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Hungary, and Dr. Lajos Kemecsi, Director General of the Museum of Ethnography.

If you missed it: Budapest honours Peruvian Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa with major literary tribute

The event provided an opportunity to underscore the importance of international cooperation in protecting cultural heritage, as well as the fundamental role of museums, cultural institutions, and individuals in facilitating the responsible return of historical objects to their countries of origin.

Beyond the restitution of these sixteen artifacts, the ceremony symbolized the enduring friendship between Peru and Hungary and their shared recognition of cultural heritage as an essential element of national identity, historical memory, and intercultural understanding.

Photo: Dávid Demeter, Néprajzi Múzeum

The Embassy of Peru in Hungary expressed its sincere appreciation to the Museum of Ethnography, the Hungarian authorities, and all those involved in facilitating this voluntary restitution, reaffirming the importance of continued bilateral collaboration in the preservation, protection, and promotion of cultural heritage.

The return of these archaeological objects marks another meaningful chapter in Peru–Hungary cultural relations and reinforces the common commitment of both countries to preserving the legacy of ancient civilizations for present and future generations.

World.title: 18+: Young woman dragged along by train after her backpack stuck between the doors
World.content:
A 21-year-old woman suffered life-threatening injuries after her clothing and backpack became trapped in the doors of an InterCity train at Mezőkövesd railway station in north-eastern Hungary on Tuesday evening. The train reportedly dragged her along the platform for several hundred metres before the incident came to an end.

Young woman’s bag and clothes got trapped between train doors

The woman had been attempting to get off the Hernád-Zemplén InterCity, which was travelling from Füzesabony towards Mezőkövesd. According to police information reported by Hungarian media, her coat and bag became caught in the closing doors as she stepped onto the platform. The train then set off with her still trapped.

Emergency services were called to the scene, where railway employees reportedly attempted to help the injured woman before paramedics arrived. The National Ambulance Service told local media that its staff performed several life-saving interventions before transporting her to hospital in critical condition.

She is being treated at a Miskolc hospital. A friend of the woman told tabloid Blikk that she had been studying in Budapest and was travelling home to visit her parents. The family reportedly became concerned when she failed to arrive and could not be reached by telephone. According to her mother, who answered to Origo’s questions, most of her bones are broken, her ribs, hip and skull are severely injured, and they had to amputate both her legs.

Police investigate circumstances of accident

The Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Police Headquarters has launched proceedings over endangering railway transport. Investigators are examining how the woman’s belongings became trapped and why the train departed while she was being dragged. The incident has also raised questions about the safety mechanisms fitted to train doors and procedures for checking platforms before departure.

A locomotive driver, speaking anonymously to Blikk, said modern railway carriages with automatic doors generally have several safety features designed to prevent accidents. These include a switch in the steps that detects when someone is standing on them, a photocell at the bottom of the door and a pressure sensor along its edge.

According to the driver, activation of any of these mechanisms should cause the doors to reopen. Trains are also not supposed to depart while any door remains open. However, the driver suggested that visibility from the locomotive can be limited in certain conditions, particularly at night, making it difficult to spot someone caught near the doors. The investigation will need to establish which safety systems were present and whether they functioned correctly in this case.

Rail services restored after disruption

The accident initially caused significant disruption on the Budapest–Miskolc railway route. Trains were temporarily unable to run between Mezőkövesd and Mezőkeresztes-Mezőnyárád while police examined the scene.

Hungarian railway operator MÁV confirmed that the incident involved the Hernád-Zemplén InterCity, which had departed Budapest’s Keleti railway station at 18:25 and was travelling towards Košice, Slovakia, with carriages continuing to Sátoraljaújhely. Rail restrictions were lifted early on Wednesday, allowing services to resume along the entire line. The investigation into the accident is ongoing.

Zsolt Hegyi, Chief Executive of MÁV, expressed his sympathy to the young woman’s family. He also said that “the exact circumstances of the accident are being investigated by the police and MÁV’s railway safety experts”, and they will not be providing further information on the incident until the investigations have been concluded.

World.title: Hungary’s Foreign Ministry considers criminal complaint over Orbán’s luxury trips
World.content:
Hungary’s Foreign Ministry may file a criminal complaint against an unknown perpetrator following reports about former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s official foreign trips and the public money spent on them.

György Velkey, the ministry’s parliamentary state secretary, discussed the possibility in an interview with Kossuth Radio’s Felkelő programme on Wednesday morning. He said the ministry’s legal team was reviewing the documents and would decide whether there were grounds for legal action.

HUF 4.8 billion spent on Orbán’s official flights

The announcement follows an investigation by 444.hu, which obtained records of the former PM’s official air travel between 2015 and 2025 through a legal process. According to the outlet’s findings, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade spent HUF 4.8 billion (approximately EUR 12.8 million) on 327 trips over the ten-year period.

The most expensive journey cost HUF 180 million. Brussels was the most frequent destination, with Orbán flying there 74 times. His five trips to the United States cost a combined HUF 380 million.

Accommodation costs were also substantial. In 2025 alone, the ministry spent nearly HUF 450 million on hotel stays for Orbán and his delegations – almost as much as it had spent between 2016 and 2021 combined.

Velkey criticised the former prime minister’s spending habits, arguing that the documents contradicted the public image Orbán had cultivated as a politician close to ordinary people.

He said Orbán and his delegations had favoured five-star hotels and luxury restaurants, with taxpayers footing the bill. Velkey also claimed that Orbán had used public money to pursue his hobby of attending football matches.

Read our article about the travels: Orbán’s foreign trips cost Hungarian taxpayers EUR 13 million – luxury hotels, Michelin-starred dinners and football matches included

Legal team reviewing documents

Velkey said the ministry would examine the records with lawyers and file a complaint against an unknown perpetrator if the spending raised sufficient legal concerns.

“We will, of course, file a complaint against an unknown perpetrator, as we have done before, if it is justified,” he said, adding that any further steps would depend on the legal team’s assessment.

Asked how soon a complaint might be filed, Velkey said the timing would depend on the outcome of the internal review. He stressed that the ministry’s responsibility was to act if it found anything suspicious, while the justice system would have to handle the rest.

The state secretary also said that the ministry’s wider review had already examined tens of thousands of documents, although a significant number of records still remained to be checked.

During the same radio interview, Velkey raised another issue involving Orbán’s brother, Áron Orbán. He alleged that the former prime minister’s brother had used his family connection to seek help with arranging visas. According to Velkey, a 2023 letter to Iraq’s ambassador requesting assistance with visas was signed by Áron Orbán, who identified himself in brackets as the prime minister’s brother.

World.title: Budapest is beating Vienna and Prague in race for Christmas season visitors
World.content:
Budapest has emerged as Europe’s most popular destination for Christmas market visits this Advent season, attracting more flight bookings than traditional favourites Vienna and Prague, according to travel platform Kiwi.com.

Travel site measured ticket sale surge for Budapest flights

Booking data collected up to 23 November 2026 show that the Hungarian capital is experiencing an almost 25 per cent increase in air arrivals during the weeks leading up to Christmas compared with the same period last year.

The trend comes amid growing demand for festive city breaks across Europe. Overall, bookings for Advent travel are up 18.1 per cent year on year, while Budapest is recording stronger growth than the regional competitors included in the ranking, reports 24.hu.

Vienna, by contrast, has seen the number of travellers booking flights fall by 18.7 per cent. Berlin and Copenhagen are also gaining popularity, with bookings rising by 26.1 per cent and 33.4 per cent respectively.

The typical European Advent getaway lasts four days, according to Kiwi.com. However, the average flight ticket price per passenger has increased from EUR 167 last year to EUR 184 this season.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Budapest attracts more visitors from abroad

The capital’s popularity is also reflected in bookings covering the wider year-end holiday period, from the start of Advent through to New Year’s Eve. The number of passengers flying to Hungary during this period is up 30.5 per cent compared with last year.

Spain and Italy are the leading source markets, with arrivals from both countries increasing by around a fifth. Romanian, French and British travellers complete the top five nationalities visiting Hungary by air.

Some smaller markets have recorded particularly sharp growth. The number of Albanian visitors has more than quadrupled, while Norwegian arrivals have risen almost two-and-a-half times. Bulgarian visitor numbers have also increased by approximately a third.

Kiwi.com spokesperson Daniela Chovancová said the first weekend of December was expected to be the busiest period for Advent travel across Europe. Friday 4 December is forecast to see the highest number of departures, while Thursday departures are also becoming increasingly popular as travellers combine Christmas market visits with long weekends.

In case you missed it: Budapest finishes at the bottom of air pollution rankings among European capitals

Festive attractions draw international visitors

Budapest’s seasonal appeal includes the Christmas market at Vörösmarty Square, illuminated displays on the façade of St Stephen’s Basilica and the city’s festive light tram services.

The booking figures suggest that the Hungarian capital is benefiting from the wider popularity of European Christmas market breaks, although they reflect reservations made through one travel platform rather than total visitor numbers.

Travellers arriving in Hungary are also booking slightly larger groups than last year, while the typical return trip remains four days.
