World.title: [Rear View] Sara Duterte’s farewell walk?
World.content:
This is not a declared presidential candidate showing off the breadth of her political coalition. This is more like one thanking the people who stood by her as she prepares her exit.

Is it just me or is Vice President Sara Duterte doing the political version of a farewell walk?

Pageant bekis know the ritual, the one where the reigning queen, before relinquishing her crown, takes a long, almost leisurely walk on the runway, all smiles, waving at the adoring crowd while sentimental music plays in the background.

A pre-recorded speech plays alongside, where she takes stock of her reign, of her experiences and lessons learned, and ends with grateful thank yous to the organization and her fans. The camera follows her as she fades into the background. Behind the curtains, she no longer holds the spotlight, and she knows it.

Watch the Vice President these past days and you will see that walk.

A round of visits to Duterte strongholds, a profuse thanks to supporters for keeping her strong despite adversities, a year-end thanksgiving brunch with political personalities known for loyalty, but no heavyweights who signal leverage and clout.

This is not a declared presidential candidate showing off the breadth of her political coalition. This is more like one thanking the people who stood by her as she prepares her exit.

The whisper in political circles is that the 14 votes needed to convict are there.

Until the votes are in, it remains a whisper, and who knows, the Vice President might pull off a surprise in the Q&A or the Marcos administration’s operators might trip at the runway. But the Duterte camp surely has heard the whisper, and its behavior says it believes the whisper.

A Christmas verdict?

The impeachment trial resumes on Tuesday, December 1, and if the schedule holds, the verdict could come before Congress adjourns for Christmas. The verdict will surely be the topic at every family reunion and Noche Buena, along with grumblings over how this administration has made this Christmas season the most miserable since the pandemic lockdown.

Her critics, of course, do not expect her to walk off a winner. The Vice President has long proven she is no Miss Congeniality and after November, certainly not Best in National Costume either. Her defense spent the month showing us how ill-fitting the costume of a public servant living a simple lifestyle is.

The impeachment trial rests on a single article of unexplained wealth. The defense expressed confidence it could make a rebuttal on the prosecution’s forensic report showing alleged unexplained wealth and undeclared assets at P817.87 million. So far, it has failed to make a convincing one.

Why not take the stand?

After announcing, then dropping, 16 bank officials from the list of witnesses, a move that, had it proceeded, would have provided an opening to question her joint account with her father, detained former President Rodrigo Duterte, the defense brought in their anti-money-laundering expert. But the said expert attacked the methodology of a forensic report he admitted he had not read. He also conceded the other claims he made in open court were outside his expertise.

A witness testifying on the banana chip company tied to the Vice President’s husband admitted that the company lacks the property, plant, equipment, and personnel needed to run a manufacturing business. Other witnesses tested the patience of senator-judges with their selective amnesia. Their testimonies only raised more questions and bolstered the case against the Vice President.

And through all of this, the Vice President herself has not taken the stand. The public, says a recent survey, now wants to hear her testify.

In 2012, then-chief justice Renato Corona took the stand at his impeachment trial. He was convicted anyway, but he showed up for his own Q&A. Sara Duterte has chosen to let her lawyers do the talking for her. That’s no way to keep the crown.

When the senator-judges hand in their scorecards, and if the whisper turn out to be true, it would be difficult, if not impossible, for the Vice President to wave and smile, or deliver a generous and sincere thank you for the memories. – Rappler.com

Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

World.title: Sandiganbayan suspends Pasay judge over bribery case
World.content:
The judge contests the suspension, claiming only the Supreme Court has the authority to discipline judges, but the Sandiganbayan maintains that its criminal proceedings are separate from administrative actions taken by the SC

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan has ordered the three-month preventive suspension of a Pasay City regional judge who is facing a direct bribery charge filed in August by the Office of the Ombudsman.

The Sandiganbayan’s 6th Division rejected Pasay Regional Trial Court Branch 108 Judge Albert Cansino’s opposition, citing Section 13 of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, which makes preventive suspension mandatory for public officials facing a valid charge under the law involving fraud against the government or public funds or property.

Cansino was charged together with court interpreter Mariejoy Lagman over the alleged solicitation and receipt, directly or indirectly, of P6 million from a litigant in a property dispute.

The order was signed by associate justices Sarah Jane Fernandez, Kevin Narce Vivero and Lord Villanueva, and directed the Office of the Court Administrator to enforce the suspension.

The bribery case stemmed from the May 23, 2024 arrest of Lagman in an entrapment operation conducted by the National Bureau of Investigation. The operation followed an anonymous complaint sent to the Judicial Integrity Board.

NBI agents found during the arrest a copy of a May 15, 2024 order signed by Cansino. A certified true copy of the order had been received by a representative of the defendants in the Pasay court property dispute.

The P6 million was allegedly sought as a “consideration for a favorable decision” in the civil case.

Cansino argued against the Sandiganbayan’s authority to suspend him, arguing that only the Supreme Court had the power to discipline and suspend judges.

He said the SC had already placed him under preventive suspension for 90 days in 2024 over the same allegations, extending the measure twice for a total of nine months.

Cansino said he resumed his judicial duties in February 2025 “without issue, interference, or untoward incident.”

But the Sandiganbayan rejected the argument, saying the SC’s suspension was imposed in an administrative proceeding, while the case before it was criminal in nature.

“This Court must, however, emphasize that administrative proceedings are separate and distinct from criminal proceedings, even if the said proceedings arose from the same facts and circumstances,” the anti-graft court said. – Rappler.com

World.title: How China got access to Nvidia’s AI chips despite rules to stop them
World.content:
NVIDIA AND CHINA. The Nvidia logo and Chinese flag are seen in this illustration taken August 27, 2025.

The drama around Nvidia, the top US exporter of AI chips to China, thrusts the rules into the spotlight

AI chips are a central battleground in the US-China technology race. To preserve its lead, in recent years Washington has imposed and revised rules to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors and chipmaking technology, while balancing national security concerns with trade considerations.

The drama around Nvidia, the top US exporter of AI chips to China, has thrust those rules into the spotlight.

Delving into the resulting regulations is a quagmire. Export control rules are often likened to the US tax code in their complexity and constant revision.

Here are some basics for understanding what’s legal, and what’s not, when it comes to China’s access to US AI chips:

When did the US start to restrict chips to China?

In October 2022, the US unveiled sweeping restrictions on advanced chips to China, marking the biggest shift in US policy toward exporting technology to China in decades.

A year later, it tightened the rules to capture more chips and stop chip designers such as Nvidia from selling products engineered to fall just below the performance thresholds of the earlier restrictions. It also expanded the restrictions to countries in the Middle East and restricted chips to overseas companies headquartered in China.

In January 2025, the Biden administration extended the restrictions globally, imposing a worldwide license requirement. But in May, days before it was set to take effect, the Trump administration announced it would not enforce that rule.

The Trump administration only formally rescinded and replaced the rule last week, leaving a gap that allowed data center capacity to proliferate in countries such as Singapore, where Chinese companies could rent computing power remotely to train and deploy AI models.

Did Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud company whose former executive allegedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, operate legally?

For over two years, authorities have been investigating whether Megaspeed diverted chips to China, which would be illegal. But companies in countries including Singapore were allowed to buy advanced AI chips for their data centers license-free until the US issued a new rule last week cutting off that practice.

Megaspeed likely won’t be getting any more chips. It was added to a US trade blacklist this week, along with its Thai and Malaysian subsidiaries, essentially blocking shipments. Nvidia also said it cut off sales to Megaspeed in June 2025.

Are Nvidia’s shipments of AI chips to China legal?

About a year ago, President Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, drawing criticism from experts who said the chips would help jumpstart China’s military modernization and erode the US lead in AI. The H200 chip is one of Nvidia’s more advanced chips, but not top-of-the-line.

Nvidia cannot simply ship the chips to Chinese companies that pay for them. Nvidia must apply for licenses from the US Department of Commerce, which has issued them since last spring on a case-by-case basis.

Last week, the House foreign affairs committee released licensing data showing the Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026.

What does the new Trump administration rule do?

Last week, the Trump administration issued a new regulation, adding license requirements for five countries including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, in an effort to crack down on chips being smuggled into China.

Prior to that, the chip-based license requirement generally applied to countries like Russia that raise national security concerns, along with companies headquartered in arms-embargoed countries. Now they also apply to Southeast Asian countries viewed as transshipment points with a high risk for illegal diversion to China.

The rule also clamped down on AI chip sales to non-US data centers that supply a high volume of computing power to Chinese-headquartered firms.

How big a problem is chip smuggling?

For years, Nvidia’s Huang has said there is no evidence of chip smuggling to China.

But that assertion, which experts already viewed skeptically, was further questioned in March when US prosecutors charged three people associated with California-based AI server maker Super Micro Computer SMCI.O, including its co-founder, in a scheme to divert about $2.5 billion of US technology into China, including AI servers packed with Nvidia AI chips.

Critics say Nvidia has tried to minimize a well-known risk. Huang once said Nvidia’s sophisticated Grace Blackwell AI chip platform weighed nearly 1.8 metric tons and could not fit into a pocket or backpack. But servers are not smuggled in backpacks. They are routed through third countries and intermediary companies.

Supporters say Nvidia may not have had verified evidence of diversion and that the company cannot keep tabs on all its products after they’re sold.

Can Nvidia track its chips to see where they end up?

Nvidia has built location verification technology that could indicate which country its chips are operating in, the company confirmed in December 2025. It has offered the feature as a software option for customers.

But the company has opposed proposed legislation that would require location verification and diversion reporting for advanced AI processors.

A measure known as the Chip Security Act is among several export control bills that gained new momentum in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, and may be included in the National Defense Authorization Act that Congress is expected to pass next month. – Rappler.com

World.title: 76% of Australians struggling to tell apart real and AI content – new report
World.content:
The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognize it at all.

Most Australians are using – or at least have tried out – generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini, among many others.

We can use them to search for information, answer questions, and generate text, images, sound and video. As generative AI becomes more sophisticated and ubiquitous, many people are no longer able to distinguish AI-generated content from authentic, human-made content.

Our new representative survey of 2,000 Australian adults conducted in August and September 2026 found 76% of Australians had recently encountered content they initially believed was real, only to later discover that it had been generated by AI.

The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognize it at all.

The synthetic trap

People with high levels of education who are interested in the technology and have high AI literacy are the most likely to report having mistaken AI content for real.

However, this doesn’t mean these groups are more exposed or susceptible to AI-generated content. Instead, the data suggests these people are better at recognizing when they’ve been misled.

In fact, people with low education and lower AI literacy are the most likely to say they don’t know whether they have mistaken AI content for real.

Therefore, many Australians may not recognize when they have encountered synthetic content. This presents a dilemma for users who are increasingly turning to AI tools to seek information.

Trust in AI is low

While AI use has grown rapidly, many are skeptical of the technology and concerned about how it might impact society. About half (51%) of Australian respondents said they use AI chatbots or tools at least weekly, and more than one quarter (28%) use them daily. Almost everyone (96%) is aware of at least one generative AI platform.

Despite widespread awareness and usage, trust in major AI tools remains very low. When asked “how much do you trust or distrust generative AI chatbots or tools?” only a minority said they trust ChatGPT (34%), Microsoft Copilot (24%), Google Gemini (24%) and Claude (17%).

Our survey also shows people are particularly distrustful of politicians and social media companies that use generative AI. More than half of Australians believe the use of AI by politicians and political parties will make society worse, with social media companies and news media viewed almost as negatively.

In contrast, the report reveals that people view scientists and healthcare professionals as the most trustworthy and benevolent users of AI, with around half saying their use of the technology will improve society.

How do people verify content?

Despite this high level of exposure to AI-generated content and low levels of trust, people rarely use proactive measures to identify or verify if content was AI-generated.

When people suspect AI-generated content, the majority simply take a closer look and examine the content carefully, relying on their intuition. Some check comments made by other online users. But few people look for disclosure statements or labels to identify whether it was made with AI, and even fewer turn to trusted sources of news.

Rather than engaging in lateral reading – leaving the content and checking independent sources – most people engage in vertical reading, which involves only looking within the source. They scrutinize the content itself and rely on their own judgment. This approach becomes less effective as AI-generated content becomes increasingly convincing.

Generally, younger people are more likely to check whether information is true, using a range of verification strategies. The exception is checking a trusted news source, which is more common among those aged 45 and over. Instead, young adults are far more likely to look at comments from other users than older age groups.

Additionally, AI literacy plays an important role in people’s verification strategies. Those with high AI literacy are much more likely to closely examine content than those with low understanding of the technology, suggesting that education about how AI works supports more active and critical evaluation of online information.

People want strong safeguards

Because of the low levels of trust in the technology, Australians say they want strong safeguards around it.

Most importantly, they want protections to ensure accuracy and reliable responses when they are using an AI platform.

They also want guardrails in place to prevent AI from generating illegal, dangerous or harmful content, and protections to reduce the presence of bias and ensure fairness and equity in the content it generates.

This points to the need for a multi-pronged response from the tech platforms and government.

First, digital platforms need clearer and more consistent labeling of AI-generated content. If people are expected to make informed decisions about what they’re seeing, they need transparent information about where that content comes from.

Second, the findings show people with higher levels of AI literacy are better equipped to recognize synthetic content and engage in more critical evaluation practices.

We need to educate all Australians with media and AI literacy. Education in schools is important, but adults need training too. We need a whole-of-society approach where adults can have access to education through local community or workplace initiatives.

Australia already lags behind other countries when it comes to media literacy education, and the rapid increase in AI only makes the need for a national approach more urgent. – via Reuters/Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] The Marcos estate tax: A test of presidential statesmanship
World.content:
Taking the high ground would give real substance to the President’s own appeals for tax compliance

Ferdinand Marcos Jr. can help settle his father’s estate tax and show Filipinos that the law applies with equal force when the taxpayer is the President’s own family.

When President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. opened the 2025 tax campaign of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), he asked Filipinos to pay what they owe. That call for civic duty gained urgency on November 13, when he swore in Rolando Ligon Jr. as BIR commissioner.

Ligon takes office facing a test that strikes at his bureau’s credibility: what has the government done to collect the unpaid estate tax of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.? While the duty to account and collect rests with the commissioner, the President can make that work far easier.

By publicly assuring the BIR that it has his full backing to pursue every lawful remedy—even when the taxpayer is his own family—Marcos Jr. can turn a decades-old stalemate into an act of true statesmanship.

Understanding what is at stake begins with the record. The starting figure is P23,293,607,638, per the assessment made by the BIR in July 1991 after a special audit found that no estate tax return had been filed.

PCGG, BIR Letters Re Marcos Estate Tax by Nami Buan on Scribd

Because Philippine jurisprudence, as affirmed in Lorenzo v. Posadas, establishes that succession taxes accrue at death, the original assessment is governed by the tax laws in force when the elder Marcos died in 1989.

The flat 6% estate tax rate introduced decades later under the TRAIN Law (Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion Act or Republic Act No. 10963) does not apply to that assessment. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] Estate tax amnesty: Essential compliance guide)

Instead, the tax code then in force imposed a graduated schedule peaking at 60% on any portion of a net estate exceeding P3 million, plus a P1,393,450 base tax on the first P3 million.

Working backward from the P23.29 billion assessment—subtracting the base tax, dividing the remainder by 60%, and adding back the initial P3 million—implies a taxable net estate of roughly P38.82 billion if the assessment consisted entirely of basic tax. (READ: Facts and lies: the Marcoses’ unpaid estate tax)

While that arithmetic illustrates the assessment’s scale, reconstructing the actual tax base requires the audit schedules showing which assets were included, how they were valued, and what deductions were allowed.

Public debate, however, has often centered on P203.819 billion. That figure stems from a 2021 calculation by retired Supreme Court senior associate justice Antonio Carpio, who took the P23.294 billion assessment and added a 25% surcharge of P5.823 billion, P139.762 billion in interest at 20% a year over 30 years, and P34.940 billion in interest on the surcharge. (READ: [ANALYSIS] The estate tax liability of the Marcos Estate)

The math explains how the headline number grew, yet its assumptions require an official accounting. The TRAIN Law changed how statutory interest is calculated starting January 1, 2018, and the Supreme Court has applied the transition from 20% to 12% in tax cases. The BIR should clarify which rates and periods govern this account, how each charge was computed, and what credits reduce the balance.

What is beyond dispute is that the assessment itself is legally settled. Marcos personally challenged the collection measures decades ago, leading to the Supreme Court’s 1997 ruling in Marcos II v. Court of Appeals.

The Court held that the assessment became final and unappealable after the heirs failed to protest it through proper channels, finding sufficient notice and timely levies under the three-year prescriptive period then applicable.

LOOK: Supreme Court's Entry of Judgment which shows that GR 120880, where the High Court ordered Marcos heirs to pay P23 billion in estate tax, became final and executory on March 9, 1999. @rapplerdotcom pic.twitter.com/p9XbJxiIGZ — Lian Buan (@lianbuan) March 30, 2022

Crucially, the justices ruled that the BIR could proceed against estate property without waiting for probate court approval. Though Marcos claimed in 2022 that his family could not argue its case while in Hawaii, the Court’s decision records that notices were served after his return to the Philippines—including papers for his mother delivered through his office at the House of Representatives.

The coalition 1Sambayan is urging Ligon to act before December 2, marking five years since the BIR sent a written demand to the heirs—a notice confirmed by then-commissioner Caesar Dulay.

Determining whether another demand letter is legally necessary to preserve the government’s claims requires reviewing the statute and the collection record. As the Supreme Court showed in Republic v. Hizon—where a collection suit was deemed time-barred even as the BIR was allowed to proceed against properties covered by timely warrants—deadlines matter. Ligon must swiftly establish which remedies remain live and act accordingly before any applicable window closes. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] The new BIR chief’s 3 crosses: Will he dare audit the powerful?)

Just as importantly, the BIR owes the public a transparent accounting of past collection steps. Court records show that 11 Tacloban, Leyte, parcels went to auction in 1993. When no one bid, the properties were declared forfeited to the government.

What became of those lands, and what value, if any, was credited against the tax? Subject to lawful disclosure limits, the bureau should lay out the full ledger: the original assessment, accrued charges, recoveries, and collectible balance. If any remedy has lapsed, it should explain when and why. After years of competing figures, Filipinos deserve a clear record they can examine.

This moment gives Marcos a rare chance to show statesmanship. As an heir, he can help produce estate records, authorize disclosures where his consent can lawfully enable them, and work with the other heirs to settle what the BIR confirms is due.

As President, he can give Ligon the space to reach and explain his own conclusions, even those inconvenient to the Marcos family. He can do both before December 2, while the bureau determines that date’s legal significance.

Taking the high ground would give real substance to the President’s own appeals for tax compliance and hand revenue officers a powerful precedent the next time a well-connected taxpayer expects special treatment.

Marcos has spent years asking Filipinos to judge his administration on its merits. Now, the choice is his. By using the authority of his office to protect the BIR’s independence in pursuing his father’s estate, he can show Filipinos that the law bends for no one. – Rappler.com

World.title: Duran Duran guitarist and songwriter Andy Taylor dies at 65
World.content:
DURAN DURAN. Members of British band Duran Duran (from left) Andy Taylor, Roger Taylor, Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and John Taylor arrive at the 2003 MTV Video Music Awards in Radio City Music Hall in New York in this August 28, 2003 file photo.

'To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,' says Taylor's wife, Tracy Wilson-Taylor

LOS ANGELES, USA – Andy Taylor, the guitarist and songwriter for pop-rock band Duran Duran and a Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee, died at age 65 on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates released on Wednesday, November 25.

Taylor, who co-wrote some of the group’s biggest hits, including “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “Rio,” and “Girls on Film,” died from metastatic prostate cancer. He was diagnosed in 2018.

The first section of the statement came from his family, while the second was from Duran Duran members Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor.

“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” Taylor’s wife, Tracy Wilson-Taylor, said on behalf of his family.

The members of the Grammy-winning band noted that Taylor brought a unique style to their sound.

“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music,” they said, adding that he faced his illness with courage, honesty and grace.

Born in 1961 in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, Taylor began learning guitar at age 11 and later dropped out of school to tour England and Europe with several bands. He moved to Birmingham and joined Duran Duran in 1980.

The group signed with EMI Records and released its debut album, “Duran Duran,” in 1981. While the record was successful in the United Kingdom, global fame followed with 1982’s “Rio.”

Taylor later launched a solo career, releasing his debut studio album, “Thunder,” in 1987.

The late musician has four children with Wilson-Taylor. – Rappler.com

World.title: EXPLAINER: How scammers reach you, with or without your data
World.content:
Scammers are no longer just sliding into your DMs; they have found new ways to slip onto your screen

Recent data breaches have exposed personal records across Philippine government agencies and private firms, making it more important than ever to stay alert to targeted scams.

The National Privacy Commission has advised the public to remain cautious about possible attempts at phishing, smishing, and other scams that may arise after the wave of cybersecurity incidents in the country.

In its State of Scams Report, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA) found that 84% of Filipinos have encountered a scam this year. This is an increase from 77% in 2025. The survey, which had 1,160 Filipino adult respondents, was conducted from March 16 to April 13, 2026.

Knowing what a scam looks like is no longer enough, as scammers have upgraded their techniques to catch you. Here is how scammers reach you today.

Email messages

With your real name or account details, scammers can send convincing fake promotions, receipts, password-reset prompts, and even account-suspension warnings.

Since emails allow you to enhance your text with styles, scammers can easily mimic official branding of government agencies, banks, and organizations to trick you into opening malicious attachments or clicking links.

SHAM PRIZE. A phishing email notifies the recipient that they have won free products from a hardware retailer. Rappler screenshot

Your email service can often detect whether a message is suspicious or not. But you must watch out for mismatched sender domains, unusual requests, or unexpected links and attachments.

Social media and messaging apps

As more telecommunication companies tighten SMS filters, scammers have migrated to Facebook, Instagram, Viber, Telegram, WhatsApp, and other social media platforms.

When they gain unauthorized access to your social media accounts, they target more victims by impersonating you and sending suspicious direct messages (DMs) or links to your contacts.

Some even casually ask how you are and proceed to offer you job opportunities or paid tasks.

FAKE JOB SCAMS. Individuals claiming ot be human resources (HR) staff of marketing agencies reach out on online messaging apps to offer virtual jobs or paid tasks. Rappler screenshots

Be mindful of engaging with messages not only from unknown contacts, but also from your loved ones. If you notice something suspicious, you may use your online messaging app’s report and block option.

Phone calls

Scammers do not only use unknown numbers to contact you. They can spoof their caller ID to imitate banks, digital wallets, government employees, and courier companies using Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP).

It allows users to make phone calls via an internet connection instead of an analog phone line, according to the Federal Communications Commission.

Fraudsters utilize VoIP to lure you into sharing sensitive information by telling you that you have unauthorized transactions or your account has been compromised. They cause panic and urgency, so they can access your account information.

Be cautious when answering phone calls from unknown numbers. Do not share sensitive account details or passwords, as banks and e-wallets will never ask for those details, and scammers can also spoof caller IDs.

Hang up and verify whether a phone number is associated with legitimate institutions by checking their official channels or by searching this list of hotlines and telemarketing SIM numbers published by local banks and e-wallets:

SMS and text messages

GASA also discovered that Filipinos mostly experience scams conducted through text messages this year.

Scammers used to deliver spam texts to you through an unknown phone number, which you can easily identify as suspicious.

DELIVERY FRAUD. A smishing text message from an international number informs the recipient that they have a pending delivery from PHLPost and includes a malicious website link. Rappler screenshot

But now they have found a workaround that does not require your phone number to reach you: International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) catchers.

These are surveillance devices acting as fake cell towers that can intercept your mobile phone, access your device’s location, and manipulate message threads by sending spoofed messages to you.

Such messages slip straight into your legitimate message threads because they are undetected by telco spam filters as they bypass cell towers.

BOGUS, NOT BONUS. Smishing messages from banks and a water service provider indicate that the recipient has expiring credit card points and a cash prize, which can be claimed by accessing the provided phishing links. Rappler screenshots

Cybersecurity advocacy group Scam Watch Pilipinas documented spoofed messages through IMSI catchers as early as 2024, according to an investigative report by The Philippine STAR.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas already released Memorandum No. M-2022-015 in 2022, prohibiting banks from sending clickable links through text, email, or messaging apps.

If you receive a text message with a link to your device, do not click it, since it may be a smishing scam.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security also advised turning off the 2G network connection of your device, if the option is available.

Websites

Unlike texts or calls that interrupt you, fake websites serve as the final trap.

Fraudsters draw you in through a link in a spoofed SMS, a phishing email, a social media DM, or a sponsored search or social media ad. The goal is for you to land on a bogus website that clones a banking portal, promo page, or online store.

Even scanning QR codes can lead you to malicious website links hidden as an image instead of text until the page loads.

These fake websites often spoof banking portals that require you to enter your login credentials, card details, or one-time PINs.

Before clicking on any link, look closely at the web address for uncommon domains, misspelled or extra words, unfamiliar symbols, and numbers swapped for letters (e.g., 0 for O and 1 for l).

When scanning QR codes, check first if the printed image has signs of tampering. You may also read the link preview first before accessing the site after scanning.

Also ensure that you have activated the built-in anti-phishing or malware protection features of your browsers and have turned on multi-factor authentication for your digital accounts.

Scammers can spoof phone numbers, clone websites, or imitate cell towers. But they cannot get through a user who stops to verify first.

If you encounter any online scams, you may report them to the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center by dialing 1326. – Rappler.com

World.title: PNP hunts ‘digital predator’ linked to Caloocan school stabbing
World.content:
Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. — Photo from Office of the Chief PNP/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines—The Philippine National Police’s (PNP) cybercrime investigators are tracking down an alleged online groomer or “digital predator” who encouraged a 12-year-old student to stab two classmates inside a public elementary school in Caloocan City.

“I have ordered the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group to immediately trace, identify, and hunt down this digital predator in full coordination with foreign and local cyber-intelligence partners,” PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said on Thursday.

“Exploiting a minor’s vulnerability to incite real-world violence is a serious crime, and we will pursue this perpetrator wherever they are hiding online,” he added.

Article continues after this 

READ: 2 students injured in stabbing incident in Caloocan elementary school

An 11-year-old Grade 6 pupil sustained seven stab wounds, while a 9-year-old Grade 4 student suffered two wounds after another student allegedly attacked them with a kitchen knife hidden inside a thick book in his bag.

The attack occurred around 6 a.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 25, while students were assembled in the school lobby for their morning formation.

Both victims were taken to Dr. Jose N. Rodriguez Memorial Hospital, where they were declared out of danger and recommended for discharge.

They are also set to undergo psychological debriefing.

Article continues after this 

A teacher apprehended the suspect and sought assistance from barangay security personnel.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said police arrived within three minutes of receiving the initial call.

Article continues after this 

Initial police findings indicated that the suspect may have experienced bullying, including physical abuse and ridicule from classmates. Investigators have yet to establish these claims.

The minor who attacked the two students is now in the custody of the Caloocan City Social Welfare and Development Office.

“We strongly condemn this senseless act of violence, especially one that victimized children in a place where they should feel safe,” Nartatez said.

World.title: PH seeks 6 Chinook helicopters under $2-B US defense loan package
World.content:
Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. (Photo by Gabryelle Dumalag)

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has requested six CH-47 Chinook heavy-lift helicopters from the United States under a proposed $2-billion military financing package, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said Thursday.

Teodoro said all six brand-new helicopters could be delivered as early as 2029 if Washington agrees to prioritize the Philippine order.

“Nag-request kami sa US government doon sa $2-billion financing ng anim na Chinook. That is the only thing I can disclose out of that package (We made a request to the US government regarding the $2-billion financing for six Chinooks. That is the only thing I can disclose out of that package),” Teodoro told reporters after the closing ceremony of the Armed Forces of the Philippines’ Joint Exercise Dagat-Langit-Lupa (AJEX Dagit-Pa).

Article continues after this 

Otherwise, delivery could take about six years, he said.

Teodoro said earlier delivery would depend on whether the US would agree to reallocate six helicopters intended for the US Army to the Philippines.

The helicopters would initially be assigned to the Philippine Air Force, and the acquisition request would also cover integrated logistics support and crew training.

While the Philippines has the capacity to accommodate six Chinooks, Teodoro said maintenance would be a bigger concern than basing infrastructure.

“A Chinook can carry about four times a Black Hawk, so it saves you time. And it saves you logistical space,” Teodoro said.

Article continues after this 

He said the helicopters could transport large artillery pieces and vehicles, citing the need for heavy-lift capabilities given the country’s archipelagic geography.

READ: US to spend $400M for PH sea defense

Article continues after this 

Asked whether the Philippines intended to acquire more Chinooks, Teodoro cited budget constraints, adding that the country should have acquired such helicopters long ago.

“Kung puwede lang eh, kulang nga ’yun eh. Pero siyempre, hanggang doon lang ang kaya natin (If only we could. That is not enough. But of course, that’s all we can manage),” he said.

Proposed US defense loan

The disclosure came a week after the White House announced that the Philippines and the United States would pursue a Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan package worth more than $2 billion to acquire defense and security equipment.

The announcement followed the bilateral meeting between President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and US President Donald Trump in Malacañang on Nov. 18.

READ: PH, US eye $2-billion defense loan, expanded trade ties

The Department of National Defense earlier clarified that the announcement reflected an intent to negotiate financing, with details of the arrangement still to be discussed.

World.title: Davao Oriental Army battalion completes military evaluation
World.content:
The 67th Infantry Battalion, based in Baganga, Davao Oriental, completed the 10-day Battalion Evaluation and Certification Program (BECP) on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Photo by 10th Infantry “Agila” Division

DAVAO CITY – The 67th Infantry Battalion (67IB) under the 10th Infantry “Agila” Division (10ID) completed the 10-day Battalion Evaluation and Certification Program (BECP) on Wednesday, earning the highest score among other units in Mindanao.

The battalion’s performance further strengthened 10ID’s operational readiness in support of its Comprehensive Archipelagic Defense Operations (CADO).

67IB underwent a 10-day comprehensive assessment of its operational capabilities through different exercises, including live-fire drills, field training, and sustainment activities.

Article continues after this 

READ: Army conducts large-scale ‘Katihan’ in Northern Luzon

BECP is a continuous initiative of the Philippine Army to standardize the operational competence of different army battalions in the country. This includes enhancing mission readiness and effectiveness, operational planning, execution capabilities, tactical decision-making, and strategic readiness in addressing security challenges in its environs.

The 67IB, which is under the operational control of the 1001st Infantry “Pag-asa” Brigade (1001IB), was the 10th Army battalion evaluated in Mindanao.

Maj. Gen. Alvin Luzon, 10ID commander, recognized the BECP evaluation team, headed by Colonel Jerome Peñalosa and the 10ID BECP Training Directorate, for their professionalism, objectivity, and dedication to ensure the program’s integrity.

In his message to the troops, Luzon urged them to embrace the evaluation results and put them into concrete actions and continuously improve their capabilities.

Article continues after this 

“Maintain the standard. Improve the standard. And always be ready for the next mission,” he said.

He also emphasized the need to integrate lessons learned into training programs, standard operating procedures, plans, and daily operations.

Article continues after this 

Luzon presided over the closing ceremony at Camp Ramon Apostol, Barangay Salingcomoto, Baganga in Davao Oriental, on Wednesday morning.

Also in attendance were Brigadier General Vince James Bantilan, 1001IB commander, and Lt. Col. Noe Venancio Baluyan Jr., 67IB commander.

Local government officials headed by Davao Oriental Governor Nelson Dayanghirang Sr., Baganga Mayor Laureano Taya, Cateel Mayor Emilou Nuñez, and Boston Mayor Rowell Rosit also attended the ceremony.

“The presence of local government officials and civilian stakeholders underscores the importance of inter-agency cooperation and community support in strengthening territorial defense readiness,” Maj. Ruben Gadut, chief of 10ID’s Public Affairs Office, said in a statement.

World.title: New Subic hangar expands capacity for business jet maintenance
World.content:
Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority Chairman and Administrator Eduardo Jose L. Aliño (second from right) joins Aviation Concepts Technical Services Inc. President Raul F. Trinidad Jr. (left) and Subic Bay International Airport Department Manager Zharrex Santos (second from left) during the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the company’s new 7,000-square-meter Hangar B on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo courtesy of SBMA)

SUBIC BAY FREEPORT — An aircraft maintenance facility based at the Subic Freeport has expanded its capacity to accommodate more business jets with the inauguration of a new 7,000-square-meter hangar at the Subic Bay International Airport (SBIA).

Aviation Concepts Technical Services, Inc. (ACTSI) inaugurated Hangar B last week, according to the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA) in a statement on Thursday.

The new facility can accommodate up to 10 long-range business jets or 12 large-cabin aircraft of mixed types, increasing ACTSI’s maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) facilities from 5,600 to 12,600 square meters.

Article continues after this 

READ: Most rich people opt to charter than own aircraft

Designed in partnership with Prime Metro BMD Corp. (PrimeBMD) and Colliers, the hangar was built to meet international aviation maintenance standards.

“Hangar B’s additional 7,000 square meters gives us greater capacity and flexibility to serve the customers who have placed their trust in us,” said ACTSI President Raul Trinidad Jr., who led the inauguration with SBMA Chairman and Administrator Eduardo Jose Aliño.

“As plans to modernize and develop the airport move forward, we see opportunities to attract more operators, strengthen aviation services, and create skilled employment. ACTSI intends to contribute to that future,” he added.

The expansion comes as the SBMA seeks a private-sector partner to rehabilitate and expand the airport through a proposed P7-billion public-private partnership (PPP) project.

Article continues after this 

Under the proposed 25-year concession, the airport is envisioned as a cargo and logistics hub, with improvements to its existing facilities and the development of additional infrastructure.

READ: Guess who are flying in style: Philippines now home to 50 private jets

Article continues after this 

New York-based private investment firm Cerberus Capital Management, through its affiliate Cerberus Asia Pacific Investments LLC, submitted an unsolicited proposal to rehabilitate, expand, and operate the airport.

The affiliate was granted original proponent status, allowing the proposal to undergo a comparative challenge, also known as a Swiss challenge. The SBMA scheduled the submission and opening of competing bids for Nov. 26.

SBIA previously served as the Asia-Pacific hub of cargo company FedEx from 1995 until 2009, when the company transferred its regional operations to Guangzhou, China.

Aliño said the expansion comes as private aircraft owners across Southeast Asia are seeking faster cabin internet, reliable voice connectivity, and improved in-flight entertainment systems.

“More hangar space, like Aviation Concepts’ Hangar B, also brings real benefits. It supports stronger operations and finances, and better asset protection for aircraft owners, fixed-base operators, cargo handlers, and our airport,” he said.

World.title: Cultural agencies flag overlap in proposed Bonifacio museum plan
World.content:
Screengrab from Senate of the Philippines / YouTube

MANILA, Philippines — Cultural agencies on Thursday raised concerns about the possible overlap with existing historical facilities as the Senate deliberates on a proposal to establish a museum dedicated to revolutionary leader Andres Bonifacio.

During the Senate committee on culture and the arts hearing, representatives of the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) urged lawmakers to carefully assess the need for a separate institution.

Reading from the NHCP’s position paper on the proposed museum, its Supervising Historic Sites Development Officer, Bryan Anthony Paraiso, cited the existing Museo ng Katipunan at the Pinaglabanan Memorial Shrine in San Juan City.

Article continues after this 

“Since the latter already interprets the history of the Katipunan in the Philippine revolution, there is a possibility of overlapping historical narratives, exhibition themes, and educational programs,” Paraiso said.

READ: Andres Bonifacio: A monument of lies

Paraiso likewise raised a “curatorial challenge,” noting that Bonifacio’s belongings were “reportedly destroyed when his house in Tondo, Manila was burned on the 3rd of April 1896.”

However, King Cortez, founder of Bantay Kasaysayan, said the existence of the Museo ng Katipunan should not prevent the establishment of a separate museum dedicated to Bonifacio.

“I don’t see anything that should stand in the way. First of all, Rizal has museums in Dapitan, Calamba, and Fort Santiago. So if the reason is that there is already a Katipunan museum in San Juan, perhaps we should look at our heroes equally, especially if there is much we can learn from them,” Cortez said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Where is Bonifacio’s bolo?

National Commission for Culture and the Arts Culture and Arts Officer Eric Adriano also supported the proposal in principle, but recommended conducting a feasibility study before establishing the museum.

Article continues after this 

He also recommended calling the proposed facility the “Andres Bonifacio Museum” rather than the “Andres Bonifacio National Museum,” as the term “National Museum” is reserved for the National Museum of the Philippines under Republic Act No. 11333.

Meanwhile, National Museum Director General Jeremy Barnes suggested using “Andres Bonifacio National Shrine,” with a museum inside it, to avoid confusion with his institution.

According to Barnes, concerns about the scarcity of artifacts relating to Bonifacio could also “make the few remaining even more priceless.”

Barnes said Manila needed a stronger presence honoring Bonifacio, particularly in the areas where he lived and worked, so his legacy could be better highlighted beyond existing monuments and historical markers.

Sen. Robinhood Padilla, who sponsored the proposed Andres Bonifacio Museum Act under Senate Bill No. 1589, said he was open to the recommendations and suggested further discussions through a technical working group.

World.title: Harvard study puts spotlight on resource demands of AI, Pax Silica
World.content:
A Harvard study underscores that artificial intelligence is not an invisible technology in the cloud. It relies on massive physical infrastructure whose demands on energy, water, land and public resources deserve transparency and public scrutiny.

Recent remarks by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. suggesting that proposed investments in the Philippines involve “AI technology” rather than “data centers” raise important questions about the relationship between artificial intelligence infrastructure and its physical resource requirements.

Scientific evidence indicates that advanced AI systems are inseparable from the data centers that power them. A study published in Nature Sustainability by Gianluca Guidi and Francesca Dominici of Harvard University documented the electricity consumption and carbon footprint of 403 hyperscale data centers in the United States, demonstrating that AI expansion carries significant demands for electricity, water, land and cooling infrastructure.

Article continues after this 

This paper examines the scientific relationship between AI and data centers, evaluates the implications of the Harvard findings for the proposed Pax Silica development in New Clark City, and argues that informed public discussion requires transparency about resource use, environmental impacts and social consequences.

The issue is not whether AI is desirable but whether policymakers and citizens fully understand the physical systems on which AI depends.

Artificial intelligence has become a defining technological narrative of the 21st century. Governments court AI investments. Corporations race to develop increasingly powerful models. Policymakers speak of innovation, competitiveness and digital transformation.

Yet amid the excitement, a fundamental misconception persists: the belief that artificial intelligence exists apart from the physical world.

Recently, Marcos reportedly emphasized that a proposed investment project involves “AI technology” rather than data centers. While such a distinction may appear reasonable to the public, it does not reflect the technological reality of modern artificial intelligence.

Article continues after this 

AI is not an alternative to data centers. AI depends on data centers. The two are inseparable.

This is a matter of computer science, engineering, energy systems and, increasingly, environmental science.

Article continues after this 

A recent study published in Nature Sustainability by researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health offers one of the most comprehensive assessments yet of the energy and carbon footprint associated with hyperscale data centers in the United States.

The findings should be of interest not only to scientists and engineers but also to policymakers and citizens in countries such as the Philippines that are considering large-scale AI-related infrastructure investments.

The peer-reviewed Harvard study is:

Guidi, G., Dominici, F., Squartini, T., Sprinkle, C., Gilmour, J., Butler, K., Bell, E., Delaney, S., Bargagli-Stoffi, F.J. (2026). “Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of U.S. Hyperscale Data Centers.” Nature Sustainability. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7.

The Nature abstract, the Nature Asia press summary of Nov. 17, 2026, and the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health press release of Nov. 16, 2026, are openly accessible.

What Guidi et al. actually did and why it matters

The Harvard study is not an opinion piece, a model of a hypothetical future or a corporate sustainability report. It is the first peer-reviewed, facility-level, bottom-up accounting of the electricity use and carbon emissions of U.S. hyperscale data centers, or HDCs, since the rise of generative AI.

The research was undertaken because no government agency tracks such data.

Lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in Harvard’s Department of Biostatistics, said: “Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now. But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint. Our study helps fill that gap.”

Corresponding author Francesca Dominici, Clarence James Gamble Professor of Biostatistics, Population and Data Science and director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative, added: “Our goal is to give the public, policymakers, investors, and developers a much more concrete, up-to-date picture than was available before.”

The researchers compiled facility-level information on 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers operating between May 2024 and April 2025. They used satellite imagery, building footprints and industry data to identify and validate each facility, beginning with 675 candidate sites and excluding hundreds for which verifiable data were unavailable.

They then estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility under low-, central- and high-load operating scenarios because operators do not disclose actual metered loads.

The researchers used U.S. Environmental Protection Agency eGRID data to attribute carbon emissions to each facility based on the mix of power plants in its regional grid, using a location-based, total-output balancing-authority attribution method in the published version.

That method assigns emissions based on the average carbon intensity of all generation in the balancing authority, including nuclear power and renewables, rather than only fossil-fuel generation.

The preprint, by contrast, explored a residual or consumption-based method that assigns a higher intensity because it allocates dirtier marginal generation to the data center.

The published version reports a lower intensity — 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour, compared with a U.S. total-output average of 348 grams per kilowatt-hour.

The preprint and Harvard’s public press material emphasized a higher, fossil-heavy intensity of about 545 grams per kilowatt-hour and a fossil-fuel share of 54%, consisting mainly of natural gas at 38% and coal at 15%, with nuclear power at 21% and renewables at 25%.

Both figures result from different accounting methods. The authors report their methodology, present a range and acknowledge uncertainty.

The study’s broader implication is that discussions about AI also involve electricity, water, land, carbon emissions and public resources.

The myth of the weightless digital economy

For years, technology companies have used the metaphor of “the cloud.” Information is stored in the cloud. Applications run in the cloud. AI operates in the cloud.

The metaphor, however, can obscure the physical infrastructure behind these services.

The cloud is an immense network of physical facilities containing servers, processors, fiber-optic networks, cooling systems, backup generators, substations, transformers, batteries and transmission lines.

Every search query, online video, digital payment and AI interaction ultimately depends on hardware operating somewhere.

When a person asks an AI chatbot a question, the answer is not generated inside a smartphone. It is generated through computations carried out by powerful processors in highly specialized data centers.

These facilities consume large amounts of electricity because advanced AI systems require billions or even trillions of calculations every second. They generate substantial heat and therefore require sophisticated cooling systems.

They must also operate continuously because interruptions can compromise reliability and business operations.

In other words, AI has a physical footprint.

Just as airports are essential to aviation, data centers are essential to artificial intelligence.

Without data centers, there is no large-scale AI.

What the Harvard research reveals

The Harvard-led study published in Nature Sustainability examined hundreds of hyperscale data centers in the United States and estimated their electricity consumption and related carbon emissions.

The findings challenge the perception that digital technologies are environmentally neutral.

The researchers found that data centers consume large quantities of electricity, much of it still derived from fossil-fuel sources. They also highlighted transparency gaps that make it difficult to fully assess the environmental costs of the rapidly expanding AI sector.

The study demonstrates that the AI revolution is not solely a software revolution. It is also an energy revolution.

Every expansion of AI capability requires a corresponding expansion of computational infrastructure.

Every new generation of AI models requires more computing power.

Every increase in computing power requires more electricity.

And every increase in electricity demand raises questions about energy supply, carbon emissions, infrastructure development and environmental sustainability.

These realities cannot be separated from discussions about AI investment.

Why terminology matters

Some may dismiss the distinction between AI and data centers as merely semantic. But language shapes public understanding and public policy.

When citizens hear the phrase “AI technology,” they may imagine software developers, algorithms and digital innovation. They may not immediately think about electrical substations, transmission lines, cooling towers, groundwater extraction, land conversion or long-term resource consumption.

Conversely, the term “data center” more clearly conveys that physical infrastructure is involved.

The risk of emphasizing AI while downplaying data centers is that the public may underestimate the scale of the associated resource requirements.

Scientific accuracy requires acknowledging that artificial intelligence is not a substitute for data centers. Rather, data centers form the essential infrastructure on which AI operates.

Describing an AI project without discussing data centers is analogous to discussing a hydroelectric dam without mentioning the reservoir or commercial aviation without mentioning airports.

One cannot meaningfully exist at scale without the other.

The Pax Silica question

The relevance of the Harvard study becomes particularly evident when examining proposals such as Pax Silica and other large-scale technology developments being promoted in the Philippines.

Supporters frequently highlight potential benefits, including foreign direct investment, job creation, technological modernization, increased digital capacity, higher tax revenues and enhanced competitiveness.

These are legitimate considerations that deserve serious attention.

RELATED STORY: Pax Silica: Development at what cost?

However, responsible policymaking requires evaluating both benefits and costs.

Large AI-oriented technology complexes do not merely process information. They consume resources. The critical question is whether those resources are available, sustainable and equitably allocated.

Several issues therefore require transparent public discussion.

Electricity

If large-scale AI facilities require substantial power supplies, where will the electricity come from?

Will new generation capacity be required?

Will electricity be derived primarily from renewable energy sources, natural gas, coal or imported fuels?

Will local communities face increased competition for power during periods of peak demand?

The Philippines already struggles with some of the highest electricity costs in Southeast Asia. Any project involving exceptionally large electricity demand merits thorough analysis.

Water

Cooling systems are among the less-discussed aspects of the digital economy.

Yet cooling represents one of the most critical operational requirements of modern data centers.

Processing equipment generates heat continuously. Unless that heat is removed efficiently, equipment performance declines and system reliability suffers.

As a result, major facilities may require substantial quantities of water for cooling operations.

For a country already facing periodic droughts, growing urban demand, declining watershed conditions and climate-related water stress, water allocation deserves careful scrutiny.

Questions about water withdrawals are questions of sustainable resource management.

Land use

Technological development is often portrayed as less land-intensive than traditional industries.

Yet hyperscale facilities require significant physical footprints.

Additional infrastructure may include substations, transmission corridors, access roads, water systems, support buildings and logistics facilities.

Consequently, project evaluation should examine not only economic outputs but also land-use implications, biodiversity impacts and potential effects on agriculture and local communities.

Climate commitments

The Philippines is among the countries most vulnerable to climate change. The nation experiences increasingly severe typhoons, flooding, droughts, sea-level rise and agricultural disruption.

At the same time, the country has committed itself to climate mitigation efforts and sustainable development goals.

This raises an important policy question: How should rapidly expanding AI infrastructure fit within broader national climate objectives?

The issue is not whether technology should advance. The issue is whether technological development aligns with environmental sustainability goals.

Learning from the Green Revolution

The Philippines has experienced similar debates before.

The Green Revolution was promoted primarily in terms of production gains and technological progress. It contributed to higher yields and increased food production.

Yet subsequent decades revealed associated challenges involving chemical dependence, groundwater depletion, ecological degradation, biodiversity loss and farmer indebtedness.

The lesson is not that innovation is undesirable. The lesson is that innovation should be examined holistically.

Societies should evaluate technologies not only by the benefits they promise but also by the costs they impose.

The same principle applies to artificial intelligence.

AI offers significant opportunities in education, research, agriculture, health care, disaster management, governance and productivity.

Yet those benefits do not negate the need for discussions about energy demand, water use, emissions and resource allocation.

Transparency is not opposition

Questioning a project does not necessarily imply opposition to it.

Transparency can strengthen investment, improve public trust, reduce misinformation and increase the likelihood that projects proceed with social legitimacy.

When citizens ask how much electricity a project will consume, they are seeking information about development.

When communities ask where water will come from, they are seeking information about resource use.

When researchers seek environmental impact assessments, they are evaluating evidence before long-term commitments are made.

The Harvard study reinforces this principle by emphasizing the need for better reporting and greater transparency about the environmental impacts of data centers.

The researchers are not advocating rejection of AI. They are advocating informed decision-making.

The same standard should apply in the Philippines.

Beyond hype and fear

Public discourse around AI often oscillates between two extremes.

One side portrays AI as a solution to a broad range of economic and social challenges.

The other portrays AI as an existential threat.

Neither perspective alone adequately addresses the central issue: governance.

How should societies deploy AI responsibly?

How should benefits be distributed?

How should environmental costs be measured?

How should scarce resources be allocated?

And who ultimately bears the risks?

These are governance questions rather than purely technological ones. Their answers require transparency, accountability, scientific evidence, public participation and rigorous policy analysis.

The real conversation the Philippines needs

The most important contribution of the Harvard research is not simply its statistics on energy consumption or carbon emissions.

Its broader contribution is a reminder that digital technologies are not disconnected from physical realities.

AI is not floating in cyberspace. It is embedded in electrical grids. It is connected to water systems. It occupies physical land.

It requires minerals, metals, semiconductors, cables and cooling infrastructure.

Its impacts extend beyond software into ecology, economics and governance.

Consequently, the Philippine discussion should not revolve solely around whether a project is an AI facility or a data center.

The more important question is whether the public is receiving a complete and scientifically accurate picture of what such projects entail.

If artificial intelligence is indeed the future, citizens deserve full disclosure about the infrastructure that will support that future.

The challenge before the Philippines is not whether to embrace AI. The challenge is whether to do so transparently, sustainably and in a manner consistent with national interests.

The questions are straightforward:

Who will supply the electricity?

Who will provide the water?

What lands will be affected?

How will environmental impacts be managed?

Who will capture the economic benefits?

And how will the public be assured that the promises of technological progress outweigh the costs?

These are questions that responsible democracies should ask before committing vast public resources to the infrastructure of the digital age. /dm

World.title: Distillers: Since youth prefer coffee, just tax that instead
World.content:
Coffee and croissant. STOCK PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — The group of major liquor companies recommended to the House of Representatives committee on ways and means to explore imposing additional taxes on coffee instead of alcoholic drinks, as the younger generation leans towards the brewed beverage.

During the House committee hearing on proposed additional taxation for alcopops, 1Tahanan party-list Rep. Elmer Catulpos asked Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines (DSAP) president Olivia Limpe-Aw if the local liquor industry was growing. The DSAP was asking the government to ease on further imposing taxes on alcoholic products.

Limpe-Aw replied that there was no growth, since their removals or shipments of liquor in 2025 have not even matched the figures for 2021 because higher prices and changing consumer behavior.

Article continues after this 

“Wala nga po, kasi no’ng 2025 ang volume namin, hindi pa niya na-reach ‘yong 2021 levels. So in 2021, ang removals namin is 527 million, sa 2025 ang removals is 512 million. So talagang nagko-contract talaga siya kasi nga, tumataas ang presyo,” Limpe-Aw said.

(There’s no growth, because in 2025 our volume of removals did not reach the 2021 levels. So in 2021, our removals were at 527 million, but in 2025 the removals dipped to 512 million. So there’s really a contraction because prices increased.)

“Siyempre ‘di ba the law of supply and demand ‘pag tumaas ang presyo, bababa ang demand. So kaka-increase ng presyo, talagang bababa ang demand. Plus of course, ‘yong na-mention po natin, nag-iiba din ‘yong consumer behavior, like ‘yong mga Gen Z natin hindi na sila masyadong umiinom ng alak, gusto nila kape,” she added.

(Of course, this law of supply and demand: when prices go up, demand goes down. So every time you increase prices, demand goes down. Plus, of course, we have mentioned this before: consumer behavior also changes, like those from Gen Z do not drink much liquor anymore; they prefer coffee.)

Focus on alcopops first

Limpe-Aw said she and other distillers suggested that the committee chairperson and Marikina Rep. Miro Quimbo tax coffee instead, but the lawmaker relented, saying they will focus on liquor first.

Article continues after this 

“Kaya nga ang sabi namin kay Cong. Miro baka gusto niyong i-tax ‘yong kape kasi ‘yon ang malaki ‘di ba, hindi talaga ‘yong alak. And ang laki, ang mahal ng kape,” Limpe-Aw said.

(That’s why we told Cong. Miro that maybe they want to tax coffee because it has more volume of consumption, not liquor. Coffee is really a big market and it’s expensive.)

Article continues after this 

“‘Wag muna tayo, sa alak muna tayo, baka dumami (ang) antukin kapag kape ang pinag-usapan,” Quimbo replied.

(Let’s not go there, let’s focus on liquor, maybe a lot of people will be sleepy if we tax coffee.)

Quimbo in particular said that the committee was considering how to tax alcopops, or sweet carbonated drinks containing alcohol, as a way of deterring young Filipinos from drinking it.

The lawmaker added that the low prices of these products and the wide range of flavors have made alcopops appealing.

“Sa huling pagtalakay natin sa proposed policy na ito, nakita natin ang mga datos sa pagtaas ng alcohol consumption ng ating mga kabataan,” Quimbo said. “We need to take a closer look at the products they consume, particularly alcopops, which, because of their affordability, flavors, and packaging, are appealing to our youth.”

(In our last discussion on this proposed policy, we saw data indicating a rise in alcohol consumption among our youth. We need to take a closer look at the products they consume, particularly alcopops, which, because of their affordability, flavors, and packaging, are appealing to our youth.)

“Ang bawat batang nailalayo natin sa pagkalulong sa alak ay may mas magandang pagkakataong lumaking malusog at makapag-ambag sa kanyang pamilya at sa ating bansa,” Quimbo said.

(Every young Filipino whom we can pull away from alcohol addiction will have a greater chance of growing up healthy and able to contribute to his family and our country.)

However, Quimbo maintained that any increase in excise taxes for alcoholic drinks should serve a clear public health purpose, while also examining how the liquor industry will be impacted.

“But as I have emphasized in our previous hearing, we need to be surgical in our approach. Hindi lang basta pagtataas ng buwis ang gusto nating gawin. Kailangan nating matukoy kung ano talaga ang problemang nais nating tugunan at masigurong tama ang calibration ng ating pagbubuwis,” he noted.

(But as I have emphasized in our previous hearing, we need to be surgical in our approach. We cannot just increase taxes because we want it. We have to specify what problem we want to solve and ensure that there is correct calibration in our taxation efforts.)

The Philippines has been increasing taxes for so-called sin products, or vices like alcohol and cigarettes. In January 2020, former president Rodrigo Duterte signed into law a measure imposing additional excise taxes on alcoholic beverages and e-cigarettes, more commonly known as the Sin Tax Law.

READ: Duterte signs law increasing taxes on alcohol, e-cigarettes

The new law was expected to generate around P24.9 billion in revenues for the government, which were channeled into the Universal Health Care program.

Despite the higher taxes, several health advocates have urged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to raise sin taxes even more, as the current preventive measures were no longer enough to curb unhealthful habits among the youth.

In a press briefing last July 2026, members of the Youth for Health coalition called on the government to allocate more funds for health programs targeting youth, citing rising cases of stunting and obesity nationwide.

READ: Increase in taxes pushed to protect youth from vices

World.title: LTFRB probes InDrive operator after driver’s row with passengers
World.content:
.

MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has issued a show cause order against the operator of an InDrive partner involved in a viral video showing a heated dispute with passengers over an additional tollway charge.

LTFRB Acting Chairperson Greg Pua said the operator was directed to explain in writing why its authority to operate a transport network company (TNC) should not be suspended or canceled.

The hearing is scheduled for Dec. 9.

Article continues after this 

The case stemmed from a viral video showing a transport network vehicle service (TNVS) driver charging passengers an additional P39 for using an expressway without first informing them or obtaining their consent.

READ: DOTr seeks probe of inDrive driver over tollway dispute with passengers

The disagreement escalated when the driver allegedly told the passengers to get out of the vehicle, prompting them to insist that the matter be settled at a police station.

Pua reminded taxi and ride-hailing drivers to inform passengers and secure their approval before making decisions that would result in additional charges, such as taking expressways.

“We understand the concerns being raised by some taxi drivers and TNVS partners on this particular issue, but unless they are willing to shoulder the additional cost, they must always inform their passengers and seek their approval first before entering expressways,” Pua said.

Article continues after this 

He explained that using expressways entails toll fees, which should be discussed with passengers, particularly when the cost will be charged to them.

READ: LTFRB: Over 600 TNVS partners under ‘tempo’ status to be regularized

Article continues after this 

The video also sparked discussions on social media, with some netizens siding with the passengers while others cited heavy traffic and other possible reasons for the driver’s decision to take the expressway.

Pua urged public utility vehicle operators, particularly taxi and TNC operators, to remind their drivers of LTFRB rules on expressway use to prevent similar incidents.

“Let this serve as a lesson for all the drivers to keep their passengers informed and ask for their consent first before making any decision that will result in additional cost,” he said.

“This is not only about the LTFRB rule on the use of expressways for PUVs (public utility vehicles), this is also a matter of respecting the passengers,” he added.

Earlier, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon also said passengers must be given the option to take the toll road or an alternative route.

“Drivers cannot make that decision on their own without the passenger’s consent,” he added.

World.title: Myanmar Records Worst Landmine Casualties in the World for 3rd Year
World.content:
Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties from landmines and unexploded ordnance in the world last year with nearly 1,900, according to the Landmine Monitor report released Tuesday.

The group’s research shows that Myanmar was the country worst affected by deaths from landmines and so-called “explosive remnants of war” for the third year running.

Worldwide, some 6,929 casualties were recorded in 2025, counting both civilians and military personnel. Myanmar accounted for a massive proportion of over 27 percent or nearly one-third with 1,891.

The military has regularly used antipersonnel mines since 1999 and increased their use notably after the coup in February 2021, the report pointed out.

Casualties soared as a result, from just 368 in 2021 to 1,003 in 2023 before doubling to 2,029 the following year.

They are regularly planted around military bases and outposts as well as mobile phone towers, mining operations and fuel pipelines.

One regime combat engineer reported that he was ordered to plant mines in Kachin and Rakhine states near populated areas, marked only by “Danger Do Not Enter” signs without mentioning mines.

“Often there are no signs,” said Thet Oo of the resistance Yinmabin–Salingyi Strike Committee in heavily mined Sagaing Region.

He said the regime frequently plants landmines when launching offensives or raiding villages, placing them at the entrance of houses.

They are designed to sever legs.

He admitted that the heartland resistance People’s Defense Forces (PDF) also used remote-controlled handmade landmines across the country after the coup. But when resistance governing bodies were formed, they banned mines near settled areas except for military purposes that require their authorization.

“The mines are meant to injure or delay the enemy,” he added. But he claimed they are always cleared before residents return.

The report says ethnic armed organizations reported seizing regime landmines almost every month between January 2022 and this September 2026, showing how prevalent their use is.

Regime-aligned ethnic Border Guard Forces (BGF) and the militias under the regime’s command also use landmines, it says.

“We urge all states to reject the production and use of antipersonnel mines, by any actor, under any circumstances,” Tamar Gabelnick, director of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told AFP.

Syria was the second-most affected country with an equally massive 1,602 casualties, trailed at a substantial distance by Afghanistan with 497.

World.title: Myanmar’s China Dilemma: Turning Beijing’s Need Into Leverage Requires Legitimate Leaders
World.content:
Anyone seeking clarity on China-Myanmar relations must first ask one crucial question: does China need Myanmar, or does Myanmar need China?

Some argue that Beijing’s often-cited desire for access to the Indian Ocean through Myanmar is overstated. Others contend that China barely needs Myanmar at all, and that the relationship matters far more to Naypyitaw than to Beijing.

The reality is more complicated.

The Malacca Dilemma

Some analysts state that China needs Myanmar to secure overland access to the Indian Ocean, bypassing the Malacca Strait chokepoint. Others dismiss this view, saying the chokepoint is no longer a problem for a country which now boasts the world’s largest navy.

Chinese leaders began wrestling with the “Malacca Dilemma” in the early 2000s under President Hu Jintao. Around the same time, Beijing and Myanmar’s previous junta began talks on pipelines to transport oil and gas from the Bay of Bengal to Yunnan Province. Agreements were reached in 2007-2008, and construction began in June 2010.

At that point, China had yet to commission a single aircraft carrier. Its first carrier — a Soviet-made ship bought from Ukraine in 1998 and modified — did not enter service until 2012.
