Razmadze denies publishing the post and says he has no connection to the page. According to him, the page was created a long time ago and regularly published videos featuring other opposition figures. Razmadze has demanded that the Imedi, Rustavi 2 and POSTV television channels remove the false information and apologise.

What do human rights organisations say?

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) described the actions targeting Razmadze across various platforms as “a coordinated, targeted and systematic harassment campaign”.

The organisation says the materials published as part of the campaign amount to identity theft, as the videos reproduce Razmadze’s appearance and voice without his consent.

GYLA notes that the videos contain no elements of satire or parody, which “aggravates the negative impact on Tornike Razmadze’s rights – his rights to honour, privacy, identity and security”.

The organisation says the state has an obligation to assess such risks promptly, take protective measures and provide effective legal remedies for violations of these rights.

Reaction on social media

The story sparked widespread discussion on social media. Razmadze faced a wave of insults and accusations that echoed the narrative promoted by the fake videos. At the same time, many users expressed their support. Other bloggers and government critics voiced solidarity with Razmadze, warning the authorities that such campaigns could have dangerous consequences. YouTube bloggers and sports commentators also expressed their support.

Comedian Onise Okriashvili wrote on Facebook that this appeared to be the first case in Georgia in which someone had tried to discredit a person using hyper-realistic AI-generated videos rather than satirical ones.

Background: fined over remarks about Russian propagandists

A month before the campaign began, Razmadze was fined 3,000 lari. In September, the Interior Ministry opened administrative proceedings against him. The case concerned a Facebook comment containing obscene language directed at Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov. They had previously described Georgian King Erekle II as a ruler who “knelt down”. Razmadze’s video addressed those remarks.

A newly established Interior Ministry unit responsible for combating “hate speech” initiated the case. The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association described it at the time as a precedent for censorship.

Razmadze says he expected a campaign against him after the authorities opened the case.

What happens next?

Razmadze is discussing further legal action with his lawyers. The Interior Ministry has yet to say whether it has launched an investigation following his complaint.

Georgia’s first AI smear campaign against an activist

World.title: Georgia awarded contracts worth nearly $499m without competitive tenders – TI
World.content:
Non-competitive public procurement in Georgia

Between January and October 2026, almost half (45%) of tenders announced in Georgia attracted only one bidder. The lack of competition meant that these contracts cost the state around 150 million lari (approximately $57.5 million) more.

This is according to a new study by Transparency International Georgia.

According to the study, in the first ten months of 2026, government agencies awarded contracts worth a total of 4.09 billion lari (approximately $1.57 billion) through 16,222 electronic tenders.

A total of 7,364 tenders – 45% of all those announced – attracted only one bidder, either a company or an individual entrepreneur. The contracts were worth a combined 1.31 billion lari (approximately $499 million), accounting for almost a third of all public procurement spending.

According to the organisation, the winning bids in single-bidder tenders were, on average, just 4.3% below the initial estimated value set by the authorities. By comparison, prices in competitive tenders fell by an average of 15.4%.

TI estimates that if prices in non-competitive tenders had fallen by the same proportion, public contracts would have cost the state around 150 million lari (approximately $57.5 million) less.

The study also found that in 2,883 tenders, worth a total of 572 million lari (approximately $219.6 million), the winning bid exactly matched the estimated value set by the government in advance. In these cases, the state made no savings.

The largest public procurer using non-competitive procedures is the Special Penitentiary Service

According to TI, in 2026 the Special Penitentiary Service was the largest public procurer using non-competitive tenders. Through this mechanism, the agency awarded contracts worth a total of 203.7 million lari (approximately $78.6 million).

Almost the entire amount – 201.4 million lari – went towards two contracts for providing meals to prisoners.

In May 2026, the Special Penitentiary Service awarded contracts worth 152.4 million lari to Giorgi 2020 and 49 million lari to Delfood.

Both companies were the sole bidders in their respective tenders. Moreover, their bids exactly matched the estimated values set in advance.

The contracts were awarded amid a scandal over the quality of food served in Georgian prisons. Earlier, in March, the Special Penitentiary Service terminated its contract with Ili Group, which had been responsible for providing meals to prisoners.

According to TI, Giorgi 2020 had never previously won a public procurement tender.

On 3 April 2026 – the day the tender was announced – the company’s owners transferred 33% of its shares to Irakli Letodiani free of charge.

According to the TV Pirveli television channel, Letodiani is a former employee of the State Security Service.

Which sectors have the least competition?

According to the study, several sectors have particularly high proportions of tenders with only one bidder:

Transport services – 85%;

Software and information systems – 81%;

Repair and maintenance – 78%;

Medical equipment and medicines – 59%.

The proportion of construction tenders attracting only one bidder was relatively low, at 29%. However, construction ranked first in terms of the total value of contracts awarded.

Non-competitive construction contracts were worth a total of 517.9 million lari (approximately $199.8 million).

Tbilisi and Batumi account for the largest sums in non-competitive procurement

According to TI, 43% of tenders organised by municipalities – including those run by mayors and bodies established by them – attracted no competition. The figure for central government agencies and other state institutions was 48%.

Municipalities awarded contracts worth a total of 625 million lari (approximately $241.1 million) without any competition.

In monetary terms, Tbilisi ranked first, with 277 million lari, accounting for 38% of the capital’s procurement spending. Batumi came second, with 63 million lari, or 30% of its procurement spending.

In terms of the proportion of non-competitive tenders, the highest figures were recorded in Ambrolauri (61%), Terjola (59%) and Khulo (55%).

The risk of tailoring tender requirements to specific companies

TI notes that one possible reason for the high proportion of tenders with only one bidder is that authorities tailor procurement requirements to suit specific suppliers. The organisation cites several examples of this practice.

In June 2026, TI reported on five road repair tenders announced by Batumi’s Department of Infrastructure and Improvement.

Under the terms of the tender, bidders had to either own an asphalt plant within a 30km radius of the work site or provide a contract with such a facility. This requirement applied to a tender worth 29.2 million lari (approximately $11.3 million), in which Gza was the sole bidder.

Another example is a security services tender announced by Georgian Railway in 2023. To qualify for the contract, worth 7.8 million lari (approximately $3 million), bidders had to demonstrate at least 20 years of uninterrupted experience.

According to Transparency International (TI), only two companies in the entire country met this requirement. The sole bidder was Intersecurity Georgia LLC, owned by Ioseb Alavidze, a former head of the Tbilisi police. The company’s bid exactly matched the estimated contract value.

The organisation also cites a tender for the provision of social canteen services announced by Rustavi City Hall in 2022.

In that case, the company offering the lowest price was excluded from the tender because its revised price schedule listed figures to four decimal places instead of two. The contract was ultimately awarded to a company whose bid was 155,000 lari (approximately $59,800) higher.

The problem extends beyond large-scale tenders

TI says that a lack of competition in public procurement is not a new problem. The organisation refers to a 2024 study which found that half of the large tenders – those worth more than five million lari – announced between January and July 2024 attracted no competition.

Figures for 2026 show that the problem is not limited to large-scale procurement: only one bidder took part in half of all tenders worth up to 100,000 lari.

The organisation also criticises reports prepared by the State Procurement Agency. TI notes that although the agency’s reports point to an increase in competition, none of its annual reports published since 2019 has mentioned that almost half of all public tenders attract only one bidder.

Non-competitive public procurement in Georgia

World.title: NEST Centre: 408 Azerbaijani citizens killed while fighting in Ukraine for Russian forces. What is known in Baku?
World.content:
Azerbaijani citizens killed while serving in Russian army

At least 408 Azerbaijani citizens who fought in the ranks of the Russian army have been killed in Russia’s war against Ukraine. The figures come from a study published on 23 November by the independent think tank NEST Centre (New Eurasian Strategies Centre). The study draws on registered death records obtained through a data leak from Russia’s Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).

According to NEST Centre’s calculations, 6,947 foreign nationals who fought on Russia’s side were confirmed killed between 24 February 2022 and 29 September 2026. Azerbaijan ranks sixth in the number of fatalities, after Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

Earlier this year, the authorities in Azerbaijan acknowledged that a “significant number” of the country’s citizens had died in the war between Russia and Ukraine, but did not specify how many. The leaked data help to fill some of this information gap.

What does the figure of 408 deaths tell us, what does it leave out, and how does Baku view the deaths of its citizens in this war?

How did the data leak happen?

In late October, the Belarusian hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian group Silent Crow said they had gained access to Rosstat’s information systems. The agency confirmed that it had come under cyberattacks between 29 October and 1 November, but denied that hackers had breached its databases or leaked confidential information.

Several international media outlets and research centres subsequently analysed the database. Janis Kluge, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said there was no longer any doubt about its authenticity. Bloomberg, meanwhile, reported that it had been unable to verify the data using cryptographic methods, but had found no signs of falsification.

Why could the death toll be higher than 408?

NEST Centre stresses that the list of fatalities is incomplete and that the figures do not reflect the true scale of Russia’s losses. There are several reasons for this.

First, the figure of 408 includes only Azerbaijani citizens. According to a Bloomberg analysis based on the same database, more than 6,000 of the 11,335 foreign-born servicemen killed had acquired Russian citizenship before their deaths. Russia offers foreigners a simplified and accelerated path to citizenship in exchange for military service. The figures for Azerbaijan do not include people born in Azerbaijan who died as Russian citizens.

Second, researchers say that if Russian civil registry offices did not register a foreign national’s death, the information may have remained only in the Ministry of Defence’s internal records. Third, the database contains no information about people missing in action. In 2025, the average delay in registering deaths exceeded four months.

How did they end up in the Russian army?

NEST Centre provides no specific information about how Azerbaijani citizens joined the Russian army. However, the study says that recruiters promised foreigners – primarily migrants from Central Asia – civilian jobs, help with paperwork or release from detention centres, before sending them to military units. In some cases, researchers say, recruiters used threats and physical violence to force migrants to sign military contracts.

There have also been individual reports of Azerbaijani citizens ending up on the front line under similar circumstances. In August this year, the Azerbaijani news website Modern.az published a video in which an Azerbaijani man serving in the Russian army claimed that authorities had unlawfully sent him to the combat zone.

What does Baku say?

Azerbaijan criminalises participation in armed conflicts abroad. On 3 February 2026, the State Security Service (SSS) said that “a significant number of citizens of the Republic of Azerbaijan have taken part in hostilities between Russia and Ukraine, been killed, gone missing or been wounded, while some remain in captivity”. According to the agency, in January that year authorities detained four Azerbaijani citizens suspected of fighting on the side of Russia or Ukraine. A court ordered their pre-trial detention.

The SSS warned citizens that “participation in such armed conflicts entails criminal liability in the Republic of Azerbaijan”. However, it did not specify how many Azerbaijani citizens had been killed, gone missing or been taken prisoner.

Azerbaijanis are also fighting on Ukraine’s side. In September 2024, Galib Osmanly, a representative of the United Azerbaijani Diaspora of Ukraine, told the Turan news agency that at least 60 ethnic Azerbaijanis had been killed while serving in the Ukrainian army since the start of the war. They included both Ukrainian citizens and Azerbaijanis who held residence permits in the country.

Against the backdrop of tensions with Moscow

The figures on those killed have emerged amid tensions between Baku and Moscow. The crash of an AZAL passenger plane in December 2024 and the disagreements that followed undermined trust between the two countries. In September this year, Azerbaijan placed three Russian propagandists on its wanted list.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry and State Security Service have yet to comment on the findings of the NEST Centre study. Russia’s Defence Ministry, meanwhile, does not disclose figures for the number of foreign nationals serving in its army or the casualties among them.



Azerbaijani citizens killed while serving in Russian army

World.title: Opinion: ‘Pashinyan’s proposal is aimed at Russia, not Armenian opposition’
World.content:
Who did Pashinyan address his referendum proposal to?

Experts in Armenia are debating Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s proposal to the parliamentary opposition. He suggested that opposition MPs vote to put the draft of a new constitution to a referendum. In return, he promised to resign as prime minister regardless of the referendum’s outcome.

Local analysts describe the offer as a “deal” with the opposition. Under its terms, if opposition MPs do not obstruct the constitutional referendum, Pashinyan will voluntarily step down. Opposition figures have repeatedly stated that their main goal is to remove him from office. Pashinyan, meanwhile, wants to change the Constitution. He believes a new version would allow Armenia to live in peace and resolve conflicts with its neighbours.

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan, discussing the opposition forces that could theoretically vote in favour of the referendum, highlights the following points:

“They are part of, and even lead, political forces that have ‘united’ to overthrow the government;

The political capital of these forces lies neither in their members, nor in their standing at home, nor in the other groups they have joined forces with.”

According to the analyst, the political capital of both opposition factions – “Strong Armenia” and “Armenia” – lies in “Moscow’s patronage”.

“They will only be able to respond to Pashinyan’s proposal after agreeing on their answer with the Kremlin. In reality, Russia is the party responding to the proposal,” Robert Gevondyan argues.

The political analyst also puts forward scenarios in which Moscow might allow the pro-Russian opposition to “make a deal” with the Armenian authorities.

“The opposition rejects the offer of its dreams”

In recent days, Armenia’s prime minister has repeatedly presented his proposal in public appearances. Pashinyan is asking opposition MPs to vote in favour of holding a referendum on the draft Constitution. In return, he promises to resign if voters reject it. If they approve it, the ruling party will not nominate him for prime minister in the next election.

The opposition factions “Armenia” and “Strong Armenia” have rejected the offer.

They believe the incumbent prime minister will step down anyway and refuse to accept his proposed “deal”.

Opposition figures describe the draft of the new Constitution as “Aliyev’s Constitution”. They believe Armenia is changing its supreme law at Azerbaijan’s request.

Azerbaijan refuses to sign a peace treaty until Armenia changes its Constitution. Baku considers the reference in its preamble to the Declaration of Independence problematic. The declaration calls for the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. The new draft omits this reference. Parliament must first approve the proposal to put the draft Constitution to a referendum. At least two-thirds of MPs must vote in favour. The ruling Civil Contract party does not have enough seats to secure the required majority. It is six votes short.

Commenting on the opposition’s refusal, ruling party representative and Speaker of the National Assembly Ruben Rubinyan said that, for them, “obstructing peace matters more than removing Pashinyan from power”.

He also suggested that the opposition was seeking to “make peace impossible and incorporate Armenia into another state – the Union State of Russia and Belarus”.

Pashinyan himself describes his proposal as an unprecedented opportunity for the opposition.

He explains the opposition’s refusal by saying that “their mission is to prevent the country from achieving both peace and independence”.

Analysis

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan has outlined his views on the issue in an article titled “The new Constitution and Pashinyan’s proposal to Russia”:

“Pashinyan apparently understands that the Kremlin will make the final decision on the issue he has raised.

The proposal, made just days before three visits to Moscow scheduled for December this year, is addressed not to Armenia’s parliamentary opposition, but to the Kremlin.

The Armenian prime minister has announced that he will visit Russia on 3, 11 and 22 December. According to a preliminary agreement, Pashinyan will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on 3 December. The Armenian prime minister also said that a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, bringing together the heads of government of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), is scheduled for 11–12 December. The annual meetings of the leaders of the EAEU and Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries will take place in St Petersburg at the end of the year.

There is little doubt that Armenia’s new Constitution will be on the agenda when Pashinyan meets Putin. The draft was published ahead of the planned visits.

But under what circumstances could Pashinyan secure the six votes he needs with Russia’s help? There are two theoretical scenarios.

First, Moscow could give the green light to a constitutional referendum if the new Constitution takes Russia’s interests and demands into account.

However, the draft has already been published, and it contains provisions that are clearly problematic for Moscow. In particular, removing the reference to Armenia’s Declaration of Independence from the preamble is primarily a geopolitical issue. But another provision, which bars political parties from operating with foreign funding, would directly limit Russia’s ability to exert influence in Armenia.

Under the current Constitution, the Constitutional Court may ban only parties that have advocated violence or used it to overthrow the constitutional order. The new draft introduces the following additional grounds for banning a political party: receiving funding from foreign sources;

advocating the renunciation of state independence;

inciting ethnic or religious hatred;

taking actions that obstruct the free expression of voters’ will.

The second way to secure Moscow’s approval for the six votes needed to hold a constitutional referendum would be to reach agreements on other issues.

These could include Armenia’s railway network, the construction of a new nuclear power plant, Russia’s 102nd military base in Gyumri, Armenia’s European integration process and other matters.

In other words, if Pashinyan and Putin reach agreements on key issues, Russia could “give the green light” to a referendum on constitutional amendments. The question is whether Yerevan is prepared to pay such a price.”

Who did Pashinyan address his referendum proposal to?

World.title: Georgian Dream propaganda network ran coordinated campaign against Metropolitan Iov – ISFED
World.content:
Campaign against Metropolitan Iov in Georgia

Following a sermon that included criticism of the Georgian government, a coordinated disinformation campaign against Metropolitan Iov was launched on social media. Dozens of social media pages published posts with identical content at almost exactly the same time.

As part of the campaign, at least 20 paid s appeared on Meta platforms, generating between 77,600 and 107,180 views in total.

Pro-government media outlets, Facebook pages and individuals affiliated with Georgian Dream’s propaganda network stepped up the campaign against Metropolitan Iov following his critical sermon.

The campaign was investigated by the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED).

The organisation analysed how identical quotes targeting the metropolitan spread across dozens of pages within minutes of each other; how videos from previous years were used in a new context; and how paid advertising complemented the campaign’s organic reach.

What Iov said and why it led to a confrontation with the authorities

The confrontation followed a sermon that Metropolitan Iov delivered at Urbnisi Cathedral on 10 November. He called government officials “non-believers” and “alien to the Church”, saying that the government had exhausted its potential and that the Georgian people should choose more worthy leaders in the future.

The metropolitan criticised the Church’s dependence on state funding, saying that the authorities were trying to merge Church and state.

He also raised issues such as corruption, the prevalence of drug addiction among young people and the widespread popularity of gambling. In addition, he referred to information allegedly leaked from the State Security Service in 2021, which contained details of surveillance of members of the clergy.

In his sermon, Iov also mentioned Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the Georgian Dream party. He also referred to the previous administration, saying: “We know what the previous government was doing; everything is obvious – the people voted against it.”

Metropolitan Iov’s remarks attracted particular attention because he had previously supported Georgian Dream.

On 21 November, during another sermon, he explained that although he had supported the ruling party, he believed it had since changed course, making criticism necessary.

“I supported Georgian Dream and stood by them, but I saw that they had gone astray. The situation had changed, and it became necessary to speak out against such actions. If they put things right, take these remarks into account and bring about change in Georgia – if they change the course of these developments – I may support them again,” he said.

Metropolitan Iov was also among the candidates for the post of patriarch in May 2026. Metropolitan Shio Mujiri was elected patriarch.

Identical posts and quotes from ‘experts’

According to ISFED’s monitoring, representatives of Georgian Dream were the first to react to Metropolitan Iov’s sermon.

MP Levan Machavariani called it “irresponsible”, saying that a senior clergyman should not use the pulpit to make political statements. Meanwhile, MP Mariam Lashkhi, responding to journalists’ questions, remarked: “May God forgive him.”

Meanwhile, pro-government figures began posting their views on social media.

On 11 November, news agencies and television channels linked to Georgian Dream published the same quote from a Facebook post by Gia Abashidze. He claimed that Bishop Iov was using the church pulpit to call for a change of government.

Screenshots of the posts. Source: ISFED

Thirteen minutes after Abashidze’s statement, a quote from Davit Kartvelishvili was circulated. He accused the metropolitan of having links to Saakashvili’s political forces, referred to criminal cases involving the metropolitan’s diocese and raised the issue of the seizure of agricultural land.

According to ISFED, these allegations came without references to specific sources or any particular case. Nevertheless, the text appeared on 14 pages within a few hours.

Screenshots of the posts. Source: ISFED

Tamta Megrelishvili, Davit Chikhelidze and Zaal Anjaparidze also joined the campaign. In their posts, they accused Metropolitan Iov of making political statements against the government, supporting Saakashvili and taking a position that ran counter to the country’s interests.

Davit Chikhelidze even linked the metropolitan’s diocese to harbouring criminals and “gangland-style disputes”.

A fake Facebook profile also took part in the campaign

The campaign also involved a Facebook profile that Myth Detector had previously identified as fake. The account, registered under the name Ketevan Mikiashvili, published two posts targeting Bishop Iov, just a few hours apart.

In her first post, Mikiashvili addressed the metropolitan ironically, referring to the election of the new patriarch. She remarked that Bishop Iov had “dropped his mask” after Shio became patriarch. The post included an archive television report captioned “Call to release Saakashvili”.

In her second post, she shared a video recorded on 25 September 2019, titled “Bishop Iov on Petre Tsaava”, implying that the footage revealed the metropolitan’s true motives.

These posts highlighted another narrative promoted by the campaign: Bishop Iov’s criticism of the authorities was presented not as a political or ecclesiastical disagreement, but as a personal grievance stemming from his defeat in the patriarchal election.

Mikiashvili later published another post portraying Bishop Iov’s sermon as yet another attempt to stage a revolution.

Personal attacks also appeared in posts by other figures.

On 11 November, Lasha Natsvlishvili, a Georgian Dream supporter and propagandist, published a Facebook post containing insults directed at Metropolitan Iov. [Fact-checkers say Lasha Natsvlishvili is behind the fake “Ketevan Mikiashvili” profile – JAMnews].

The post prompted a strong reaction, including from members of the clergy.

In 2012, Lasha Natsvlishvili became an MP on the Georgian Dream party list. He later served as first deputy interior minister and deputy chief prosecutor, before working as a public relations adviser to Georgian Dream.

The Interior Ministry launched administrative proceedings against Lasha Natsvlishvili over the post containing insults directed at Metropolitan Iov. On 16 November, Judge Manuchar Tsatsua fined Natsvlishvili 2,500 lari.

20 adverts and nearly 107,000 views

According to ISFED, part of the campaign was paid for. Data from the Meta Ad Library as of 17 November showed that at least 20 adverts targeting Metropolitan Iov’s reputation had appeared on five Facebook pages.

All the adverts ran between 11 and 14 November, with up to $100 spent on each. ISFED estimated that they generated between 77,600 and 107,180 views in total.

The adverts published on an anonymous page called Ganulebuli Opozitsia (“Cancelled Opposition”) attracted the most views – between 47,000 and 60,094. The same page also shared a post about Metropolitan Iov’s “vast wealth”.

Screenshots of the posts. Source: ISFED

Advertising materials also appeared on the pages Fact • ფაქტი, Ustari, Akhla • ახლა and Saerto Gazeti.

According to ISFED’s research, Jaba Khubua, the head of Fact • ფაქტი, is a presenter on the pro-government Imedi TV channel. Shako Kuchashvili, the owner of Ustari, is a Georgian Dream supporter and one of the presenters of the Fake Control programme on the same channel.

ISFED notes that the Fact and Ustari pages were created in 2026 and that the people behind them have links to the pro-government Imedi TV channel and Georgian Dream.

ISFED says this is significant because, following sanctions imposed by the UK, the main pages of the pro-government Imedi and POSTV channels faced restrictions on placing s. This forced them to use new pages to distribute their content.

The disinformation campaign also circulated footage from previous years. One advert used a recording of a sermon delivered by Metropolitan Iov in 2024, in which he discussed the release of Mikheil Saakashvili from prison. The video was accompanied by footage from Saakashvili’s time in power showing police storming a church in Gldani. However, the post did not mention that the sermon had been recorded two years earlier.

Government response and reaction within the Church

The campaign against Metropolitan Iov extended beyond social media. On 15 November, Imedi TV broadcast a 17-minute report as part of its Imedis Kvira (“Imedi Week”) programme, titled “A political manifesto from the pulpit”.

On the same day, Goga Khaindrava, a film director and Georgian Dream supporter, described the sermons delivered by Metropolitan Iov and the clergy who supported him as political statements.

Other members of the clergy, including Metropolitan Ilarion of Svaneti, expressed support for Metropolitan Iov. They criticised the ruling party’s policies and drew attention to issues such as the demographic crisis, gambling and drug addiction.

On 16 November, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze commented on the dispute. He said that public arguments between the clergy and the authorities harmed both the Church and the country, adding that the government had no intention of joining the dispute.

Campaign against Metropolitan Iov in Georgia

World.title: Seven people detained during protests in Georgia released: What do we know about them?
World.content:
Pardoning of protesters in Georgia

Seven people detained during the 2024 protests have been released from custody. They were among 232 people pardoned by President Mikheil Kavelashvili to mark St George’s Day.

Those released include Giorgi Okmelashvili, Irakli Metvinetukhutsesi, Giorgi Mindadze, Anri Kvaratskhelia, Nikoloz Javakhishvili, Davit Lomidze and Temur Zasokhashvili.

News of the pardons emerged late on Sunday, 22 November. The full list was not initially made public, but some of the names became known.

It also remained unclear exactly when those pardoned would be released. Some relatives and friends spent the entire night outside detention facilities, waiting for their release.

The prisoners were freed in the morning, shortly after 11:00. Footage of the moment shows highly emotional scenes.

Over the past two years, a period marked by protests in Georgia, more than 100 protesters have been arrested and prosecuted. All but three were sentenced to prison.

None of those detained admitted guilt during their trials.

Who was released and what were they accused of?

Two of the seven, Irakli Megvinetukhutsesi and Giorgi Okmelashvili, were arrested in May 2024 during protests against the so-called “Russian law” (the law on “foreign agents”).

The other five were arrested during pro-European protests that began in November-December 2024, after Irakli Kobakhidze announced the suspension of EU accession talks.

Giorgi Okmelashvili – 922 days in prison

Giorgi Okmelashvili reunites with his family. Photo: Publika, Mindia Gabadze

Giorgi Okmelashvili is a film director and producer who works in marketing. He is the founder of Limoni, an advertising and video production company.

He was detained on 15 May 2024 while on his way to work. At the time, protesters were holding demonstrations outside the Georgian parliament against the “Russian law” on “foreign agents”.

His arrest stemmed from an incident during a protest outside parliament on 13 May. The day before the legal affairs committee was due to hold a third-reading vote on the “Russian law”, protesters spent the night outside the parliament building under the slogan: “We will stay awake all night for Georgia”.

According to the prosecutor’s office, Okmelashvili struck a police officer in the face with his elbow during the protest. After his arrest, the Interior Ministry released video footage in an attempt to substantiate the charge. Okmelashvili and his lawyers insisted that his actions were an instinctive response to defend himself: at the time, riot police were trying to push protesters back.

On 3 February 2025, Giorgi Okmelashvili was sentenced to five years in prison.

“Rock’n’roll goes on. It wasn’t easy – that’s all I can say. Greetings to cell 414. I’m pretty much the same person I was before. Nothing has changed, except that I’ve read a lot of books and thought about many things,” Okmelashvili said after his release.

His young wife, their child, who is in the first year of primary school, and his parents were waiting for him at home.

🟥 Giorgi Okmelashvili spent 922 days in detention, from 15 May 2024 to 23 November 2026. That is 2 years, 6 months and 8 days.

Irakli Megvinetukhutsesi – 928 days in prison

Irakli Megvinetukhutsesi was arrested in the spring of 2024 during protests against the “foreign agents” law. He was taken into custody on 9 May 2024.

Little information about Megvinetukhutsesi’s background is publicly available. His family rarely speaks to the media. It is known that he was over 21 at the time of his arrest.

Megvinetukhutsesi faced two charges: assaulting a police officer and illegally acquiring and possessing marijuana. According to the prosecution, he threatened police officers with a knife during the protest. The prosecution claimed that one officer was injured while disarming him.

The defence insisted that Megvinetukhutsesi had no intention of harming the officer and had merely raised the knife in a demonstrative gesture.

On 30 December 2024, Tbilisi City Court found Megvinetukhutsesi guilty on both charges. He was sentenced to five years in prison.

🟥 Irakli Megvinetukhutsesi spent 928 days in prison – 2 years, 6 months and 14 days.

Giorgi Mindadze – 722 days in prison

Giorgi Mindadze reunites with his adoptive mother, Nani Tsulaia. Photo: MO SE

Giorgi Mindadze is a student who was arrested during the pro-European protests in November–December 2024. He was 21 at the time of his arrest and was in his third year at medical university.

On the evening of 1 December 2024, police arrived at his relatives’ home in the village of Tsilkani, where Mindadze was staying at the time, and detained him. They gave no explanation for his arrest at the scene.

It later emerged that investigators had accused him of setting off pyrotechnics during a protest on 29 November. He faced a criminal charge of assaulting a police officer. According to the prosecution, a firework launched by Mindadze struck a police officer, injuring his leg.

The defence lawyer noted that the case file contained no direct evidence that the officer had been injured by pyrotechnics launched by Mindadze. The prosecution presented a photograph taken on 29 November showing Mindadze holding a pyrotechnic device, as well as testimony from the police officer.

On 3 July 2025, the court found Mindadze guilty and sentenced him to five years in prison.

Giorgi has no mother – she died when he was very young. His neighbour, Nani Tsulaia, adopted him and raised him as her own son. Nani was with Giorgi when police arrested him. Officers took him away without telling her where they were taking him.

She went from one police station to another, trying to find out where they were holding her adopted son.

Nani Tsulaia has become one of the prominent figures in the protest movement. Since Giorgi’s arrest, she has taken part in street protests without fail. Along with other parents, she travelled across Georgia to tell the public the truth about those detained.

“I really want to go home… Freedom for everyone!” were Giorgi’s first words after his release from prison.

🟥 Giorgi Mindadze spent 722 days in detention, from 1 December 2024 to 23 November 2026. That is 1 year, 11 months and 22 days.

Anri (Anzor) Kvaratskhelia – 718 days in prison

Anri Kvaratskhelia after his release from prison. Photo: MO SE

Anri (Anzor) Kvaratskhelia also took part in the pro-European protests in November and December 2024. He was among those charged with assaulting a police officer.

Anri was arrested at his home on 5 December 2024. He was 25 at the time. According to the prosecution, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue on the night of 1 December, Kvaratskhelia threw a Molotov cocktail towards riot police officers.

His defence lawyers stressed that no law enforcement officers were injured in the incident. They argued that there was no actual victim who had sustained physical injuries and that the bottle had not reached the police cordon.

On 18 July 2025, Tbilisi City Court found him guilty and sentenced him to four years and six months in prison.

Anri was born on 20 January 1999 to a family of internally displaced people from Abkhazia. His mother is an emigrant.

“I’ll visit the guys. I hope they’ll be released soon. They’re great guys – they know what they’re doing!” he said after his release.

🟥 Anri Kvaratskhelia spent 718 days in detention, from 5 December 2024 to 23 November 2026. That is 1 year, 11 months and 18 days.

Nikoloz Javakhishvili – 723 days in prison

Nikoloz Javakhishvili after his release from prison. Photo: MO SE

Nikoloz Javakhishvili was arrested on 30 November 2024. He also took part in the autumn protests. He was 20 at the time of his arrest and worked as a DJ before his detention.

Javakhishvili, along with seven other protesters, was charged with participating in group violence. The case became known in the media as the “case of the eight”.

Javakhishvili was accused of throwing pyrotechnics at police during a protest. As part of its evidence, the prosecution presented video footage showing a young man with a Georgian flag draped over his shoulders and a brown blanket thrown over it. The footage shows him throwing pyrotechnic devices. Investigators claimed that the person in the video was Javakhishvili.

The defence challenged this identification from the outset, arguing that the person could not be identified from the footage. Lawyers also insisted that the protesters had formed neither an organised group nor a prior conspiracy.

On 2 September 2025, the court sentenced Nikoloz Javakhishvili to two years in prison. He had been in custody since 30 November 2024. His sentence was due to end on 4 December 2026. The pardon secured his release 11 days before the end of his sentence.

🟥 Nikoloz Javakhishvili spent 723 days in prison – 1 year, 11 months and 23 days.

Davit Lomidze – 722 days in prison

Davit Lomidze and Temur Zasokhashvili after their release from prison. Photo: MO SE

Davit Lomidze was 53 when police arrested him on 1 December 2024 during a pro-European protest on Rustaveli Avenue.

Police initially detained him on an administrative offence charge. However, just as he was due to be released, they took him into custody again, this time as part of a criminal case opened against him.

According to the prosecution, on the night of 1 December, during a protest outside parliament, Lomidze threw a Molotov cocktail towards riot police officers and a water cannon. Investigators claim that the water cannon caught fire as a result.

According to Lomidze’s lawyer, the case file contained two video recordings and a police report. The footage did not show who had thrown the Molotov cocktail, making it impossible to identify Lomidze as the perpetrator.

Moreover, riot police officers brutally beat and mistreated Lomidze during his arrest.

On 8 August 2025, Tbilisi City Court found Davit Lomidze guilty of assaulting a police officer. It sentenced him to four years and six months in prison.

🟥 Davit Lomidze spent 722 days in prison – 1 year, 11 months and 22 days.

Temur Zasokhashvili – 722 days in prison

Temur Zasokhashvili was arrested on 1 December 2024 alongside Davit Lomidze. The court heard their cases together.

He was 39 at the time of his arrest. He lived in Tbilisi with his father; his mother and brother had been living abroad for many years. He previously worked for the State Security Service and, before his arrest, was employed in the technical department of a hotel.

Zasokhashvili faced the same charge as Lomidze: setting fire to a water cannon using a Molotov cocktail. He denied the charges. His defence also questioned whether investigators could identify the person in the video footage.

His lawyer, Dimitri Vardiashvili, said he saw Zasokhashvili after his arrest at the detention centre. He had been beaten, his eyes were swollen and guards had to support him to prevent him from falling.

On 8 August 2025, the court sentenced him to four years and six months in prison.

🟥 Temur Zasokhashvili spent 722 days in detention – 1 year, 11 months and 22 days.

The pardon process

Under Georgia’s Constitution, granting pardons is the exclusive prerogative of the president and constitutes an individual act of clemency.

The president may exercise this power at any time. Traditionally, pardons are granted to mark significant religious holidays.

The president’s power to grant pardons allows them to:

Grant a full pardon;

Reduce a sentence;

Remove a criminal conviction.

A pardon is not the same as an amnesty. A pardon is an individual decision by the president concerning specific people, while an amnesty involves the mass release of certain categories of convicted people and is granted by parliament.

When making a decision, the president may consult relevant government agencies or experts, although this is not mandatory.

Representatives of the Georgian Dream party have repeatedly raised the possibility of pardoning people arrested during protests. The ruling party has set a condition: those seeking a pardon must admit their guilt and express remorse.

In December 2025, Mikheil Kavelashvili said that people described as “prisoners of conscience” were in fact guilty and should admit their mistakes.

In May 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also said that “repentance, remorse and admission of guilt” were essential conditions for receiving a pardon.

In June, he urged prisoners to admit their guilt and submit pardon applications to the president.

In September, Kobakhidze again stressed that there were no “prisoners of conscience” in Georgia. Nevertheless, the authorities said they were willing to grant pardons on condition that prisoners admitted their guilt and expressed remorse.

Some prisoners rejected this demand. They insist they have committed no crimes and refuse to admit guilt in exchange for their freedom. Some continue to hold this position. They include journalist Mzia Amaglobeli, actor Andro Chichinadze, 19-year-old Mate Davitdze, doctor Irakli Kerashvili and many others.

Dozens of people arrested during the protests remain in Georgian prisons. Some are due to complete their sentences by the end of this year, while others are scheduled for release in early 2027. However, some have received prison terms of four years or more.

“We all need to be free now. None of us belongs in prison. I would advise them to take this opportunity [for a pardon] and get out. The situation in the country is such that we – young people – are needed here,” pardoned protester Nikoloz Javakhishvili said, addressing those who remain behind bars.

World.title: Iran's Isfahan Province exports rise 54% to $1.1B in eight months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Exports of goods through the customs offices of Isfahan Province, located in central Iran, rose by 54% in value to $1.1 billion over the first eight months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through November 21, 2026), compared to the same period last year (March 21 through November 21, 2025).

According to the Iranian Customs Administration, the Director General of the Isfahan Province Customs Administration, Rasul Kuhestani, announced the figures.

According to him, in the reporting period, the exports grew by 37% in weight to 1.5 million tons year on year.

Kuhestani added that 162,000 tons of goods, valued at $574 million, were imported into the country through the province's customs offices over an eight-month period. Compared to the same period last year, imports increased by 30% in terms of value and 67% in terms of weight.

The customs official noted that revenue from the province's customs offices reached 112 trillion rials (approximately $57.4 million) during this period, an increase of 425% compared to the corresponding period last year.

According to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Islamic Republic of Iran Customs Administration, 1.78 million tons of goods worth $1.16 billion were exported, and 138,000 tons of goods worth $661 million were imported through customs offices in Iran's Isfahan province during the past Iranian year (from March 21, 2025, through March 20, 2026). Revenue from the province's customs offices totaled 61.8 trillion rials (approximately $35.5 million) for that year.

For the record, Iran uses the Solar Hijri calendar, also known as the Persian calendar. The country is currently in the year 1405. The Iranian year begins on March 20 or 21. The first six months of the year each have 31 days; the following five months have 30 days, while the final month has 29 days in three out of every four years and 30 days in the fourth year. Consequently, the months of the Iranian calendar begin on the 21st, 22nd, or 23rd day of the corresponding Gregorian calendar month.

World.title: Kazakhstan boosts oil exports to France by 34% in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Kazakhstan exported 5.06 million tonnes of crude oil and crude oil products obtained from bituminous minerals to France in January-September 2026, up 33.98% year-on-year from 3.78 million tonnes in the corresponding period of 2025, according to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan.

In value terms, exports of these products to France rose by 62.29% year-on-year to $3.36 billion from $2.07 billion.

In September 2026, Kazakhstan exported 429,690 tonnes of these products to France, worth $265.89 million.

Overall, Kazakhstan exported 53.12 million tonnes of crude oil and crude oil products obtained from bituminous minerals in January-September 2026, including 6.07 million tonnes in September. This was down 5.43% from 56.16 million tonnes in the same period of 2025. In value terms, exports of these products increased by 13.46% to $33.73 billion, including $3.59 billion in September, compared with $29.73 billion a year earlier.

Bilateral trade turnover between Kazakhstan and France reached $4.83 billion in January-September 2026, up 39% from $3.48 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, accounting for 4.1% of Kazakhstan’s total foreign trade. Kazakhstan’s exports to France surged by 73.9% to $3.93 billion (5.7% of total exports), while imports from France decreased by 25.7% to $904.72 million (1.9% of total imports).

Kazakhstan’s overall foreign trade turnover reached $116.8 billion in January-September 2026, up 11.81% compared with $104.46 billion in the same period of 2025. Exports totaled $68.44 billion, increasing by 18.12% from $57.95 billion, while imports reached $48.36 billion, up 3.96% from $46.52 billion.

Crude oil and crude oil products obtained from bituminous minerals accounted for 85.5% of Kazakhstan’s exports to France and 49.3% of Kazakhstan’s total exports in January-September 2026.

World.title: Uzbekistan's accommodation and food services output rises 11.3%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Uzbekistan's accommodation and food services sector generated 179.7 trillion soums (about $15.05 billion) in January-September 2026, up 11.3% year over year, with Tashkent city and Samarkand region recording the highest output, according to the country's National Statistics Committee.

Tashkent city led the country with 32.6 trillion soums (around $2.73 billion) in accommodation and food services, followed by Samarkand region with 21.6 trillion soums (approx. $1.81 billion).

Namangan region ranked third, with 17.8 trillion soums (approx. $1.49 billion), narrowly ahead of Fergana region, which recorded 17.6 trillion soums (about $1.47 billion). Kashkadarya region followed with 15.4 trillion soums (around $1.29 billion), while Tashkent region accounted for 13.3 trillion soums (approx. $1.11 billion).

Andijan region generated 11.6 trillion soums (about $971.52 million), followed by Khorezm region with 10.2 trillion soums (around $854.27 million). The Republic of Karakalpakstan and Bukhara region recorded 9.1 trillion soums (approx. $762.14 million) and 8.9 trillion soums (about $745.39 million), respectively.

Surkhandarya region reported 7.5 trillion soums (around $628.14 million), while Navoi and Jizzakh regions recorded 5.5 trillion soums (approx. $460.63 million) and 5.3 trillion soums (about $443.89 million), respectively. Syrdarya region had the lowest output among the regions, at 3.4 trillion soums (around $284.76 million).

According to Trend's calculations based on the committee's figures, Tashkent city accounted for approximately 18.1% of the country's total accommodation and food services output. Samarkand region contributed around 12%.

Combined, the two leading areas generated 54.2 trillion soums (approx. $4.54 billion), equivalent to approximately 30.2% of the national total.

Based on the reported annual growth rate of 11.3%, accommodation and food services output in January-September 2025 is estimated at approximately 161.5 trillion soums (about $13.53 billion). This indicates an increase of around 18.2 trillion soums (approximately $1.52 billion) during the first nine months of 2026.

World.title: Kazakhstan-Kyrgyzstan trade rises to $1.99 billion in nine months
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Investment, Industry and Science of the Moscow region of Russia

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Bilateral trade turnover between Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan reached $1.99 billion in January-September 2026, up 17.9% year-on-year from $1.69 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, according to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan.

Kyrgyzstan accounted for 1.7% of Kazakhstan’s total foreign trade turnover during the reporting period, compared with 1.6% a year earlier.

Kazakh exports to Kyrgyzstan rose by 14.9% year-on-year to $1.46 billion from $1.27 billion, accounting for 2.1% of Kazakhstan’s total exports (compared with 2.19% in January-September 2025).

Meanwhile, imports from Kyrgyzstan increased by 25.9% year-on-year to $530.58 million from $421.32 million, representing 1.1% of Kazakhstan’s total imports (up from 0.91% a year earlier).

Overall, Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover reached $116.8 billion in January-September 2026, up 11.8% in nominal terms compared with $104.46 billion in the same period of 2025.

Exports totaled $68.44 billion, increasing by 18.1% in nominal terms from $57.95 billion, while imports reached $48.36 billion, up 3.9% from $46.52 billion.

China was Kazakhstan’s largest export destination, accounting for 17.9% of exports, followed by Italy (17.6%), Russia (8.5%), Türkiye (7.7%), the Netherlands (6.2%), and France (5.7%).

Russia was Kazakhstan’s largest import partner, accounting for 31% of imports, followed by China (30.3%), Germany (4.6%), the United States (3.7%), South Korea (2.4%), and Türkiye (2.1%).

World.title: Iran's Bank Keshavarzi boosts lending 58% to nearly $1.1B in eight months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Bank Keshavarzi increased its lending by 58% year on year to 2.15 quadrillion rials (approximately $1.1 billion) in the first eight months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through November 21, 2026), the bank said in a statement.

"During the eight-month period, Bank Keshavarzi provided loans worth 2.15 quadrillion rials (approximately $1.1 billion) to boost production and create jobs in the country's food security sector," the statement said.

In the first seven months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through October 22, 2026), the bank issued loans worth 1.77 quadrillion rials (about $907 million). Lending in the eighth month (October 23 through November 21, 2026) amounted to 380 trillion rials (nearly $195 million).

Among the bank's financing products, interest-free loans recorded the highest growth, rising by 87.4% compared with the first eight months of the previous Iranian year. Murabaha financing ranked second, with an increase of 65.4%, while civil partnership contracts grew by 54.4%.

Of the total loans issued during the reporting period, 62% went toward working-capital financing, while the remaining 38% was allocated to capital investments. Working-capital financing helps maintain the continuity of producers' operations, while loans for capital investments support investment and the expansion of production capacity.

Bank Keshavarzi offers a wide range of services aimed at increasing agricultural and food production and strengthening food security.

According to Trend's calculations based on the bank's statistical data, Bank Keshavarzi issued loans totaling 3.56 quadrillion rials (roughly $1.82 billion) in the previous Iranian year (March 21, 2025 through March 20, 2026). This was 48% higher than the amount issued in the preceding year (March 20, 2024 through March 20, 2025).

The bank's total revenue reached 1.16 quadrillion rials (approximately $594 million) in the previous Iranian year, up 35% from the preceding year. Its net profit for the year amounted to 53 trillion rials (approximately $27.1 million).

For the record, Iran uses the Solar Hijri calendar, also known as the Persian calendar. The country is currently in the year 1405. The Iranian year begins on March 20 or 21. The first six months of the year each have 31 days; the following five months have 30 days, while the final month has 29 days in three out of every four years and 30 days in the fourth year. Consequently, the months of the Iranian calendar begin on the 21st, 22nd, or 23rd day of the corresponding Gregorian calendar month.

World.title: Iran's Kerman Province point-to-point inflation reaches 97% in October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Inflation in Iran’s southeastern Kerman Province reached 97% year-on-year in the seventh month of the Iranian calendar (September 23 through October 22, 2026), compared with the same month of the previous year (September 23 through October 22, 2025).

According to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Statistical Center of Iran, point-to-point inflation refers to the percentage change in the price index compared with the corresponding period of the previous year.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) in Kerman Province stood at 796.5 in the seventh month.

During the seventh month, point-to-point inflation in Kerman Province stood at 127.8% in the food, beverages, and tobacco products category and 73.2% in the non-food goods and services category.

Monthly inflation in Kerman Province stood at 4.4% in the seventh month compared with the sixth month (from August 23 through September 22, 2026).

Monthly inflation refers to the percentage change in the price index compared with the previous month.

In the seventh month, monthly inflation in Kerman stood at 3.3% in the food, beverages, and tobacco products category and 5.5% in the non-food goods and services category.

At the end of the seventh month, annual inflation stood at 80.3% compared with the previous corresponding 12-month period.

Annual inflation refers to the average percentage change in the price index over the past year.

At the end of the seventh month, annual inflation in Kerman stood at 113.6% in the food, beverages, and tobacco products category and 55.8% in the non-food goods and services category.

In Iran, inflation statistics are published by both the Central Bank and the Statistical Center. The figures reported by these two statistical agencies may differ.

In the seventh month, point-to-point inflation across Iran reached 88.7% compared to the same month of the previous year.

For the record, Iran uses the Solar Hijri calendar, also known as the Persian calendar. The country is currently in the year 1405. The Iranian year begins on March 20 or 21. The first six months of the year each have 31 days, the following five months have 30 days, while the final month has 29 days in three out of every four years and 30 days in the fourth year. Consequently, the months of the Iranian calendar begin on the 21st, 22nd or 23rd day of the corresponding Gregorian calendar month.

World.title: Azerbaijan is strategic partner for Georgia – Maka Botchorishvili
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Azerbaijan is a strategic partner for Georgia, and the two countries have been jointly implementing important projects in the region for many years, Georgia's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Maka Botchorishvili said.

According to her, amid global challenges and the current geopolitical context, greater importance is being attached to relations between Georgia and Azerbaijan, the dynamics of bilateral engagement, and the potential for cooperation.

Botchorishvili noted that regular exchanges of views and continuous work on various issues are essential to ensure that both countries are better represented in the current geopolitical environment.

"Our strategic partnership with Azerbaijan is very rich in substance. It also encompasses intensive political dialogue. A number of high-level state visits have taken place this year. The President of Azerbaijan visited Georgia, while the Prime Minister of Georgia paid an official visit to Azerbaijan. In addition, the Prime Minister of Azerbaijan has visited Georgia, and reciprocal visits by ministers responsible for various sectors in the two countries are continuing," Botchorishvili said.

The Foreign Minister emphasized that political dialogue between Georgia and Azerbaijan covers specific projects, the current situation in the region, and the potential for cooperation between the two countries.

According to her, cooperation in the development of the transport corridor, the transit of energy resources, and other areas is of particular importance.

"All of this creates prospects for the development of the Middle Corridor, which is extremely important," Botchorishvili added.
