World.title: Anti-Netanyahu bloc vows to swear in Israel's new government by end of week
World.content:
Israeli Opposition Leader Gadi Eisenkot says efforts to form a new government are moving at "full speed", but more than two weeks since the nation's election, it is not clear how it will unfold.

On Wednesday Israeli media reported Mr Eisenkot was hoping to form a new government by next Wednesday — before the December 6 deadline.

Late on Tuesday the Yashar leader agreed to sign a coalition pact with Avigdor Liberman's right-wing Yisrael Beytenu, the first alliance formally agreed since the election.

The move sparked backlash from The Democrats, who said they were halting talks with Yashar after the deal.

The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, have been frustrated by Mr Eisenkot's overtures to Likud and the ultra-Orthodox.

How did we get here?

After no bloc managed to secure a 61-seat majority in the October 27 election, Israel's parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government.

Mr Eisenkot was tasked by President Isaac Herzog with forming a government after 67 of the 120 members of the Knesset backed him as prime minister, with Benjamin Netanyahu in position as caretaker prime minister.

Mr Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, though Mr Herzog could extend it by two weeks.

In recent days he has held a series of smaller meetings across party lines, including with Likud, and advanced talks with ultra-Orthodox party United Torah Judaism.

The agreement with Yisrael Beytenu is the first clear result of the efforts to formulate a coalition that could form government.

Mr Liberman said a government with a Jewish majority that included ultra-Orthodox parties "can be formed by the end of next week".

The Arab parties dilemma

The sticking point is the Arab parties.

Mr Liberman has ruled out a government with the Arab-led parties.

Where to next in the Israeli election? The inconclusive result of the Israeli election with neither Netanyahu nor the opposition gaining majority, means weeks of messy and complicated negotiations.

Two members of the opposition bloc have said they will not sit with the Joint List or United Arab List, leaving Mr Eisenkot with a few main options.

These include bringing in the ultra-Orthodox parties, a unity government, or a minority government.

Mr Golan has pushed Mr Eisenkot to reach a deal with the Arab parties, but other sides of the anti-Netanyahu camp like Mr Liberman are not in favour.

Mr Netanyahu also urged against forming government with the Arab parties, posting on social media: "You must not form a government with supporters of terrorism!"

Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused him of fuelling hostility toward Israel's Arab population.

Mairav Zonszein from non-government organisation International Crisis Group said Mr Eisenkot was testing how big and wide a government he could form.

"I think these talks are in part genuine, but in part a performance in order to have the legitimacy to go to go further because he's going to have to rely on the 19 seats of the Palestinian Arab parties in order to have a government," she said.

Mr Eisenkot said the talks reflected "a genuine commitment to forming the broadest government possible".

Mr Netanyahu and his allies have been ramping up a racially charged campaign of de-legitimisation against the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who represent 21 per cent of the population.

A court boost for Netanyahu

Meanwhile, a corruption trial against Mr Netanyahu continues in a court in Jerusalem.

Netanyahu and the 'deep state' Benjamin Netanyahu's opponents say he is an "enemy of the state". Supporters say he is all Israel has.

On Wednesday, judges in the trial urged Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara to consider dropping Case 4000, the only bribery charge against Mr Netanyahu.

Summoned to the Jerusalem District Court in a rare move, the judges questioned whether the evidence supported a second case: Case 2000.

The judges said they were open to options for resolving a third case, Case 1000, which involves Australian billionaire James Packer, who has been called to testify at the trial.

James Packer reportedly gave lavish gifts to Benjamin Netanyahu and his family. (AAP: Dean Lewins/Reuters: Abir Sultan)

According to Israeli media, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman said there was little chance of conviction in Case 4000.

Ms Baharav-Miara said she would review the proposals with the prosecution team.

Mr Netanyahu demanded an end to his corruption trial in a televised statement from the Knesset.

"Today the trial fell apart," he declared.

Under current law, Mr Netanyahu cannot be appointed a minister while indicted on serious offences.

If the charges are dropped, that could change.

Former Israeli diplomat Alon Pinkas told the ABC the court developments would not affect the coalition-building process.

He said the attorney general had "no choice but to accept the judge's recommendation", given that the judges saw a very low probability of conviction.

Mr Pinkas said if Mr Eisenkot succeeded, "all this will be forgotten".

If he does not, and Israel heads to a new election in March or April, the developments could somewhat factor in.

With the clock running down on Mr Eisenkot's mandate, coalition talks are now entering a decisive phase as the opposition leader looks to keep Mr Netanyahu from returning to office.

The court's decision has landed in Mr Netanyahu's favour.

World.title: Witness recounts dramatic 'crash tackle' arrest of balaclava-clad men
World.content:
Police have thwarted an attempted kidnapping with the dramatic arrest of four balaclava-clad men in Sydney's west.

About 5pm on Wednesday, Auburn police responded to reports that three men, allegedly armed with firearms, had attempted to enter an occupied SUV on Gormley Avenue in Lidcombe.

Multiple police officers swarmed the scene and carried out the arrests. (ABC News)

Police said the male driver of the SUV reversed through a nearby fence and drove off, while the three men and a fourth man drove away in an allegedly stolen Mercedes sedan.

Traffic and Highway Patrol officers located the sedan and attempted to stop it, before it collided with two other vehicles on Olympic Drive in Lidcombe.

A person was injured when their vehicle was struck by the sedan, and they were taken to hospital for non-life-threatening injuries.

The four men were caught by police. (ABC News)

The four occupants of the sedan ran from the vehicle, but were arrested nearby with the assistance of officers from the Public Order and Riot Squad, Burwood Police Area Command and Raptor Squad.

Police seized two firearms, ammunition, zip ties, bleach, balaclavas and rolls of duct tape from the sedan.

Following further inquiries, police located a staged vehicle in Fairfield, which contained bleach and gloves.

The aftermath of when the allegedly stolen Mercedes sedan crashed into two other vehicles. (ABC News)

The four alleged assailants — aged 22, 23, 25 and 38 — were charged with a series of offences including take/detain person in company with intent to obtain advantage, participate in a criminal group and contribute to criminal activity, and possess unregistered firearm in a public place.

'They crash tackled him'

Tanya Hamilton witnessed the arrests, and her CCTV captured the incident unfold.

Tanya Hamilton witnessed the arrests in Lidcombe on Wednesday. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

She first heard the sirens and then walked outside her residence to see what was happening.

"As I've come out, there was this almighty crash, and there were three cars just over the back here all collided," she said.

"I raced immediately to the gate to see if I could help and next minute I see there's two guys all dressed in black with black balaclavas on running down here and there's two female police officers chasing after them."

Ms Hamilton's CCTV captured the arrests. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Ms Hamilton said she yelled out to the first alleged assailant, before noticing other men running away from the scene.

"One of them circled around this block here and tried to hide behind a tree over there, and I yelled out to the police, 'He's hiding'. It took two guys [officers] and they crash tackled him and got him."

She said she saw the other three alleged assailants "go up a dead-end street" where they were caught by police.

" It was quite frightening at the time," Ms Hamilton said. "I've had enough of it around this area. "

Acting Superintendent Darren Sly says the men involved in the incident are known to police. (ABC News)

Acting Superintendent Darren Sly, commander of the Auburn Police Area Command, said it was possible the incident was linked to "a crime for hire".

"There's every possibility that this is a crime for hire, that these men have been hired to do this," he said.

"The victim and four men are all known to police and linked to organised crime activity," Acting Superintendent Sly said, noting it was a "targeted attack" and that the five individuals were not cooperating with police.

" I'd also like to say for those who wish to undertake this type of criminal activity, who believe they are the hunters, will quickly become the hunted. "

Ten alleged crime network arrests

It comes as 10 people suspected of being part of a "broad organised criminal enterprise", were arrested for their alleged roles in an "extensive dial-a-dealer drug supply network" across Sydney.

Police allege the network is responsible for carrying out shootings and facilitating drug supply across Sydney's south-west, and that the group supplied firearms and stolen vehicles, organised violent home invasions and carried out robberies.

Detective Superintendent Jason Box, the head of Taskforce Falcon, said detectives executed 10 search warrants on Thursday across Punchbowl, Greenacre, Auburn, Merrylands, Gladesville and Hillsdale.

Ten people were arrested on Thursday as part of Taskforce Falcon. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Those arrested are suspected as being part of a "broad organised criminal enterprise". (Supplied: NSW Police)

Seven men and two women were arrested and taken to various police stations, where inquiries continue.

A 17-year-old boy was also arrested at Sydney International Airport in Mascot.

He was charged with a series of offences including aggravated break and enter, robbery in company and participate in a criminal group and contribute to criminal activity.

Jason Box issued a warning to 'crime for hire' criminals. (ABC News)

"All these 10 offenders are being charged with offences including supply prohibited drug commercial quantity, aggravated break and enter, aggravated robbery and criminal group offences," Superintendent Box said.

"We allege they [the 10 in total] conducted more than 1,600 drug deals between December 25 [2025], and July 2026 and they generated approximately $650,000 in revenue from those drug sales."

When asked who police believed the group was loyal to, Detective Superintendent Box said, "Whoever pays them."

World.title: Breaking: Insurance giant AIG sued by corporate regulator over complaints handling
World.content:
Major insurer AIG is being sued by the corporate regulator for its handling of hundreds of customer complaints regarding general insurance claims.

ASIC alleged AIG Australia, which offers travel insurance and consumer device insurance, failed to provide complaint responses or delay notifications within the required 30-day timeframe in 534 cases.

Some customers waited for months for complaint decisions, including those who were unwell, injured or recently bereaved, between October 2021 and December 2025.

ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said policyholders should not have to fight their insurer for basic communication.

"Making a complaint to your insurer should be a pathway to resolving a problem, not the beginning of another one," he said.

Mr Kirkland alleged some customers were also given inaccurate explanations for the delays.

"Complaint handling is a fundamental obligation for insurers, who must take complaints seriously," he said.

Alan Kirkland says insurers need to take complaints seriously. (ABC News: Adam Wyatt)

"Insurers must have effective systems for recording complaints and should not have to search personal drives and emails to know whether a complaint was responded to."

ASIC alleged the delays caused uncertainty, frustration and emotional distress, and that some customers faced delays receiving insurance payments, refunds or compensation.

AIG Australia is a publicly listed subsidiary of the global American International Group, headquartered in New York.

The parent company saw a net income of $US3.1 billion in the 2025 financial year.

AIG has been approached for comment.

AIG is a prominent sponsor of women's golf. (Getty Images: Andrew Redington)

Automated 'complexity' excuse

The corporate regulator also alleged AIG used a standard template for communications about delays that pre-populated "complexity" as the reason for the delay, and failed to inform customers of their rights to escalate complaints to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).

ASIC alleged the insurer failed to have an effective system for recording information about complaints and keeping track of their progress.

This system did not provide an alert when a complaint response was due, or reliably record whether complaints had been answered.

The news comes weeks after the federal court fined insurance giant Hollard $2 million for taking so long to process a home insurance claim that a house in regional Victoria became uninhabitable.

ASIC sued Hollard in April last year, alleging the insurer "breached its duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of a claim made by a couple in October 2021, two days after a storm damaged their roof.

The outcome was the first civil penalty ordered against an insurer for breaching its duty of utmost good faith.

Hollard admitted contravening the Insurance Contracts Act.

Loading...

ASIC put insurers on notice

In December 2024, ASIC put general insurers on notice after a review of 11 insurers found they failed to identify one in six complaints, alongside shortcomings in customer communications, complaints-handling systems and the identification of systemic issues.

"ASIC has put insurers on notice about complaints-handling failures. Those that continue to fall short of their legal obligations should expect enforcement action," Mr Kirkland said.

ASIC said it was seeking declarations, pecuniary penalties, adverse publicity orders and orders requiring AIG to engage an independent expert to review its complaints-handling arrangements and implement recommendations.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this investigation, you can securely contact reporter Adelaide Miller at miller.adelaide@proton.me

The enforcement action also comes as the Insurance Council of Australia's redrafted code of practice is under review by ASIC.

The corporate regulator is seeking public feedback on the redrafted code, before deciding whether to approve to proposed changes.

World.title: Child protection inquiry announced after sustained pressure on government
World.content:
The delivery of child protection services in WA will be investigated by a parliamentary committee after months of intense focus on the care of children in the Pilbara.

Port Hedland has been subject to intense media, political and community focus in recent months after evidence of systemic child protection failings in the mining town emerged.

Last week, an independent review found staffing levels at the child protection department have still not been fully addressed, four years after the murder of three children by their mother Margaret Hawke in Port Hedland in 2022.

Port Hedland, the Pilbara's second-largest town, has been under scrutiny for child protection shortcomings.

The review found while staffing recommendations made in an internal review of the case had been "substantially implemented," shortages had not been fixed.

It found an inability to attract staff to the region was impacting the department's ability to deliver its service.

Child Protection staffing levels still not addressed Staffing levels at WA's beleaguered Child Protection department have still not been fully addressed, four years after the murder of three children by their mother in the state's north.

Those problems will now be investigated by the Standing Committee on Public Administration, as well as the effectiveness of current child protection responses, workforce capability, caseload pressures, and outcomes for children and young people in care.

It will also look at how well agencies coordinate across the child protection, education, health, police and justice systems, as well as with non-government service providers and Aboriginal community-controlled organisations.

The committee will consider "any legislative, policy or structural reforms required to improve outcomes for the protection of children and young people in Western Australia" and any other matters the committee considers relevant.

Problems ongoing

Last week, Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski said the child protection workforce had increased by 40 per cent statewide but could not provide figures specifically for the Pilbara.

Ms Stojovski admitted while measures had been taken to address shortages, the problem was ongoing.

The government also last week announced $22.6 million in funding to address the staffing shortages.

The night before murdering her children, Ms Hawke had been turned away from a women's refuge which was full.

Dorothy Papertalk believes a coronial inquest would provide answers about what happened to her grandchildren. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

The children's grandmother Dorothy Papertalk had been campaigning for a coronial inquest into their deaths which was approved last month.

Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch has been under sustained pressure to do more to address the crisis, but at one time suggested child protection was not directly part of his portfolio.

He has since walked back those comments.

Don Punch has been under intense scrutiny over his comments about child protection not being directly part of his portfolio. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

"My job is to go out and listen to Aboriginal people, Aboriginal elders, talk with communities and understand the issues that they're facing," he said last month.

Some local elders have called for Mr Punch to be sacked, but Premier Roger Cook has stood by him.

World.title: Meet the 'meavers' tagging along on their graduating kids' celebrations
World.content:
Parents of teens are flooding traditional Leavers Week hot spots in Western Australia as they too celebrate the end of their children's school years.

Mothers affectionately dubbed "meavers", a portmanteau of mums and leavers, are taking their own chance to holiday after dropping their children at official schoolies celebrations around Dunsborough, south of Perth.

Official celebrations for Leavers, known as Schoolies in the rest of the country, have attracted more than 8,000 teenagers to Dunsborough this week, and are due to finish tonight.

Perth woman Louise Deshon and five friends stayed at a holiday house this week, while their daughters were in designated leavers' accommodation nearby.

Louise Deshon and friends say leavers week has been an opportunity to take a break themselves. (ABC News: Anthony Pancia)

Enjoying lunch at a Margaret River winery on Tuesday, Ms Deshon stressed they were not in the South West to supervise their children, but to take a break themselves after supporting their children through Year 12.

"What were my options?" she said.

"Stay at home and go to work, or come down and have a bit of a shop and go to lunch?

"It's more a celebration than keeping tabs on them."

The group said it was also a chance to mark the strong friendships they had formed with other parents during their children's time at school.

The so-called meavers said parents should also celebrate the end of schooling. (ABC News: Anthony Pancia)

Parents urged to behave

While most parents have been simply enjoying a quiet glass of wine during leavers, support agencies have urged they keep themselves in check.

Red Frogs' spokesperson Michael Croot said he had noticed an increase in parents travelling with leavers in recent years.

"That support network is really important, as long as the parents are behaving themselves as well," he said.

South West Police Superintendent Paul Van Noort said his officers had also picked up on the phenomenon.

"Look, some of them give it a good crack," he joked.

But he said parents had every right to enjoy themselves.

Leavers have been celebrating throughout the South West this week. (ABC News: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

"They're equally celebrating their leavers' success, and there is nothing wrong with that; all that we ask is that everyone just parties responsibly," he said.

"We just want everyone to stay safe."

Changes to P-plate rules linked

The growing number of parents in attendance, also welcomed by local tourism operators housing the young partygoers, coincides with a change to WA's probationary driving laws.

Since 2024, WA P-platers are only allowed to have one passenger in their vehicle for the first six months of their licence.

There are 8,000 registered leavers in the South West this week. (ABC News: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

Four Seasons Caravan Park manager Angie Kartsioukas believes this has led to more parents driving school leavers down and dropping them off.

With no adults permitted at the park during the celebration, Ms Kartsioukas said the bulk of them stayed nearby.

"A lot more parents did come down this year we found, and then they would go on to stay in Dunsborough," she said.

"The mums I did speak to in the car, they were looking forward to their week away and staying closer to the kids."

World.title: Teacher who had sex with student after principal's warning avoids jail
World.content:
A Hunter Valley teacher who had sex with a 17-year-old schoolboy has been spared jail after, in part, a judge found she had already been punished by the loss of her career and public humiliation.

In April, Zoe Jade Hodges, 31, pleaded guilty to two counts of having sexual intercourse with a person under her special care in 2023.

Today, Judge Miiko Kumar sentenced her to a three-year community correction order (CCO).

Judge Kumar said Hodges had been warned by the principal at the school where she taught, but offended anyway.

Zoe Hodges had sex with the boy in 2023. (Supplied: Facebook)

"I take into account the offence involved a breach of trust involving a child," Judge Kumar said.

" I find she knew that relationship was not only inappropriate, but also illegal. "

Judge Kumar said the former teacher organised for the two to meet outside of school hours.

"The offending was instigated by the offender inviting the victim to rock up to her house during school holidays," she said.

Special care relationship

Last week in her sentencing submission, defence barrister April Francis said the offending was in the context of a "special care" relationship.

"It’s not a sexual offence against a child; it is offence of a special care relationship," Ms Francis said.

Crown prosecutor Emily Winborne said there was a "power imbalance" and jail was the only sentence appropriate.

Zoe Hodges will serve a community correction order. (Supplied: Facebook)

"It is the Crown's submission that the relationship was inherently one that arose from a power imbalance," Ms Winborne said.

"The power imbalance existed by virtue of the offender's position as a teacher."

Teacher warned

Judge Kumar said Hodges knew pursuing a student was wrong.

"In December 2022, she was formally counselled by the principal about allegations she had had inappropriate contact with male students," Judge Kumar said.

"The principal emailed copies of policies and she responded by an email and thanked the principal for bringing them to her attention."

Zoe Hodges pleaded guilty in April. (Supplied: Facebook)

The judge said she accepted Hodges had borderline personality disorder and said that played a role in her offending.

"I find there is a nexus between her mental health and her offending and I therefore find this reduces her moral culpability," she said.

'Humiliation and isolation'

Judge Kumar said while there was a breach of trust, "agreed police facts do not disclose efforts of pressure or persuasion" in relation to the schoolboy.



The judge said Hodges had suffered what was known as extra-curial punishment.

"Her financial future has suffered, she has suffered humiliation and isolation as a result of the offending," she said.

"Her profession is lost to her."

Judge Kumar noted her prior good character and said she had good prospects for rehabilitation.

"I find the offender is remorseful and contrite, she has made efforts at rehabilitation and taken material steps to retrain through TAFE," she said.

As part of her CCO, Hodges must be of good behaviour and do 250 hours of community service work.

The 31-year-old has also been placed on the child protection register for 15 years.

World.title: Court hears victim of alleged schoolies bashing has no sign of brain activity
World.content:
The victim of an alleged group bashing during schoolies week celebrations on the Gold Coast is showing no sign of brain activity, a court has heard.

Zion Pisia, 18, faced Southport Magistrates Court today charged with acts intended to cause grievous bodily harm over his alleged involvement in the early-morning attack at Surfers Paradise on Tuesday.

He is one of 11 teenagers, including seven juveniles, charged over the incident, which left a 15-year-old with a broken jaw and fractured skull.

The court today heard the victim remained on life support at Gold Coast University Hospital, with recent scans showing no sign of brain activity.

Police prosecutor Matt Gilles told the court Mr Pisia was one of the principal offenders and his involvement was clearly captured on CCTV.

Loading...

"He does initiate the assault — he is the first to throw a punch at the victim," Mr Gilles told the court.

Mr Gilles said the victim escaped Mr Pisia's first attack, and escaped a second assault involving the larger group, before being knocked to the ground by several of the teens chasing him.

"[What followed] was a far more horrific assault," Mr Gilles told the court.

"He [Mr Pisia] is observed to stomp and kick the victim's head while he lay on the ground.

The incident happened metres from the official Gold Coast schoolies celebration area. (ABC News: Shari Hams)

Mr Gilles said the victim's family remained with him in the intensive care unit.

" The most recent update I've got is that an EEG was conducted and didn't provide any indication of brain activity. "

Family releases statement

The 15-year-old boy's parents today released a statement describing the distress the incident had caused them, their family and their friends.

"This has been made more difficult by videos and commentary relating to the incident circulating on social media," the parents wrote.

"Our son remains in a critical condition … we are deeply grateful to the doctors, nurses and all staff providing him with ongoing care."

"We have been overwhelmed by the kindness and generosity of the local community. Please know all your messages of support, concern and encouragement have meant a great deal to our family during this difficult time."

The 15-year-old remains in intensive care at Gold Coast University Hospital. (ABC Gold Coast: Heidi Sheehan)

They said while they appreciated the public interest and media attention that surrounded the incident, their focus was on supporting their son's recovery.

"We request privacy as we navigate the challenging days ahead."

'He hopes he pulls through'

Mr Pisia's lawyer, Ashkan Tai, initially intended to apply for bail but withdrew the application when the victim's condition was detailed.

Speaking outside court, Mr Tai said his client was "extremely worried" about the 15-year-old.

"He really hopes he pulls through," Mr Tai said.

"He knows he's dealing with something very serious and only time will tell how things work out."

Three other adults, also charged with one count each of acts intended to cause grievous bodily harm, were yesterday remanded in custody.

All four men will next face Southport Magistrates Court on December 17.

The seven 17-year-olds charged with the same offence are being dealt with by the Children's Court.

One of those 17-year-olds, also alleged to be a principal offender, did not apply for bail yesterday.

World.title: Mother accused of attempted murder of two boys granted bail
World.content:
A woman charged with attempted domestic violence murder of two boys with gas was granted bail after the court heard she was drunk and her boyfriend had just broken up with her.

Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide

The 47-year-old nurse, who cannot be named to protect the children's identities, appeared in the Brisbane Magistrates Court today, where she applied for bail.

She is facing two counts of attempted murder as a domestic violence offence against a child.

Police had previously alleged the woman exposed two boys, aged 12 and 15, to a noxious substance at a Mitchelton home in Brisbane's north-west on September 24.

The court heard that, leading up to the alleged incident, the woman's boyfriend had ended the relationship and had left their home.

It is alleged that hours later she turned on the kitchen's gas burners and sent him a photo with a message.

"I did ask for help. I am begging for help. Bye," the text, read to the court, said.

The court heard the boyfriend contacted her eldest son, who went downstairs to the kitchen, and his mother told him to pack a bag and leave.

The youngest son was still asleep upstairs.

The court heard the boyfriend returned to the home that day to find the burners turned off and the woman intoxicated.

He stayed the evening and left the following morning.

It is alleged the woman turned the burners on again.

She was then taken to hospital and spent about 10 days in the mental health unit.

Police arrested the nurse after being discharged from the hospital.

Authorities had previously said the boys were not injured and were "safe and well".

Defence tells court 'likely a cry for attention'

The woman's defence lawyer argued the prosecution's case was "very weak", and it would take about two years before the attempted murder charge went to trial.

He said the woman had "a bit of a breakdown" after receiving bad news from her boyfriend.

"In my submission that's just as likely to be a cry for attention or for help."

"When one looks at what happened on those two events, it's difficult to say that the only reasonable inference is that she was trying to kill herself.

"And the risk is ameliorated. She's not allowed to drink. She was drunk at the time," the defence lawyer said.

The court heard the woman was being treated for depression before the alleged incident.

Her lawyer said there was "no chance" she would be able to access or contact her children, with the two boys living with their father in an undisclosed location in north Queensland.

He also said the woman had support in the community, including her brother who was in the courtroom today.

The prosecutor told the court he accepted attempted murder was a "particularly difficult charge to prove" but said there were "a number of offences which will effectively form backups".

"Either she has intended to kill the children and undertaken acts preparatory to that, or she has done something almost as sinister, namely endangered the lives of her children and herself as part of some obscene charade," he said.

The 47-year-old woman appeared in the Brisbane Magistrates Court on Thursday. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The prosecutor told the court the woman had allegedly made two similar threats or indications to friends that she was going to die by suicide and take the children with her.

"That doesn't necessarily prove that she does have an intention at any point to actually do it, but it does indicate … [a] weaponisation of her capacity to endanger the lives of the children to provoke responses," he said.

The prosecutor said the children living in North Queensland "largely ameliorate the direct risk to the children".

"However, what we have here is an applicant who is willing to go to extreme and potentially lethal lengths," he said.

The judge accepted that the alleged behaviour was dangerous and reckless but was satisfied to grant her bail because of the "inherent weaknesses" in the prosecution case on these charges.

In delivering her verdict, the Judge also took into account the time already spent in custody and expected delays before the matter was finalised.

The woman has spent 49 days in custody and will be released on bail, upon her passport being surrendered, with several conditions such as not drinking alcohol.

A protection order is also in place preventing contact with the children.

The matter will next be heard at a committal mention in January.

World.title: Maddy riding on to make Izzy proud after heart-breaking farewell
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Maddy riding on to make Izzy proud after heart-breaking farewell Craig Kerry November 26, 2026 — 3:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Maddy Owen had already been through the hardest part before she gave a beautiful and heart-wrenching eulogy for her best friend and fellow jockey Izzy Neale. Owen, like many friends and family, had rushed to be at Neale’s bedside at Dubbo Hospital after her fatal fall at Warren on November 8. Neale’s family announced the 22-year-old’s passing two days later, and the racing community has struggled since to come to terms with the devastating loss of the promising apprentice. Maddy Owen after a win at Rosehill on Swift Charm in January 2025. Getty Images Neale was farewelled at Merriwa Showground on Wednesday and Owen was among those to speak. The 25-year-old shared memories of their friendship as well as glimpses of Izzy’s fun-loving personality, loyalty, work ethic and passion for horses.



And, through tears, there was the hurt of an exciting future taken away, and a final thank you to her “pretty girl, best friend and partner in crime” for their time together. Owen, who has three rides at Rosehill on Saturday, is determined to make Neale proud, push through the pain and carry on their shared dreams in racing. “It’s been tough being at the races or even trackwork, around places where she would usually be, but it’s our life and what we do,” Owen said on Thursday. “I guess the funeral probably brought a little bit of closure, and it was nice seeing her family and everyone in racing come together there. There were lots of people who attended, so I thought it was quite nice. “We’d already been through the hardest part. When it happened, we all drove out to Dubbo from different places.



Izzy Neale, Mikayla Weir and Maddy Owen together at Randwick on Everest day this year. Instagram “Chelsea [Hillier] was actually with her at the track. It was a hard few days following that … so I think the funeral was just a really nice send-off and a little bit of closure.” Owen, who became friends with Neale while working at Scone five years ago, said the tragedy had not changed her riding ambitions and those in racing who knew Izzy had found solace together at the track. “When I think about what happened, I think of it more as a freak accident,” she said. “I don’t blame it on racing, or what we do, and it’s what we both loved to do. It was our passion. It was really our whole lives.



“That’s what she loved to do, that’s how most of us were friends. That was our one common interest, so we’re just getting back out there and being together. That actually helps. “She was very positive, happy and talented. I said in my speech that the hardest part will be, I always looked forward to when we were racing at the same location and we could hang out. “It would be like Muswellbrook tomorrow. Because we raced in different areas, it wasn’t that often that we got to hang out. Then there were the times calling each other to and from the races, all those little things.” Tamworth-based Owen has two rides on Friday at Muswellbrook for the Scone stable of Brett and Georgie Cavanough, where she worked initially as an apprentice, then three for them at Rosehill. “I’ve been in Scone a little bit the last few weeks, just organising and doing some things, so I’ve been doing a bit of riding for Brett and he’s been really good,” she said.



Related Article Horse racing ‘It doesn’t feel right’: Jockey riding through grief for fallen friend “He’s given me some good rides and opportunities, and it’s good to have something to focus on, which I am. I’m really looking forward to all the rides, but especially the stakes race.” Owen rides Pride To Follow ($61) in the listed Starlight Stakes (1100m), where the five-year-old mare rises in class from wins at Port Macquarie then Randwick. “She’s in really good form,” said Owen, who rode her at Port Macquarie. “When I won on her, it was a quality, and then she raced at Randwick in a benchmark 84, so she’s stepping up to the mark each time.



“She’ll have to step up again on Saturday, but she’s racing in good form, she puts herself into the race and she gets in with a light weight, so I’m sure on her best run, she will be thereabouts.” Owen also rides Indifference ($34) in the Country Classic (2000m) and Arapawa ($17) in the benchmark 78 handicap over 1800m. “Indifference is a nice horse, I rode him this morning and he’s well, so I’m sure he’ll put in a good performance,” she said. “And Arapawa is first time over that trip, but hopefully the track stays soft and he’ll enjoy that. He’s won at Rosehill before and I think he’ll be in with a chance.”

World.title: ‘Turncoat town’: Liberal senator defects to One Nation
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation ‘Turncoat town’: Liberal senator defects to One Nation Brittany Busch and Michelle Griffin Updated November 26, 2026 — 3:14pm ,first published November 26, 2026 — 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Liberals have scorned One Nation defector Leah Blyth for abandoning the party, in a shock exit that derailed the Coalition’s momentum on the final sitting week of the year. The senator, who lost the South Australian party presidency to hard-right powerbroker Alex Antic in September, said the Liberals had lost their way and One Nation was the only party that could be trusted to make hard decisions. One Nation defector Senator Leah Blyth with Pauline Hanson at Parliament House on Thursday. Dominic Lorrimer The former opposition spokeswoman for defence infrastructure said she did not feel safe in her old party, and the factional infighting in her state branch was such that private security was employed for her protection. Blyth had been appointed to the Senate in February 2025 to fill a casual vacancy left by retiring leading moderate Simon Birmingham, and was not expected to secure a winnable spot on the Liberal ballot for next year’s election.



Blyth’s defection brings the number of One Nation senators to five, with two MPs in the lower house. While Hanson had regularly fanned speculation throughout the year that other members of parliament had approached her to join the party, Blyth is the first federal politician to make the switch since Joyce. One Nation’s popularity has surged in all the polls this year and was the first preference of one in four voters in the latest Resolve Political Monitor. Loading Her departure was a blow to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who had overseen 10 months of relative stability in the Coalition and told his party room on Tuesday that they could win the next election as Labor struggles with grim economic results and the fallout from tax hikes introduced at the last federal budget. Blyth’s colleagues and staff were blindsided by her move even after Pauline Hanson teased a defection on Wednesday night with a video of her preparing a steak in a sandwich press, imitating her wooing of Barnaby Joyce a year previously.



Federal party president Tony Abbott suggested Blyth was leaving because she was on the wrong side of a factional battle. “This has got nothing whatsoever to do with principle, nothing whatsoever to do with the national interest. I think the public will see through what this is,” he said in a video posted to Instagram. Senator Leah Blyth has joined the growing ranks of One Nation. Dominic Lorrimer Fellow South Australian senator Anne Ruston wrote to the party’s state membership on Thursday afternoon saying Blyth had put her own interests first and thrown away the trust of those who had voted for a Liberal. “Leah was never elected to the Senate seat she holds. That seat was won by Simon Birmingham on the Liberal ticket, with the votes of South Australians and the hard work of members like you,” Ruston said.



“She told [delegates]: ‘My word can be trusted. My promises will be kept.’ Today we found out that those promises were worth nothing.” Related Article Opinion

One Nation One Nation shock defection an exercise in hypocrisy and a blow to Taylor Paul Sakkal Chief political correspondent Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume denied internal divisions were to blame, adding Blyth “wasn’t a big contributor to the party room”. Asked whether the move was a surprise, backbencher Scott Buchholz said: “Of course it was. I’ve just got to go and find out who she is now.” Taylor, who had largely left the South Australian state division to its factional fight, did not appear before media on Thursday.



Nationals leader Matt Canavan said One Nation was turning into “turncoat town” and Blyth’s defection smacked of self-interest. “To turn around now … and say ‘my principles and policies are more aligned with One Nation’ – I mean, give me a break,” he told Radio National earlier. Pauline Hanson said Blyth was a true conservative. Dominic Lorrimer Canavan insisted he was not concerned about any further defections, but when asked whether he had talked anyone out of leaving the Coalition, conceded he had worked hard to keep people together during a tough period. Blyth went on the attack during a press conference with Hanson on Thursday morning, saying it was “pretty grubby” for Coalition MPs to background media about what her staff knew, but admitted she had not spoken to anyone in the party about her decision. Tony Abbott’s accusations she acted from self-interest were a “complete and utter falsehood”, she said.



The senator said the Liberal Party had abandoned her by forsaking its principles and making too many compromises on policy. Related Article Political leadership ‘He used me’: Nationals veteran accuses Barnaby Joyce of hypocrisy and misleading party faithful Unable to identify any points of difference she had with the Coalition on current issues such as the digital duty of care, Blyth criticised the Liberals for not being willing to withdraw from the Paris climate agreement, even as the party ditched net zero. She then said there had not been enough debate before the Coalition backed a defence bill that gave the minister sweeping powers to designate military zones. One Nation also voted to pass that law. In a later interview on News24, Blyth said she did not know what the minor party’s position had been. The senator swerved questions about the times she had described One Nation as a corrosive force – a central part of her fight with Antic, seen by some in the Coalition as too willing to cosy to the minor party.



She paid tribute to Antic at her One Nation press conference. “I will shout out to Senator Alex Antic; he was a voice of reason in the party room on [net zero],” she said. She added that she had taken a pay cut to move to One Nation and insisted the party had not promised her anything. Hanson’s chief of staff Chris Taylor confirmed Blyth would not be guaranteed preselection. “She’s going to have to prove herself. She has to prove herself to the people of South Australia and to the party. She’ll have plenty of time to do that,” he told News24.



Hanson said Blyth had approached her, and that the decision would resonate with former Liberal supporters who felt the party had abandoned them. The minor party leader, who has previously vowed to reject “opportunistic” Coalition defectors, welcomed Blyth as a true conservative. Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Labor frontbencher Murray Watt mocked Taylor over the defection, saying if he could not control his party, he could not govern the country. World.title: Sunshine grocer’s death over stolen $17 pants leaves harrowing impact
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Sunshine grocer’s death over stolen $17 pants leaves harrowing impact Erin Pearson November 26, 2026 — 3:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A 14-year-old girl pleaded guilty to her role in a street attack that left a Sunshine grocer dead after she stole $17 blue teddy bear pants from a neighbouring store. The owner of Diamond Valley Fashions says her life has been forever changed after losing her friend of nearly three decades, Van Viet Truong, 60, who came to her and her husband’s aid as they were attacked while attempting to retrieve their stolen stock in August. Tributes laid at Hong Hung Asian Grocer on Hampshire Road in Sunshine. Ruby Alexander One of the two 14-year-old girls, whose action led to the fatal attack, pleaded guilty in a children’s court on Thursday to affray, assault and two counts of shop theft after more serious charges including violent disorder and intentionally causing serious injury were withdrawn. A co-accused, aged 15, is facing jail time for alleged manslaughter relating to Truong’s daylight killing.



In a victim impact statement read to the court, the woman said her friend’s death had left a void in her life that could never be filled. Sixty-year-old Van Viet Truong, who died in August. “The memories are difficult to escape, my mind remains consumed by the attack. Once a place that represented familiarity and hard work is a constant reminder of violence and trauma,” she said. “I never imagined someone attempting to protect their property, could be confronted with such violence. “No sentence imposed by the court can undo what happened [and] I fear the effects of this ... will remain with me for many years to come.



“We were simply trying to protect our business and the livelihood we’ve worked so hard to build. We no longer enjoy the same freedom or piece of mind we once took for granted.” The court heard Truong migrated from Vietnam to Australia in 1990 before marrying and having two children. He owned the grocery store neighbouring Diamond Valley Fashions on Hampshire Road in Sunshine. About 1.30pm on August 1, the court heard a group of youths met at Sunshine railway station, with CCTV capturing a 12-year-old boy kicking a passing bike and laughing as they made their way to Sunshine Marketplace. Soon after, some of the group stole energy drinks and party poppers from a supermarket, with the 12-year-old drawing the attention of security staff when he set the poppers off.



Shortly before 2pm, the prosecutor said two 14-year-old girls in the group stole two pairs of blue teddy bear pyjama pants worth $17 each from a sale rack outside the fashion store and ran from the scene, chased by the male owner and his wife. Truong heard the commotion, the court heard, and followed along Hampshire Road. CCTV footage has captured an attack on a man in his 60s who attempted to stop alleged shoplifters in Sunshine. Nine News When the second 14-year-old girl allegedly assaulted the male fashion store owner, Truong tried to intervene. The 15-year-old boy then allegedly punched Truong in the head, forcing him to the ground. When he got back on his feet, the boy charged at Truong with such force that it picked the grocer up and drove him backwards, causing his head to hit the ground.



“Witnesses reported hearing a loud sound as his head hit pavement, a very loud crack. As he lay unresponsive on the ground, his glasses lay broken next to him,” the prosecutor said. When the girls attempted to rejoin the fight, they were stopped, with the second kicking Truong as he lay motionless on the ground. The Sunshine community gathered for a rally on Hampshire Road last month. Chris Hopkins The court heard it was a busy weekend, with the incident witnessed by many bystanders and children, prompting six separate calls to Triple Zero for help. The second 14-year-old girl then allegedly turned back towards Truong and said, “that’s what you get”, while smiling, before others in the group appeared to celebrate.



Truong was rushed to hospital but died on August 5. Related Article Crime A violent crime shocked this community. Now locals are calling for change The two other shopkeepers sustained minor injuries. The 14-year-old girl’s lawyer said they accepted that the incident had a harrowing effect but reminded the court her client had not been charged over Truong’s death. They maintained the 14-year-old was remorseful and disappointed in herself but came from a fractured family and had not been attending school, where she’d previously been a captain. The girl was also using drugs and alcohol at the time but had no prior convictions.



Both the prosecution and defence submitted that probation or a youth supervision order would be appropriate punishment, despite the child receiving a caution for an unrelated incident since being placed on bail. The magistrate is expected to sentence the girl in December. The prosecution earlier withdrew charges against the 12-year-old boy, due to his age. The 15-year-old remains in custody after being charged with manslaughter. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Broken Hill Gold swoops on two historic SA goldfields
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Broken Hill Gold swoops on two historic SA goldfields Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd November 26, 2026 — 3:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Broken Hill Gold has beefed up its South Australian Curnamona Province stranglehold, doubling its regional exploration tenure to more than 1500 square kilometres with the grant of two new exploration licences in the historic high-grade goldfields. The company’s new ground sits just 50km from its flagship White Dam gold-copper project and takes in the historic Manna Hill and Waukaringa goldfields, where old-timers chased mouth-watering grades during the late-1800’s heyday. Historic workings at Broken Hill Gold’s new exploration tenure in South Australia near its flagship White Dam copper-gold project. The move comes as South Australia actively encourages new mineral exploration through government initiatives, providing a favourable backdrop for explorers looking to unlock the state’s potential. The Early prospectors certainly had an eye for grade in this district. Historical records show the Manna Hill goldfield produced roughly 3400 ounces of gold at a stellar 18 grams per tonne (g/t), while the Waukaringa goldfield churned out some 45,000 ounces at a serious 23 g/t gold from a 5km strike littered with historical workings and shafts.



‘These two blocks have been left dormant after multiple years tied up in litigation before being released for tender.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes What makes the opportunity on the new grounds particularly compelling is the lack of modern exploration. According to the company, a review of historical data shows that while some work was done between the 1950’s and 2015, no modern drilling has been conducted on the main goldfields since the 1990’s. Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “These two blocks have been left dormant after multiple years tied up in litigation before being released for tender and to give a new motivated company the chance to explore and develop areas which have seen little to no exploration spend for at least 30 years.” The acquisition solidifies the company’s ambitions of a dual-pronged strategy in the region. Broken Hill could potentially supplement near-term oxide gold production at its existing White Dam facility with ore from its newly acquired ground, generating cash flow to help bankroll exploration. Meanwhile, its emerging Icebreaker copper-gold discovery, also at White Dam, could ultimately turbocharge the scale of the company’s operations. The wider Curnamona IOCG district is geological big-game country, featuring numerous iron-oxide-copper-gold systems that have become BHP’s bread and butter this century in South Australia. The district also hosts the giant Kalkaroo deposit, just 40km north of White Dam, with a resource of 1.1 million tonnes of copper and 3.1 million ounces of gold. It’s enough to get the imagination running wild about the potential scale of Broken Hill Gold’s recent Icebreaker discovery, where early drilling delivered standout early holes up to 28m at 2.4g/t gold and 0.7 per cent copper from 93m, with the emerging sulphide system remaining open at depth and along strike.



Back at the new ground, the company says it’s now compiling historical exploration data to define priority areas for first-pass exploration, slated to begin in Q1 2027. In the meantime, initial fieldwork will involve geological mapping, surface sampling and geophysics. While plans for the new tenure are being drawn up, the rods are still turning at the company’s existing White Dam project. Diamond drilling is in full swing at Icebreaker, with five holes now complete. In addition, reverse-circulation drilling to upgrade and expand the shallow Icebreaker oxide mineral resource is complete. The rig has now moved to the adjacent Rolling prospect to advance it towards a resource estimate. After demerging its Queensland assets, Broken Hill Gold has gone all-in on South Australia and this latest land grab shows serious intent. By locking up ground with a rich high-grade history and barely a scratch of modern exploration, Broken Hill Gold has opened up a serious new discovery front. Better still, existing infrastructure offers a pathway to modest production and early cash flow, potentially helping fund the hunt for something much bigger. Broken Hill Gold has staked out a sizeable patch of elephant country – now comes the hunt for a giant lurking beneath its feet. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: How a mix-up with a Formula 1 star has left Min Woo Lee short in Sydney
World.content:
SportGolfAustralian Open How a mix-up with a Formula 1 star has left Min Woo Lee short in Sydney Evin Priest November 26, 2026 — 2:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Min Woo Lee has been forced to roll the dice with his equipment set-up for the first two days at the Australian PGA after leaving his 8-iron at his Las Vegas base during a content filming session with Formula 1 driver Carlos Sainz Jr. The West Australian star was a pre-tournament favourite for the PGA but realised he was without one of his trusty short irons when practising at The Lakes Golf Club earlier in the week. Min Woo Lee on the 12th during his opening round at the PGA Championships on Thursday. Getty Images It didn’t stop the 28-year-old star from playing his way into contention during round one of the PGA, finishing with three birdies in his final four holes for a four-under-par 68. Lee sat four shots behind fellow West Australian Haydn Barron, whose 64 took the clubhouse lead at eight under from the morning wave of players. “I felt like I hit the ball pretty good – the pins are in very tricky positions,” Lee said after his round. “Didn’t really get too many chances or close chances [early on] so, yeah, happy to end like that.”



The PGA Tour winner played just two holes of the PGA on Thursday morning when his approach to the par-4 12th, his third hole of the day, called for the only club he couldn’t hit. “I [needed] to hit an 8-iron and had to hit a 9-iron because of that,” said Lee, who played with countryman Adam Scott (71) and Sweden’s Alex Noren (70). A natural entertainer and one of golf’s most popular players on social media, Lee said there was a good story behind the gaffe. “On Monday, when I was practising [here], I was like, ‘Where’s my 8-iron?’ And it’s funny because I did a lot of videos with ... I practised and [gave a golf lesson to] Carlos Sainz from the Williams [F1] team,” Lee said.



“He was at the same golf club [in Las Vegas] with [fellow F1 driver] Lance Stroll, and they were all touching my clubs and swinging with it and trying it out. It’s got mixed up somewhere, for good reason.” Min Woo Lee on the 11th hole at The Lakes during day one of the PGA Championships. Getty Images Lee is a creative shot maker known for shaping the ball and chipping in from difficult positions, as he did during the final round of his 2023 Australia PGA victory at Royal Queensland. So, he played the cards he was dealt and produced a round featuring five birdies and one bogey at the par-3 15th. “It actually makes golf kind of fun; you’ve got to play different shots,” Lee said. “[A replacement 8-iron] is on the way [from clubmaker Callaway in California]. They said tomorrow afternoon, so I won’t use it for the first two days. I just put a hybrid in there, which I used on the eighth hole, par 5, second last hole. I hit it good [and made birdie].” Lee had a good year on the PGA Tour with four top-five results, including two runner-up finishes en route to a fourth place on the season-long standings. But the world No.28, and Australia’s top-ranked male, is still without a victory in 2026 and hopes to bag at least one of the two Australian majors at the PGA or next week’s Open in Melbourne.

World.title: Auric beefs up gold inventory ahead of WA Munda mine restart
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Auric beefs up gold inventory ahead of WA Munda mine restart Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 26, 2026 — 2:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Auric Mining has hit a brace of high-grade, near-surface gold intercepts and uncovered new mineralisation beneath the current pit design at its Munda gold deposit near Widgiemooltha in Western Australia. Drilling at the western end of the proposed open pit returned a suite of impressive results that look set to sweeten the project’s early-stage mining economics. Top hits include a shallow nine-metre intersection grading 7.05 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 4m along with a three-metre hit assaying 7.17g/t gold from only 9m. Auric Mining’s soon-to-be-refurbished Burbanks processing facility, 87km from its Munda gold project near Coolgardie, WA. Other notable near-surface intervals featured 11m running 2.54g/t gold from 8m, 6m going 3.85g/t from 29m and 8m at 2.71g/t from 9m. The company says the latest results from this area are averaging around 56 per cent higher in grade than predicted by the existing resource model for the same volume of rock, a cracking outcome ahead of a planned mining restart. In what could prove to be an even more significant development for the project’s longer-term potential, the drilling program has also identified a new zone of footwall mineralisation below the base of the current pit design. The discovery hints at the potential for both resource growth and an expansion of the planned open pit. Results from this deeper footwall zone include a three-metre intercept of 4.88g/t gold from 42m and two further holes landing 8m at 1.27g/t from 31m and 7m at 1.36 g/t from 51m.



‘With drilling at Munda continuing into 2027, we see considerable scope to build on the ounces we already own.’ Auric Mining managing director Mark English Alongside its extensional work, Auric is running an operational grade control program at Munda, with recent results continuing to exceed expectations, confirming thick, high-grade mineralisation. The latest batch of grade control results delivered some solid grades, including a standout five-metre hit grading 16.72g/t gold from 11m and 4m at 10.33g/t from 14m. The Munda deposit was originally discovered in the 1990’s during nickel exploration, and historical drilling often stopped once it passed out of the prospective ultramafic rocks and into the underlying basalt footwall. The company has been systematically testing this footwall zone for extensions to the known gold system and that strategy appears to be paying dividends. Auric Mining managing director Mark English said: “Defining higher-than-expected, near-surface mineralisation is an excellent outcome. Results such as 9m @ 7.05 g/t and 3m @ 7.17 g/t will contribute to the early success of the next stage of mining whilst additional mineralisation intersected below the current pit design could lead to expansion of the open pit.” The positive results from Munda are timely, since its 194,000-ounce gold resource is earmarked as the cornerstone feed for the company’s ambitious plan to become a standalone gold producer. Auric is establishing its own integrated mining and processing operation centred at its Burbanks hub, 9km south of Coolgardie and just 87km by road from Munda.



The company recently kicked its producer plan into high gear, revealing the relocation of a recently acquired processing plant from Queensland is running ahead of schedule, with components set to start arriving at Burbanks in December. While the old Burbanks plant previously handled just 180,000 tonnes annually, Auric’s July scoping study envisages a revamped 600,000-tonne-per-annum carbon-in-leach operation using cyanide to extract gold. Management has also pointed to potential expansion to double capacity to 1.2 million tonnes, targeting first processing in April 2028, subject to approvals and funding. The company snapped up the plant infrastructure package from Queensland just two months ago, securing a three-stage crushing circuit, mill deck structures, dust extraction system, critical spares, store inventory and supporting steelwork for a paltry $1.2M. The buy followed its $4.4M acquisition of the historic Burbanks processing site in late 2024, giving Auric an established brownfields location for its proposed gold processing hub with existing power and water. Management estimates equivalent new equipment would cost between $15 million and $25 million, representing a substantial capital saving. That leaves serious daylight between the purchase price and replacement cost, even after allowing for refurbishment, relocation and installation expenses. Auric has already shown a knack for turning a relatively modest outlay into a tidy payday. Its Jeffreys Find joint venture near Norseman parlayed a $1.2M investment into a $16.5M cash distribution, while the starter pit at Munda coughed up 8886 ounces of gold, a whopping 46 per cent ahead of budget, leaving the coffers bulging with almost $48M in cash by the start of 2026.



The company has also been bolstering its gold inventory, recently snapping up the 102,000-ounce Union Jack resource just 15km away, in addition to eyeing a further 68,500 ounces of historically estimated gold at Iron Maiden near Norseman, subject to due diligence. Notably, Auric’s war chest, which stood at $33M at the end of September, has subsequently risen to $53 million following a recent $17M placement and a $3M share purchase plan, leaving Auric well-funded to execute its strategy. With its own mill on the way and the drills delivering grades well above expectations at its cornerstone Munda deposit, Auric looks to be piecing together its production puzzle. The arrival of the trucks at Burbanks next month will likely represent more than just a logistical milestone; it will signal the start of construction for a potential new Goldfields producer. World.title: Hundreds of home buyers in limbo after $20m in deposits goes missing
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWInvestigation Hundreds of home buyers in limbo after $20m in deposits goes missing Lucy Macken Updated November 26, 2026 — 2:25pm ,first published 1:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Hundreds of home buyers who were due to take possession of newly built apartments in Dee Why and Blacktown have had their plans thrown into doubt after most of their deposits went missing. The developer behind the large-scale projects, Landmark Group, has launched Supreme Court proceedings to recoup almost $20 million worth of deposits alleged to be unaccounted for from the trust account of law firm Branston Neville Lawyers. Millions of dollars in deposits in Landmark Group’s Casa Delmar are in doubt. Landmark Group Justice Anthony McGrath has ordered an account of the project’s funds from solicitor Ken Neville, who heads up the Bella Vista-based firm, and for the funds to be transferred to a new trust account. Freeze orders have been issued over the law firm’s bank accounts.



The eastern suburbs developer behind Landmark Group, Arash Tavakoli, issued a statement on Thursday saying he was dismayed by the situation, particularly for first home buyers and families who had planned to move in before Christmas. Lawyer Ken Neville at Branston Neville Lawyers is the subject of Supreme Court orders seeking an account of millions of dollars of missing deposit funds. “[Buyers] did everything right,” Tavakoli said. “They paid their deposits into a solicitor’s trust account, which should be the safest place their money could be. We are committed to every one of these sales, and we will keep fighting until every deposit is accounted for.” An estimated 285 buyers have been impacted by the missing deposits. A spokesperson for Landmark Group said no purchaser has been asked to pay their deposit again, and the solicitors of affected purchasers have been advised. Landmark is yet to confirm the revised settlement date.



The Dee Why development, known as Casa Delmar, is a six-to- ten storey complex of 288 apartments, almost all of which had already sold before the project was completed. Of those, about 140 apartment sales are affected by the missing deposit funds. The 21-storey development at Blacktown, Second Avenue, is almost complete and almost entirely sold. Of its 343 apartments, 145 apartments are affected. Of 285 unit sales, more than $24 million in deposits was held in the trust account of Branston Neville Lawyers. Of the 343 apartments in Landmark’s Second Avenue development at Blacktown, about 145 apartments are affected by the missing deposit funds. However, according to a source familiar with the operations at Landmark Group, when the developer changed law firms a few months ago, only about $5 million of those deposits were transferred to the trust account of their newly appointed law firm Hendrix Legal.



When the deposits were not transferred, Landmark reported the matter to the Law Society of NSW and commenced proceedings in the Supreme Court. A Landmark spokesperson said freeze orders have been issued against the firm and its principal’s bank accounts. Included in the orders was a Neville family company, Kensue Pty Ltd, of which the director is Neville’s wife Suzanne Neville, who is a senior associate at the law firm. David Winning, founder and head of YM Conveyancing, has four clients who purchased apartments in the Dee Why development whose purchases have been delayed. One is a woman who was due to settle on Wednesday but was advised at the 11th hour she was unable to do so. “As far as we are concerned the contract between buyers and the developer is still legally enforceable,” Winning said.



“While the issue of settlement and the deposit funds is a matter for the courts, technically the developer is in breach of contract for not settling.” Winning said there will be ancillary costs to account for through this process as buyers are left with removalist and rent costs while they can’t move into their homes. “Investors will also have mounting costs as they will be unable to rent out apartments,” Winning said. In a statement issued on behalf of Tavakoli on Thursday, he said: “These are extraordinary circumstances, and I know how unsettling they are for our buyers, including first home buyers. “Buying a home is hard enough. People need to know that their deposits are protected when paid into solicitor’s trust accounts. Currently, whatever guardrails that were meant to protect a home buyer’s deposit failed. We are doing everything we can to get our buyers into their homes as soon as possible.”



Landmark Group is expected to turn to the Law Society of NSW to access the compensation Fidelity Fund, administered by the law society. The fund is capped at $1 million payable on all claims against a law firm. It is at the discretion of the law society’s committee if it will allow that cap to be exceeded in special circumstances. Ken Neville and the Branston Neville Lawyers law firm did not respond to questions before publication. The matter returns to court on Monday, November 30. World.title: NRL clubs want players paid $3000 per match. Here’s how it will impact the salary cap
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL clubs want players paid $3000 per match. Here’s how it will impact the salary cap Christian Nicolussi November 26, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

NRL clubs have been urged to back the introduction of $3000 match payments which would allow players at the lower end of the pay scale to earn up to $72,000 extra a season. Club chief executives were told at a meeting with ARL Commission executive chairman Peter V’landys on Wednesday the salary cap was expected to rise to $16 million in 2028, but there is a big chance $1.25m of that money would be dedicated to match payments. South Sydney CEO Blake Solly is a huge fan of introducing match payments. Fairfax Media The real cap would sit at $14.75 million, which would impact the percentage rise for most players who have signed new deals with ratchet clauses. The Rugby League Players’ Association has previously tried to push through weekly match payments, without success, but there is now growing support in clubland to introduce the measure in the next collective bargaining agreement.



“We are 100 per cent supportive of match payments,” South Sydney CEO Blake Solly said. “During the last CBA, all clubs and the RLPA were committed to introducing match payments, but one club derailed it at the last minute. “We think this is a great way to reward players who are performing on the field, and producing the wonderful entertainment that is driving the revenue into the game in terms of gate receipts and broadcast. Cooper Clarke had an outstanding rookie season for the Storm, and would have been one of the big winners from match payments. Getty Images “It’s fair. If you play, you get it. If not, you don’t. It’s not so significant that it will disrupt all the other benefits that will go into the cap as part of the new broadcast deal. “The indication at the CEO’s conference was the cap would rise to $16 million. But having been around three previous CBA negotiations, that sounds wonderful as a headline figure, but there’s an awful lot of complexity that sits inside that.



“The club consultation committee is looking forward to working with Peter and his team and the RLPA on trying to get the CBA and club funding deal as son as we can. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Are the PNG Chiefs blowing their money? We crunch the numbers Christian Nicolussi Sports reporter “As for the match payments, it certainly benefits the guys at the lower end of the scale who are performing and playing – an extra $60,000 or $70,000 for someone on $80,000 or $150,000 is material, and deserved.” Solly is a member of the committee negotiating the next CBA, along with Brisbane counterpart Dave Donaghy, Warriors boss Cameron George and Dolphins CEO Terry Reader. This masthead revealed this week the PNG Chiefs were keener than most clubs to know what the next cap will be. The Chiefs can offer tax-free wages so have not included ratchet clauses in their players’ contracts, but a salary cap set at $14 million or $16 million – or $14.75m in real terms once match payments are factored in – will make a real difference in how hard they keep going at top talent.



Match payments would be paid to all players who take the field, from million-dollar stars like Nathan Cleary and Kalyn Ponga to the very bottom earners on a team’s roster. “And given Peter has for a long time supported ‘battlers’, match fees will be right in his wheelhouse,” Solly said.
