World.title: Vance has aligned himself with the tech bros. Has he miscalculated?
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Vance has aligned himself with the tech bros. Has he miscalculated? Benedict Smith November 26, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: When Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia boss following revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Donald Trump leapt to his defence. The US president is determined to maintain his country’s lead over China in the AI race and holds significant shares in the company. He also considers the leather-jacketed 63-year-old tech bro a friend. Much has been made of JD Vance’s background in Rust Belt Ohio, but not enough of his affiliation with the tech world. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin But as Trump put pressure on Nvidia board members to return Huang to the throne, he had a partner who at first sight may seem more surprising: JD Vance. Stepping in was a significant risk for the US vice president. He harbours presidential ambitions for 2028 – and may have disastrously miscalculated by throwing in his lot with big tech.



“Vance is toast right now,” said Brett Loyd, a former pollster to Trump. “Absolutely toast.” Related Article Updated

AI Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after direct lobbying by Trump “I don’t think anybody’s a fan of big tech right now,” said Brent Buchanan, the president of the Republican pollster Cygnal. “[It] doesn’t really benefit Republicans who just got waxed for not paying attention to regular people.” So why did Vance reportedly use his Silicon Valley connections to push Nvidia’s board for Huang’s return? And having done so, why did he so publicly welcome the tech boss’s return? From Yale to Silicon Valley



Part of the reason is surely Vance’s political history. Much has been made of the self-proclaimed hillbilly’s background in Rust Belt Ohio, but not enough of his affiliation with the tech world. As a Yale Law School student he met and befriended Peter Thiel, the co-founder of PayPal. He later described him as “possibly the smartest person I’d ever met”, crediting the billionaire’s influence on his faith and personal philosophy. Loading After graduating, Vance worked for Thiel’s venture capital firm, Mithril Capital, and lived for a time in San Francisco when he joined a biotech company. Thiel donated $US15 million ($23 million) to Vance’s Senate campaign in 2022, which was also supported by David Sacks, the Silicon Valley investor who later became Trump’s AI tsar. True, Vance sounded sceptical of Silicon Valley early in Trump’s second term, when he declared big tech had “too much power” and that he wanted to “break ’em up”, Teddy Roosevelt-style.



But that may have been populist posturing from Vance, who has shown little interest in dismantling tech monopolies in office. Related Article Analysis

Trump's America National security has been sacrificed for the stock market – and that’s a scandal At any rate, he has since argued that technological advances would usher in a renaissance in American manufacturing, restoring those communities hollowed out by deindustrialisation. “When you erect a tariff wall around a critical industry like auto manufacturing, and you combine that with advanced robotics and lower energy costs and other tools that increase the productivity of US labour, you give American workers a multiplying effect,” he claimed in March last year. “That, in turn, allows firms to make things here at a price-competitive basis.” That might be a genuine economic philosophy. It might also be an attempt by him to attract blue-collar workers while reassuring his Silicon Valley backers – a kind of elitist populism.



Eyes on 2028 Buchanan believes Vance’s lobbying of Nvidia’s board was an attempt to stem the economic damage from Huang’s abrupt fall from grace a fortnight ago. “We need a healthy Nvidia to have a healthy economy,” he said. “Our current entire economy is based on Nvidia succeeding and funding other things within the ecosystem. But that doesn’t make good politics.” Donald Trump believes Jensen Huang is too important to the fate of Nvidia and the US economy writ large. NYT There is another factor, which is that should he run in 2028, Vance stands to benefit from donations from exceptionally wealthy and politically conscious tech bosses.



Chief among them will be Elon Musk, assuming he has not been scarred by wasting some $US445 million in a futile attempt to shore up Republican control of Congress. The Tesla boss has been a vocal supporter of Vance. Related Article Elon Musk ‘I feel pretty foolish’: Musk rues election cash splash, declares he’s not MAGA But Vance’s decision to throw in his lot with the tech bros now appears to have been exceptionally ill-timed. And in politics, timing is everything. Americans are deeply alarmed by the rapid expansion of data centres and advances in artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities. More than half of voters in an NBC exit poll said the centres were a “crucial or major” factor in their vote in the midterms, a shattering experience for Republicans. Democrats conquered what should have been Republican strongholds by capitalising on voters’ anxieties and levelling accusations of cronyism between the administration and Silicon Valley. Hundreds of millions of dollars spent by Musk and fellow tech bosses for the Republicans failed to stem the blue tsunami.



Many predicted MAGA would worm its way out of its embrace with big tech after the humiliating defeat. That has not been the case. “It’s clear that the Republican Party’s closeness with big tech contributed to major electoral losses this year,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist and chief executive of The Alliance for Secure AI. “The voters overwhelmingly rejected the big tech oligarchy and Jensen Huang’s reinstatement ignores that.” Hawks on the right Vance’s intervention with Nvidia also leaves him vulnerable to a challenge from hawkish Republicans who believe Huang poses a threat to US national security.



One such figure is Marco Rubio, who warned top administration officials in March that the tech boss was in a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Related Article Trump's America ‘Vibes have definitely shifted’: The perfect storm that changed how America sees big tech Loyd believes the US secretary of state is already quietly distancing himself from Trump – unlike Vance. Vance has long presented himself as MAGA personified: the product of American communities failed by a vapid political consensus that let jobs flee abroad while letting in drugs and cheap immigration. But he embodies its contradictions too, and he is just as much a product of Silicon Valley as he is of Middletown, Ohio. Huang has been lucky enough to have a second chance at the reins of Nvidia. But politics can be less forgiving than business, and voters may not be so lenient with Vance.

World.title: Maddy riding on to make Izzy proud after heart-breaking farewell
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Maddy riding on to make Izzy proud after heart-breaking farewell Craig Kerry November 26, 2026 — 3:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Maddy Owen had already been through the hardest part before she gave a beautiful and heart-wrenching eulogy for her best friend and fellow jockey Izzy Neale. Owen, like many friends and family, had rushed to be at Neale’s bedside at Dubbo Hospital after her fatal fall at Warren on November 8. Neale’s family announced the 22-year-old’s passing two days later, and the racing community has struggled since to come to terms with the devastating loss of the promising apprentice. Maddy Owen after a win at Rosehill on Swift Charm in January 2025. Getty Images Neale was farewelled at Merriwa Showground on Wednesday and Owen was among those to speak. The 25-year-old shared memories of their friendship as well as glimpses of Izzy’s fun-loving personality, loyalty, work ethic and passion for horses.



And, through tears, there was the hurt of an exciting future taken away, and a final thank you to her “pretty girl, best friend and partner in crime” for their time together. Owen, who has three rides at Rosehill on Saturday, is determined to make Neale proud, push through the pain and carry on their shared dreams in racing. “It’s been tough being at the races or even trackwork, around places where she would usually be, but it’s our life and what we do,” Owen said on Thursday. “I guess the funeral probably brought a little bit of closure, and it was nice seeing her family and everyone in racing come together there. There were lots of people who attended, so I thought it was quite nice. “We’d already been through the hardest part. When it happened, we all drove out to Dubbo from different places.



Izzy Neale, Mikayla Weir and Maddy Owen together at Randwick on Everest day this year. Instagram “Chelsea [Hillier] was actually with her at the track. It was a hard few days following that … so I think the funeral was just a really nice send-off and a little bit of closure.” Owen, who became friends with Neale while working at Scone five years ago, said the tragedy had not changed her riding ambitions and those in racing who knew Izzy had found solace together at the track. “When I think about what happened, I think of it more as a freak accident,” she said. “I don’t blame it on racing, or what we do, and it’s what we both loved to do. It was our passion. It was really our whole lives.



“That’s what she loved to do, that’s how most of us were friends. That was our one common interest, so we’re just getting back out there and being together. That actually helps. “She was very positive, happy and talented. I said in my speech that the hardest part will be, I always looked forward to when we were racing at the same location and we could hang out. “It would be like Muswellbrook tomorrow. Because we raced in different areas, it wasn’t that often that we got to hang out. Then there were the times calling each other to and from the races, all those little things.” Tamworth-based Owen has two rides on Friday at Muswellbrook for the Scone stable of Brett and Georgie Cavanough, where she worked initially as an apprentice, then three for them at Rosehill. “I’ve been in Scone a little bit the last few weeks, just organising and doing some things, so I’ve been doing a bit of riding for Brett and he’s been really good,” she said.



Related Article Horse racing ‘It doesn’t feel right’: Jockey riding through grief for fallen friend “He’s given me some good rides and opportunities, and it’s good to have something to focus on, which I am. I’m really looking forward to all the rides, but especially the stakes race.” Owen rides Pride To Follow ($61) in the listed Starlight Stakes (1100m), where the five-year-old mare rises in class from wins at Port Macquarie then Randwick. “She’s in really good form,” said Owen, who rode her at Port Macquarie. “When I won on her, it was a quality, and then she raced at Randwick in a benchmark 84, so she’s stepping up to the mark each time.



“She’ll have to step up again on Saturday, but she’s racing in good form, she puts herself into the race and she gets in with a light weight, so I’m sure on her best run, she will be thereabouts.” Owen also rides Indifference ($34) in the Country Classic (2000m) and Arapawa ($17) in the benchmark 78 handicap over 1800m. “Indifference is a nice horse, I rode him this morning and he’s well, so I’m sure he’ll put in a good performance,” she said. “And Arapawa is first time over that trip, but hopefully the track stays soft and he’ll enjoy that. He’s won at Rosehill before and I think he’ll be in with a chance.”

World.title: ‘Turncoat town’: Liberal senator defects to One Nation
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation ‘Turncoat town’: Liberal senator defects to One Nation Brittany Busch and Michelle Griffin Updated November 26, 2026 — 3:14pm ,first published November 26, 2026 — 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Liberals have scorned One Nation defector Leah Blyth for abandoning the party, in a shock exit that derailed the Coalition’s momentum on the final sitting week of the year. The senator, who lost the South Australian party presidency to hard-right powerbroker Alex Antic in September, said the Liberals had lost their way and One Nation was the only party that could be trusted to make hard decisions. One Nation defector Senator Leah Blyth with Pauline Hanson at Parliament House on Thursday. Dominic Lorrimer The former opposition spokeswoman for defence infrastructure said she did not feel safe in her old party, and the factional infighting in her state branch was such that private security was employed for her protection. Blyth had been appointed to the Senate in February 2025 to fill a casual vacancy left by retiring leading moderate Simon Birmingham, and was not expected to secure a winnable spot on the Liberal ballot for next year’s election.



Blyth’s defection brings the number of One Nation senators to five, with two MPs in the lower house. While Hanson had regularly fanned speculation throughout the year that other members of parliament had approached her to join the party, Blyth is the first federal politician to make the switch since Joyce. One Nation’s popularity has surged in all the polls this year and was the first preference of one in four voters in the latest Resolve Political Monitor. Loading Her departure was a blow to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who had overseen 10 months of relative stability in the Coalition and told his party room on Tuesday that they could win the next election as Labor struggles with grim economic results and the fallout from tax hikes introduced at the last federal budget. Blyth’s colleagues and staff were blindsided by her move even after Pauline Hanson teased a defection on Wednesday night with a video of her preparing a steak in a sandwich press, imitating her wooing of Barnaby Joyce a year previously.



Federal party president Tony Abbott suggested Blyth was leaving because she was on the wrong side of a factional battle. “This has got nothing whatsoever to do with principle, nothing whatsoever to do with the national interest. I think the public will see through what this is,” he said in a video posted to Instagram. Senator Leah Blyth has joined the growing ranks of One Nation. Dominic Lorrimer Fellow South Australian senator Anne Ruston wrote to the party’s state membership on Thursday afternoon saying Blyth had put her own interests first and thrown away the trust of those who had voted for a Liberal. “Leah was never elected to the Senate seat she holds. That seat was won by Simon Birmingham on the Liberal ticket, with the votes of South Australians and the hard work of members like you,” Ruston said.



“She told [delegates]: ‘My word can be trusted. My promises will be kept.’ Today we found out that those promises were worth nothing.” Related Article Opinion

One Nation One Nation shock defection an exercise in hypocrisy and a blow to Taylor Paul Sakkal Chief political correspondent Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume denied internal divisions were to blame, adding Blyth “wasn’t a big contributor to the party room”. Asked whether the move was a surprise, backbencher Scott Buchholz said: “Of course it was. I’ve just got to go and find out who she is now.” Taylor, who had largely left the South Australian state division to its factional fight, did not appear before media on Thursday.



Nationals leader Matt Canavan said One Nation was turning into “turncoat town” and Blyth’s defection smacked of self-interest. “To turn around now … and say ‘my principles and policies are more aligned with One Nation’ – I mean, give me a break,” he told Radio National earlier. Pauline Hanson said Blyth was a true conservative. Dominic Lorrimer Canavan insisted he was not concerned about any further defections, but when asked whether he had talked anyone out of leaving the Coalition, conceded he had worked hard to keep people together during a tough period. Blyth went on the attack during a press conference with Hanson on Thursday morning, saying it was “pretty grubby” for Coalition MPs to background media about what her staff knew, but admitted she had not spoken to anyone in the party about her decision. Tony Abbott’s accusations she acted from self-interest were a “complete and utter falsehood”, she said.



The senator said the Liberal Party had abandoned her by forsaking its principles and making too many compromises on policy. Related Article Political leadership ‘He used me’: Nationals veteran accuses Barnaby Joyce of hypocrisy and misleading party faithful Unable to identify any points of difference she had with the Coalition on current issues such as the digital duty of care, Blyth criticised the Liberals for not being willing to withdraw from the Paris climate agreement, even as the party ditched net zero. She then said there had not been enough debate before the Coalition backed a defence bill that gave the minister sweeping powers to designate military zones. One Nation also voted to pass that law. In a later interview on News24, Blyth said she did not know what the minor party’s position had been. The senator swerved questions about the times she had described One Nation as a corrosive force – a central part of her fight with Antic, seen by some in the Coalition as too willing to cosy to the minor party.



She paid tribute to Antic at her One Nation press conference. “I will shout out to Senator Alex Antic; he was a voice of reason in the party room on [net zero],” she said. She added that she had taken a pay cut to move to One Nation and insisted the party had not promised her anything. Hanson’s chief of staff Chris Taylor confirmed Blyth would not be guaranteed preselection. “She’s going to have to prove herself. She has to prove herself to the people of South Australia and to the party. She’ll have plenty of time to do that,” he told News24.



Hanson said Blyth had approached her, and that the decision would resonate with former Liberal supporters who felt the party had abandoned them. The minor party leader, who has previously vowed to reject “opportunistic” Coalition defectors, welcomed Blyth as a true conservative. Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Labor frontbencher Murray Watt mocked Taylor over the defection, saying if he could not control his party, he could not govern the country. World.title: Sunshine grocer’s death over stolen $17 pants leaves harrowing impact
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Sunshine grocer’s death over stolen $17 pants leaves harrowing impact Erin Pearson November 26, 2026 — 3:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A 14-year-old girl pleaded guilty to her role in a street attack that left a Sunshine grocer dead after she stole $17 blue teddy bear pants from a neighbouring store. The owner of Diamond Valley Fashions says her life has been forever changed after losing her friend of nearly three decades, Van Viet Truong, 60, who came to her and her husband’s aid as they were attacked while attempting to retrieve their stolen stock in August. Tributes laid at Hong Hung Asian Grocer on Hampshire Road in Sunshine. Ruby Alexander One of the two 14-year-old girls, whose action led to the fatal attack, pleaded guilty in a children’s court on Thursday to affray, assault and two counts of shop theft after more serious charges including violent disorder and intentionally causing serious injury were withdrawn. A co-accused, aged 15, is facing jail time for alleged manslaughter relating to Truong’s daylight killing.



In a victim impact statement read to the court, the woman said her friend’s death had left a void in her life that could never be filled. Sixty-year-old Van Viet Truong, who died in August. “The memories are difficult to escape, my mind remains consumed by the attack. Once a place that represented familiarity and hard work is a constant reminder of violence and trauma,” she said. “I never imagined someone attempting to protect their property, could be confronted with such violence. “No sentence imposed by the court can undo what happened [and] I fear the effects of this ... will remain with me for many years to come.



“We were simply trying to protect our business and the livelihood we’ve worked so hard to build. We no longer enjoy the same freedom or piece of mind we once took for granted.” The court heard Truong migrated from Vietnam to Australia in 1990 before marrying and having two children. He owned the grocery store neighbouring Diamond Valley Fashions on Hampshire Road in Sunshine. About 1.30pm on August 1, the court heard a group of youths met at Sunshine railway station, with CCTV capturing a 12-year-old boy kicking a passing bike and laughing as they made their way to Sunshine Marketplace. Soon after, some of the group stole energy drinks and party poppers from a supermarket, with the 12-year-old drawing the attention of security staff when he set the poppers off.



Shortly before 2pm, the prosecutor said two 14-year-old girls in the group stole two pairs of blue teddy bear pyjama pants worth $17 each from a sale rack outside the fashion store and ran from the scene, chased by the male owner and his wife. Truong heard the commotion, the court heard, and followed along Hampshire Road. CCTV footage has captured an attack on a man in his 60s who attempted to stop alleged shoplifters in Sunshine. Nine News When the second 14-year-old girl allegedly assaulted the male fashion store owner, Truong tried to intervene. The 15-year-old boy then allegedly punched Truong in the head, forcing him to the ground. When he got back on his feet, the boy charged at Truong with such force that it picked the grocer up and drove him backwards, causing his head to hit the ground.



“Witnesses reported hearing a loud sound as his head hit pavement, a very loud crack. As he lay unresponsive on the ground, his glasses lay broken next to him,” the prosecutor said. When the girls attempted to rejoin the fight, they were stopped, with the second kicking Truong as he lay motionless on the ground. The Sunshine community gathered for a rally on Hampshire Road last month. Chris Hopkins The court heard it was a busy weekend, with the incident witnessed by many bystanders and children, prompting six separate calls to Triple Zero for help. The second 14-year-old girl then allegedly turned back towards Truong and said, “that’s what you get”, while smiling, before others in the group appeared to celebrate.



Truong was rushed to hospital but died on August 5. Related Article Crime A violent crime shocked this community. Now locals are calling for change The two other shopkeepers sustained minor injuries. The 14-year-old girl’s lawyer said they accepted that the incident had a harrowing effect but reminded the court her client had not been charged over Truong’s death. They maintained the 14-year-old was remorseful and disappointed in herself but came from a fractured family and had not been attending school, where she’d previously been a captain. The girl was also using drugs and alcohol at the time but had no prior convictions.



Both the prosecution and defence submitted that probation or a youth supervision order would be appropriate punishment, despite the child receiving a caution for an unrelated incident since being placed on bail. The magistrate is expected to sentence the girl in December. The prosecution earlier withdrew charges against the 12-year-old boy, due to his age. The 15-year-old remains in custody after being charged with manslaughter. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Broken Hill Gold swoops on two historic SA goldfields
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Broken Hill Gold swoops on two historic SA goldfields Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd November 26, 2026 — 3:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Broken Hill Gold has beefed up its South Australian Curnamona Province stranglehold, doubling its regional exploration tenure to more than 1500 square kilometres with the grant of two new exploration licences in the historic high-grade goldfields. The company’s new ground sits just 50km from its flagship White Dam gold-copper project and takes in the historic Manna Hill and Waukaringa goldfields, where old-timers chased mouth-watering grades during the late-1800’s heyday. Historic workings at Broken Hill Gold’s new exploration tenure in South Australia near its flagship White Dam copper-gold project. The move comes as South Australia actively encourages new mineral exploration through government initiatives, providing a favourable backdrop for explorers looking to unlock the state’s potential. The Early prospectors certainly had an eye for grade in this district. Historical records show the Manna Hill goldfield produced roughly 3400 ounces of gold at a stellar 18 grams per tonne (g/t), while the Waukaringa goldfield churned out some 45,000 ounces at a serious 23 g/t gold from a 5km strike littered with historical workings and shafts.



‘These two blocks have been left dormant after multiple years tied up in litigation before being released for tender.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes What makes the opportunity on the new grounds particularly compelling is the lack of modern exploration. According to the company, a review of historical data shows that while some work was done between the 1950’s and 2015, no modern drilling has been conducted on the main goldfields since the 1990’s. Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “These two blocks have been left dormant after multiple years tied up in litigation before being released for tender and to give a new motivated company the chance to explore and develop areas which have seen little to no exploration spend for at least 30 years.” The acquisition solidifies the company’s ambitions of a dual-pronged strategy in the region. Broken Hill could potentially supplement near-term oxide gold production at its existing White Dam facility with ore from its newly acquired ground, generating cash flow to help bankroll exploration. Meanwhile, its emerging Icebreaker copper-gold discovery, also at White Dam, could ultimately turbocharge the scale of the company’s operations. The wider Curnamona IOCG district is geological big-game country, featuring numerous iron-oxide-copper-gold systems that have become BHP’s bread and butter this century in South Australia. The district also hosts the giant Kalkaroo deposit, just 40km north of White Dam, with a resource of 1.1 million tonnes of copper and 3.1 million ounces of gold. It’s enough to get the imagination running wild about the potential scale of Broken Hill Gold’s recent Icebreaker discovery, where early drilling delivered standout early holes up to 28m at 2.4g/t gold and 0.7 per cent copper from 93m, with the emerging sulphide system remaining open at depth and along strike.



Back at the new ground, the company says it’s now compiling historical exploration data to define priority areas for first-pass exploration, slated to begin in Q1 2027. In the meantime, initial fieldwork will involve geological mapping, surface sampling and geophysics. While plans for the new tenure are being drawn up, the rods are still turning at the company’s existing White Dam project. Diamond drilling is in full swing at Icebreaker, with five holes now complete. In addition, reverse-circulation drilling to upgrade and expand the shallow Icebreaker oxide mineral resource is complete. The rig has now moved to the adjacent Rolling prospect to advance it towards a resource estimate. After demerging its Queensland assets, Broken Hill Gold has gone all-in on South Australia and this latest land grab shows serious intent. By locking up ground with a rich high-grade history and barely a scratch of modern exploration, Broken Hill Gold has opened up a serious new discovery front. Better still, existing infrastructure offers a pathway to modest production and early cash flow, potentially helping fund the hunt for something much bigger. Broken Hill Gold has staked out a sizeable patch of elephant country – now comes the hunt for a giant lurking beneath its feet. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: How a mix-up with a Formula 1 star has left Min Woo Lee short in Sydney
World.content:
SportGolfAustralian Open How a mix-up with a Formula 1 star has left Min Woo Lee short in Sydney Evin Priest November 26, 2026 — 2:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Min Woo Lee has been forced to roll the dice with his equipment set-up for the first two days at the Australian PGA after leaving his 8-iron at his Las Vegas base during a content filming session with Formula 1 driver Carlos Sainz Jr. The West Australian star was a pre-tournament favourite for the PGA but realised he was without one of his trusty short irons when practising at The Lakes Golf Club earlier in the week. Min Woo Lee on the 12th during his opening round at the PGA Championships on Thursday. Getty Images It didn’t stop the 28-year-old star from playing his way into contention during round one of the PGA, finishing with three birdies in his final four holes for a four-under-par 68. Lee sat four shots behind fellow West Australian Haydn Barron, whose 64 took the clubhouse lead at eight under from the morning wave of players. “I felt like I hit the ball pretty good – the pins are in very tricky positions,” Lee said after his round. “Didn’t really get too many chances or close chances [early on] so, yeah, happy to end like that.”



The PGA Tour winner played just two holes of the PGA on Thursday morning when his approach to the par-4 12th, his third hole of the day, called for the only club he couldn’t hit. “I [needed] to hit an 8-iron and had to hit a 9-iron because of that,” said Lee, who played with countryman Adam Scott (71) and Sweden’s Alex Noren (70). A natural entertainer and one of golf’s most popular players on social media, Lee said there was a good story behind the gaffe. “On Monday, when I was practising [here], I was like, ‘Where’s my 8-iron?’ And it’s funny because I did a lot of videos with ... I practised and [gave a golf lesson to] Carlos Sainz from the Williams [F1] team,” Lee said.



“He was at the same golf club [in Las Vegas] with [fellow F1 driver] Lance Stroll, and they were all touching my clubs and swinging with it and trying it out. It’s got mixed up somewhere, for good reason.” Min Woo Lee on the 11th hole at The Lakes during day one of the PGA Championships. Getty Images Lee is a creative shot maker known for shaping the ball and chipping in from difficult positions, as he did during the final round of his 2023 Australia PGA victory at Royal Queensland. So, he played the cards he was dealt and produced a round featuring five birdies and one bogey at the par-3 15th. “It actually makes golf kind of fun; you’ve got to play different shots,” Lee said. “[A replacement 8-iron] is on the way [from clubmaker Callaway in California]. They said tomorrow afternoon, so I won’t use it for the first two days. I just put a hybrid in there, which I used on the eighth hole, par 5, second last hole. I hit it good [and made birdie].” Lee had a good year on the PGA Tour with four top-five results, including two runner-up finishes en route to a fourth place on the season-long standings. But the world No.28, and Australia’s top-ranked male, is still without a victory in 2026 and hopes to bag at least one of the two Australian majors at the PGA or next week’s Open in Melbourne.

World.title: NZ burying valuable energy source in landfills, biogas company says
World.content:
Audio player for " Biogas company wants to see more waste collection " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment/2799873%2Fnz-burying-valuable-energy-source-in-landfills-biogas-company-says

Biogas company wants to see more waste collection Nine To Noon Download MP3 12m

A biogas company says New Zealand is burying a valuable energy source by not coordinating a system to divert organic waste away from landfill.

Ecogas takes residential and industrial organic waste, and through anaerobic digestion at two facilities in the North Island, turns it into a gas that was pumped into the national grid.

But the company was frustrated about the uncertainty around feedstock - with a report for the government last year finding 622,000 tonnes of food was put into landfill each year.

Some of the gas from the waste was collected and used by landfill gas operators, but Ecogas chief technical officer Dr Alzbeta Bouskova Houghton said this was an inefficient system, with half of the gas going to the atmosphere.

Houghton told Nine to Noon it could all be used by a facility like Ecogas - which was set to open a new site in Canterbury next year.

"The facility in Canterbury will process the council's kerbside collections from organics, so that's the household green and garden and food scraps, together with other industrial and commercial organics, into bioenergy and biofertiliser," she said.

Houghton said the plant was purposely designed for that type of feedstock and for the region's needs.

She said it would use its gas to process one of the by-products of the digestion process into biomass fuel.

"That is for two reasons," Houghton said.

"One, that there is no national gas grid in the South Island. And the second reason is that there's a high demand for biomass fuel in the Canterbury region from the industrial processes."

Mandated diversion targets

Houghton said Christchurch Council had been collecting organic waste from households for over a decade.

She said waste was going to a composting plant, which had issues, such as its smell.

Houghton said their plant needed 50,000 to 75,000 tonnes of feedstock a year to pay its way.

"But it's not a technology limit. It's the current settings that produce this, and at the moment, the waste that comes to us only comes when it's substantially cheaper than landfill," she said.

"And so, every, and with the current settings, every tonne is carrying an uncertainty, and investor has to price in the risk.

"So, what we are asking for is a mandated diversion target that changes that, and this would essentially achieve two things.

"It would signal a commitment to divert organics from landfill towards more sustainable uses, and it will then enable the councils and businesses to commit to long-term feedstock supply contract that facilities like ours rely on."

Shifting rubbish collections to fortnightly

Houghton said around 40 percent of general rubbish was food waste.

She said by separating that rubbish into a different bin, the rubbish collection did not have to happen weekly and could be dropped down to fortnightly.

"The savings generated from avoiding the landfill cost and the weekly collection is then able to offset the cost of additional collection of the food scraps.

"So, it can be done viably, it is being done viably, and there's obviously councils that have figured this out already."

Houghton said participation was critical and councils did monitor that.

She said that it often depended on the message the public was receiving.

"We are basically asking people to change their habits, and it often comes with a bit of a friction," Houghton said.

"But what we are finding is that once people understand what happens to their food scraps, they are a lot more willing to engage with the service."

Houghton said what they were calling for was essentially a binding target for the diversion.

World.title: RNZ Asia, business and technology teams face cuts as fallout continues
World.content:
A further three teams have received change proposals, impacting jobs at public broadcaster RNZ.

RNZ Asia, the business team, and technology team, have all received proposals, according to the Public Service Association and E tū unions, joining the rural reporters.

In a joint letter on Thursday, the unions disclosed these teams had received change proposals as RNZ addressed its financial woes; the revelation of a nearly $12 million deficit.

In the intensive five page letter, about 20 points were made challenging the proposals being undertaken in response to failures that would be subject to independent review.

As well as targeting the substance and processes involved, the unions highlighted a "remarkable statement" in the change proposals that they said was "offensively tone-deaf".

The line in the proposals had said: "Even with good planning, it [change] can raise questions and uncertainty. That's completely normal. What matters is that we stay in conversation and work it through together."

The unions said in their joint letter this was "offensively tone-deaf" because there had been "a total absence of good planning at RNZ and that staff are being asked to face the consequences".

This included the "loss of their livelihood before any answers are provided through the independent review".

"Further, the suggestion that 'we stay in conversation' is the opposite of the approach that RNZ is taking to this consultation period, which is woefully short and does not allow anyone to 'stay in conversation'."

In response to the unions' comments, a RNZ spokesperson said: "RNZ will respond directly to the unions about the matters they have raised."

"RNZ is following a full consultation process and meeting its obligations to staff and the unions under the Employment Relations Act and the collective agreement."

What's happening at RNZ Asia?

RNZ said the proposal for change to RNZ Asia would see staffing in that group reduced from eight full-time equivalents to five.

"The challenge RNZ is facing is that it currently costs more to run than we are funded for, and we need to address that," a RNZ spokesperson said.

"We have shared the proposal with impacted staff and will not be commenting further on the proposal while we await their feedback."

The situation was further explained, saying, "RNZ is proposing to no longer provide a regular translation service as part of its digital coverage and integrate RNZ Asia with the wider newsroom."

"This proposal balances the need for RNZ to reduce costs while maintaining a focus on creation of original reporting in English for Asian communities, acknowledging the importance of these communities in Auckland and for wider New Zealand."

Proposed changes to rural news a 'kick in the guts'

Federated Farmers says proposed changes to RNZ's rural reporting team come as a huge blow to communities across the country.

Learning about the proposal from leaked confidential documents, Federated Farmers North Canterbury president Bex Green said it was a total "kick in the guts for New Zealand's hard working rural people".

The proposal is believed to affect 75 percent of specialist rural reporter roles, as the public broadcaster seeks to axe 58 jobs in response to its nearly $12 million deficit.

The challenges at RNZ come against a backdrop of wider turmoil in the media sector, with other news publishers and broadcasters reducing operations, publications and programming.

In a statement, Green said rural New Zealand was already losing its local newspapers and other sources of news, and "now our state broadcaster is looking to abandon us too".

"For decades, farmers have tuned in during morning milking, while they're having lunch or out working on the farm. It's how we find out what's happening in the wider farming world, keep up with important agricultural and trade news, and stay connected to other rural communities," Green said.

"You might be miles from the nearest town, but you can always switch on the radio and hear what's happening across the country. That's worth protecting, but instead, we're seeing it gradually stripped away."

Ruapehu mayor Weston Kirton echoed the sentiment, warning the proposed cuts would weaken the voice of rural New Zealand and reduce coverage of the regions that drive the country's economy.

"Food and fibre production and international tourism together generate around seven in every 10 export dollars New Zealand earns. Rural New Zealand is not a niche interest. It is central to the country's success," he said.

"This proposal sends the wrong message to rural communities. It is another signal to rural communities that government isn't listening to the hard-working people who are paying most of New Zealand's bills."

RNZ response

Responding to questions about the proposal affecting rural reporting, a RNZ spokesperson said, "We will continue to produce news and stories relevant to rural communities".

"We are proposing to do this by protecting rural coverage on Morning Report, continuing the popular award-winning Country Life podcast and radio programme, and making rural coverage of agribusiness issues part of our business team's remit.

"We continue to have RNZ-employed regional reporters across the nation, including Central Lakes Queenstown, Nelson, New Plymouth, Palmerston North, Hawke's Bay, Waikato, and Northland," the spokesperson said.

"Additionally, we partially fund over 20 Local Democracy Reporters to cover local and rural issues in non-RNZ newsrooms across the country.

"The proposal balances the importance of rural news to our audience and Charter delivery, with the need for RNZ to reduce its costs. We will always deliver heartland coverage and have specialised focus on rural issues."

'Deeply inappropriate'

The comments came after Public Service Association national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons told RNZ's Morning Report on Thursday that cutting roles before a review into the public broadcaster's financial problems was complete were "deeply inappropriate".

"It will undermine RNZ's ability to comply with its own charter, and board members should be very conscious of that," Fitzsimons said.

The RNZ charter required the broadcaster to fulfil a range of roles, including to "endeavour to provide services of the highest quality, which provide comprehensive, independent, accurate, impartial, and balanced regional, national, and international news and current affairs".

Fitzsimons said RNZ was rushing to respond to its financial challenges, and it should wait until a government was in place before acting. The final election result is due to be announced on Friday, with potential coalition negotiations to follow.

"The last thing the RNZ board and management should be doing is making irreversible destructive cuts to our national broadcaster. The stakes are high, RNZ is a statutory civil defence lifeline radio broadcaster, New Zealanders rely on it to provide reliable lifesaving information. These cuts put RNZ at risk and they should be stopped immediately."

There were more immediate hurdles though, and Fitzsimons acknowledged RNZ's "cash situation is problematic".

"This is where we call on Treasury to intervene. It's a public broadcaster. This isn't a private company that can go bust," Fitzsimons said.

"RNZ is a public broadcaster. We need Treasury to support them, we've already had indications from politicians that a bailout is possible, the last thing RNZ should be doing is panicking and cutting jobs."

Labour commitment

Labour media spokesperson Reuben Davidson said this week his party would bail out RNZ by "writing off the deficit" if they were in government, and had called for the board to be sacked.

ACT leader David Seymour, who has shareholding responsibilities for RNZ, said he and Media Minister Paul Goldsmith had requested changes to the draft terms of reference after receiving them late last week.

"Our overall feedback was: let's toughen it up," he told RNZ. "I would hope that it will be wrapped up by Christmas."

In a statement, RNZ said its board had "committed to a thorough and robust independent review into what happened and why, including RNZ's financial controls, reporting, assurance and governance".
