World.title: 'Neutral from the outset': Wellington mayor Andrew Little still holding back over rates controversy
World.content:
After weeks of controversial headlines and hours of public submissions, Wellington's mayor is still holding back from stating his position on the capital's major rating debate.

Andrew Little said he's forming a "very clear picture" of his view on the ratings system proposal, but didn't want to get ahead of the process with final submissions underway.

One long-standing Wellington councillor said the proposal to change the rating system from a land-value to capital-value system has caused the most concern she's ever seen in the city, with people stopping her in the street "worried sick".

The council received about 5700 public submissions and over 450 requests to speak on the city's rating review - which also includes proposals to decrease businesses rates and an extension.

The capital-value/land-value debate has struck a nerve, with some cinemas and central-city bars warning they are facing closure over rates increases, and supporters urging the change to stamp out land-banking in the city and saying other rates would decrease.

In an interview with RNZ, Little was asked what his view was on the controversial policy. He said he did not want to pre-empt the process.

"The whole issue of pre-determination does loom large in local government, so we are sensitive to it, particularly on big and controversial questions like this, so it is important we don't look like we've made up our minds before we've made a decision - otherwise people get cynical about the whole consultation process."

Little, however, said feedback from the community, and information received in the consultation process, would "weigh heavily" on the council's decision over its rating system, and suggested it would feature in his.

"I was neutral from the outset, although I'd met with people who were kind of, championing the cause, they could never explain to me what the impact would be, and until I was clear about that I didn't have a view one way or the other, but now I've got some good information to make a decision."

The campaign has involved vocal lobby groups on either side of the debate - Common Ground Aotearoa and Voice for Wellington, including donations for some councillors during the campaign from Common Ground Aotearoa and donations to other councillors from businesses or property developers.

Little said that was the nature of politics in New Zealand, where public funding wasn't provided for those who wanted to stand.

"There wouldn't be a councillor who hasn't had a donation from somebody who represents one view or another."

When asked whether the presence of these groups had influenced councillors, Little said he wasn't concerned.

"I'm not fazed by lobby groups, interest groups, pressure groups - whatever. It actually enriches our public debate. I think the job of those in elected public office is to use those discriminatory tools and understand that things said with the greatest passion or volume aren't necessarily correct."

'Most concern I've ever seen'

Independent councillor for the Pukehīnau Lambton ward, Nicola Young, said the ratings debate was "boiling over" in the city.

"I've been a councillor for 13 years, and never have I experienced the level of public concern that I have about this.

"I went to the orchestra, people came to me beforehand, during the interval and as I was going home. I'm getting emails all the time, people will stop me in the street - people are worried sick about it."

Nicola Young. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Hours of back-to-back public hearings held in council offices this week have canvassed a range of views on the different proposals.

Ngaio resident Michelle Rush said her rates would go up under a land value system, but she wanted the change, because it supported townhouse development.

Curbing expensive greenfield development in areas without existing infrastructure was crucial for the council, she said.

"It does help to contain urban sprawl, and spatial studies from both North America and Australia show that land taxation channels growth inward onto under-utilised, infill parcels near key infrastructure."

But architect and urban designer Graeme McIndoe, founding director of McIndoe Urban, told councillors he didn't believe a change to land-value rates would incentivise development, or efficient land-use.

McIndoe said inner-city development relied on market demand, interest rates, district plan controls - which had levers for intensive development.

World.title: More driving licence test options called for as wait times stretch
World.content:
Road safety advocates are calling for more driving licence testing options as wait times at VTNZ stretched past 80 days at some sites.

Driving Change Network said New Zealanders trying to get their licence before Summer were stuck in long queues for a test.

It said it was the second time in three years that a "poorly timed policy change" had pushed wait times out.

National director of the network, Wendy Robertson, told Checkpoint the graduated driver licensing changes on 25 January were causing the rush.

"Three pressures are landing at the same time," Robertson said.

"Learners who already qualify to sit their restricted test are trying to book before the changes add another six months to their time.

"Restricted drivers who have picked up police driving infringements since May are trying to sit their full test before an extra six-month penalty applies. And on top of that comes the usual December rush, when young people finish exams and get ready for holiday jobs, summer travel and moving to uni."

Robertson said VTNZ would have known demand was going to be higher at this time of year.

"Letting staffing drop so it can't keep up is really not good enough."

Figures extracted from NZTA's Driver Licence Register showed North and West Auckland wait times were more than 42 days for a restricted test and 36 days for a full test, while in South Auckland it was more than 50 days for a restricted test and more than 37 for a full test, the network said.

In Canterbury it was more than 46 days for a restricted test and 38 for a full test.

Some individual sites were under severe pressure - Auckland's New Lynn was more than 62 days for a practical test, Auckland's Wiri was more than 82 and Nelson was more than 60.

"We understand demand will drop from late January when the full licence test is removed, and we can see why VTNZ may not have replaced staff who resigned," Robertson said.

"But VTNZ is contracted by the government to deliver this service, and it should still be able to deliver it."

Robertson said NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi (NZTA) was helping by pressing VTNZ to add testing days and hours.

"This shows exactly why New Zealand needs two testing options, not the monopoly VTNZ has held since 2014."

Under the new system, learners could shorten the restricted period back to six months, with more supervised driving or paying for an approved course.

NZTA's head of driving regulation, Chris Rodley, said NZTA was working with VTNZ and the network to create more testing capacity in Canterbury.

At least 200 extra testing days would be introduced in the next eight weeks in the region, he said, through travelling driver testing officers, while recruitment and training of additional officers was completed.

World.title: 'Ripped the Band-Aid off': Israel Adesanya opens up on bitter CKB breakup
World.content:
For more than a decade Israel Adesanya was the face and force of City Kickboxing.

His success put the Morningside gym on the map as a global powerhouse in MMA.

The first man to bring gold to Aotearoa, Adesanya ignited the sport and inspired countless others to strap on some gloves.

But the former king of CKB has endured a brutal fall from the top, losing his belt, his top 10 ranking, and now his team.

The former UFC middleweight champion parted ways with his gym of 16-years back in July following his most recent defeat in the octagon.

After losing his title to Sean Strickland in Sydney in 2023, Adesanya's standing has declined rapidly. He is now riding a four-fight losing streak.

However, a new gym has brought new hope of a career resurgence for the country's most decorated mixed martial artist.

In a bid to reclaim his spot among the best middleweights in the world, 'the Last Stylebender' has moved training camps across the Harbour Bridge to Unity MMA in Rosedale.

Reflecting on the decision in a recent video on his Youtube channel, Adesanya compared leaving CKB to ending a long term relationship.

"It was a hard decision It could have been worse than a breakup but you've had bad breakups before, we all have," he said.

"Sometimes when I was younger you feel I've spent so much time with this person, I've invested so much, I don't want to lose all those years. Then you stick to it, regardless of the disrespect, the manipulation. You stick with them because you don't want those to go to waste."

Adesanya went on to say time away from the gym helped cement his decision.

"As I got older, I can see things for what they are. As hard as it was, it was also really easy once I got it done.

"I ripped the Band-Aid off. I could see the forest for the trees. It was good to get clarity. I trusted my intuition, I trusted my instincts and I trusted my judgement. I stayed away from the gym for months before I made the decision. So that way I couldn't be clouded."

However, it seems Adesanya was not just looking for a change of scenery, with evidence of a rift between him and the new UFC Light Heavyweight champion Carlos Ulberg growing stronger.

He did not elaborate on the allegations of manipulation or disrespect, however, a fan commented eluding to a possible personal feud with Ulberg.

And Ulberg chimed in.

"False accusations, I don't move like that. Someone tag Israel, that's his move."

Adesanya is set to return to the Octagon next month for the first time without CKB.

Beaten by Joe Pyfer in March in what was his second consecutive TKO and fourth loss on the trot, Adesanya is fighting to keep his career alive against the dangerous Sharaputdin Magomedov on 6 December.

Meanwhile, Ulberg continues to recover from the knee injury he suffered during his UFC light heavyweight title win over Jiri Procházka in April.

Things may get even more tense at the famed gym, with rising star Navajo Stirling now ranked third in Ulberg's division, and seriously pushing for a title shot.

The pair have maintained that a fight between them would not affect the CKB team, with Stirling telling RNZ earlier this month he has a strong relationship with Ulberg.

World.title: Person who chopped branches from Ōmārama oak to receive council bill
World.content:
Waitaki District Council wants the person who cut branches off a scarlet oak tree in central Ōmārama to pay for its removal and replacement.

The council said the 30-year-old tree, which is on council land in front of a row of shops, was pruned without permission. The damage was reported on 4 November.

"Council received reports of the damage and contacted an arborist whose assessment determined the tree is likely to incur further damage, as it is top-heavy. Removal is recommended," a spokesperson said.

The council said it had worked with police to identify who was responsible and the person would be asked to pay "all costs incurred from the tree replacement and beautification work".

Waitaki mayor Mel Tavendale said the tree had been "well hacked at" because of what she believed was an issue with visibility.

"This is something that is really important to our community and it certainly has created a fair bit of chatter. I guess at the end of the day we need to be really clear on what people should and shouldn't be doing," she said.

The council said it was yet to determine how much the tree's replacement would cost.

Tavendale said the council planned to plant a new, mature tree that "hopefully won't look hugely different".

World.title: Health NZ hires at least 166 workers back after redundancy
World.content:
Health NZ has made hundreds of workers redundant since it was formed in 2022, only to hire at least 166 of them back again.

That's according to documents obtained under the Official Information Act (OIA) by the Public Service Association (PSA).

"Health NZ has identified 166 former employees across the organisation who were made redundant and subsequently returned to work for Health NZ as employees," it said.

The data did not count staff who were made redundant and returned as contractors.

Health NZ (HNZ) said it could not provide data on contractors - generally paid a higher rate than employees - as they were "generally not engaged or paid through Health NZ's payroll systems and are instead recorded through financial systems as vendors".

It said that information would take staff away from their other work for too long to collate.

The 166 staff were from across the organisation and it was not clear what their roles were and whether they were frontline, clinical, or back-office.

Agency-wide, 1907 redundancy payments had been logged in the payroll system since 1 July 2022.

"This figure has been compiled from more than 20 payroll systems and may include both voluntary redundancies and redundancies arising from organisational change."

HNZ could not immediately provide answers on how much had been paid out in redundancies, saying the request would be treated as another OIA, along with questions from RNZ about what exact roles those 166 staff were in, and the amount of time between their dismissal and rehire.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons. Supplied

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said the data revealed "a senseless merry-go-round where health workers lose their jobs creating serious stress to them and their colleagues only to be hired back when Health NZ realised how critical their work was".

"This is exactly why we need a public good test," she said. "Before any major restructure, agencies should have to show what it will do to services and what it will really cost. A public good test would have prevented much of this waste.

"Instead, we've had short-sighted cuts that leave the country less able to cope with an ageing population and growing health needs."

The rehiring data came as part of a request by the union for information regarding data and digital staff in particular.

According to the health agency's employee payroll systems, there were 292 staff members working in a data or digital function who were made redundant since the district health boards (DHBs) were amalgamated to form Health NZ four years ago.

"Employees may be made redundant in one district and rehired in another," it said. "Employees may be made redundant from one role and continue working in another - these employees are excluded from this total."

Robyn Shearer, HNZ's executive national director for people and culture, health and safety, said the agency had combined 20 former district health boards and other health entities when it was established in 2022, and inherited a range of legacy systems, structures and ways of working.

Since then it had undergone "significant organisational change", including the disestablishment of some roles and the creation of new ones.

"We continue to actively recruit to frontline clinical and support roles across Health New Zealand," Shearer said.

World.title: NRL scraps All Stars game for 2027 preseason
World.content:
The NRL is looking at whether the All Stars clash could form part of an expanded grand-final week in 2027, after a cluttered preseason squeezed the annual fixture off the calendar.

The sheer number of players returning to training late from the World Cup, as well as early-season overseas travel, has left no room for the match next February.

The fixture has been part of every NRL preseason since 2010, except in 2014 and 2018, when it was skipped due to World Cups.

Earlier this year, NRL executive chair Peter V'landys floated permanently shifting the game to grand-final week, before the idea was talked down by Maori and Indigenous players.

The All Stars game has been a fixture on the NRL calender since 2010. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Chief among their concerns was the unavailability of players from teams in grand-final sides, and that players would be carrying injuries that could stop them playing.

But the nature of next year's schedule means an end-of-season fixture may be the only way the match could be fit in.

"Ideally, and it's a matter of getting everybody on the same page, we should be holding the All Stars at the end of the year," V'landys said.

"We want to give the All Stars a much greater profile. It doesn't get that profile at the beginning of the year.

"It should be right at the end in the grand-final week.

"What was proven from this World Cup: if you've got clean air, look at the ratings you get."

V'landys still has his sights set on the All Stars match being one of several in grand-final week, as part of an expanded carnival.

Part of that could still include the NRLW grand final being played as a standalone event, with V'landys leaving the door open to that in 2027.

The NRLW grand final could become a standalone event in 2027. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"You could have it at Allianz Stadium on a Friday night," V'landys said.

"Because I'm proud of how good the women are going, we want to take them to the next level at some point.

"We've got the best women's sport in Australia. Cricket has always been pretty high up there, but I think we've caught them.

"Our ratings show it. They got over a million viewers [for the World Cup final]. What did the Bleeding Cup [Bledisloe Cup] get? It got 600,000. The women beat them."

NRL to tweak rules again for 2027 The NRL will come down harder on hip-drop tackles in 2027 but has ruled out the possibility of rolling back the controversial set restart rule.

An underage State of Origin match has also been proposed as an option to be played in grand-final week.

A third-place playoff between the two losing preliminary finalists was also floated in August, before it was largely laughed down by critics and players.

"I know that it got, everybody wanted to pot it. But it was the highest-rating FIFA [World Cup] match," V'landys said.

"If you're a Tigers' fan and you're up against the Eels, you'll watch it. It's third against fourth.

"It's like anything else. You've got to market it properly and have prize money or sponsors involved.

"If we listen to all the traditionalists all the time, we'd be playing for a couple of hundred dollars a game because you wouldn't get the revenue."

AAP

World.title: Kurtley Beale back in Wallabies team for first time in five years
World.content:
Kurtley Beale's return to the gold jumper is no sentimental, one-off reward for the veteran playing a selfless backroom role and being a mentor to young Wallabies this past month.

Coach Les Kiss says Australia's great rugby maverick has won his place back at the age of 37 absolutely on merit.

There's not a soul in the Wallabies' camp who has not been enthusing about the 37-year-old's return to the starting 23 in Friday's (Saturday AEDT) Nations Championship finale against Ireland at Twickenham.

Players such as Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii have been gushing about how he has been an inspirational presence in the team room and on the training park following his shock call-up to the squad for the spring tour to the UK.

But Kiss was quick to make it clear on Wednesday that Beale's selection on the Test team's bench for the first time since he won cap number 95 for the Wallabies against Wales in 2021 was no sentimental end-of-tour present.

"This isn't a gift to Kurtley," Kiss said.

"I couldn't speak highly enough of him. He has been unbelievable and he's been selected on merit. He's earned it; that's the bottom line."

With Australia going for a six-two split of forwards and backs on the bench, Kiss felt Beale's remarkable versatility — he has played in five different positions in the Wallabies' back line over his 17-year international career — could be crucial on Friday.

It means he has jettisoned both Ben Donaldson and Filipo Daugunu, two of the rare Australian success stories off the bench on a trying trip this past month, with Kiss admitting it was tough on the pair.

"But if you saw Kurtley's Super Aus games [for the Western Force], he played at 10, then he went to 12. He helped engineer those wins,'' the coach said.

"He was kicking goals from everywhere, kicking corners. And that type of influence has come through in every session, every video session, every computer session on this trip.

"He's earned his call. He's been nothing short of exceptional, really, how he's worked with the group, brought his wisdom, been patient, and he's clearly earned his spot, not only in my eyes but in his peers' eyes."

Les Kiss has praised Kurtley Beale's contribution to the squad on tour, despite not playing a minute yet. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Jan Kruger)

Suaalii was among those singing Beale's praises.

"I grew up watching Kurtley. I've always admired him from afar,'' he said.

"I've enjoyed working with him, just sitting at computers, picking his brain off the field, and just seeing what he's like as a person and how much he loves the game.

"How he sees the game is different from a lot of people, and I've just been asking him different questions and just trying to grow my game as a player. He's a great man, and the crew love him."

Up front, Allan Alaalatoa will earn a 100th cap while, at the other end of the spectrum, winger James Ramm will make his debut.

Prop Alaalatoa is the 14th Wallabies centurion, having made his debut in 2016. He will line up with Isaac Kailea and hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa in the front row, with Harry Wilson dropping to the bench.

"We've taken some steps forward, grown our game and tested our squad depth this year and I know the team is highly motivated to put in a performance that reflects the hard work put in by everyone in our final test," Kiss said.

Ireland, meanwhile, has made two changes from the side that beat the Springboks last week in Dublin, with Australian-born winger Mack Hansen out of the squad.

Wires/ABC

World.title: David Warner takes aim at 'bullying' journalists
World.content:
David Warner has accused the media of "perpetuating speculation", intimating he is being bullied as the sandpaper scandal continues to simmer.

Warner has called for media to substantiate allegations that he used superglue and grit on finger strapping to tamper with the ball on the infamous 2018 tour of South Africa.

The claims, published by News Corp and SEN radio, were penned by prominent broadcaster Gerard Whateley.

"I'm not entirely sure where Gerard's assertions have come from, as they certainly do not align with my recollection of events," Warner posted on Instagram.

"In relation to the alleged use of superglue and grit, and the more recent claims regarding the finger, could I respectfully ask what credible evidence exists to substantiate these allegations?

"Before further unverified claims are circulated publicly, I would suggest establishing the facts rather than perpetuating speculation."

Australia's ball tampering with sandpaper during the 2018 Test series in South Africa is under fresh scrutiny following the release of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.

Khawaja's claims of the entire team knowing of the ball tampering have been backed by Warner and Cameron Bancroft, but rejected by current Test captain Pat Cummins and fellow bowlers Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc.

Usman Khawaja (left) and David Warner have been at the heart of the renewed speculation over the Cape Town Test. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Khawaja completed a lengthy interview with The Grade Cricketer this week, where he revealed that he had issued a draft statement that hoped to find some "middle ground" between the two warring factions.

He doubled down though in saying that the whole squad knew about the ball tampering.

Khawaja also confirmed Whateley's report that a player had asked in Australia's first Test under Langer where the mints or red frogs were, with the ball not swinging.

Warner also replied to an Instagram user's comment that Whateley "is a long-time hater" of the internationally retired batsman.

Justin Langer's spray An Australian player suggested tampering with the ball in the nation's first Test after Sandpapergate before the intervention of then-coach Justin Langer.

"Refreshing to see someone willing to speak honestly," Warner replied.

"Education and eloquence are admirable qualities, but they should never be used to undermine those who weren't afforded the same opportunities.

"When someone uses their public platform to control a narrative without affording others the same voice, it raises a legitimate question about the distinction between journalism and bullying."

Steve Smith — who is yet to comment publicly amid the fresh furore — and Warner were banned by Cricket Australia for 12 months and lost the captaincy and vice-captaincy respectively for their role in the ball-tampering controversy.

Bancroft, who has admitted using sandpaper on the ball, was suspended for nine months.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: North star's path from family tragedy to a fourth AFLW flag tilt
World.content:
Football is emotional, and big games even more so.

It's something North Melbourne players are becoming veterans at understanding as their club heads into its fourth straight grand final this week. They are aiming for a third consecutive premiership.

But for Kangaroo star forward Jenna Bruton, there's an extra layer to it.

This season, she marked her 100th game in the qualifying final against Carlton.

She deeply wished her mum and aunt, who both died from brain cancer a few years before, could have been there.

"It made me pretty sad, obviously. But it is sad," she said of achieving her milestone without them.

"I want people to know that mum was a massive part of my journey."

Bruton's story is well known in AFLW circles. In late 2015 her mum, Suzy, was diagnosed with cancer. A top draft prospect, Bruton omitted herself from the historic inaugural 2016 draft to become her full-time carer.

Loading Instagram content

She didn't want to commit to anything if she couldn't manage her mum's treatments and help her where needed.

And with her mother's diagnosis, she "fell out of love with the game for a little bit".

"They did say mum, her life expectancy was probably lucky to get one year [after diagnosis], and she lasted five or six," she said.

During that time, Bruton made her way into the AFLW system after her partner and star player, Jasmine Garner, submitted her belated draft nomination for her.

"She did it for me," Bruton said. "I wasn't actually going to do it. She did the application and I didn't have a choice. I'm glad she did."

Bruton was taken with pick 11 by the Western Bulldogs in 2017, before signing with North Melbourne as an expansion player for the 2019 season.

Her mother died a week before the first game of the 2022 season.

Jenna Bruton is close with her family. (Getty)

Just three months earlier, her aunt Andrea, her mother's sister, died from the same cancer.

"You're more likely to win TattsLotto than two people in your family get the same brain cancer. So it was pretty hard on my nan and everyone," Bruton said.

"They said it's not genetic at all, which is crazy that it was both of them. They say it's just bad luck.

"We think about them a lot."

Bruton said her aunt's Facebook posts about her football journey now came up as memories.

If Garner had never put Bruton's name down, she would probably still be back in Trentham, working the 400-hectare potato farm she grew up on.

Jenna Bruton runs through the banner for her 100th match with niece Polly. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Her goal song, Hot Potato by The Wiggles, is a call back to this, along with being a favourite of her niece and nephew.

She is now a three-time premiership player; once with the Western Bulldogs and twice with North Melbourne.

A big part of that journey has been her family, Garner and their dogs Bronson and Honey.

"My mum's other sister is just up the road from dad, so I go up and see her a lot and she comes down to the footy. I feel like I'm closer to mum through them," she said.

"Then I've got a niece and nephew. Sort of feel like they're a part of mum. So, they've helped us a lot through losing mum.

Jasmine Garner and Jenna Bruton have been partners for 13 years. (Getty)

"Polly, my niece, she was born a couple of months before mum passed away. So mum did get to meet her, which was so good. She definitely keeps the family together."

She said her sadness during big games was also mixed with a lot of good emotions.

"I actually said to Jammin [Garner] after my 100th, it was probably like the best day," she said.

"Just with family and it was just so good. I don't really like the attention, but it was one of my favourite days."

The pair will be hoping those emotions come flooding back this Friday with another premiership, the club's third straight, if they are able to defeat Melbourne in the grand final.

World.title: Sydney Swans player has driving charge dismissed by judge
World.content:
Sydney Swans player Tom Papley has had a charge of driving while suspended dismissed in court.

Mr Papley was stopped on November 2 and charged with driving while suspended due to an unpaid parking fine, with a drug test later returning positive results for MDMA and cocaine.

The driving charge was heard in Waverley Local Court, with the court hearing Mr Papley had paid the fine two days earlier but had not checked whether the suspension had been lifted.

Judge Michael Barko dismissed the charge.

"I accept he genuinely honestly believed he was OK to drive," Judge Barko said.

"One can only say that he had the right attitude in relation to paying his fines. He should have simply waited until it was all clear before he drove."

The drug matter was not mentioned in the proceedings.

Outside court, Mr Papley apologised to his "family, the football club and my fans".

"My sole focus is earning their respect back," he said.

Banned by AFL

Police said at the time of the incident that the 30-year-old tested positive for illicit drugs, with a second sample confirming the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

NSW Police fined Mr Papley $722 and suspended his drivers licence for three months for that matter.

He was also banned by the AFL from the Swans' preseason game and the first three matches of the 2027 season due to "conduct unbecoming" under the league's Illicit Drugs Policy.

The league issued him a suspended $5,000 fine.

AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley last week said the sanction reflected the seriousness of the breach.

"AFL players are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with illicit drug use," Mr Harley said in a statement.

"The player is being held accountable for his actions and has acknowledged he made a grave mistake."

World.title: Jack Clayton draws on AFL draft experience to chase Test cricket debut
World.content:
Missing selection in the AFL draft has helped Australia hopeful Jack Clayton deal with the pressure of fighting for a Test debut.

Clayton made his final pitch to the selectors with an unbeaten 84 for Queensland on Wednesday, before NSW clung on for a draw at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

Australia will on Saturday name its squad for next month's first Test against New Zealand in Perth.

Clayton is considered an outside chance of a call-up, after starting the Shield season with 449 runs at an average of 74.83.

The 27-year-old was thrust into the spotlight in late October, as Australia's batting failed in its last Test in Cape Town at the same time as he was racking up 104 runs against Victoria.

While being talked up for international selection brings its own kind of pressure, Clayton has leaned on the experience he gained from being in the Brisbane Lions' academy before he was told by the AFL club in 2017 they would not draft him.

Loading Instagram content

"Something I learned playing AFL was about … thinking about getting drafted or things out of my control," Clayton said.

"As soon as I start thinking about what may happen, I don't play that well.

"I know as soon as I get into that mindset that it's taking me out of what I need to do and what I need to focus on. That's a skill I've developed over time."

Instead of worrying about what the future might hold, Clayton is focusing on his job of scoring runs for Queensland.

"And those things [such as selection], other people can control that; I can't control that," he said.

Clayton's hopes are likely to hinge on where the opening is in Australia's batting.

There could be just one change to the side from Cape Town, with the fit-again Steve Smith in at number three for the axed Marnus Labuschagne.

NSW draw against Queensland Thanks to a sporting declaration by Queensland and some exceptional bowling, the SCG was treated to one of the best Sheffield Shield finishes in years as New South Wales hung on for a draw.

And the option is there to shake up the openers, with Sam Konstas or Jake Weatherald selected.

But if Smith wants to stay at number four, Clayton is confident he can go to first drop if the opportunity arises.

"I've batted there before. I feel comfortable. I batted all my juniors there," he said.

After four seasons of first-class cricket with Queensland, Clayton is comfortable with his game.

"You never know if you're actually ready for Test cricket," he said.

"But I feel like I've been performing well, doing all the things I've been doing for the last three years.

"I try and take into account the shots I think are going to be low-risk scoring options and do that over and over again.

"That's what I've had success with."

AAP

World.title: The reason why North Melbourne dominates the AFLW landscape
World.content:
A North Melbourne victory has been a near certainty heading into almost every AFLW match of late.

The Kangaroos have lost just one game in their last 43, and boast a 96 per cent winning rate since losing the 2023 grand final.

At the opposite end of the scale, struggling teams Collingwood and GWS have winning percentages closer to just 15 per cent.

Tomorrow, North will play Melbourne in its fourth consecutive grand final, aiming to be the first side in competition history to secure a three-peat.

Despite the gap between either end of the ladder, AFL Hall of Famer and former Western Bulldogs coach Nathan Burke said it will benefit the league's competitiveness long-term.

"I think it's outstanding for the competition, because this is still a fledgling competition … to have North Melbourne so far out in front, it just means that everyone has to catch up," he said.

"The downside is that the competition becomes a little bit more predictable … and there are some people that just see that and think, 'Oh, North Melbourne are going to win,' and just turn off.

"They don't look at it closely and see the improvement that's coming from underneath because we're trying to catch North Melbourne."

The rest of the pack are trying desperately to chase down the Kangaroos. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

The Kangaroos have not been the only dominant side in the competition over the past 11 seasons.

This is the first year neither Adelaide nor Brisbane will feature in the AFLW grand final.

Want to win an AFLW flag? Club culture matters, data shows AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

The Lions have played in seven grand finals, yielding two wins, while the Crows currently hold the record for most premierships in the competition with three.

That record will be equalled if the Kangaroos salute at Princes Park tomorrow night.

AFLW commentator Chyloe Kurdas said a win would edge the Roos ahead when ranking the best sides across the competition's history.

"[They are] interesting comparisons because of the flags Adelaide have won. You look at the conversion rate for Brisbane [of grand finals into premierships], and you look at North Melbourne's conversion rate into their fourth grand final," she said.

"[To win] Three from four, I guess, on the conversion rate, North Melbourne — should they get over the line — will be the number one of those three sides."

Kurdas said the club is being rewarded for the efforts it put into a women's team well before the AFLW's inception.

Melbourne University Women's Football Club developed a partnership with the Kangaroos so players could train at Arden St, and remained the club's VFLW affiliate until 2019.

Emma Kearney has played over 100 games for North Melbourne. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Robert Cianflone)

"It's the groundwork North Melbourne did in 2009, 2010 to invest in the really early days, even before AFLW was on the radar … they used a lot of that intel to build a culture that was ready for women and girls to come into the game at a professional level," Kurdas said.

"And of course, how they built their list. They prioritised footballers at the time, really prioritised skills, and they were able to leverage the draft rules at the time and bring in a really strong group of players from day one."

Melbourne University alumni Emma Kearney and Ash Riddell joined North Melbourne in its first season in the AFLW and remain key pillars of the side leading into tomorrow's grand final.

This year, North lost its first match since the 2023 grand final and recorded its lowest score since that season, while still clearly remaining the premiership favourites.

"Slowly they're [other teams] catching up; it's not happening as fast as everyone would like," Burke said.

"I think Geelong made the biggest strides getting closest to North Melbourne … we'll see how close Melbourne get this weekend, but I do still think there's a bit of a gulf from those top three teams," Burke said.

The statistic in Melbourne's favour tomorrow is its win-loss record against the Roos.

The Demons are the only team in the AFLW to have a better head-to-head record against North since the two-time reigning champions entered the competition.

World.title: Renegades WBBL player bowled without facing a ball
World.content:
The Melbourne Renegades have pipped Brisbane Heat by three wickets in a last-ball thriller highlighted by a bizarre diamond duck to Deandra Dottin.

Chasing 138, Dottin came in at 4-97 and was adjusting her helmet strap and was gloveless on arrival at the crease outside the allotted 75 seconds time limit.

She was ordered by umpires to stand aside while Heat spinner Sarah Glenn had a free bowl at the stumps. She was on target and Dottin departed without facing a ball.

The drama preceded a tense final over when the Renegades required nine runs from Lucy Hamilton's bowling.

Annie Wikman smacked the first ball for four, and five singles followed, including Wikman's winning run from an inside edge.

Tess Flintoff top-scored in the chase with 30 from 32 balls and Georgia Wareham made a valuable 29 from 26 against a Heat bowling attack led by Glenn's 2-15 and Sienna Ginger's 2-13.

The Renegades (nine points) replaced the Heat (eight points) in fourth spot and, if they beat the Melbourne Stars on Saturday, will feature in the finals.

Renegades captain Sophie Molineux was instrumental in Wednesday night's win at Melbourne's Junction Oval, taking 4-20.

Earlier, Molineux produced her superb bowling spell to stymie the Heat batters.

The Australian captain claimed a wicket in her first over, bowling dangerous opener Grace Harris for a golden duck, and another in her second.

Molineux returned to bowl the 13th over and took two more wickets in three balls, while Orla Prendergast top-scored with 23 from 15 balls, and Lucy Hamilton (21 from 15) and Sienna Ginger (21 from 21) played handy knocks.

Sophie Molineux ripped through the Heat's top order. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Brisbane must now hope the Renegades are defeated by the Stars on Saturday to have any hope of reaching the play-offs.

The Heat will know their fate by the time they host the Perth Scorchers on Sunday.

Sydney Thunder, on six points, remain the only other chance to reach the finals. They meet the finals-bound Adelaide Strikers on Thursday and the Sydney Sixers on Saturday.

The Thunder must win both games but, even then, they're relying on the Renegades and Heat to both lose their respective last matches.

AAP

Tech.content:
Notification:

On the day CPSC publishes the recall releases, Amazon must notify the public by posting the recall releases to Amazon.com; notify original purchasers directly via email and by providing information regarding the recalls on each purchaser’s “Your Orders” page.

Tech.title: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
Tech.content:
Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and s based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.

First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers.

According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall. The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out.

Image: Google

Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google.

My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes.

When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch.

Tech.title: WhatsApp’s new scheduled messages let you choose the right time to send
Tech.content:
To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

Tech.title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.

Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press.

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here.

The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.

Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.

To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

Tech.title: 1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. It’s unclear how many users are affected.

The password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.

It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to users to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.

Related 1Password lets AI agents use your passwords without seeing them

The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

Tech.title: The Fairphone 6 Plus is modular, repairable, and $100 off right now
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Unlike most smartphones, the Fairphone 6 Plus is designed for home repair, with easily replaceable parts that could help extend its lifespan well into the future. That makes its midrange price point easier to justify, especially now that it’s dropped to a new low of $552.49 (about $98 off) at Amazon as part of the retailer’s ongoing Black Friday sale.

The 6.3-inch Fairphone 6 Plus features 12 user-replaceable parts, including the battery, screen, USB-C port, and cameras, all of which you can swap out with the included screwdriver. Replacement parts are relatively affordable, too; a new battery costs $39.99, which helps offset its middling battery life and lack of wireless charging. It also comes with a five-year warranty and up to six Android OS upgrades, making it a good option if you want a phone you can keep using for years.

Although repairability is its marquee feature, the 6 Plus is also a solid midrange Android device. Fairphone prioritizes ethically sourced materials, making it a strong choice for environmentally conscious buyers who don’t want to sacrifice performance. Its Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor handles everyday tasks well, and its cameras take decent photos, though they’re not quite on par with those of pricier phones.

What’s more, it offers a clean, bloatware-free Android experience and modular back panels, which you can swap for optional accessories like a card holder or crossbody strap. Our own Allison Johnson particularly liked the phone’s dedicated switch for turning on customizable focus modes called Moments, which can simplify your homescreen and limit access to distracting apps — something we could all use a little less of.

Tech.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
Tech.content:
In Brief

S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.

The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.

A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

Tech.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
Tech.content:
SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”

The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”

This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

Tech.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
Tech.content:
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.

While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.

Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
Tech.content:
When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”

The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”

Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”

Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”

In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

Tech.title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America
Tech.content:
Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com.

The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.

According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.

Karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.

Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said.

“The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.

The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.

“The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”

Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.

“When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
Tech.content:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”

Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

“Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”

Tech.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
Tech.content:
Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.

The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

Tech.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
Tech.content:
Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.

Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.

The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”

When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”

When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.

The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero‘s AI Puppy.

The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules.

While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study.

Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors.

It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January, finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns.

While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them.

“These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.”

TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.

Tech.title: The Iowa Lead Detonation Happened. Now the Real Work Begins to Study It
Tech.content:
On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site.

But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days. A barrage of government, university, and citizen monitoring and testing projects are underway. Air, soil, and water samples they’ve collected will determine the extent of lead exposure, if any, in Middletown and the surrounding area.

The lead azide has been on the base near Middletown for decades, but recently the Army deemed it unstable and too dangerous to move and remediate. Poor communication between the Army and towns in the path of the fallout led to a public uproar. While the federal government stepped up its mitigation measures—the Army dug a dam around the detonation site, while NASA stepped in with research jets and satellites for monitoring—universities had already been swinging into action due to the chaotic rollout.

Several departments at the University of Iowa kicked into gear to begin to set up air and soil monitoring stations late last week. “Initially we did not know that [the] EPA or Army or anybody else was going to be doing anything,” says Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the university.
